Though this is true, yet if that had been the reason, the following plagues too would have been inflicted on him without forewarning. Someone might, however, suppose that this third plague was brought on the Egyptians with a threat beforehand, though Scripture does not say so, because it is sufficiently suggested by what goes before and what follows. But if this plague was not announced to Pharao beforehand, it can be said that God admonished Pharao in both ways, so that his heart might be softened: namely by inflicting some plagues on him and his people without forewarning (for he inflicted the last two in this way too, as is related below), and some with forewarning. God also sent this plague not only on the men but on their beasts as well, so that they might be afflicted not only in their own persons but also in their goods, their possessions and their beasts.

paras.t: Feceruntque similiter malefici incantationibus suis, ut educerent scinifes, id est, similia facere nitebantur per suas incantationes, extendendo manum suam cum virgis, ut fertur in Glossa. Ex quo apparenter oritur, quod viderunt qualiter Aaron fecit, scinifes producendo. Et non potuerunt educere scinifes. Quare non potuerunt hoc per subsidia dæmonum, naturalesque causas, quum majora potuerint, nec istud excedat naturalium vires causarum, magis quam productio draconum atque ranarum, aut conversio aquarum in sanguinem? Ad hoc beatus Augustinus tertio de Trinitate respondet: Ex ineffabili, inquiens, Creatoris potentatu fit, ut quod possent angeli mali si permitterentur, ideo non possunt, quia non permittuntur. Neque enim occurrit alia ratio, cur non potuerunt facere minutissimas muscas, qui ranas serpentesque fecerunt, nisi quia major erat dominatio prohibentis Dei per Spiritum Sanctum. Quod etiam ipsi magi confessi sunt, dicentes: Digitus Dei est hic. Hæc Augustinus.
paras.en: [[8:18|And the magicians with their enchantments practised in like manner, to bring forth sciniphs|Feceruntque similiter malefici incantationibus suis, ut educerent scinifes]], that is, they strove to do the like by their enchantments, stretching out their hands with rods, as is reported in the Gloss. From this it would appear that they had seen how Aaron went about producing the sciniphs. [[8:18|and they could not|Et non potuerunt]] bring forth sciniphs. Why could they not do this with the help of the demons and of natural causes, since they had been able to do greater things, and this does not exceed the powers of natural causes any more than the producing of serpents and frogs, or the turning of the waters into blood? To this blessed Augustine replies in the third book On the Trinity: It comes, he says, of the unspeakable might of the Creator, that what the evil angels could do if they were permitted, they cannot do because they are not permitted. For no other reason occurs why they who made frogs and serpents could not make the tiniest flies, except that the dominion of God forbidding them through the Holy Ghost was greater. And this the magicians themselves confessed, saying: [[8:19|This is the finger of God|Digitus Dei est hic]]. Thus far Augustine.

paras.t: Sed tunc quæritur, cur potius Deus prohibuit spiritus malignos ab isto effectu, quam a factis majoribus jam præfatis. Dicunt quidam, quod ideo, ut malefici amplius confunderentur, quod quamminimas muscas nequibant producere. Hinc dicere sunt compulsi, Digitus Dei est hic, id est, potestas nos impediens ab hoc effectu, demonstrat nobis omnipotentiam et excellentiam Dei, nostras artes viresque refrenantis, sicut digitus rem quamcumque ostendit.
paras.en: But then it is asked why God forbade the evil spirits this effect rather than the greater deeds already mentioned. Some say: so that the sorcerers might be the more confounded, in that they could not produce even the tiniest flies. Hence they were compelled to say, [[8:19|This is the finger of God|Digitus Dei est hic]], that is, the power that hinders us from this effect shows us the almighty power and excellence of God, who curbs our arts and our powers, as a finger points out any thing.

paras.t: Augustinus vero aliam causam assignat, cur Deus fecit magos deficere in tertio signo, non in primo neque secundo. Nam ait: Commendatur nobis Trinitas, et quod verum est, summi philosophi gentium, quantum in eorum litteris indagatur, sine Spiritu Sancto philosophati sunt, quamvis de Patre et Filio non tacuerunt. Hinc Magister in historiis dicit: Philosophi habuerunt notitiam Patris et Filii, non tamen Spiritus Sancti.
paras.en: Augustine, however, gives another reason why God made the magicians fail at the third sign, and not at the first or the second. For he says: The Trinity is commended to us [that is, by their failing at the third sign, which points to the third Person]; and, what is true, the greatest philosophers of the Gentiles, so far as can be traced in their writings, philosophized without the Holy Ghost, though they were not silent about the Father and the Son. Hence the Master says in the Histories [that is, Peter Comestor, in the Historia Scholastica]: The philosophers had knowledge of the Father and the Son, but not of the Holy Ghost.

paras.t: Circa hoc quæri posset, qualiter istud verum sit, et an trinitas vel saltem dualitas Personarum, videlicet deitas et consubstantialitas Patris ac Filii, per rationem valeat naturalem cognosci, et utrum philosophus quibusdam innuit. Et videtur quod imo, quoniam decimo de Civitate Dei, capitulo 23 loquitur Augustinus: Plotinus Platonicus disputans de tribus principalibus substantiis, ponit Deum patrem et mentem paternam seu intellectum paternum, per quos Patrem et Filium videtur insinuare. Trismegistus quoque in libro de Verbo perfecto, aperte effatur de Patre æterno, et unico ejus Filio. Insuper dixit: Monas gignit monadem, et in se suum reflectit ardorem. Denique Augustinus decimo de Civitate Dei apertissime refert: Porphyrius divinis oraculis dicit esse expressum, principia posse purgare. Quæ autem dicit principia tanquam Platonicus, novimus. Dicit enim Deum Patrem, et Deum Filium, quem appellat paternum intellectum aut mentem paternam, et medium horum: quem medium quem alium dicat, nisi Spiritum Sanctum, non intelligo. Amplius, septimo Confessionum dicit se in libris Platonicorum sub aliis verbis invenisse, quod in exordio sui Evangelii ait evangelista Joannes: In principio erat Verbum, etc. Ad ista Thomas in prima parte Summæ suæ, quæstione 32, satis aperte respondet, dicendo: Deus per naturalem rationem cognosci non potest, nisi ex creaturis, prout causa cognoscitur per effectum. Quum ergo trium Personarum sit una potentia creativa, seu una virtus agendi, et actio indivisa ad extra, ex creaturis cognosci non possunt, nisi quæ ad essentiæ pertinent unitatem. Ideo trinitas Personarum per naturalem rationem non patuit. Platonici autem per verbum Dei intellexerunt, vel idealem rationem in Deo, vel mentem quamdam a summo Deo immediate creatam, in qua omnium rerum species relucerent, et mentem illam ob præcipuam suam cum Deo similitudinem, vocabant Prolem seu Filium Dei. De hac materia alibi plenius scripsi, idcirco pertranseo.
paras.en: On this one might ask how this is true, and whether the trinity, or at least the duality, of the Persons (that is, the deity and consubstantiality of the Father and the Son) can be known by natural reason, and whether a philosopher has hinted at it in certain words. And it seems that it can, since Augustine says in the tenth book of the City of God, chapter 23: Plotinus the Platonist, treating of the three principal substances, posits God the Father and the paternal mind, or paternal intellect, by which he seems to suggest the Father and the Son. Trismegistus too, in the book On the Perfect Word, speaks openly of the eternal Father and of his only Son. He said besides: The monad begets a monad, and reflects its own ardour back upon itself. Again, Augustine in the tenth book of the City of God relates most plainly: Porphyry says that it was declared by divine oracles that the principles are able to purify. And what principles he means, as a Platonist, we know. For he speaks of God the Father and God the Son, whom he calls the paternal intellect or paternal mind, and of a mean between them; and what other he means by this mean than the Holy Ghost, I do not understand. Further, in the seventh book of the Confessions he says that he found in the books of the Platonists, in other words, what John the Evangelist says at the opening of his Gospel: [[John 1:1|In the beginning was the Word|In principio erat Verbum]], etc. To these things Thomas replies clearly enough in the first part of his Summa, question 32, saying: God cannot be known by natural reason except from creatures, as a cause is known by its effect. Since, then, the three Persons have one creative power, or one power of acting, and an undivided action ad extra [that is, towards what is outside God, the creatures], from creatures only what belongs to the unity of the essence can be known. Therefore the trinity of the Persons was not made known by natural reason. But the Platonists understood by the Word of God either the ideal reason in God [that is, the pattern of all things in the divine mind], or a certain mind created immediately by the supreme God, in which the forms of all things shone; and because of its special likeness to God they called that mind the Offspring, or Son, of God. I have written more fully of this matter elsewhere, and so I pass it by.

paras.t: Præterea, sicut recitat Lyra, Hebræi dicunt magos defecisse in tertio signo, quoniam dæmones quorum auxilio magi utuntur, non habent potestatem super aliquod corpus quod minus est hordei grano. Quod reprobat Lyra: quia quod habet potestatem super majus, habet potestatem super minus, sed non econverso. Circa hoc asserit Rabbi Paulus: Hebræi dicentes quod dæmones non habent potestatem super aliquod corpus minus grano hordei seu lenticulæ, intelligunt hoc de corpore animalis: quorum ratio est, quia quum in corpore animalis requirantur multa organa corporaliter distincta, ad diversa opera sensus et motus exercenda, major potentia activa requiritur ad formandum unum animal in quantitate modica aut minima, quam in quantitate ad hoc competenti: sicut major potestas seu ars scriptoris requiritur ad scribendum litteram tam parvam, ut totum psalterium contineatur in folio uno, quam ad scribendum illud in foliis multis: ideo ratio postillatoris, videlicet Lyræ, contra Hebræos inducta, non est sufficiens, nisi addatur quod dæmones non producunt aliquam formam, nisi applicando activa passivis. Ex quo sequitur, quod quum movere possint ad magna animalia producenda, movere etiam valent ad producendum animalia parva ac minima.
paras.en: Further, as Lyra relates, the Hebrews say that the magicians failed at the third sign because the demons, whose help the magicians use, have no power over any body smaller than a grain of barley. This Lyra rejects: because what has power over the greater has power over the less, though not the other way about. On this Rabbi Paul [that is, Paul of Burgos, a converted rabbi, in his Additions to Lyra's Postill] says: The Hebrews who say that the demons have no power over any body smaller than a grain of barley or a lentil understand this of the body of an animal. Their reason is this: since in the body of an animal many organs, bodily distinct, are needed to carry out the various works of sense and motion, a greater active power is needed to form an animal of small or very small size than one of the size suited to it; just as a greater skill, or art, in a scribe is needed to write letters so small that the whole psalter is contained on one leaf than to write it on many leaves. Therefore the argument of the Postillator, that is, Lyra, brought against the Hebrews, is not sufficient unless it is added that the demons produce no form except by applying actives to passives [that is, by bringing natural agents to bear on matter that can receive their action]. From which it follows that, since they can set things in motion to produce large animals, they can also set them in motion to produce small and very small ones.

paras.t: Insuper circa illud, Digitus Dei est, asserit Rabbi Paulus: Per hoc confessi sunt magi virtutem divinam, non tamen sic, quod crediderunt quod Adonai seu Dominus, quem profitebantur Moyses et Aaron, esset Deus seu omnium Dominus. Quamvis enim omnes crederent aliquam primam et supremam causam, ex hoc tamen non sequitur, quod ille Adonai cujus nuntium dixit se Moyses esse, esset illa superior causa. Istud non videtur idonee dictum. Sapientes namque atque philosophi Pharaonis et Ægyptiorum, inter Hebræos quotidie conversantes, faciliter scire valebant, quod Hebræi colerent eum, quem vocabant universorum principium, primamque causam. Nam et Moyses dixit ante hæc verba ad Pharaonem: Juxta verbum tuum faciam, ut scias quod non est sicut Dominus Deus noster, sicut in isto capitulo patuit modo: per quæ verba evidenter significavit, summum et verum Deum, esse Deum ac Dominum Hebræorum.
paras.en: Moreover, on the words [[8:19|This is the finger of God|Digitus Dei est]], Rabbi Paul says: By this the magicians confessed a divine power, yet not in such a way that they believed that Adonai, or the Lord, whom Moses and Aaron professed, was God, or the Lord of all. For although all believed in some first and supreme cause, it does not follow from this that that Adonai whose messenger Moses said he was, was that higher cause. This does not seem to be well said. For the wise men and philosophers of Pharao and of the Egyptians, living every day among the Hebrews, could easily know that the Hebrews worshipped him whom they called the beginning of all things and the first cause. For Moses too had said to Pharao before these words: [[8:10|I will do according to thy word; that thou mayest know that there is none like to the Lord our God|Juxta verbum tuum faciam, ut scias quod non est sicut Dominus Deus noster]], as was shown just now in this chapter: by which words he plainly signified that the supreme and true God is the God and Lord of the Hebrews.

paras.t: Præterea Rabbi Paulus scribit, quod tres primæ plagæ non attigerunt ad mollificationem cordis Pharaonis, nec in toto, neque in parte. Cujus contrarium ex hoc probatur, quod Pharao qui antea dixerat, Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam, in secunda plaga magnitudinem cordis sui parumper depressit. Siquidem Moysen Aaronque vocavit, et dixit: Orate Dominum, ut auferat ranas a me, etc. Ranis vero ablatis, rursus intumuit ac induravit cor suum. Ideo Origenes et Glossa affirmant, quod per verbera aliqualiter emendatus, petiit pro se orari. At vero quod post verba illa, Digitus Dei est hic, in textu subjungitur, Induratumque est cor Pharaonis, et non audivit eos, Rabbi Paulus exponit, quod Pharao non audivit maleficos profitentes divinam esse virtutem. Cui expositioni obsistit, quod post verba illa, Non audivit eos, mox subditur, sicut præceperat Dominus. Non enim præceperat Dominus Pharaoni, ut audiret maleficos. Ideo sensus est, quod non audivit eos, utpote Moysen et Aaron, de quibus paulo ante eadem verba sunt scripta.
paras.en: Further, Rabbi Paul writes that the first three plagues did nothing to soften Pharao's heart, either wholly or in part. The contrary of this is proved by the fact that Pharao, who had said before, [[Ex 5:2|I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go|Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam]], in the second plague lowered the pride of his heart for a little. For he called Moses and Aaron and said: [[8:8|Pray ye to the Lord to take away the frogs from me|Orate Dominum, ut auferat ranas a me]], etc. But once the frogs were taken away, he swelled up again and hardened his heart. Therefore Origen and the Gloss affirm that, somewhat amended by the blows, he asked to be prayed for. But as for what is added in the text after the words [[8:19|This is the finger of God|Digitus Dei est hic]], namely [[8:19|And Pharao's heart was hardened, and he hearkened not unto them|Induratumque est cor Pharaonis, et non audivit eos]], Rabbi Paul explains that Pharao did not hearken to the sorcerers when they professed that it was a divine power. Against this explanation stands the fact that after the words [[8:19|he hearkened not unto them|Non audivit eos]] there follows at once [[8:19|as the Lord had commanded|sicut præceperat Dominus]]. For the Lord had not commanded Pharao to hearken to the sorcerers. Therefore the sense is that he did not hearken to them, that is, to Moses and Aaron, of whom the same words were written a little before.

paras.t: Porro † sicut Nicolaus de Lyra fatetur, quod intentio Pharaonis et magorum ejus ad hoc tendere videtur, ut Moyses crederetur magicis artibus facere quod agebat. Quod non apparet, quoniam Pharao visis plagis sibi ac suis inflictis, frequenter petiit, Dominum pro se rogari ut plagas auferret: per quod confitebatur plagas illas a Domino Deo Hebræorum inductas; nec negavit digitum Dei esse, quod magi sui dixerunt digitum esse Dei: non tamen voluit subdi Deo, quia de ejus providentia, gubernatione et omnipotentia non sensit fideliter: quemadmodum Syri et alii multi gentiles, imo et decem tribus idololatræ, cognoverunt quod populus Judæ serviret Deo altissimo, non tamen voluerunt eidem obedire ac obsequi.
paras.en: Further, as Nicholas of Lyra states, the intention of Pharao and his magicians seems to have been that Moses should be believed to do what he did by magic arts. This does not appear to be so, since Pharao, seeing the plagues inflicted on himself and his people, often asked that the Lord be prayed to for him, to take the plagues away: by which he confessed that those plagues were brought on by the Lord God of the Hebrews. Nor did he deny that it was the finger of God, as his magicians said it was the finger of God. Yet he would not be subject to God, because he did not think faithfully of his providence, government and almighty power: just as the Syrians and many other Gentiles[[1 Kings 6:3||]], and even the ten idolatrous tribes[[3 Kings 13:6||]][[3 Kings 13:33||]], knew that the people of Juda served the most high God, and yet would not obey and serve him [the margin cites 1 Kings 6:3 ff., where the Philistines own the hand of the God of Israel, and 3 Kings 13:6, 33, where Jeroboam asks the man of God to pray for him and yet does not turn from his wicked way].

paras.t: Præterea dicit Lyra, quod post tertiam plagam et prolationem verborum illorum, Digitus Dei est hic, magi non cessaverunt resistere Moysi, et adsistere Pharaoni. Quod reprobat Rabbi Paulus, affirmans quod in tertia plaga omnino victi fuerunt, et præ verecundia vel horrore non comparuerunt. Cui obviat quod sequenti habetur capitulo: Non poterant malefici stare coram Moyse, propter vulnera quæ erant in eis. Et hoc fuit Moyse stante coram Pharaone. Ergo et magi tunc adstabant contra Moysen Pharaoni. Quamvis autem non legantur post tertiam plagam conati facere similia operibus Moysis aut Aaron, attamen restiterunt eis, ut poterant. Principales autem inter hos magos, fuerunt Jannes et Mambres, quemadmodum ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus: Sicut Jannes et Mambres restiterunt Moysi, etc. In Alcorano sceleratissimi Mahometi habetur, quod magi ad Deum Israel fuerunt conversi, statim post primum signum, devoratis eorum draconibus a virga seu colubro Aaron seu Moysis: quod est apertissime contra textum.
paras.en: Lyra says moreover that after the third plague and the uttering of the words [[8:19|This is the finger of God|Digitus Dei est hic]], the magicians did not cease to resist Moses and to stand by Pharao. This Rabbi Paul rejects, affirming that in the third plague they were utterly overcome, and for shame or dread did not appear again. Against this stands what is found in the following chapter: [[Ex 9:11|Neither could the magicians stand before Moses, for the boils that were upon them|Non poterant malefici stare coram Moyse, propter vulnera quæ erant in eis]] [the margin note here cannot be read; Denis has vulnera, "wounds", where the Vulgate has ulcera, "boils"]. And this was while Moses was standing before Pharao. Therefore the magicians too were then standing by Pharao against Moses. And though we do not read that after the third plague they tried to do things like the works of Moses or Aaron, yet they resisted them as far as they could. The chief among these magicians were Jannes and Mambres, as the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[2 Tim 3:8|as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses|Sicut Jannes et Mambres restiterunt Moysi]], etc. In the Koran of the most wicked Mahomet it is said that the magicians were converted to the God of Israel immediately after the first sign, when their serpents had been devoured by the rod, or serpent, of Aaron or of Moses: which is most plainly against the text.

paras.t: Deinde quarta describitur plaga. Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen: Consurge diluculo, et sta coram Pharaone, hoc est, in ripa circa fluvium Nili obvia ei. Egredietur enim ad aquas, id est ad deambulandum super littus fluvii decurrentis prope mansionem ipsius, vel pro sanitate, vel ut aliqui opinantur, causa idololatriæ, ut scilicet fluvium tanquam Deum coleret, quoniam tam utilis erat Ægyptiis, irrigando et fecundando terram eorum, vel quoniam taurus quem colebant Ægyptii, interdum apparuit super aquas. Et dices ad eum: Hæc dicit Dominus: Dimitte populum meum, ut sacrificet mihi. Quod si non dimiseris eum, ecce ego immittam in te et in servos tuos, etc., omne genus muscarum; et implebuntur omnes domus Ægyptiorum muscis diversi generis, id est muscis diversarum specierum, quarum nonnullæ fuerunt venenosæ. Pro Muscis diversi generis, Septuaginta transtulerunt Cynomyiam, id est muscam caninam quæ acriter pupugit vel punxit. Verum (ut recitat Lyra) in Hebræo habetur: Mittam in te commixtionem. Et dicunt Hebræi ac Josephus, quod per istam commixtionem non intelligitur multitudo muscarum, sed multitudo animalium diversorum generum, quæ terribilia erant adspectu, atque nociva morsu, quæ de suis exeuntia cavernis, necabant homines et jumenta. Denique duæ hæ plagæ quibus affligebantur Ægyptii ab istis scinifum et diversarum muscarum punctionibus, inquietudinibus, tædiosisque sonis, correspondent impietatibus Ægyptiorum, quas exercuerunt in Hebræos, impellendo, trudendo, pungendo, et cum cachinno subsannando eosdem.
paras.en: Then the fourth plague is described. [[8:20|The Lord also said to Moses: Arise early, and stand before Pharao|Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen: Consurge diluculo, et sta coram Pharaone]], that is, on the bank by the river Nile, meeting him; [[8:20|for he will go forth to the waters|Egredietur enim ad aquas]], that is, to walk along the shore of the river that flowed near his dwelling, either for his health or, as some think, for the sake of idolatry, namely to worship the river as a god, because it was so useful to the Egyptians in watering and fertilizing their land, or because the bull that the Egyptians worshipped sometimes appeared above the waters. [[8:20|and thou shalt say to him: Thus saith the Lord: Let my people go to sacrifice to me|Et dices ad eum: Hæc dicit Dominus: Dimitte populum meum, ut sacrificet mihi]]. [[8:21|But if thou wilt not let them go, behold I will send in upon thee, and upon thy servants|Quod si non dimiseris eum, ecce ego immittam in te et in servos tuos]], etc., [[8:21|all kind of flies|omne genus muscarum]]: [[8:21|and the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with flies of divers kinds|et implebuntur omnes domus Ægyptiorum muscis diversi generis]], that is, with flies of different species, some of which were poisonous. For "flies of divers kinds" the Septuagint translated Cynomyia, that is, the dog-fly, which stung sharply. But (as Lyra relates) the Hebrew has: I will send upon thee a mixture. And the Hebrews and Josephus say that by this mixture is meant not a multitude of flies but a multitude of animals of different kinds, terrible to look on and harmful in their bite, which came out of their dens and killed men and beasts. Lastly, these two plagues, in which the Egyptians were afflicted by the stinging, the disquiet and the wearisome noise of these sciniphs and of the flies of divers kinds, answer to the wickedness of the Egyptians which they practised against the Hebrews, driving them, thrusting them, goading them, and mocking them with jeers.

paras.t: Faciamque mirabile in die illa in terra Gessen, in qua populus meus est, id est, grande miraculum faciam in illa parte Ægypti, ut non sint ibi muscæ. Istud secundum Augustinum etiam de præcedentibus plagis est intelligendum, quod scilicet non fuerunt in terra Gessen, in qua morabantur Hebræi. Sed quia in terra illa etiam multi Ægyptii habitabant (unde et infra Dominus legitur Hebræorum mulieribus præcepisse, ut mutuarent vasa pretiosa ab Ægyptiis sibi vicinis), alii dicunt, quod plagæ istæ fuerunt et in terra Gessen: non tamen affligebantur ab eis Hebræi, sed soli Ægyptii. Propter quod subditur: Ponamque divisionem inter populum meum, et populum tuum, hoc est inter Hebræos et Ægyptios, ita quod bestiolæ istæ non transgredientur terminum eis mea jussione præfixum. Cras erit signum istud.
paras.en: [[8:22|And I will make the land of Gessen wonderful in that day|Faciamque mirabile in die illa in terra Gessen]] [Denis's text reads "I will work a wonder in that day in the land of Gessen"], in which my people is, that is, I will work a great miracle in that part of Egypt, [[8:22|so that flies shall not be there|ut non sint ibi muscæ]]. This, according to Augustine, is to be understood of the preceding plagues too, namely that they were not in the land of Gessen, where the Hebrews dwelt. But because many Egyptians also lived in that land (whence we read below that the Lord commanded the women of the Hebrews to borrow precious vessels from the Egyptians who were their neighbours[[Ex 11:2||]] [the margin gives Exod. v, 2, which does not fit; the command is at Ex 11:2, compare 3:22]), others say that these plagues were in the land of Gessen too, yet the Hebrews were not afflicted by them, but the Egyptians alone. For this reason it is added: [[8:23|And I will put a division between my people and thy people|Ponamque divisionem inter populum meum, et populum tuum]], that is, between the Hebrews and the Egyptians, so that these little beasts would not pass the bound set for them by my command. [[8:23|to morrow shall this sign be|Cras erit signum istud]].

paras.t: Fecitque Dominus ita. Et venit musca gravissima, id est multitudo muscarum tædiosissima sono, punctione, atque adspectu molesta, in omnem terram Ægypti. Corruptaque est terra ab hujuscemodi muscis, id est deformata, habitatoresque terræ Ægypti læsi et inquinati sunt a muscis præfatis.
paras.en: [[8:24|And the Lord did so. And there came a very grievous swarm of flies|Fecitque Dominus ita. Et venit musca gravissima]] [musca, literally "fly", in the singular], that is, a multitude of flies, most wearisome with their noise and troublesome with their stinging and their sight, [[8:24|into all the land of Egypt|in omnem terram Ægypti]]: [[8:24|and the land was corrupted by this kind of flies|Corruptaque est terra ab hujuscemodi muscis]], that is, disfigured; and the inhabitants of the land of Egypt were hurt and defiled by those flies.

paras.t: Vocavitque Pharao Moysen et Aaron, et ait illis: Ite, et sacrificate Deo vestro in terra hac. Et ait Moyses: Non potest ita fieri. Abominationes enim Ægyptiorum, id est animalia quædam quæ Ægyptii abominabiliter colunt, videlicet ovem, bovem et taurum, immolabimus Domino Deo nostro. Quod si mactaverimus ea quæ Ægyptii colunt, coram eis, lapidibus nos obruent: quia reputarent sibi ac diis suis injurias maximas fieri in tali mactatione. Circa hoc loquitur Strabus: Ægyptii ovem adorabant propter Jovem Ammonem, id est Jovem in specie ovis seu arietis, nam et cum capite arietino depingebatur; bovem quoque seu taurum, qui consecratus exstitit Api seu Apidi in specie tauri. Et vaccam colebant pro Iside. Apis autem erat maximum numen apud Ægyptios.
paras.en: [[8:25|And Pharao called Moses and Aaron, and said to them: Go and sacrifice to your God in this land|Vocavitque Pharao Moysen et Aaron, et ait illis: Ite, et sacrificate Deo vestro in terra hac]]. [[8:26|And Moses said: It cannot be so|Et ait Moyses: Non potest ita fieri]]. For [[8:26|the abominations of the Egyptians|Abominationes enim Ægyptiorum]], that is, certain animals that the Egyptians abominably worship, namely the sheep, the ox and the bull, [[8:26|we shall sacrifice|immolabimus]] [[8:26|to the Lord our God|Domino Deo nostro]]. [[8:26|now if we kill those things which the Egyptians worship, in their presence, they will stone us|Quod si mactaverimus ea quæ Ægyptii colunt, coram eis, lapidibus nos obruent]]: because they would reckon that the greatest wrong was done to themselves and their gods by such a slaughter. On this Strabo says: The Egyptians adored the sheep for the sake of Jupiter Ammon, that is, Jupiter in the form of a sheep or ram, for he was also painted with a ram's head; and the ox, or bull, which was consecrated to Apis, in the form of a bull. And they worshipped the cow for Isis. And Apis was the greatest deity among the Egyptians.

paras.t: Dixitque Pharao: Ego dimittam vos, ut sacrificetis Domino Deo vestro in deserto, etc. Hoc dixit vel ficte, vel ex intentione propter angustiam plagæ. Rogate pro me. Et ait Moyses: Egressus a te, orabo Dominum, et recedet musca a Pharaone, etc. Oravitque Moyses Dominum, et recessit plaga illa omnino. Quo viso, rursus induratus est Pharao.
paras.en: [[8:28|And Pharao said: I will let you go to sacrifice to the Lord your God in the wilderness|Dixitque Pharao: Ego dimittam vos, ut sacrificetis Domino Deo vestro in deserto]], etc. This he said either feignedly or in earnest, because of the distress of the plague. [[8:28|pray for me|Rogate pro me]]. [[8:29|And Moses said: I will go out from thee, and will pray to the Lord: and the flies shall depart from Pharao|Et ait Moyses: Egressus a te, orabo Dominum, et recedet musca a Pharaone]], etc. And Moses prayed to the Lord, and that plague departed altogether. Seeing this, Pharao was hardened again.

paras.t: Circa hæc in Scholastica fertur historia: Pro his duabus plagis dicit Josephus, quod innumerabilis multitudo pediculorum in Ægyptiis pullulavit ex interioribus ebulliens, quos nec lavacris nec medicamentorum unguentis exterminare valebant. Credibile quippe est, Ægyptios fuisse percussos multis plagis, præter decem plagas famosas et principales.
paras.en: On these things it is reported in the Scholastic History [of Peter Comestor]: In place of these two plagues Josephus says that a countless multitude of lice swarmed on the Egyptians, bubbling up from within, which they could not get rid of either by baths or by medicinal ointments. For it is credible that the Egyptians were struck with many plagues besides the ten famous and principal ones.

8.title: De spirituali ejusdem capituli octavi sensu
8.title_en: On the spiritual sense of the same eighth chapter

paras.t: Dixit Dominus ad Moysen, etc. Secunda Ægyptiorum plaga fuit ebullitio ranarum copiosissima. Per Ægyptum, ut patuit, sæculum nequam exprimitur: per ranas autem designantur deceptores verbosi, præsertim loquaces et inverecundi hæretici, qui instar ranarum semper eumdem deformem et falsum emittunt sonum perfidorum verborum, quidquid eis dicatur, et quantumcumque eorum reprobentur errores. Rursus, per ranas designantur hypocritæ et vitiosi doctores, qui intus pleni sunt omni spurcitia, et inefficacia resonant verba: quæ coram Deo turpiter sonant, quia quod docent et prædicant, non adimplent. Universi demum, qui veritati fidei christianæ atque ecclesiasticæ unitati improbis et pertinacibus oblatrant clamoribus, recte designantur per ranas. Hi omnes plagant et lædunt eos, qui carni ac mundo inhærent. De quibus in prima Joannis Canonica habetur: Ipsi de mundo sunt, et de mundo loquuntur, et mundus eos audit. Hi sunt subditi Pharaonis, id est vitiosis præsidentibus subjecti et conformati in vitiis, quoniam qualis est rector civitatis, tales et habitantes in ea. Sed quomodo Aaron Deo jubente producit has ranas, nisi quoniam (teste Scriptura) Deus propter peccata populi facit regnare hypocritam, et in furore suo dat reprobis et perversis talem, qualem merentur, rectorem? Quemadmodum ait per Isaiam: Dabo pueros principes eorum, et effeminati dominabuntur eis.
paras.en: [[8:1|And the Lord said to Moses|Dixit Dominus ad Moysen]], etc. The second plague of the Egyptians was a most abundant swarming forth of frogs. By Egypt, as has been shown, this wicked world is expressed; and by the frogs are signified wordy deceivers, above all talkative and shameless heretics, who like frogs always give out the same ugly and false sound of faithless words, whatever is said to them and however much their errors are refuted. Again, by the frogs are signified hypocrites and vicious teachers, who within are full of all filth and sound forth ineffectual words, which ring foully before God, because what they teach and preach they do not fulfil. Lastly, all who bark against the truth of the Christian faith and the unity of the Church with wicked and stubborn clamour are rightly signified by the frogs. All these plague and harm those who cleave to the flesh and the world, of whom it is said in the first canonical Epistle of John: [[1 John 4:5|They are of the world. Therefore of the world they speak: and the world heareth them|Ipsi de mundo sunt, et de mundo loquuntur, et mundus eos audit]]. These are the subjects of Pharao, that is, those who are subject to vicious rulers and conformed to them in vices, since [[Ecclus 10:2|what manner of man the ruler of a city is, such also are they that dwell therein|qualis est rector civitatis, tales et habitantes in ea]]. But how does Aaron at God's command bring forth these frogs, unless because (as Scripture testifies) God [[Job 34:30|maketh a man that is a hypocrite to reign for the sins of the people|propter peccata populi facit regnare hypocritam]], and in his fury gives the reprobate and perverse such a ruler as they deserve? As he says by Isaias: [[Is 3:4|I will give children to be their princes, and the effeminate shall rule over them|Dabo pueros principes eorum, et effeminati dominabuntur eis]].

paras.t: Quemadmodum autem Pharao petiit ranas auferri a se, sic frequenter perversi prælati, principesque iniqui propriorum subditorum rebellium importunitatem, inquietudinem, obstrepentesque clamores ferre non valentes, precantur liberari ab illis. Quod si ipsi qui præsunt, propriam emendaverint vitam, experientur mores subditorum suorum in melius commutari: quia secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus.
paras.en: And as Pharao asked that the frogs be taken away from him, so perverse prelates and wicked princes, unable to bear the importunity, the unrest and the noisy clamour of their own rebellious subjects, often pray to be delivered from them. But if those who rule amend their own life, they will find the manners of their subjects changed for the better: because [[Ecclus 10:2|As the judge of the people is himself, so also are his ministers|secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus]].

paras.t: Insuper, per tertiam plagam Ægypti, hoc est per scinifes, designantur versuti et callidi, ac duplices corde, et mendaciter blandientes: qui tunc gravius nocent et pungunt, dum magis prætendunt favorem ac famulatum. De quibus loquitur Jeremias: Sagitta vulnerans lingua eorum. In ore suo pacem cum amico suo loquitur, et occulte ponit ei insidias. Talium insidiæ sunt ita latentes, ut prius sentiantur, quam prævideantur; et vix ab oculatissimis viris queunt perpendi. Ideo recte ait Scriptura: Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei. Et rursus: Qui sophistice loquitur, odibilis est. Et: Homo qui blandis fictisque sermonibus decipit proximum suum, maledicetur. Tales sunt et detestandi bilingues. Contra quos Ecclesiasticus asserit: Susurro et bilinguis, maledictus; multos enim turbavit, pacem habentes. Et alibi: Denotatio pessima super bilinguem. Hi omnes vicissitudinem sortientur, et qua mensura metiuntur, eis remetietur. Nam et impietates eorum redundabunt in eos, quum in Ecclesiaste scriptum sit: Qui fodit foveam, incidit in eam; et qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber. Alibi quoque: Facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur, et non cognoscet unde illi adveniet illusio.
paras.en: Further, by the third plague of Egypt, that is, by the sciniphs [that is, gnats or midges], are signified the cunning and crafty, the double-hearted and those who flatter with lies: who wound and sting most grievously when they make the greatest show of favour and service. Of these Jeremias speaks: [[Jer 9:8|Their tongue is a piercing arrow|Sagitta vulnerans lingua eorum]]. [[Jer 9:8|with his mouth one speaketh peace with his friend, and secretly he lieth in wait for him|In ore suo pacem cum amico suo loquitur, et occulte ponit ei insidias]]. The snares of such men lie so hidden that they are felt before they are foreseen, and can scarcely be detected even by the most clear-sighted men. Therefore Scripture rightly says: [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei]]. And again: [[Ecclus 37:23|He that speaketh sophistically, is hateful|Qui sophistice loquitur, odibilis est]]. And: A man who deceives his neighbour with flattering and feigned words shall be cursed[[Prov 29:5||]] [Denis's wording differs from Prov 29:5, which reads: "A man that speaketh to his friend with flattering and dissembling words, spreadeth a net for his feet"]. Such too are the detestable double-tongued, against whom Ecclesiasticus declares: [[Ecclus 28:15|The whisperer and the double tongue is accursed: for he hath troubled many that were at peace|Susurro et bilinguis, maledictus; multos enim turbavit, pacem habentes]]. And elsewhere: [[Ecclus 5:17|an evil mark of disgrace upon the double tongued|Denotatio pessima super bilinguem]]. All these shall receive like for like, and with what measure they mete, it shall be measured to them again[[Matt 7:2||]]. For their wickedness too shall recoil upon them, since it is written in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 10:8|He that diggeth a pit, shall fall into it: and he that breaketh a hedge, a serpent shall bite him|Qui fodit foveam, incidit in eam; et qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber]]. And elsewhere too: [[Ecclus 27:30|A mischievous counsel shall be rolled back upon the author, and he shall not know from whence it cometh to him|Facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur, et non cognoscet unde illi adveniet illusio]] [Denis's text reads "whence the mockery cometh to him" (*unde illi adveniet illusio*)].

paras.t: Rursus, per scinifes significantur logicorum et sophistarum argumentationes curiosæ, et superfluæ concertationes. Sed et pulvis terræ in scinifes vertitur, dum homines intimorati ac leves, præinductis vanitatibus atque versutiis student.
paras.en: Again, by the sciniphs are signified the curious arguments of logicians and sophists, and their superfluous disputes. And the dust of the earth is turned into sciniphs when men without the fear of God, and light-minded, give themselves to the vanities and subtleties aforesaid.

paras.t: Præterea per muscas diversarum specierum, rite intelliguntur carnalia vitia, ac variæ species gulæ, et item luxuriæ, quibus Ægypti, id est mundani et falsi nominis religiosi ac clerici, mente et corpore inquinantur, vitam suam abbreviant, et diversimode periclitantur: tandemque in profundissima Acherontis labuntur: et quantum glorificaverunt se, in deliciisque fuerunt, tantum de tormento ac luctu recipiunt in æternum. Sed in terra Gessen, videlicet inter eos qui veri sunt Israelitæ, religiosi et contemplativi, non invenitur hæc plaga.
paras.en: Moreover, by the flies of divers kinds are fittingly understood the carnal vices, the various kinds of gluttony and likewise of lust, by which the Egyptians, that is, worldly men, and religious and clerics in name only, are defiled in mind and body, shorten their life and are endangered in divers ways; and at last they sink into the lowest depths of Acheron, and as much as they have glorified themselves and lived in delights, so much torment and sorrow do they receive for ever[[Apoc 18:7||]] [the margin note here is illegible; the words are adapted from Apoc 18:7]. But in the land of Gessen, that is, among those who are true Israelites, religious and contemplatives, this plague is not found.

paras.t: Præterea abominationes Ægyptiorum Hebræi offerunt Deo, quoniam temporalia et terrena, quibus avari et vitiosi tanquam idolis serviunt, et plus quam vero Deo adhærent, ipsi ad spiritualia ordinant, atque pauperibus largiuntur: et de mammona iniquitatis, vitam sibi mercantur æternam: et quæ receperunt de manu Domini, immolant ei. Iterum, abominationes Ægyptiorum sunt mundi contemptus, religionis ingressus, paupertas spontanea, conversatio pœnitentialis, sancta simplicitas, profunda humilitas, inimicorum dilectio, beneficentia malefacientibus facta, omnium adversitatum et injuriarum tranquilla perpessio: quæ omnia a carnalibus et superbis hominibus, quasi abominabilia reputantur aut evitantur: sed electi Dei et veraciter virtuosi, hæc amplectuntur et offerunt Deo, cui omne bonum adscribunt, et ad ejus honorem ac gloriam bona ista exerceant: quæ etiam in diversis locis religionis, mansionibusque secretis liberius exhibent, expeditiusque observant, ne ab Ægyptiis lapidibus obruantur, hoc est, ne verbis detractoriis et mundanis tumultibus, asperisque injuriis infestentur, atque a Dei obsequio retrahantur, et pectoris pace priventur.
paras.en: Further, the Hebrews offer to God [[8:26|the abominations of the Egyptians|abominationes Ægyptiorum]], since temporal and earthly things, which the covetous and vicious serve as idols and cleave to more than to the true God, these men direct to spiritual ends and bestow on the poor; and with the mammon of iniquity they purchase for themselves eternal life, and what they have received from the hand of the Lord they sacrifice to him. Again, [[8:26|the abominations of the Egyptians|abominationes Ægyptiorum]] are contempt of the world, entrance into religion [that is, into a religious order], voluntary poverty, a life of penance, holy simplicity, deep humility, love of enemies, kindness done to those who do us harm, and the calm bearing of all adversities and injuries: all of which carnal and proud men regard as abominable, or shun. But the elect of God and the truly virtuous embrace these and offer them to God, to whom they ascribe all good, and they practise these good things to his honour and glory; and they show them forth more freely and keep them more readily in the various houses of religion and in secret dwellings, lest they be overwhelmed with stones by the Egyptians[[8:26||]], that is, lest they be harassed by detracting words, worldly tumults and harsh injuries, and drawn back from the service of God and robbed of peace of heart.

paras.t: Postremo circa istud, Egredietur ad aquas, scribit Lyra: Forsan Pharao credidit, quod sicut aqua purgat fæces corporales, ita et mentales. Ad quod argumentum est, quoniam Sarraceni terram Ægypti nunc inhabitantes, talibus ablutionibus ad emendationem peccatorum utuntur: et forte tenent hoc ex ritu antiquo Ægyptiorum. Contra hoc ultimum verbum, quod scilicet Sarraceni tenent hoc, etc.: quod tamen Lyra non scribit affirmando, sed dubitando, quia adjungit, forte: multa scribit Rabbi Paulus, inter cetera dicens, quod Sarraceni præcipiuntur a Mahometo custodire legem Mosaicam et Evangelium, ut in Alcorano expresse habetur. Ideo simulando observationem Mosaicæ legis, se circumcidunt, non tamen octavo die, sed post lapsum cujuscumque temporis indifferenter; simulando quoque observationem Evangelii, utuntur quibusdam ablutionibus seu baptismis.
paras.en: Lastly, on the words [[8:20|he will go forth to the waters|Egredietur ad aquas]], Lyra writes: Perhaps Pharao believed that as water cleanses the filth of the body, so it cleanses that of the mind too. An argument for this is that the Saracens who now inhabit the land of Egypt use such washings for the amendment of sins; and perhaps they hold this from an ancient rite of the Egyptians. Against this last statement, namely that the Saracens hold this, etc. (which Lyra, however, writes not affirming but doubting, for he adds "perhaps"), Rabbi Paul [that is, Paul of Burgos, a converted Jew who wrote Additions to Lyra's Postill] writes much, saying among other things that the Saracens are commanded by Mahomet to keep the Mosaic law and the Gospel, as is expressly found in the Alcoran. Therefore, feigning observance of the Mosaic law, they circumcise themselves, though not on the eighth day but indifferently after any lapse of time; and feigning observance of the Gospel as well, they use certain washings or baptisms.

paras.t: Circa hæc dico, quod impius ac perfidissimus Mahometus finxit se esse prophetam et nuntium Dei, specialiter missum Sarracenis, sicut Moysen dixit specialiter missum Hebræis, et Christum Christianis. Iterum dixit, quod sicut Deus Moysi Testamentum et Christo Evangelium, sic sibi Alcoranum dedit, sicque dixit sibi a Deo missam ac datam specialem legem, ut eam proponeret Sarracenis. Ideo nullibi præcipit in Alcorano, ut Sarraceni absolute aut in toto observent legem Moysis et Evangelium Christi. Aliqua tamen ex lege et Evangelio præcipit eis servanda, et tamen in Alcorano nullam facit mentionem de observanda circumcisione a Sarracenis, nec præcipit eis servare sacramentum Baptismi, imo omnia sacramenta evangelicæ legis abjecit. Verum est tamen, quod in Alcorano suo affirmat legem suam in nullo discrepare a lege Moysis et Evangelio Christi. Quod tamen omnino falsissimum est, sicut hoc clarissime et copiosissime demonstravi in tractatu quem contra Alcoranum composui. Insuper dico, quod Sarraceni observant circumcisionem non indifferenter post cujuscumque temporis lapsum, sed regulariter circumcidunt filios suos quum tredecim annorum exstiterint, quia tot annorum fuerat Ismael, de quo natos se dicunt, quando circumcisus est, ut in Genesi continetur. Hoc autem cum Rabbi Paulo concedo, quod Sarraceni Ægypti ritum suarum ablutionum potius habent ex traditione sui pseudoprophetæ, quam ex antiqua consuetudine Ægyptiorum. Nam in omni terra et regione qua degunt, ablutiones tales observant.
paras.en: On these matters I say that the impious and most faithless Mahomet pretended that he was a prophet and messenger of God, sent specially to the Saracens, just as he said that Moses was sent specially to the Hebrews and Christ to the Christians. He said further that as God gave the Testament to Moses and the Gospel to Christ, so he gave the Alcoran to him; and so he said that a special law had been sent and given him by God, for him to set before the Saracens. Hence nowhere in the Alcoran does he command the Saracens to keep the law of Moses and the Gospel of Christ absolutely or entirely. Some things from the law and the Gospel he does command them to keep; and yet in the Alcoran he makes no mention of the Saracens keeping circumcision, nor does he command them to keep the sacrament of Baptism; rather, he cast away all the sacraments of the law of the Gospel. It is true, however, that in his Alcoran he affirms that his law in no way differs from the law of Moses and the Gospel of Christ. Yet this is utterly false, as I have shown most clearly and at great length in the treatise I composed against the Alcoran [*Contra perfidiam Mahometi*]. Moreover, I say that the Saracens keep circumcision not indifferently after any lapse of time, but as a rule circumcise their sons when they are thirteen years old, because Ismael, from whom they say they are descended, was of that age when he was circumcised, as is contained in Genesis[[Gen 17:25||]]. But this I grant with Rabbi Paul: that the Saracens of Egypt have the rite of their washings from the tradition of their false prophet rather than from the ancient custom of the Egyptians. For in every land and region where they live they keep such washings.

9.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli noni : Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen : Ingredere ad Pharaonem
9.title_en: Literal explanation of the ninth chapter: And the Lord said to Moses: Go in to Pharao

paras.t: Tres plagæ sequentes, videlicet quinta, sexta et septima, in isto describuntur capitulo. Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen: Ingredere ad Pharaonem, etc. Hæc dicit Dominus Deus Hebræorum, etc. Ecce manus mea erit super agros tuos, super equos et asinos et camelos et oves et boves, id est, potestas mea agris et jumentis tuis inferet læsionem et destructionem. Unde quasi expositorie subditur: pestis valde gravis. Quæ autem fuerit pestis hæc, in littera non narratur in speciali: sed aliqui putant quod solo Dei imperio facta fuit corruptio ista jumentis et herbis agrorum, quia nec Moyses nec Aaron legitur in hac plaga aliquod exhibuisse obsequium. Verumtamen tales effectus solet Deus magis per angelica ministeria, quam per se ipsum immediate producere. Aliqui vero dicunt, quod ex corruptione aeris infecta fuerunt pascua, et ex consequenti jumenta ex pascuis ipsis vescentia.
paras.en: The three following plagues, namely the fifth, sixth and seventh, are described in this chapter. [[9:1|And the Lord said to Moses: Go in to Pharao|Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen: Ingredere ad Pharaonem]], etc. [[9:1|Thus saith the Lord God of the Hebrews|Hæc dicit Dominus Deus Hebræorum]], etc. [[9:3|Behold my hand shall be upon thy fields|Ecce manus mea erit super agros tuos]], [[9:3|upon thy horses, and asses, and camels, and oxen, and sheep|super equos et asinos et camelos et oves et boves]], that is, my power will bring harm and destruction upon thy fields and thy beasts. Hence, by way of explanation as it were, is added: [[9:3|a very grievous murrain|pestis valde gravis]]. What this murrain was is not told in particular in the text; but some think that this blight came upon the beasts and the grass of the fields by the command of God alone, since neither Moses nor Aaron is read to have rendered any service in this plague. Yet God is wont to produce such effects through the ministry of angels rather than by himself immediately. Others say that the pastures were infected by a corruption of the air, and in consequence the beasts that fed on those pastures.

paras.t: Et faciet Dominus mirabile, id est miram divisionem et distinctionem, inter possessiones Israel, et possessiones Ægyptiorum: ita ut nihil omnino pereat ex his quæ pertinent ad filios Israel: quia nec pascua, nec jumenta Hebræorum læsa fuerunt hac plaga. Et dicunt nonnulli, quod in eisdem agris seu campis corrupta fuerunt animalia Ægyptiorum, non Hebræorum: alias non videtur probabile, quod Ægyptii permiserunt jumenta Hebræorum ire et pasci in eisdem campis cum animalibus suis. Ideo dicunt, quod infectio illa seu pestis non fuit in locis et pascuis ac jumentis ad Hebræos spectantibus: quod verius reor.
paras.en: [[9:4|And the Lord will make a wonderful|Et faciet Dominus mirabile]] thing, that is, a wonderful division and distinction, [[9:4|between the possessions of Israel and the possessions of the Egyptians|inter possessiones Israel, et possessiones Ægyptiorum]]; so [[9:4|that nothing at all shall die of those things that belong to the children of Israel|ut nihil omnino pereat ex his quæ pertinent ad filios Israel]]: for neither the pastures nor the beasts of the Hebrews were harmed by this plague. And some say that it was in the same fields or plains that the animals of the Egyptians were stricken, and not those of the Hebrews; but it does not seem likely that the Egyptians allowed the beasts of the Hebrews to go and graze in the same plains with their own animals. Therefore it is said that this infection or murrain was not in the places, pastures and beasts belonging to the Hebrews: which I think the truer view.

paras.t: Constituitque Dominus tempus, dicens per Moysen ad Pharaonem: Cras faciet, id est implebit, Dominus verbum istud in terra Ægypti. Circa hoc recitat Lyra: Dicunt Hebræi, quod Moyses fecit lineam in pariete, dicens: Cras sole hanc lineam attingente, fiet hæc plaga: et hoc, ad insinuandum certitudinem divinæ providentiæ.
paras.en: [[9:5|And the Lord appointed a time, saying|Constituitque Dominus tempus, dicens]] through Moses to Pharao: [[9:5|To morrow will the Lord do|Cras faciet]], that is, fulfil, [[9:5|this thing in the land|Dominus verbum istud in terra]] of Egypt. On this Lyra relates: The Hebrews say that Moses drew a line on the wall, saying: Tomorrow, when the sun reaches this line, this plague shall come; and this to make known the certainty of divine providence.

paras.t: Mortuaque sunt omnia animantia Ægyptiorum. Istud quidam exponunt de animalibus quæ fuerunt in domibus: quia de animalibus quæ fuerunt in agris et campis, paulo post dicitur quod grandine perierunt. Alii hoc exponunt de animalibus quæ fuerunt in agris et campis: quod magis consonat litteræ, sicut nunc patuit. De quibus autem animalibus verificetur, quod grandine perierunt, statim discutietur.
paras.en: [[9:6|and all the beasts of the Egyptians died|Mortuaque sunt omnia animantia Ægyptiorum]]. Some explain this of the animals that were in the houses, since of the animals that were in the fields and plains it is said a little later that they perished by the hail. Others explain it of the animals that were in the fields and plains, which agrees better with the text, as has just been seen. Of which animals it is true that they perished by the hail will be discussed shortly.

paras.t: Et misit Pharao ad videndum, an nihil obiisset de pecoribus Hebræorum, ut exploraret an verba Moysis essent impleta. Si quæratur, cur non misit similiter ad videndum de plaga præcedenti, in qua etiam Moyses de hujusmodi divisione prædixit: respondetur, quod propter molestiam muscarum in aere copiosissime volitantium, nuntii non potuissent expedite ire per terram. Vel forte Pharao magis reputavit hanc plagam, quæ sibi exstitit tam noxia. Denique, quia Ægyptii non solum afflixerunt Hebræos, sed et jumenta eorum, imponendo utrisque grandes labores ac onera deportanda, idcirco Ægyptii juste puniti sunt in morte jumentorum suorum corresponditque pœna culpæ.
paras.en: [[9:7|And Pharao sent to see|Et misit Pharao ad videndum]] whether nothing had died of the herds of the Hebrews, to find out whether the words of Moses had been fulfilled. If it be asked why he did not likewise send to see in the preceding plague, in which Moses had also foretold such a division, the answer is that because of the plague of the flies swarming in the air in great numbers, messengers could not have gone readily through the land. Or perhaps Pharao made more of this plague, which was so harmful to him. Lastly, since the Egyptians afflicted not only the Hebrews but their beasts too, laying great labours and burdens to be carried upon both, the Egyptians were justly punished in the death of their own beasts, and the punishment answered to the fault.

paras.t: Deinde describitur sexta plaga. Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen et Aaron: Tollite plenas manus cineris, id est, unusquisque vestrum impleat manum suam cineribus, de camino, et adspergat illum Moyses in cœlum coram Pharaone; atque pulvis super omnem terram Ægypti. Circa hæc quæri plurima possunt. Primo, cur Dominus fecit præcedens miraculum et flagellum, quo occisa sunt Ægyptiorum jumenta, sine ministerio Moysis et Aaron, et non istud, quo puniti sunt homines et jumenta. Secundo, cur Dominus jussit tam Moysi quam Aaron implere manus cineribus; et item, cur cineribus de camino. Tertio, cur solus Moyses jussus est pulverem spargere. Quarto, cur adjecit, Et sit pulvis super omnem terram Ægypti, quasi ante non fuerit ibi pulvis.
paras.en: Next the sixth plague is described. [[9:8|And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: Take to you handfuls of ashes|Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen et Aaron: Tollite plenas manus cineris]], that is, let each of you fill his hand with ashes, [[9:8|out of the chimney, and let Moses sprinkle it in the air in the presence of Pharao|de camino, et adspergat illum Moyses in cœlum coram Pharaone]]; [[9:9|And be there dust upon all the land of Egypt|atque pulvis super omnem terram Ægypti]]. Many questions can be asked about this. First, why the Lord worked the preceding miracle and scourge, by which the beasts of the Egyptians were killed, without the ministry of Moses and Aaron, and not this one, by which men and beasts were punished. Second, why the Lord bade both Moses and Aaron fill their hands with ashes; and again, why ashes from the furnace [caminus, a furnace or kiln; the Douay-Rheims has "chimney"]. Third, why Moses alone was bidden to scatter the dust. Fourth, why he added, [[9:9|And be there dust upon all the land of Egypt|Et sit pulvis super omnem terram Ægypti]], as if there had been no dust there before.

paras.t: Ad ista quis dicere posset, Quis cognovit sensum Domini? aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit? Verumtamen conjiciendo et opinando, potest aliqualis dari responsio: dicendo ad primum, quod Dominus fecit quædam signa per Aaron, propter causam supra inductam: quædam per Moysen, ad ostendendum ejus principalitatem in ista legatione. Nam et ea quæ Aaron egit, ex Moysis imperio fecit, ita quod Dominus dixit ad Moysen: Dic ad Aaron, Extende manum: vel, Tolle virgam, aut aliquid simile. Aliqua vero signa fecit Dominus per se, ad ostendendum, quod ipse nullius eget obsequio. Ad secundum dici potest, quod utrisque jussit Dominus manus implere cineribus, ad declarandum commune et sociale ac concors eorum obsequium. Ad tertium, quod soli Moysi, tanquam principali, jussit spargere cinerem. Nam et sparsio ista est facta sursum in cœlum: ideo Moysi competebat, qui constitutus est mediator quoad pertinentia ad Deum. Ad quartum, quod pulvis de quo nunc sermo, de terra consurgens, circa eam volitabat in aere: et forte fuerat infectivus et inflictivus plagæ, quæ statim narratur. Cur autem est sumptus cinis de camino? Dici potest quod plaga ista correspondebat iniquitati Ægyptiorum, qua oppresserunt filios Israel, imponendo eis decoctionem laterum in fornace ardente.
paras.en: To these one might say: [[Rom 11:34|who hath known the mind of the Lord? Or who hath been his counsellor?|Quis cognovit sensum Domini? aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit?]] Yet by conjecture and opinion some kind of answer can be given. To the first one may say that the Lord worked certain signs through Aaron, for the reason given above, and certain ones through Moses, to show that he was the principal in this embassy. For even what Aaron did he did at Moses' command, so that the Lord said to Moses: Say to Aaron: Stretch forth thy hand; or, Take the rod; or something of the kind. And some signs the Lord worked by himself, to show that he needs the service of none. To the second it can be said that the Lord bade both of them fill their hands with ashes, to declare that their service was common, shared and of one accord. To the third, that he bade Moses alone scatter the ashes, as the principal. For this sprinkling was also made upwards into the air; therefore it was fitting for Moses, who was appointed mediator in the things that pertain to God. To the fourth, that the dust spoken of here, rising from the earth, was flying about it in the air, and perhaps it was what carried and inflicted the plague that is told straight after. But why were the ashes taken from the furnace? It can be said that this plague answered to the wickedness of the Egyptians by which they oppressed the children of Israel, laying on them the baking of bricks in the burning furnace.

paras.t: Erant enim in hominibus et jumentis ulcera et vesicæ turgentes in universa terra Ægypti, in qua morabantur Ægyptii, non tamen in mansionibus Hebræorum. Itaque in vesicis Ægyptiorum fuit interior læsio, scilicet calefactio pungens, ex qua primo ulcera nascebantur, deinde ruptis vesicis facta sunt vulnera in eisdem. Et hoc justo Dei judicio, quia in filiis Israel ex magnitudine oppressionum, dolorum, laborum, angustiarumque fuit multiplex læsio viscerum interiorum ex persecutione Ægyptiorum.
paras.en: [[9:9|for there shall be boils and swelling blains both in men and beasts, in the whole land of Egypt|Erant enim in hominibus et jumentis ulcera et vesicæ turgentes in universa terra Ægypti]], in which the Egyptians dwelt, but not in the dwellings of the Hebrews. So in the blains of the Egyptians there was an inward hurt, namely a stinging heat, from which first the boils arose; then, when the blains burst, sores were made in them. And this by the just judgement of God, because in the children of Israel, from the greatness of their oppressions, pains, labours and distresses, there was a manifold hurt of the inward parts through the persecution of the Egyptians.

paras.t: Nec poterant malefici stare coram Moyse propter vulnera quæ in illis erant. Unde elicitur, quod plaga ista acrius eos torsit, quia quum ante dixissent, Digitus Dei est hic, utpote cognoscentes plagas istas esse a summo Deo, non tamen cessaverunt a sua malitia.
paras.en: [[9:11|Neither could the magicians stand before Moses, for the boils that were upon them|Nec poterant malefici stare coram Moyse propter vulnera quæ in illis erant]] [Denis's text reads vulnera, sores; the margin gives ulcera, boils, the reading of the Vulgate]. From this it is gathered that this plague tormented them more sharply, because though they had said before, [[Ex 8:19|This is the finger of God|Digitus Dei est hic]], as knowing that these plagues were from the most high God, yet they had not ceased from their malice.

paras.t: Sequitur septima plaga. Dixit quoque Dominus ad Moysen: Mane consurge et sta coram Pharaone, et dices ad eum: Hæc dicit Dominus: Dimitte populum meum, ut sacrificet mihi; quia in hac vice, id est, nisi dimiseris eos in hoc tempore, mittam omnes plagas meas super cor tuum, id est super te totum, ita quod intus et extra affligeris, et cordis tui penetralia perforabuntur dolore. Per cor autem, tanquam per partem principalem, totus homo accipitur. Nam et Philosophus ait, quod homo est maxime suus intellectus. Nec sine causa dixit, Super cor tuum, sed ad insinuandum penetrativam hujus plagæ severitatem. Denique, quia nunc dicitur, Omnes plagas meas, quidam exponunt istud non solum de hac plaga, sed simul de ea et plagis sequentibus. Potest tamen exponi de sola hac plaga totali, quæ plures partiales plagas in se comprehendebat, quemadmodum nunc patebit. Frequenter etiam ponitur numerus pluralis pro singulari, et econverso. Omne quoque interdum accipitur pro perfecto aut toto. Et sic nunc accipi potest. Omnes, id est perfectas et totales has plagas, quia in hac plaga multa fuerunt afflictiva atque nociva.
paras.en: The seventh plague follows. [[9:13|And the Lord said to Moses: Arise in the morning, and stand before Pharao, and thou shalt say to him|Dixit quoque Dominus ad Moysen: Mane consurge et sta coram Pharaone, et dices ad eum]]: [[9:13|Thus saith the Lord|Hæc dicit Dominus]]: [[9:13|Let my people go to sacrifice to me|Dimitte populum meum, ut sacrificet mihi]]; [[9:14|For I will at this time|quia in hac vice]], that is, unless thou let them go at this time, [[9:14|send all my plagues upon thy heart|mittam omnes plagas meas super cor tuum]], that is, upon thy whole self, so that thou shalt be afflicted within and without, and the inmost depths of thy heart shall be pierced with pain. For by the heart, as by the principal part, the whole man is understood: for the Philosopher too says that a man is most of all his intellect. Nor did he say [[9:14|upon thy heart|Super cor tuum]] without cause, but to make known the piercing severity of this plague. Further, since it now says [[9:14|all my plagues|Omnes plagas meas]], some explain this not only of this plague but of it together with the plagues that follow. Yet it can be explained of this one complete plague alone, which contained in itself several partial plagues, as will be seen presently. The plural number is also often put for the singular, and the other way about; and "all" is sometimes taken for "perfect" or "whole", and so it can be taken here: "all", that is, these perfect and complete plagues, since in this plague there were many things that afflicted and harmed.

paras.t: Et super servos tuos et super populum tuum, id est ceteros Ægyptios qui tibi consenserunt et cooperati sunt, affligendo Hebræos; ut scias quod non sit similis mei in omni terra, id est, quod nullus sit mihi æqualis in potestate et in omni perfectione. Istud fuit una causa inductionis plagarum istarum. Aliæ quoque fuerunt causæ earum, ut scilicet per eas filii Israel instruerentur et redimerentur. Itemque, ut toti mundo tam præsentibus quam futuris innotesceret excellentia Dei, sicque converterentur ad eum.
paras.en: [[9:14|and upon thy servants, and upon thy people|Et super servos tuos et super populum tuum]], that is, the rest of the Egyptians, who consented with thee and worked with thee in afflicting the Hebrews; [[9:14|that thou mayst know that there is none like me in all the earth|ut scias quod non sit similis mei in omni terra]], that is, that none is equal to me in power and in every perfection. This was one cause of the bringing on of these plagues. There were other causes of them as well: namely, that through them the children of Israel might be instructed and redeemed; and also that the excellence of God might become known to the whole world, to those then living and to those to come, and so they might be converted to him.

paras.t: Hinc subditur: Idcirco autem posui te, id est creavi te in regno et loco hoc collocavi, ut ostendam in te fortitudinem meam, id est, omnipotentiam meam electis salubriter manifestem per effectus potentiæ atque justitiæ meæ in te: imo et cunctis hominibus, etiam reprobis, pandam virtutem ac providentiam meam ad eorum commonitionem, ut inexcusabiles inveniantur. Ideo subditur: et narretur nomen meum in omni terra, id est, cunctis hominibus prædicetur majestas mea, et fama excellentiæ meæ. Hunc passum allegat ad Romanos Apostolus, dicens: Dicit enim Scriptura Pharaoni, quia in hoc ipsum excitavi te, ut ostendam in te virtutem meam, et annuntietur nomen meum in universa terra.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[9:16|And therefore have I raised thee|Idcirco autem posui te]], that is, I created thee and placed thee in this kingdom and place, [[9:16|that I may shew my power in thee|ut ostendam in te fortitudinem meam]], that is, that I may make my omnipotence known to the elect, for their salvation, through the effects of my power and justice in thee; nay, to all men, even the reprobate, I will lay open my might and providence for their warning, that they may be found without excuse. Therefore it is added: [[9:16|and my name may be spoken of throughout all the earth|et narretur nomen meum in omni terra]], that is, may my majesty and the fame of my excellence be proclaimed to all men. The Apostle cites this passage to the Romans, saying: [[Rom 9:17|For the scripture saith to Pharao: To this purpose have I raised thee, that I may shew my power in thee and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth|Dicit enim Scriptura Pharaoni, quia in hoc ipsum excitavi te, ut ostendam in te virtutem meam, et annuntietur nomen meum in universa terra]].

paras.t: Verumtamen Deus voluntate antecedente vult omnes homines fieri salvos, atque ob æternam beatitudinem obtinendam condidit universos. Sed ipse tam bonus et sapiens est, quod malos et reprobos non crearet, nisi sciret et posset ex eorum malitia elicere multa bona. Sicque ex Pharaonis malitia elicuit Deus bona prætacta, quemadmodum ex ferocia tyrannorum et persecutorum Ecclesiæ, elicuit martyrum glorificationem, fidei corroborationem, fidelium ædificationem, conversionemque plurimorum. Porro voluntate consequente, ut loquitur Damascenus, vult Deus reprobos et præscitos damnari, considerata simul cum ea eorum malitia; sicque asseritur eos creasse, ut justitiam et fortitudinem suam demonstraret in eis. Universa equidem fecit, ut sua in eis perfectio demonstraretur. Ideo sicut in electis voluit relucere suam misericordiam, ita in reprobis suam justitiam. Propterea ad Romanos scribit Apostolus: Annon habet potestatem figulus luti ex eadem massa facere quidem unum vas in honorem, aliud vero in contumeliam? Quod si Deus volens ostendere iram et notam facere potentiam suam, sustinuit in multa patientia vasa iræ apta in interitum, ut ostenderet divitias gloriæ suæ in vasa misericordiæ quæ præparavit in gloriam.
paras.en: Yet God by his antecedent will [that is, his will considered in itself, before he regards what the creature itself does] [[1 Tim 2:4|will have all men to be saved|vult omnes homines fieri salvos]], and he made them all to obtain eternal beatitude. But he is so good and wise that he would not create the wicked and reprobate unless he knew how, and were able, to draw many goods out of their malice. And so out of Pharao's malice God drew the goods mentioned above, just as out of the ferocity of the tyrants and persecutors of the Church he drew the glorification of the martyrs, the strengthening of the faith, the edification of the faithful, and the conversion of very many. Further, by his consequent will [that is, his will as it takes account of what the creature does], as Damascene puts it, God wills the reprobate and those foreknown [to be lost] to be damned, their malice being considered together with it; and in this sense he is said to have created them in order to show his justice and might in them. Indeed he made all things so that his perfection might be shown in them. Therefore, as he willed his mercy to shine forth in the elect, so his justice in the reprobate. Hence the Apostle writes to the Romans: [[Rom 9:21|Or hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump, to make one vessel unto honour and another unto dishonour?|Annon habet potestatem figulus luti ex eadem massa facere quidem unum vas in honorem, aliud vero in contumeliam?]] [[Rom 9:22|What if God, willing to shew his wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath, fitted for destruction|Quod si Deus volens ostendere iram et notam facere potentiam suam, sustinuit in multa patientia vasa iræ apta in interitum]], [[Rom 9:23|That he might shew the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy which he hath prepared unto glory?|ut ostenderet divitias gloriæ suæ in vasa misericordiæ quæ præparavit in gloriam]] [the margin gives Rom. ix, 21, 22; the quotation runs on into v. 23]

paras.t: Circa hæc scribit Lyra: Deus non indiget malitia hominum ad declarationem fortitudinis suæ, quia per multas alias vias potest eam monstrare; sed mala permittit, ut bona eliciat. Idcirco ly ut, tenetur consecutive, non causaliter, quum dicitur: Idcirco posui te, ut ostendam in te fortitudinem meam. Sed contra hoc ultimum, scilicet quod ly ut, tenetur consecutive, non causaliter, arguit Rabbi Paulus, assumens verba Thomæ dicentis: Divina providentia non solum disponit qui effectus fiant, sed etiam ex quibus causis, et quo ordine: inter quas causas, actus humani sunt causæ quorumdam effectuum. Sicque in talibus homines aliqua agunt, ut per suos actus impleantur quidam effectus secundum ordinem a Deo dispositum. Ideo tales intermedii actus, rationem habent causalitatis respectu effectus a Deo dispositi. Unde in præsenti materia, quoniam Deus ex proposito suæ voluntatis disposuit, quod per malitiam Pharaonis a Deo toleratam et permissam, sua potentia, justitia et longanimitas hominibus declarentur: hujusmodi malitia sic a Deo permissa, habet rationem causalitatis respectu hujuscemodi declarationis a Deo intentæ: ideo ly ut, in hoc loco tenetur causaliter, ut etiam patet ex Glossa.
paras.en: On this Lyra writes: God does not need the malice of men to declare his might, since he can show it in many other ways; but he permits evils so as to draw good from them. Therefore the word "ut" [that, in order that] is taken consecutively, not causally [that is, as marking what follows from the deed, not the purpose for which it was done], when it is said: [[9:16|therefore have I raised thee, that I may shew my power in thee|Idcirco posui te, ut ostendam in te fortitudinem meam]]. But against this last point, namely that the word "ut" is taken consecutively, not causally, Rabbi Paul argues [Paul of Burgos, a convert from Judaism, whose Additions to Lyra's Postill Denis often weighs], taking up the words of Thomas, who says: Divine providence disposes not only what effects are to come about, but also from what causes and in what order; and among those causes human acts are the causes of certain effects. So in such matters men do certain things in order that through their acts certain effects may be fulfilled according to the order disposed by God. Therefore such intermediate acts have the nature of causes with respect to the effect disposed by God. Hence in the present matter, since God by the purpose of his will disposed that through the malice of Pharao, tolerated and permitted by God, his power, justice and long-suffering should be declared to men, this malice so permitted by God has the nature of a cause with respect to this declaration intended by God; therefore the word "ut" is taken causally in this place, as is also plain from the Gloss.

paras.t: Circa hæc verba Rabbi Pauli dico, quod verba S. Thomæ secundum ipsius Thomæ intentionem, vere atque catholice sunt inducta. Siquidem Doctor sanctus introduxit verba illa in secunda secundæ, quæstione 85, solvendo hanc quæstionem, an conveniens sit orare. Et declarat, quod imo, non obstante immobilitate providentiæ Dei, quia videlicet Deus prævidit ac præordinavit se daturum gratiam ac salutem hominibus per orationes et quosdam actus eorum. Hinc Thomas asserit ibi: Orandum est, non ut Deum flectamus, aut divinam dispositionem mutemus, sed ut orando id impetremus, quod Deus per orationem statuit dare aut facere. Itaque constat quod intentio Thomæ est, loqui de actibus bonis, non vitiosis, quod scilicet habeant rationem causalitatis directe respectu effectuum a Deo dispositorum. Et ita Rabbi Paulus non recte applicare videtur verba Thomæ ad probandum propositum suum, utpote quod in ordine divinæ providentiæ, obstinatio aut malitia Pharaonis habeat rationem causalitatis respectu manifestationis fortitudinis Dei. Nempe si ita esset, sequi videretur quod malitia Pharaonis fuisset a Deo intenta, atque quod Deus esset non solum permissiva, sed et effectiva seu directa causa illius malitiæ, quia Deus hoc intendit et efficit, per quod sua providentia directe causaliterque impletur. Nec Glossa videtur esse pro Rabbi Paulo, quoniam Glossa introducit verba Augustini dicentis: Novit Dominus bene uti malis, non tamen humanam naturam ad malitiam creat. Ex quibus verbis probatur, quod demonstratio fortitudinis Dei per Pharaonis malitiam, consecutive magis quam causaliter se habeat ad Pharaonis creationem et obstinationem.
paras.en: On these words of Rabbi Paul I say that the words of St Thomas, taken according to Thomas's own meaning, are truly and in a catholic sense brought forward. For the holy Doctor set down those words in the Secunda Secundæ, question 85 [in present editions question 83, article 2], in answering the question whether it is fitting to pray. And he declares that it is, notwithstanding the unchangeableness of God's providence, because God foresaw and preordained that he would give grace and salvation to men through their prayers and certain acts of theirs. Hence Thomas asserts there: We must pray, not in order to bend God or to change the divine disposition, but that by praying we may obtain what God has determined to give or to do through prayer. So it is clear that Thomas means to speak of good acts, not of sinful ones: namely, that they have the nature of causes directly with respect to the effects disposed by God. And so Rabbi Paul does not seem to apply Thomas's words rightly to prove his point, namely that in the order of divine providence the obstinacy or malice of Pharao has the nature of a cause with respect to the manifestation of God's might. For if it were so, it would seem to follow that Pharao's malice was intended by God, and that God was not only the permissive but also the effective or direct cause of that malice, since God intends and brings about that through which his providence is directly and causally fulfilled. Nor does the Gloss seem to be on Rabbi Paul's side, since the Gloss brings in the words of Augustine, who says: The Lord knows how to make good use of evils, yet he does not create human nature for malice. From these words it is proved that the showing of God's might through Pharao's malice stands to Pharao's creation and hardening consecutively rather than causally.

paras.t: Ecce pluam cras hac ipsa hora, non eadem numero, quum hora sit de numero successivorum, sed eadem in specie, grandinem multam nimis, qualis non fuit in Ægypto a die qua fundata est, usque in præsens, id est nunquam hucusque: quod fuit valde mirabile. Ægyptus namque est versus meridiem in parte australi, in qua calor plus viget: idcirco raro fit ibi grando et in modica quantitate, quum ex grandi frigore grando gignatur. Tunc autem fuit ibi grando tantæ magnitudinis ac multitudinis, quod nec in partibus borealibus seu aquilonalibus sic fieri solet, quum tamen ibidem frigus magis abundet.
paras.en: [[9:18|Behold I will cause it to rain to morrow at this same hour|Ecce pluam cras hac ipsa hora]], not the same in number, since an hour belongs to things that are successive [that is, things that pass and do not return], but the same in kind, [[9:18|an exceeding great hail; such as hath not been in Egypt from the day that it was founded, until this present|grandinem multam nimis, qualis non fuit in Ægypto a die qua fundata est, usque in præsens]], that is, never until now: which was a great wonder. For Egypt lies towards the south, in the southern region, where heat is stronger; therefore hail seldom falls there, and in small quantity, since hail is produced by great cold. But then there was hail there of such size and abundance as does not usually fall even in the northern regions, though cold is more abundant there.

paras.t: Mitte ergo jam nunc, etc. Deus in ira sua non continet misericordiam suam, sed rigori justitiæ miscet dulcorem clementiæ. Ideo admonuit Pharaonem, et in eo ejus ministros ac populum, ut servos suos ac pecora non permitterent esse in agro die quo grando erat casura.
paras.en: [[9:19|Send therefore now presently|Mitte ergo jam nunc]], etc. God in his anger does not shut up his mercy[[Ps 76:10||]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxvi, 10; the words echo Ps 76:10], but mingles the sweetness of clemency with the rigour of justice. Therefore he warned Pharao, and in him his ministers and people, not to let their servants and cattle be in the field on the day the hail was to fall.

paras.t: Qui timuit verbum Domini de servis Pharaonis, fecit confugere servos suos et jumenta in domos, id est, servi Pharaonis ac ceteri Ægyptii, ad quos comminatio Dei facta per Moysen venit, et qui crediderunt, ac servili timore et formidine timuerunt eam implendam, non permiserunt servos suos et pecora esse in agris. Qui autem neglexit sermonem Domini, id est, verba Dei prolata per Moysen sprevit, nec credidit, dimisit servos suos et jumenta in agris. Interdum enim servi et pecora quædam die ac nocte manserunt in campis et pascuis tempore ad hoc apto.
