paras.en: [[13:5|And when the Lord shall have brought thee into|Quumque introduxerit te Dominus in]] [[13:5|a land that floweth with milk and honey|terram fluentem lacte et melle]], that is, shall have incorporated thee into Christ and into his mystical body, which is the Church of the elect, in which there is an abundance of spiritual food; or shall have brought thee to holy religion; or shall have given thee a body wholly subject to reason: [[13:5|thou shalt celebrate this manner of sacred rites|celebrabis hunc morem sacrorum]], that is, thou shalt keep the Pasch spiritually, and receive Christ in the Sacrament with true preparation.

paras.t: Primogenitum asini mutabis ove. Per asinum insensata simplicitas et hebetudo atque stoliditas denotatur: per ovem, innocentia et simplicitas bona. Itaque primogenitum asini mutamus ove, quando primordia humanæ stultitiæ et inconsiderationem propriorum periculorum abjicimus, et veram puritatem innocentiamque amplectimur. Nisi enim conversi fuerimus et effecti ut parvuli, non intrabimus regnum cœlorum. Malam ergo et asininam simplicitatem mutemus in simplicitatem columbinam, innocentiamque ovinam, ut simus prudentes sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbæ. Unde hortatur et summus Apostolus: Quasi modo geniti infantes rationabiles, sine dolo, lac concupiscite. Quod si non redemeris, interficies: id est, si tam perfecte te emendare nequiveris, saltem reproba confitere, et vita pristinas tuas iniquitates. Omne autem primogenitum hominis de filiis tuis, pretio redimes: id est, opera tua præcipua rationabilia, ex tuo intellectu et voluntate nascentia, virtute et merito pretiosissimi sanguinis Christi seu passionis ipsius, non propriis viribus, de manu et rabie hostium tuæ salutis, inviolata custodire conaberis.
paras.en: [[13:13|The firstborn of an ass thou shalt change for a sheep|Primogenitum asini mutabis ove]]. By the ass is denoted senseless simplicity, dullness and stupidity; by the sheep, innocence and good simplicity. So we change the firstborn of an ass for a sheep when we cast away the beginnings of human folly and heedlessness of our own dangers, and embrace true purity and innocence. For [[Matt 18:3|unless you be converted, and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven|Nisi enim conversi fuerimus et effecti ut parvuli, non intrabimus regnum cœlorum]] [Denis puts this in the first person: "unless we be converted and become as little children, we shall not enter"]. Let us therefore change the bad simplicity of the ass into the simplicity of the dove and the innocence of the sheep, that we may be [[Matt 10:16|wise as serpents and simple as doves|prudentes sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbæ]]. Hence the chief Apostle also exhorts us: [[1 Pet 2:2|As newborn babes, desire the rational milk without guile|Quasi modo geniti infantes rationabiles, sine dolo, lac concupiscite]] [Denis reads *infantes rationabiles*, "rational babes", where the Vulgate has *rationabile … lac*, "rational milk"]. [[13:13|and if thou do not redeem it, thou shalt kill it|Quod si non redemeris, interficies]]: that is, if thou canst not amend thyself so perfectly, at least confess thy reprobate deeds, and shun thy former iniquities. [[13:13|And every firstborn of men thou shalt redeem with a price|Omne autem primogenitum hominis de filiis tuis, pretio redimes]]: that is, thou shalt strive to keep thy chief rational works, born of thy intellect and will, unharmed from the hand and the fury of the enemies of thy salvation, by the power and merit of the most precious blood of Christ, that is, of his passion, not by thy own strength.

paras.t: Igitur quum emisisset Pharao populum, non eos duxit Dominus per viam terræ Philistiim, etc. Per hoc significatum est, quod Deus noviter conversos in suæ exordio conversionis frequenter custodit a gravioribus tentamentis, et pie ac dulciter tractat eos, ne victi succumbant, atque ad pristina redeant mala. Quum vero fuerint in virtutibus exercitati, spiritualibus præliis et gravioribus tentationibus eos impugnari permittit.
paras.en: [[13:17|And when Pharao had sent out the people, the Lord led them not by the way of the land of the Philistines|Igitur quum emisisset Pharao populum, non eos duxit Dominus per viam terræ Philistiim]], etc. By this it was signified that God often guards those newly converted, at the beginning of their conversion, from the heavier temptations, and treats them kindly and gently, lest they be overcome and give way, and go back to their former evils. But when they have been exercised in the virtues, he permits them to be assailed by spiritual battles and heavier temptations.

paras.t: Et armati ascenderunt filii Israel de Ægypto. Hoc impletur in nobis, quando per veram contritionem spiritualibus implemur charismatibus Spiritus Sancti, armatura virtutum, opulentia meritorum: sicque ad excelsa tendimus internorum profectuum ac evangelicæ perfectionis. Tunc Dominus nos præcedit, et viam salutis ostendit per diem, puta in prosperis, per columnam nubis, id est per refrigerationem et irrigationem supernæ illuminationis et unctionis: atque in nocte, videlicet in adversis, per columnam ignis, hoc est per terrorem divini judicii, itemque infernalis incendii, quorum consideratione in adversis patientiam observamus, nec iter virtutum relinquimus. De horum tamen significatione infra plenius disseretur.
paras.en: [[13:18|and the children of Israel went up armed|Et armati ascenderunt filii Israel]] out of Egypt. This is fulfilled in us when, through true contrition, we are filled with the spiritual gifts of the Holy Ghost, with the armour of the virtues and a wealth of merits; and so we press on towards the heights of inward progress and of evangelical perfection. Then the Lord goes before us and shows the way of salvation: by day, that is, in prosperity, by [[13:21|a pillar of a cloud|columnam nubis]], that is, by the refreshment and watering of heavenly illumination and unction; and by night, that is, in adversity, by [[13:21|a pillar of fire|columnam ignis]], that is, by the terror of the divine judgment, and likewise of the fire of hell, by the thought of which we keep patience in adversity and do not forsake the way of the virtues. But what these signify will be treated more fully below.

14.title: Expositio litteralis capituli quartidecimi: Locutus est autem Dominus ad Moysen, dicens: Loquere filiis Israel
14.title_en: Literal exposition of the fourteenth chapter: And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel

paras.t: Capitulum istud describit, qualiter Pharao cum omni suo exercitu filios Israel persequendo penitus periit. Locutus est autem Dominus ad Moysen, dicens : Loquere filiis Israel, Reversi castrametentur e regione Phihahiroth : id est, hoc præcipe eis, ut paululum redeant versus Ægyptum, et castra seu tentoria sua collocent ex opposito loci, qui Phihahiroth nuncupatur, qui est inter Magdalum et mare contra Beelsephon, id est, qui locus situs est inter urbem nomine Magdalum, constitutam in Ægypti confinio, ad quam confugerunt Judæi tempore Jeremiæ prophetæ Godolia occiso, et inter locum Beelsephon dictum. In conspectu ejus castra ponetis super mare, hoc est, in loco præfato evidenter ponetis turmas vestras ac papiliones circa littus maris Rubri : quatenus Ægyptii mox venturi, putarent eos deviare a recto itinere, et esse in tali loco, quod manus suas non valerent evadere. Denique mare Rubrum in duos sinus seu per duo loca dividitur : unus sinus seu fundus est ab oriente, et Persicus appellatur, quoniam Persæ oram ejus inhabitant ; alter Arabicus dicitur.
paras.en: This chapter describes how Pharao, with all his army, perished utterly while pursuing the children of Israel. [[14:1|And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying|Locutus est autem Dominus ad Moysen, dicens]]: [[14:2|Speak to the children of Israel: Let them turn and encamp over against Phihahiroth|Loquere filiis Israel, Reversi castrametentur e regione Phihahiroth]]: that is, command them this, that they turn back a little toward Egypt and pitch their camp or tents opposite the place that is called Phihahiroth, [[14:2|which is between Magdal and the sea over against Beelsephon|qui est inter Magdalum et mare contra Beelsephon]]: that is, which place lies between the city named Magdal, set on the border of Egypt, to which the Jews fled in the time of the prophet Jeremias, after Godolias had been slain[[Jer 44:1||]], and the place called Beelsephon. [[14:2|you shall encamp before it upon the sea|In conspectu ejus castra ponetis super mare]], that is, in the aforesaid place you shall set your companies and pavilions in open view about the shore of the Red Sea, so that the Egyptians, who were soon to come, might think that they had strayed from the right road and were in such a place that they could not escape their hands. Further, the Red Sea is divided into two gulfs, or at two places: one gulf or basin lies to the east and is called the Persian, since the Persians dwell on its shore; the other is called the Arabian.

paras.t: Dicturusque est Pharao super filiis Israel : Coarctati sunt in terra, conclusit eos desertum : id est, Pharao cognito per exploratores et nuntios suos, quod filii Israel in loco prædicto consisterent, dicet de eis ad populum suum : Jam constituti sunt in tali loco, in terra et solitudine in qua sunt, quod evadere nequeunt ; quia (ut Josephus refert) ex una eorum parte erant asperrimi et immeabiles montes, ex alia mare Rubrum, nec patuit eis fuga, nisi per viam per quam Pharao fuit contra eos venturus. Et indurabo cor ejus, ac persequetur vos, id est, permittam eum sic indurari et excæcari, quod dolebit de hoc quod permisit vos egredi suam terram, et quasi oblitus præteritarum plagarum, insequetur vos, non attendens nec metuens potentiam atque justitiam Dei quas toties est expertus : et glorificabor in Pharaone et in omni exercitu ejus, id est, per justam ejus et suorum punitionem et submersionem, meam potentiam ac justitiam tam sublimiter declarabo, quod omnibus innotescent, et famosus ero ac gloriosus reputabor ubique. Unde supra Dominus dixit ad Pharaonem : Idcirco posui te, ut ostendam in te fortitudinem meam, et narretur nomen meum in omni terra. Scientque Ægyptii quia ego sum Dominus. Pharao namque et ejus exercitus per experientiam propriæ punitionis hoc cognoverunt, et qui in Ægypto remanserant, hoc noverunt ex mirabilibus quæ Deus tunc in mari Rubro exercuit. Verumtamen Ægyptiorum cognitio, qua Dei eminentiam dominiumque noverunt, informis fuit et imperfecta, quantum ad eos qui se non emendaverunt ex ea.
paras.en: [[14:3|And Pharao will say of the children of Israel: They are straitened in the land, the desert hath shut them in|Dicturusque est Pharao super filiis Israel : Coarctati sunt in terra, conclusit eos desertum]]: that is, when Pharao has learned through his scouts and messengers that the children of Israel have halted in the aforesaid place, he will say of them to his people: Now they are set in such a place, in the land and wilderness where they are, that they cannot escape; for (as Josephus relates) on one side of them were very rugged and impassable mountains, on the other the Red Sea, and no way of flight lay open to them except by the road by which Pharao was to come against them. [[14:4|And I shall harden his heart and he will pursue you|Et indurabo cor ejus, ac persequetur vos]], that is, I will permit him to be so hardened and blinded that he will be sorry he let you leave his land, and, as though forgetting the past plagues, he will pursue you, neither heeding nor fearing the power and justice of God which he has so many times experienced: [[14:4|and I shall be glorified in Pharao, and in all his army|et glorificabor in Pharaone et in omni exercitu ejus]], that is, by the just punishment and drowning of him and his men I will show forth my power and justice so loftily that they will become known to all, and I shall be famous and reputed glorious everywhere. Hence the Lord said above to Pharao: [[Ex 9:16|therefore have I raised thee, that I may shew my power in thee, and my name may be spoken of throughout all the earth|Idcirco posui te, ut ostendam in te fortitudinem meam, et narretur nomen meum in omni terra]]. [[14:4|and the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord|Scientque Ægyptii quia ego sum Dominus]]. For Pharao and his army came to know this by the experience of their own punishment, and those who had stayed behind in Egypt learned it from the wonders which God then worked at the Red Sea. Yet the knowledge of the Egyptians, by which they came to know God's pre-eminence and lordship, was unformed [informis: like faith not given life by charity, a knowledge that does not change the heart] and imperfect, as regards those who did not amend themselves by it.

paras.t: Feceruntque ita. Et nuntiatum est regi Ægyptiorum quod fugisset populus. Jam ante sciebat populum Hebræorum exisse de terra sua, sed eos redituros putabat, dum expleto trium dierum itinere sacrificassent. Nunc autem percepit a nuntiis suis, qui iter et processum Israelitarum exploraverunt, quod ipsi Israelitæ non disposuerunt se ad redeundum post viam trium dierum, sed quod processerunt ulterius, ideoque proponerent omnino recedere : quod fugam esse reputaverunt Ægyptii. Immutatumque est cor Pharaonis et servorum ejus super populo, id est, propositum mutaverunt, et quos egredi compulerunt, nunc ad redeundum cogere cogitabant. Et dixerunt ad invicem: Quid volumus facere, ut dimitteremus Israel, ne serviret nobis? quasi dicant, In hoc stulte fecimus; nam et signa præhabita adscripserunt (secundum Josephum) veneficiis Moysis. Junxit ergo currum, id est, proprium suum currum jussit parari sibi, et omnem populum suum, id est quosdam de singulis, assumpsit secum. In Scholastica historia fertur: Assumpsit secum quinquaginta millia equitum, et ducenta millia peditum. Tulitque sexcentos currus electos, et quidquid in Ægypto currum fuit et duces exercitus. Secundum Josephum, accepit secum proprios currus trecentos, et totidem ab Ægyptiis. Et quod ait, Quidquid currum in Ægypto fuit, intelligendum est de electis seu elegantibus curribus, qui in bellicis solent negotiis deservire, et quos expedite quivit acquirere. Et si quæratur, qualiter habebat tot equos, patet responsio ex prædictis. Non enim omnia Ægyptiorum animalia erant grandine interfecta, sed quæ erant in agris relicta.
paras.en: [[14:4|And they did so|Feceruntque ita]]. [[14:5|And it was told the king of the Egyptians that the people was fled|Et nuntiatum est regi Ægyptiorum quod fugisset populus]]. He knew already before that the people of the Hebrews had gone out of his land, but he thought they would return when they had made their three days' journey and offered sacrifice. But now he learned from his messengers, who had spied out the route and progress of the Israelites, that the Israelites had not prepared themselves to return after the three days' journey, but had gone on further, and so meant to depart altogether: and this the Egyptians reckoned to be flight. [[14:5|and the heart of Pharao and of his servants was changed with regard to the people|Immutatumque est cor Pharaonis et servorum ejus super populo]], that is, they changed their purpose, and those whom they had driven to go out they now thought to force to return. [[14:5|and they said|Et dixerunt]] to one another: [[14:5|What meant we to do, that we let Israel go from serving us?|Quid volumus facere, ut dimitteremus Israel, ne serviret nobis?]] As if to say: In this we acted foolishly; for (according to Josephus) they even put down the signs that had gone before to the sorceries of Moses. [[14:6|So he made ready his chariot|Junxit ergo currum]], that is, he had his own chariot made ready for him, [[14:6|and took all his people|et omnem populum suum]], that is, some from every part, [[14:6|with him|assumpsit secum]]. In the Scholastic History it is said: He took with him fifty thousand horsemen and two hundred thousand footmen. [[14:7|And he took six hundred chosen chariots, and all the chariots that were in Egypt: and the captains of the whole army|Tulitque sexcentos currus electos, et quidquid in Ægypto currum fuit et duces exercitus]]. According to Josephus, he took with him three hundred chariots of his own, and as many from the Egyptians. And where it says, [[14:7|all the chariots that were in Egypt|Quidquid currum in Ægypto fuit]], this is to be understood of the choice or fine chariots that are used in the business of war, and which he could readily get hold of. And if it is asked how he had so many horses, the answer is plain from what was said before: for not all the beasts of the Egyptians had been killed by the hail, but only those left in the fields.

paras.t: Quumque persequerentur Ægyptii vestigia præcedentium, scilicet Hebræorum, quorum etiam vestigia in locis arenosis potuerunt faciliter apparere, repererunt, id est a longe viderunt, eos esse in castris, id est casulis suis, super mare. Nondum tamen attigerunt Hebræos: propter quod subditur: Omnis equitatus et currus Pharaonis et universus exercitus ejus erat in Phihahiroth contra, id est ex opposito, Beelsephon: de quibus locis jam dictum est. Quumque appropinquasset Pharao, levantes filii Israel oculos, viderunt Ægyptios post se, et timuerunt valde: quoniam rudes erant et imperfecti, non habentes perfectam fidem et spem in Deo, qui toties pugnavit pro eis, et adjutorium suum eis promisit. Atque (ut Josephus addit) erat luctus et gemitus mulierum et infantium, quasi habentium ante oculos mortem, nec evadere potentium. Clamaveruntque ad Dominum, invocando ejus auxilium, quia aliqualiter speraverunt in eo; sed quam modice, constat ex eo quod subditur: et dixerunt ad Moysen aspernanter atque iracunde et increpatorie: Forsitan non erant sepulcra, id est apta loca pro sepultura, in Ægypto, et ideo tulisti, id est de Ægypto exire fecisti, nos, ut moreremur in solitudine, etc., hoc est, ut nunc in deserto hoc ab Ægyptiis occidamur.
paras.en: [[14:9|And when the Egyptians followed the steps of them who were gone before|Quumque persequerentur Ægyptii vestigia præcedentium]], namely of the Hebrews, whose footprints, too, could easily show in the sandy places, [[14:9|they found|repererunt]], that is, they saw from afar, [[14:9|them encamped|eos esse in castris]], that is, in their huts, [[14:9|at the sea side|super mare]]. Yet they had not yet reached the Hebrews; and so it is added: [[14:9|all Pharao's horse and chariots and the whole army were in Phihahiroth, before|Omnis equitatus et currus Pharaonis et universus exercitus ejus erat in Phihahiroth contra]], that is, opposite, [[14:9|Beelsephon|Beelsephon]]: places of which we have already spoken. [[14:10|And when Pharao drew near, the children of Israel lifting up their eyes, saw the Egyptians behind them: and they feared exceedingly|Quumque appropinquasset Pharao, levantes filii Israel oculos, viderunt Ægyptios post se, et timuerunt valde]]: because they were rude and imperfect, not having perfect faith and hope in God, who had so often fought for them and had promised them His help. And (as Josephus adds) there was mourning and wailing of the women and children, as of those who had death before their eyes and could not escape. [[14:10|and cried to the Lord|Clamaveruntque ad Dominum]], calling on His help, because they hoped in Him in some measure; but how little is clear from what follows: [[14:11|And they said to Moses|et dixerunt ad Moysen]], scornfully, angrily and reproachfully: [[14:11|Perhaps there were no graves|Forsitan non erant sepulcra]], that is, places fit for burial, [[14:11|in Egypt, therefore thou hast brought|in Ægypto, et ideo tulisti]], that is, made to go out of Egypt, [[14:11|us to die in the wilderness|nos, ut moreremur in solitudine]], etc., that is, so that we may now be slain by the Egyptians in this desert.

paras.t: Sed cur tantum timuerunt Hebræi, quum essent plus quam in duplo, imo quasi in triplo plures Ægyptiis illis? Respondetur, quod non erant ita periti ad bella sicut Ægyptii, nec equitibus putabant se posse resistere, atque (ut in historiis addit Magister) erant inermes. Nec obstat quod præcedenti habetur capitulo, quod ascenderunt armati: quia secundum probabiliorem expositionem, hoc intelligitur de divitiis Ægyptiorum quas asportabant, non armis proprie dictis. Vel ideo dicuntur fuisse inermes, quia non bene erant armati.
paras.en: But why did the Hebrews fear so much, when they were more than twice, nay almost three times, as many as those Egyptians? The answer is that they were not as skilled in war as the Egyptians, nor did they think they could withstand horsemen; and (as the Master [Peter Comestor, author of the Scholastic History] adds in the Histories) they were unarmed. Nor does it stand in the way that the preceding chapter has that they [[Ex 13:18|went up armed|ascenderunt armati]] [the margin gives v. 14; the words are Ex 13:18]: for according to the more probable exposition this is understood of the riches of the Egyptians which they were carrying away, not of arms properly so called. Or else they are said to have been unarmed because they were not well armed.

paras.t: Et ait Moyses ad populum: Nolite timere Ægyptios carnali et mundano timore: state firmi in fide et spe divini auxilii, et videte magnalia Domini quæ facturus est hodie, id est, quæ facere inchoabit hac die. Non tamen die illo ante noctem fuerunt submersi Ægyptii. Sed quid Dominus fecerit illo die pro filiis Israel, paulo post subditur. Ægyptios enim quos nunc videtis, nequaquam ultra videbitis usque in sempiternum, id est, nunquam post hanc diem videbitis eos vivos in vita præsenti. Tamen die sequenti viderunt eorum cadavera. In die quoque generalis judicii poterunt resuscitatos videre. Ex hac pia et dulci responsione ostenditur mira mansuetudo ac patientia Moysis, qui ad irrationabilem, improbam et ingratam populi sibi subjecti interrogationem, imo potius redargutionem, tam benigne respondit. Siquidem dicere potuisset: Quid invehimini contra me, quasi ego proprio motu vos de Ægypto eduxerim? Dominus pugnabit pro vobis, et vos tacebitis.
paras.en: [[14:13|And Moses said to the people: Fear not|Et ait Moyses ad populum: Nolite timere]] the Egyptians with a carnal and worldly fear: [[14:13|stand|state]] firm in faith and in hope of divine help, [[14:13|and see the great wonders of the Lord, which he will do this day|et videte magnalia Domini quæ facturus est hodie]], that is, which He will begin to do this day. Yet the Egyptians were not drowned on that day before nightfall. But what the Lord did for the children of Israel on that day is added a little later. [[14:13|for the Egyptians, whom you see now, you shall see no more for ever|Ægyptios enim quos nunc videtis, nequaquam ultra videbitis usque in sempiternum]], that is, you shall never after this day see them alive in the present life. Yet on the following day they saw their corpses; and on the day of the general judgement they will be able to see them raised again. This kind and gentle answer shows the wonderful meekness and patience of Moses, who answered so graciously the unreasonable, wicked and ungrateful question, or rather reproach, of the people subject to him. For he could have said: Why do you inveigh against me, as though I had led you out of Egypt of my own motion? [[14:14|The Lord will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace|Dominus pugnabit pro vobis, et vos tacebitis]].

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen : Quid clamas ad me ? Per hoc datur intelligi, quod et Moyses clamavit ad Dominum, sed non ita sicut imperfecti Hebræi. Non enim ex animi perturbatione aut diffidentia seu inordinato timore clamavit, nec clamor ejus fuit strepitus oris, sed fervor atque devotio cordis, nec cessavit Dei auxilium invocare, quamvis sciret id mox affuturum. Nam scivit quod Deus vult per orationes obtineri, quod ipse proponit misericorditer dare. Et providentia Dei hoc continet, ut multa per Sanctorum preces adimpleantur. Sic et Christus passione instante oravit pro sui corporis glorificatione, et pro sua clarificatione, pro electorum quoque finali salvatione : quæ omnia certissime scivit futura. Nec Deus increpatorie dixit ad Moysen, Quid clamas ad me ? quia non reprehendit quod oravit, sed ex familiaritate. Quasi dicat : Tam familiaris et carus es mihi, ut non oporteat diutius te clamare, quum sim paratus te exaudire. Ideo subditur : Loquere filiis Israel ut proficiscantur usque ad ripam maris, deinde per fundum ejus siccatum. Tu autem leva virgam tuam, per quam et alia signa fecisti, et extende manum tuam super mare cum virga, et divide illud, id est, dividendum designa, et ministerialiter divide illud, quemadmodum alia signa egisti. Moyses quoque meritis suis ac precibus ad maris Rubri divisionem cooperabatur. Ut gradiantur filii Israel in medio mari per siccum, id est per arefactum fundum, in quo paulo ante aqua cucurrit.
paras.en: [[14:15|And the Lord said to Moses: Why criest thou to me?|Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen : Quid clamas ad me ?]] By this we are given to understand that Moses too cried to the Lord, but not as the imperfect Hebrews did. For he did not cry out of disturbance of mind, or distrust, or inordinate fear; nor was his cry a noise of the mouth, but the fervour and devotion of the heart; nor did he cease to call on God's help, although he knew it would soon be at hand. For he knew that God wills that what He Himself purposes in His mercy to give should be obtained by prayers; and the providence of God includes this, that many things are fulfilled through the prayers of the Saints. So too Christ, when His passion was at hand, prayed for the glorification of His body, and for His own glorifying [Denis uses two words, glorificatio and clarificatio, both 'glorification'], and also for the final salvation of the elect[[John 17:1||]]: all of which He knew most certainly would come to pass. Nor did God say reproachfully to Moses, [[14:15|Why criest thou to me?|Quid clamas ad me ?]], for He did not reprove him for praying, but spoke out of familiarity; as if to say: You are so familiar and dear to me that there is no need for you to cry any longer, since I am ready to hear you. Therefore it is added: [[14:15|Speak to the children of Israel to go forward|Loquere filiis Israel ut proficiscantur]], as far as the bank of the sea, and then through its dried bed. [[14:16|But lift thou up thy rod|Tu autem leva virgam tuam]], by which you have also done the other signs, [[14:16|and stretch forth thy hand over the sea|et extende manum tuam super mare]] with the rod, [[14:16|and divide it|et divide illud]], that is, show that it is to be divided, and divide it as a minister [ministerialiter: as God's instrument, the power being God's], just as you performed the other signs. Moses also by his merits and prayers co-operated in the dividing of the Red Sea. [[14:16|that the children of Israel may go through the midst of the sea on dry ground|Ut gradiantur filii Israel in medio mari per siccum]], that is, over the dried-up bed along which the water had run a little before.

paras.t: Tollensque se angelus Domini qui præcedebat castra Israel, quia per motum nubis et ignis præcessit et viam monstravit, abiit post eos, et cum eo pariter columna nubis : id est, angelus se ipsum ac nubem illam transtulit a loco anteriori usque post dorsa Hebræorum, ponensque se inter eos atque Ægyptios : ideo subditur : priora, scilicet loca, dimittens, post tergum Hebræorum stetit invisibiliter in aere et in nube quam rexit, inter castra Ægyptiorum et castra Israel, hoc est inter turmas seu tentoria utrorumque. Et erat nubes tenebrosa et illuminans noctem. Ex hoc apparentiam habet opinio dicentium, quod columna nubis et columna ignis eadem erat. Videtur enim in textu insinuari, quod eadem columna nubis, quam scilicet angelus tulit secum, fuit tenebrosa atque illuminans : tenebrosa videlicet in ea parte, qua respiciebat Ægyptios ; et illuminans noctem, ex parte qua versa fuit ad Hebræos. Ita ut ad se invicem toto noctis tempore accedere non valerent. Non quod Hebræi optarent ad Ægyptios ire, sed quia Ægyptii appetebant Hebræos subito obruere, et violenter reducere ; sed propter interpositæ nubis teterrimam densitatem eos adspicere et aggredi non valebant. Porro qui dicunt duas fuisse columnas, affirmant quod circa noctem adveniente columna ignis, columna nubis more solito non recessit : sed mansit versus Ægyptios, et columna ignis respexit Hebræos.
paras.en: [[14:19|And the angel of God, who went before the camp of Israel|Tollensque se angelus Domini qui præcedebat castra Israel]], for by the movement of the cloud and the fire he went before them and showed the way, [[14:19|removing, went behind them|abiit post eos]], [[14:19|and together with him the pillar of the cloud|et cum eo pariter columna nubis]]: that is, the angel moved himself and that cloud from the place in front to behind the backs of the Hebrews, setting himself between them and the Egyptians; therefore it is added: [[14:19|leaving the forepart|priora]], that is, the places in front, [[14:20|stood behind|post tergum Hebræorum stetit]] the Hebrews, invisibly, in the air and in the cloud which he guided, [[14:20|between the Egyptians' camp and the camp of Israel|inter castra Ægyptiorum et castra Israel]], that is, between the companies or tents of both. [[14:20|and it was a dark cloud, and enlightening the night|Et erat nubes tenebrosa et illuminans noctem]]. From this the opinion of those who say that the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire were the same has some likelihood. For the text seems to suggest that the same pillar of cloud, namely the one the angel took with him, was both dark and enlightening: dark on the side that faced the Egyptians, and enlightening the night on the side that was turned toward the Hebrews. [[14:20|so that they could not come at one another all the night|Ita ut ad se invicem toto noctis tempore accedere non valerent]]. Not that the Hebrews wished to go to the Egyptians; but the Egyptians longed to overwhelm the Hebrews suddenly and bring them back by force, and because of the utterly black density of the cloud set between they could neither see them nor attack them. Those, however, who say that there were two pillars maintain that when the pillar of fire came on toward night, the pillar of cloud did not withdraw as usual, but stayed facing the Egyptians, while the pillar of fire faced the Hebrews.

paras.t: Cumque extendisset Moyses manum cum virga super mare, abstulit illud Dominus, id est, aquas a fundo abstraxit et ab invicem separavit, flante vento vehementi et urente tota nocte : qui ventus non divisit mare : imo vento illo incipiente, divisæ sunt aquæ, post quarum divisionem mansit flans ventus, et suo impetu ac calore desiccans terram fundi, super quam aqua paulo ante cucurrit. Ideo subditur : et vertit in siccum : non quod aqua fuit siccata, quum humiditas inseparabilis sit ab aqua, sicut calor ab igne ; sed fundum prius humidum, vertit in siccum, ne si maneret lutosus et mollis, esset ad perambulandum ineptus.
paras.en: [[14:21|And when Moses had stretched forth his hand|Cumque extendisset Moyses manum]] with the rod [[14:21|over the sea, the Lord took it away|super mare, abstulit illud Dominus]], that is, He drew the waters away from the bed and parted them from each other, [[14:21|by a strong and burning wind blowing all the night|flante vento vehementi et urente tota nocte]]. This wind did not divide the sea; rather, as that wind began, the waters were divided, and after they were divided the wind went on blowing, and by its force and heat dried the ground of the bed over which the water had run a little before. Therefore it is added: [[14:21|and turned it into dry ground|et vertit in siccum]]: not that the water was dried, since moistness is inseparable from water, as heat is from fire; but the bed, moist before, He turned into dry ground, lest, if it stayed muddy and soft, it should be unfit to walk across.

paras.t: Divisaque est aqua. Dicunt nonnulli, quod universi Hebræi per eamdem divisionem et viam divisi maris incesserunt, Moysen ducem sequentes : sicque divisa fuisset aqua in duas partes dumtaxat, inter quas una via apparuit. Probabile namque videtur, quod omnes tribus elegerunt viam incedere, in qua Moysen cernebant præcedere, et quod per alias vias formidassent intrare. Et ista est Hebræorum et multorum Catholicorum positio, quam et in expositione libri Psalmorum magis secutus sum. Alii dicunt, quod facta sunt ibi duodecim divisiones ac viæ, unicuique tribui una ; et quod singulæ tribus per singulas vias, seu unaquæque per suam ingressæ sunt. Unde Origenes circa hæc scribit : Audivi a majoribus traditum, quod in ista digressione maris, singulis tribubus Israel singulæ divisiones sunt factæ. Quod ostenditur ex eo quod scriptum est, Qui divisit mare Rubrum in divisiones : per quod plures divisiones docentur factæ ; atque per illud : Ibi Benjamin junior in stupore, princeps Juda duces eorum, principes Zabulon et principes Nephthali. Idem tenet Cassiodorus super illud, Qui divisit mare Rubrum in divisiones. Magister quoque in historiis. Verumtamen illa auctoritas, quæ magis videtur esse pro eis, sic potest intelligi : Qui divisit mare Rubrum in divisiones, id est in duas partes a se invicem divisas. Alii dicunt, quod ibi ponitur plurale pro singulari, quemadmodum in Genesi, ubi dicitur : Filii Dan, quum tamen Dan non nisi unum habuerit filium.
paras.en: [[14:21|and the water was divided|Divisaque est aqua]]. Some say that all the Hebrews went forward by one and the same division and way through the divided sea, following Moses their leader; and so the water would have been divided into two parts only, between which one way appeared. For it seems probable that all the tribes chose to go by the way in which they saw Moses go before them, and that they would have been afraid to enter by other ways. And this is the position of the Hebrews and of many Catholics, which I also chiefly followed in the exposition of the book of Psalms. Others say that twelve divisions and ways were made there, one for each tribe, and that the tribes entered each by its own way, every one by its own. Hence Origen writes on this: I have heard it handed down from the elders that in this parting of the sea a division was made for each of the tribes of Israel. This is shown from what is written: [[Ps 135:13|Who divided the Red Sea into parts|Qui divisit mare Rubrum in divisiones]] [Latin in divisiones, 'into divisions'], by which many divisions are taught to have been made; and by this: [[Ps 67:28|There is Benjamin a youth, in ecstasy of mind. The princes of Juda are their leaders: the princes of Zabulon, the princes of Nephthali|Ibi Benjamin junior in stupore, princeps Juda duces eorum, principes Zabulon et principes Nephthali]] [Denis's text reads 'Benjamin the younger, in amazement; the prince of Juda, their leaders']. Cassiodorus holds the same on the verse, [[Ps 135:13|Who divided the Red Sea into parts|Qui divisit mare Rubrum in divisiones]]; so too the Master in the Histories. Yet that authority which seems most to be in their favour can be understood thus: [[Ps 135:13|Who divided the Red Sea into parts|Qui divisit mare Rubrum in divisiones]], that is, into two parts divided from each other. Others say that the plural is put there for the singular, as in Genesis, where it says: [[Gen 46:23|The sons of Dan|Filii Dan]], though Dan had only one son.

paras.t: Et ingressi sunt filii Israel per medium sicci maris, id est per medium terræ siccatæ super quam cucurrerat aqua. Erat enim aqua quasi murus a dextra eorum et læva. Nempe si frigus potest aquæ soliditatem et immobilitatem influere, ut patet in glacie : quanto magis omnipotentia Creatoris, cui omnis creatura ad nutum obedit per ingenitam obedientialem potentiam ? Persequentesque Ægyptii, ingressi sunt post eos. Quod fuit excæcatio admiranda, et stulta ac impetuosa audacia, quia eorum ratio fuit prorsus obtenebrata.
paras.en: [[14:22|And the children of Israel went in through the midst of the sea dried up|Et ingressi sunt filii Israel per medium sicci maris]], that is, through the midst of the dried land over which the water had run. [[14:22|for the water was as a wall on their right hand and on their left|Erat enim aqua quasi murus a dextra eorum et læva]]. For indeed, if cold can give water solidity and immobility, as is plain in ice, how much more can the almighty power of the Creator, whom every creature obeys at His nod by the obediential potency [that is, a creature's capacity to be raised by God to what lies beyond its natural powers] implanted in it? [[14:23|And the Egyptians pursuing went in after them|Persequentesque Ægyptii, ingressi sunt post eos]]. This was an astonishing blindness, and a foolish and headlong boldness, because their reason was utterly darkened.

paras.t: Circa hæc in Scholastica recitatur historia : Divisum est mare in duodecim divisiones, ut quæque tribus per turmas suas incederet. Et advocans Moyses singulas tribus secundum ordinem nativitatis earum, hortabatur eas ut ipsum præeuntem sequerentur. Quumque Ruben, Simeon et Levi renuissent intrare, tribus Juda primo aggressa est iter post Moysen, per quod me[rue]runt regnum. Ægyptii vero videntes quod Hebræi ingressi essent per mare, reputabant eos vesanos ; sed quum viderent illæsos abire, ingressi sunt post eos.
paras.en: On this the Scholastic History relates: The sea was divided into twelve divisions, so that each tribe might go forward by its own companies. And Moses, calling the tribes one by one in the order of their birth, urged them to follow him as he went before. And when Ruben, Simeon and Levi refused to enter, the tribe of Juda first set out on the way after Moses, by which they merited the kingship. But the Egyptians, seeing that the Hebrews had gone into the sea, thought them mad; but when they saw them going on unharmed, they went in after them.

paras.t: Jamque advenerat vigilia matutina, in qua filii Israel jam pervenerunt ad littus. Ægyptii autem adhuc erant in medio maris siccati : et ecce respiciens Dominus supra castra, id est exercitus, Ægyptiorum, erant enim in illo totali exercitu turmæ distinctæ ac plures, subjectæ diversis ducibus belli : per columnam ignis et nubis. Iste respectus, fuit respectus justæ ac rigidæ ultionis : quia ex illa columna descenderunt super Ægyptios fulgura atque tonitrua ; imo (sicut ex Josepho Magister in historiis protestatur) intolerabiles imbres et graves tonitruos, coruscationes et lampades injecit Dominus super eos, ex quibus etiam multi occidebantur. Idcirco subjungitur : interfecit exercitum eorum, et subvertit rotas curruum, ferebanturque in profundum. Ceciderunt enim præcipites : Dixerunt ergo Ægyptii nondum occisi, neque adhuc ita præcipitati : Fugiamus Israelem, Dominus enim, cui nullus resistere valet, pugnat pro eis contra nos. Prædicta autem angelico fiebant obsequio.
paras.en: [[14:24|And now the morning watch was come|Jamque advenerat vigilia matutina]], in which the children of Israel had already reached the shore, while the Egyptians were still in the midst of the dried sea: [[14:24|and behold the Lord looking upon|et ecce respiciens Dominus supra]] the camp, that is, the army, of the Egyptians [castra Ægyptiorum, which the Douay-Rheims renders 'the Egyptian army'] (for in that whole army there were many distinct companies, under different captains of war), [[14:24|through the pillar of fire and of the cloud|per columnam ignis et nubis]]. This look was a look of just and stern vengeance: for from that pillar lightnings and thunders came down upon the Egyptians; indeed (as the Master testifies in the Histories, from Josephus) the Lord cast upon them unbearable rains and heavy thunders, flashes and fiery bolts, by which many were even killed. Therefore it is added: [[14:24|slew their host|interfecit exercitum eorum]], [[14:25|and overthrew the wheels of the chariots, and they were carried into the deep|et subvertit rotas curruum, ferebanturque in profundum]]; for they fell headlong. [[14:25|And the Egyptians said|Dixerunt ergo Ægyptii]], those not yet slain nor yet so cast down: [[14:25|Let us flee from Israel|Fugiamus Israelem]]; [[14:25|for the Lord|Dominus enim]], whom none can resist[[Esth 13:9||]], [[14:25|fighteth for them against us|pugnat pro eis contra nos]]. Now the things aforesaid were done by the service of angels.

paras.t: Et ait Dominus ad Moysen : Extende manum tuam cum virga super mare, ut revertantur aquæ ad Ægyptios super currus et equites eorum. Quumque extendisset Moyses manum contra mare, reversum est primo diluculo ad priorem locum. Fugientibusque Ægyptiis occurrerunt aquæ, etc., et operuerunt currus et equites cuncti exercitus Pharaonis, etc., in quo etiam pedites multo velocius fuerunt aquis operti.
paras.en: [[14:26|And the Lord said to Moses: Stretch forth thy hand|Et ait Dominus ad Moysen : Extende manum tuam]] with the rod [[14:26|over the sea, that the waters may come again upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots and horsemen|super mare, ut revertantur aquæ ad Ægyptios super currus et equites eorum]]. [[14:27|And when Moses had stretched forth his hand towards the sea, it returned at the first break of day to the former place|Quumque extendisset Moyses manum contra mare, reversum est primo diluculo ad priorem locum]]. [[14:27|and as the Egyptians were fleeing away, the waters came upon them|Fugientibusque Ægyptiis occurrerunt aquæ]], etc., [[14:28|and covered the chariots and the horsemen of all the army of Pharao|et operuerunt currus et equites cuncti exercitus Pharaonis]], etc.; and in this the footmen too were covered by the waters much more swiftly.

paras.t: Circa hoc scribit quidam : Ægyptii ex timore ita erant turbati et stupefacti, quod non currebant ad littus, sed magis contra aquas supervenientes. Quod non videtur idonee dictum. Aquæ enim maris divisi, stabant a littore per quod ingressi fuerunt Hebræi, usque ad locum quo exierunt, per modum murorum consolidatæ et fixæ usque ad exitum Hebræorum. Quibus egressis, cœperunt aquæ ex utraque parte a littore per totum spatium factæ divisionis, ad fundum recidere et deorsum confluere, sicque occurrerunt Ægyptiis, etiam si ad littus confugere conabantur.
paras.en: On this a certain writer says: The Egyptians were so disturbed and stunned with fear that they did not run toward the shore, but rather against the waters coming upon them. This does not seem fitly said. For the waters of the divided sea stood, from the shore by which the Hebrews went in as far as the place where they came out, made firm and fixed like walls until the Hebrews came out. When they had gone out, the waters began, on both sides, from the shore along the whole space of the division that had been made, to fall back to the bottom and flow together downward; and so they met the Egyptians, even if they were trying to flee to the shore.

paras.t: Et viderunt filii Israel Ægyptios mortuos super littus maris : mare namque ejecit corpora submersorum : et manum magnam, id est potentem effectum seu ultionem, quam exercuerat Dominus contra eos.
paras.en: [[14:31|And they saw|Et viderunt]], namely the children of Israel, [[14:31|the Egyptians dead upon the sea shore|Ægyptios mortuos super littus maris]]: for the sea cast up the bodies of the drowned: [[14:31|and the mighty hand|et manum magnam]], that is, the mighty working, or vengeance, [[14:31|that the Lord had used against them|quam exercuerat Dominus contra eos]].

paras.t: Circa hæc asserit Josephus, quod filii Israel incesserunt per fundum maris usque ad littus oppositum, ita quod pertransierunt spatium maris per latum. Porro Hebræi et multi Catholici dicunt oppositum, affirmantes quod quum Hebræi venissent ad extremum montis porrecti in mare, per longam maris viam obliquaverunt montem circumeundo, et ita ad idem littus Ægypti redierunt. Quod probant, quia natura maris est, corpora extincta ad proximum littus ejicere. Quum ergo mane jacerent corpora Ægyptiorum in eodem littore, in quo scilicet exierunt Hebræi, patet quod idem erat littus ex altera montis parte situm. Mare quoque ibidem est latitudinis tantæ, quod nec Hebræi neque Ægyptii spatio noctis unius tunc fere æquinoctialis, usque ad maris medium transcurrissent. Et nisi corpora Ægyptiorum fuissent projecta ad littus in quo exierunt Hebræi, non potuissent ea videre ex opposita ripa propter distantiam. Insuper in Numeris legitur, quod filii Israel post transitum maris Rubri fuerunt in deserto Etham, et in illo fuerunt ante transitum maris Rubri. Fuitque illud desertum in extremitate solitudinis versus Ægyptum, puta ad littus ex parte Ægypti, ut patuit capitulo præcedenti. His quoque concordare videtur quod asserit Origenes : Jubetur Moyses virga percutere mare, ut ingredienti populo Dei dehiscat et cedat. Cogitur fluctus in tumulum, et unda in semetipsam repressa, curvatur. Ex quibus videtur, quod maris divisio instar semicirculi ivit ac rediit ad idem littus, tamen ultra montem præfatum. Videtur quoque probabile, quod Ægyptii sint submersi non remote a littore quo intrabant. Non enim nisi ante aliquantulam lucem diei ingressi sunt. Mare autem primo diluculo ad pristinum rediit locum, ut in isto habetur capitulo.
paras.en: On this Josephus asserts that the children of Israel went along the bed of the sea as far as the opposite shore, so that they crossed the expanse of the sea in its breadth. But the Hebrews and many Catholics say the opposite, maintaining that when the Hebrews had come to the end of a mountain that stretched out into the sea, they slanted round the mountain by a long way through the sea, going about it, and so came back to the same shore of Egypt. This they prove because it is the nature of the sea to cast dead bodies up on the nearest shore. Since, then, in the morning the bodies of the Egyptians lay on the same shore, namely the one on which the Hebrews came out, it is plain that it was the same shore, lying on the other side of the mountain. Moreover the sea there is so broad that neither the Hebrews nor the Egyptians, in the space of one night, at that time near the equinox, could have run across as far as the middle of the sea. And unless the bodies of the Egyptians had been thrown up on the shore on which the Hebrews came out, they could not have seen them from the opposite bank because of the distance. Besides, we read in Numbers that after the crossing of the Red Sea the children of Israel were in the desert of Etham[[Num 33:8||]], and that they had been in it before the crossing of the Red Sea[[Num 33:6||]]. And that desert was at the edge of the wilderness[[Ex 13:20||]] toward Egypt, that is, on the shore on the side of Egypt, as was seen in the preceding chapter. With these, too, what Origen asserts seems to agree: Moses is bidden to strike the sea with the rod, so that it may open and give way to the people of God as they enter. The flood is driven into a heap, and the wave, pressed back upon itself, is bent. From which it seems that the division of the sea went out and came back like a half-circle to the same shore, though beyond the aforesaid mountain. It seems probable too that the Egyptians were drowned not far from the shore by which they went in; for they did not go in until a little before daylight, and the sea returned to its former place at the first break of day, as is had in this chapter.

paras.t: Idcirco quod quidam scribit, ex textu non haberi quod Ægyptii fuerunt propinquiores lateri uni, quam alteri, quando aqua irruit super eos, stare non potest ; nec valet argumentum ejusdem, quo arguit pro Josephi opinione quam sequitur : quoniam in sequenti capitulo legitur, Tulit Moyses Israel de mari Rubro, et ingressi sunt in desertum Sur. Nam ubi nos habemus, desertum Sur, Hebræus textus habet, desertum Etham, ut Magister in historiis dicit, et suo loco dicetur. Rursus, quod idem ait, desertum Etham, de quo in Numeris legitur, esse aliud ab eo, de quo fertur præcedenti capitulo, improbat Rabbi Paulus, quia sic unum illorum fuisset citra mare Rubrum, et aliud ultra : quod non habetur ex littera ; sed textus planius sonat, quod idem sit. Nec inde consequitur, quod Deus reduxit Hebræos ad terram Ægyptiorum, ut arguit quidam : quoniam mare Rubrum fuit propinquum Ægypto, quia Hebræi quamvis fessi et onerati, in tribus diebus pervenerunt ad illud ; et extendebatur usque ad terram promissionis, terminando eamdem secundum plagam orientalem, ut infra legitur. Sicque filii Israel transeundo per littus maris, secundum longitudinem ejus, ab Ægypto semper elongabantur. Unde totum illud, exsistens citra et prope mare Rubrum, est unum magnum desertum, cujus pars quædam est desertum Sur, circa quod exierunt Hebræi. Hæc Rabbi Paulus.
paras.en: Therefore what a certain writer [apparently Lyra, whom Rabbi Paul answers here] says, that it is not had from the text that the Egyptians were nearer to one side than to the other when the water rushed upon them, cannot stand; nor does the argument hold by which he argues for the opinion of Josephus, which he follows: namely that in the following chapter we read, [[Ex 15:22|And Moses brought Israel from the Red Sea, and they went forth into the wilderness of Sur|Tulit Moyses Israel de mari Rubro, et ingressi sunt in desertum Sur]]. For where we have 'the desert of Sur', the Hebrew text has 'the desert of Etham', as the Master says in the Histories, and as will be said in its place. Again, what the same writer says, that the desert of Etham of which we read in Numbers[[Num 33:6||]][[Num 33:8||]] is other than the one spoken of in the preceding chapter[[Ex 13:20||]], Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, whose Additions to Lyra Denis often cites] disproves, because in that case one of them would have been on this side of the Red Sea and the other beyond it, which is not had from the letter; rather, the text more plainly sounds as though it were the same. Nor does it follow from this that God led the Hebrews back to the land of the Egyptians, as someone argues: for the Red Sea was near Egypt, since the Hebrews, though weary and laden, reached it in three days; and it stretched as far as the land of promise, bounding it on the eastern side, as we read below[[Ex 23:31||]] [the margin gives 'Ibid. xxxiii, 31'; the passage meant seems to be Ex 23:31]. And so the children of Israel, going along the shore of the sea lengthwise, were ever drawing farther away from Egypt. Hence all that region, lying on this side of and near the Red Sea, is one great desert, a certain part of which is the desert of Sur, near which the Hebrews came out. Thus far Rabbi Paul.

paras.t: Timuitque populus Hebræorum Dominum, cujus potentiam atque justitiam in Ægyptiorum demersione, et maris Rubri divisione consideraverunt. Et quidam eorum timuerunt Deum servili, alii initiali, alii filiali timore. Et crediderunt Domino, et Moysi servo ejus, quia divina promissa in sua liberatione et Ægyptiorum plagatione viderunt impleta. Detraxerunt quoque arma Ægyptiorum ad littus ejectorum, quæ (ut dicitur) pretiosiora fuerunt, quam cetera quæ ab Ægyptiis accommodaverunt.
paras.en: [[14:31|and the people|Timuitque populus]] of the Hebrews [[14:31|feared the Lord|Dominum]], whose power and justice they had beheld in the drowning of the Egyptians and the dividing of the Red Sea. And some of them feared God with a servile fear, others with an initial fear, others with a filial fear [the three kinds of fear of the schoolmen: servile, for dread of punishment; initial, mixed with the beginning of charity; filial, out of love]. [[14:31|and they believed the Lord, and Moses his servant|Et crediderunt Domino, et Moysi servo ejus]], because they saw the divine promises fulfilled in their own deliverance and in the plaguing of the Egyptians. They also stripped off the arms of the Egyptians cast up on the shore, which (as is said) were more precious than the other things they had borrowed from the Egyptians.

paras.t: Circa hæc Josephus ait: Nemo discredat factum esse istud miraculum, dum et eis qui cum Alexandro rege Macedonum fuerunt, Pamphylicum mare divisum sit, et iter præbuit eis, quum ipsis aliud iter non esset, volente Deo per eos destruere principatum Persarum. Hoc testantur omnes qui actus Alexandri conscripserunt.
paras.en: On this Josephus says: Let no one disbelieve that this miracle took place, since for those too who were with Alexander, king of the Macedonians, the Pamphylian sea was divided and afforded them a way when they had no other way, God willing to destroy the empire of the Persians through them. All who have written the deeds of Alexander bear witness to this.

14.title: De spirituali ejusdem capituli quartidecimi intellectu
14.title_en: On the spiritual sense of the same fourteenth chapter

paras.t: Locutus est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens: Loquere filiis Israel: Reversi castrametentur, etc. Per Pharaonem et ejus exercitum, designatur princeps tenebrarum cum satellitibus suis: per filios Israel, populus christianus: per Moysen, Christus, seu quicumque fidelis prælatus Christi vicarius. Itaque per hoc quod Deus per Moysen jussit filiis Israel, ut redirent versus mare Rubrum, dum eos insecuturus fuit Pharao cum populo suo: figuratum est, quod Deus per prælatos ac prædicatores denuntiat Christifidelibus, ne penitus fugiant a campo et exercitio spiritualis militiæ contra aciem vitiorum ac dæmonum, dum invisibiles hostes insequuntur ipsos fideles ad tentandum, sed opponant se eis. Et super mare, id est super fidem gratiamque in Baptismo collatam, se fundent ac figant, imo et super contritionis confessionisque sacramentum et lacrimas pœnitentiæ salutaris: quæ omnia per mare Rubrum signantur.
paras.en: [[14:1|And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying|Locutus est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens]]: [[14:2|Speak to the children of Israel: Let them turn and encamp|Loquere filiis Israel: Reversi castrametentur]], etc. By Pharao and his army is signified the prince of darkness with his attendants; by the children of Israel, the Christian people; by Moses, Christ, or any faithful prelate who is the vicar of Christ. And so, by God's commanding the children of Israel through Moses to go back toward the Red Sea, when Pharao was about to pursue them with his people, it was figured that God, through prelates and preachers, warns the faithful of Christ not to flee altogether from the field and exercise of spiritual warfare against the battle line of vices and demons when the invisible enemies pursue the faithful themselves to tempt them, but to set themselves against them. And let them ground and fix themselves [[14:2|upon the sea|super mare]], that is, upon the faith and the grace conferred in Baptism, and indeed upon the sacrament of contrition and confession and the tears of saving penance: all of which are signified by the Red Sea.

paras.t: Dicturus est Pharao super filiis Israel: Coarctati sunt in terra, conclusit eos desertum. Sic invisibiles hostes dum vident fideles terrenis occupationibus aut peccatis carnalibus detineri, et deserto concludi, id est, fragili carne, in qua non habitat bonum, circumdari, æstimant eos suarum rabiem tentationum non posse evadere: sed cum ingenti præsumptione eos impugnant, qui jam per gratiam Dei reliquerunt Ægyptum, utpote vitiorum et errorum caligines.
paras.en: [[14:3|And Pharao will say of the children of Israel: They are straitened in the land, the desert hath shut them in|Dicturus est Pharao super filiis Israel: Coarctati sunt in terra, conclusit eos desertum]]. So the invisible enemies, when they see the faithful held fast by earthly occupations or carnal sins, and shut in by the desert, that is, hemmed in by the frail flesh, in which no good dwells, reckon that they cannot escape the fury of their temptations; and so with enormous presumption they assail those who by the grace of God have already left Egypt, that is, the darkness of vices and errors.

paras.t: Interdum autem contingit, quod fideles adhuc pusilli, videntes sibi imminere graves tentationes ac persecutiones pro justitia, quodammodo doleant se viam apprehendisse justitiæ, et eis per quos conversi sunt, indignentur, dicentes: Forsitan non erant sepulcra in Ægypto, et ideo tulisti nos, ut moreremur in solitudine. Quasi dicant: Nonne in sæculari et pristina vita manendo, poteramus satis cito devenire ad mortem? Cur ergo, inde nos retraxisti, ut tentationibus et persecutionibus obruamur, atque in hac arcta vita et pœnitentiali horrore, deficiamus sine humano ac divino solatio? Isti sunt penitus imperfecti, qui ad tempus credunt, et in hora tentationis recedunt, in tantum, ut melius arbitrentur servire Ægyptiis, hoc est carnalibus vitiis vanitatibusque mundanis, quam mori in solitudine, id est, quam pro justitia gravia pati, et in abstractione ac rigore pœnitentiæ quasi in solitudine vitam finire.
paras.en: Sometimes, however, it happens that the faithful who are still little ones, seeing grievous temptations and persecutions for justice' sake hanging over them, in a manner grieve that they have taken up the way of justice, and are indignant with those by whom they were converted, saying: [[14:11|Perhaps there were no graves in Egypt, therefore thou hast brought us to die in the wilderness|Forsitan non erant sepulcra in Ægypto, et ideo tulisti nos, ut moreremur in solitudine]]. As if they said: By staying in our former worldly life, could we not have come to death soon enough? Why then didst thou draw us away from it, that we should be overwhelmed by temptations and persecutions, and in this strait life and the harshness of penance waste away without human or divine comfort? These are the wholly imperfect, who [[Luke 8:13|believe for a while|ad tempus credunt]], [[Luke 8:13|and in time of temptation they fall away|et in hora tentationis recedunt]], so much so that they judge it better to [[14:12|serve the Egyptians|servire Ægyptiis]], that is, carnal vices and worldly vanities, [[14:12|than to die in the wilderness|quam mori in solitudine]], that is, than to suffer grievous things for justice, and to end their life in withdrawal from the world and the rigour of penance, as in a wilderness.

paras.t: Quibus bonus prælatus seu exhortator virtuosus respondet: Nolite timere, inordinata pusillanimique formidine: state per fidem et perseverantiam boni incepti; et videte magnalia Domini, quæ facturus est hodie, hoc est, sapienter pensate, quam gloriose atque magnifice Deus protinus vobis succurret, dummodo sincere confidatis in eo, implorando eum assidue cum omni affectu. Tunc enim sic conteret Satanam sub pedibus vestris, ut Ægyptios, utpote dæmones tentatores, quorum infestationem nunc graviter fertis, prorsus vincatis, ita ut nunquam de cetero eos conspiciatis taliter sicut modo. Dominus pugnabit pro vobis, et vos tacebitis. Vere enim Deus adversarios nostræ salutis expugnat: idcirco non debemus nos inaniter jactare aut reputare, dum tentationibus prævalemus, sed silere humiliter, et gratias Deo referre.
paras.en: To these a good prelate or virtuous exhorter answers: [[14:13|Fear not|Nolite timere]] with an inordinate and faint-hearted dread; [[14:13|stand|state]] by faith and by perseverance in the good you have begun; [[14:13|and see the great wonders of the Lord, which he will do this day|et videte magnalia Domini, quæ facturus est hodie]]: that is, consider wisely how gloriously and magnificently God will presently come to your help, provided you trust in him sincerely, imploring him constantly with all your heart. For then he will so [[Rom 16:20|crush Satan under your feet|conteret Satanam sub pedibus vestris]] that you will utterly overcome the Egyptians, that is, the tempting demons, whose assaults you now bear so heavily, so that you will never again see them as you see them now. [[14:14|The Lord will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace|Dominus pugnabit pro vobis, et vos tacebitis]]. For truly it is God who overcomes the adversaries of our salvation: therefore we ought not to boast vainly or think much of ourselves when we prevail over temptations, but keep silence humbly and give thanks to God.

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen: Quid clamas ad me? Saluberrime ad Deum clamamus, dum cum omni cordis recollectione et sensuum attentione oramus, dum divinæ pietatis subsidia ardenter optamus, dum ad cœlestia suspiramus. Quod dum agimus, consolatur nos Deus, inspirando quod orationes hujusmodi et sanctæ affectiones exaudiantur ab ipso.
paras.en: [[14:15|And the Lord said to Moses: Why criest thou to me?|Dixitque Dominus ad Moysen: Quid clamas ad me?]] Most wholesomely do we cry to God when we pray with all recollection of heart and attention of the senses, when we ardently long for the help of the divine goodness, when we sigh for heavenly things. And when we do this, God consoles us, breathing into us the assurance that such prayers and holy affections are heard by him.

paras.t: Præcipit quoque Dominus bono prælato, ut filiis Israel, utpote ovibus Christi sibi commissis, dicat, quatenus proficiscantur tendendo ad patriam Beatorum per profectum virtutum. Tu autem, o præsulate prædicator, eleva virgam tuam, hoc est, evangelicæ legis doctrinam exalta ac fortiter prædica, et extende manum tuam super mare, et divide illud, id est, virtutem tui sermonis applica ad declarandum fidelibus efficaciam sacramentorum Baptismi et Confessionis, quorum gratiam cunctis paratam esse doceas tempore opportuno, per quorum virtutem et gratiam prævalent et salvantur electi. Quumque ministri tenebrarum insequuntur fideles, susceptioni Baptismatis aut Pœnitentiæ actibus sacris intentos, superantur ac pereunt virtute sacramentorum evangelicæ legis: per quæ omnia glorificatur Altissimus.
paras.en: The Lord also commands the good prelate to tell the children of Israel, that is, the sheep of Christ entrusted to him, [[14:15|to go forward|proficiscantur]], making their way to the fatherland of the Blessed by progress in the virtues. [[14:16|But|Tu autem]], O preacher set over others, [[14:16|lift thou up thy rod|eleva virgam tuam]], that is, exalt the doctrine of the Gospel law and preach it boldly, [[14:16|and stretch forth thy hand over the sea, and divide it|et extende manum tuam super mare, et divide illud]], that is, apply the power of thy word to declaring to the faithful the efficacy of the sacraments of Baptism and Confession, and teach that their grace is ready for all at the fitting time; for by their power and grace the elect prevail and are saved. And when the ministers of darkness pursue the faithful who are intent on receiving Baptism or on the sacred acts of Penance, they are overcome and perish by the power of the sacraments of the Gospel law: and through all this the Most High is glorified.

paras.t: Præterea, sicut angelus cum columna nubis se posuit inter Ægyptios et Hebræos; sic angeli singuli, qui custodes sunt animarum nostrarum, scientes quanta sit dæmonum astutia atque ferocia, quanta item sit insufficientia nostra, interponunt se quasi fidelissimos muros inter illos et nos, reprimendo malignitatem illorum. Ponunt quoque columnam nubis inter illos et nos, quia auxilium gratiæ et protectionis divinæ impetrant nobis: quæ gratia sive protectio, est dæmonibus tenebrosa, nec eam æquanimiter inspicere queunt, sed per invidiam potius pejorantur, seu contabescunt de ea. Nec pro libito suo nos possunt accedere propter interposita ista subsidia.
paras.en: Moreover, as the angel with the pillar of the cloud placed himself between the Egyptians and the Hebrews, so the angels, one to each of us, who are the guardians of our souls, knowing how great is the cunning and fierceness of the demons, and how great likewise is our insufficiency, put themselves between them and us like most faithful walls, holding back their malice. They also set the pillar of the cloud between them and us, since they obtain for us the help of divine grace and protection; and this grace or protection is dark to the demons: they cannot look upon it with composure, but are rather made worse by envy, or waste away over it. Nor can they come at us as they please, because of these helps set between.

paras.t: Denique in vigilia matutina, qua Deo in mentis fervore et contemplationis sinceritate adstamus, respicit Dominus super adversarios nostros. Et sicut Pharao cum universis sibi adjunctis in Rubro periit mari, ita in Baptismo, Christi sanguine consecrato, itemque in Pœnitentiæ sacramento a Christi passione efficaciam suam sortito, pereunt invisibiles adversarii et vincuntur, cum universis tentamentis ac vitiis, ad quæ nos pertrahere enituntur.
paras.en: Lastly, in the [[14:24|morning watch|vigilia matutina]], in which we stand before God in fervour of mind and purity of contemplation, the Lord looks upon our adversaries. And as Pharao with all who were joined to him perished in the Red Sea, so in Baptism, consecrated by the blood of Christ, and likewise in the sacrament of Penance, which has received its efficacy from the passion of Christ, the invisible adversaries perish and are overcome, together with all the temptations and vices to which they strive to drag us.

paras.t: Frequenter quoque, dum cernunt quod tam gratiosissime adjuvamur a Domino, ad fugam se cohortantur, dicentes: Fugiamus Israelem, Dominus enim pugnat pro eis contra nos. Quandoque vero rursus sic indurantur, quod de novo præsumunt eos impugnare, a quibus dejecti sunt: sicut de Christo ait Evangelista, quod consummata omni tentatione, diabolus recessit ab eo ad tempus: per quod insinuatur, quod postea rediit. Idcirco oportet nos jugiter esse custoditos, sollicitos, spiritualiterque armatos.
paras.en: Often too, when they see how very graciously we are helped by the Lord, they urge one another to flight, saying: [[14:25|Let us flee from Israel; for the Lord fighteth for them against us|Fugiamus Israelem, Dominus enim pugnat pro eis contra nos]]. But at times they are hardened again, so that they presume to assail anew those by whom they were cast down: as the Evangelist says of Christ that, [[Luke 4:13|all the temptation being ended, the devil departed from him for a time|consummata omni tentatione, diabolus recessit ab eo ad tempus]]: by which it is hinted that he came back afterwards. Therefore we must at all times be on our guard, watchful, and spiritually armed.

15.title: Elucidatio capituli quintidecimi: Tunc cecinit Moyses et filii Israel carmen hoc Domino
15.title_en: Explanation of the fifteenth chapter: Then Moses and the children of Israel sung this canticle to the Lord

paras.t: Consuetudo fuit sanctis viris, imo et feminis virtuosis, spiritualia cantica Deo offerre atque componere, pro specialibus beneficiis Dei, et de magnificis ac supernaturalibus ejus operibus. Quod in veteri Testamento potissime servabatur, atque a Moyse initium sumpsisse videtur. Non enim legitur hoc factum ab aliquo ante eum. Hinc loquitur Origenes: Multa legimus cantica facta in divinis Scripturis. Horum tamen omnium primum est istud. Moris quippe Sanctorum est, ubi adversarius vincitur, hymnum congratulationis Deo offerre. In Scholastica quoque fertur historia: Moyses composuit canticum Domino hexametro carmine, quod quia ceteris prius legitur factum, dicitur Canticum canticorum. Quod intelligendum est propter prærogativam antiquitatis. Verumtamen ob mysticorum sensuum profunditatem et elegantiam, dialogus ille amoris a Salomone compositus, canticorum Canticum appellatur.
paras.en: It was the custom of holy men, and indeed of virtuous women too, to compose spiritual canticles and offer them to God for His particular benefits, and about His magnificent and supernatural works. This was observed above all in the Old Testament, and seems to have taken its beginning from Moses: for we do not read that anyone did this before him. Hence Origen says: We read of many canticles made in the divine Scriptures; but of them all this is the first. For it is the custom of the Saints, when the adversary is overcome, to offer God a hymn of thanksgiving. In the Scholastic History, too, it is related: Moses composed a canticle to the Lord in hexameter verse, which, because we read that it was made before the others, is called the Canticle of canticles. This is to be understood by the privilege of antiquity. Yet, for the depth and beauty of its mystical senses, the dialogue of love composed by Solomon is called the Canticle of canticles.

paras.t: Tunc, videlicet Pharaone Ægyptiisque submersis, cecinit Moyses et filii Israel carmen hoc Domino, et dixerunt. Moyses, Spiritu Sancto illuminante ac dirigente, edidit carmen, deinde docuit hoc filios Israel: sicque pariter cecinerunt, et se invicem ad regratiandum Deo, et ad ejus decantanda præconia, hortabantur ac invitabant, dicentes: Cantemus Domino, id est, ad ejus honorem depromamus laudes ipsius; gloriose enim magnificatus est, id est, excellentiam, omnipotentiam atque justitiam suam præclare monstravit, et famam magnificam sibi fecit per signa et mirabilia quæ contra Ægyptios egit, et nunc præcipue in maris Rubri divisione, Ægyptiorum submersione, et nostra eductione ac liberatione. In quibus omnibus suam quoque pietatem et fidelissimam veritatem declaravit in nobis. Equum et ascensorem dejecit in mare, id est, equites Pharaonis simul cum ipso eorum rege, et toto ejus exercitu, ac quadrigis eorum præcipitavit ac mersit in mari Rubro, per modum in præcedenti capitulo recitatum.
paras.en: [[15:1|Then|Tunc]], that is, when Pharao and the Egyptians had been drowned, [[15:1|Moses and the children of Israel sung this canticle to the Lord, and said|cecinit Moyses et filii Israel carmen hoc Domino, et dixerunt]]. Moses, by the light and guidance of the Holy Ghost, composed the canticle and then taught it to the children of Israel; and so they sang it together, and exhorted and invited one another to give thanks to God and to sing out His praises, saying: [[15:1|Let us sing to the Lord|Cantemus Domino]], that is, let us bring forth His praises to His honour; [[15:1|for he is gloriously magnified|gloriose enim magnificatus est]], that is, He has splendidly shown forth His excellence, almighty power and justice, and has made Himself a magnificent name by the signs and wonders which He wrought against the Egyptians, and now above all in the dividing of the Red Sea, the drowning of the Egyptians, and our leading out and deliverance. In all of which He has also shown in us His loving-kindness and most faithful truth. [[15:1|the horse and the rider he hath thrown into the sea|Equum et ascensorem dejecit in mare]], that is, He has hurled down and sunk in the Red Sea Pharao's horsemen together with their king himself and his whole army, and their chariots, in the manner related in the preceding chapter.

paras.t: Fortitudo mea et laus mea Dominus: hoc est, ipse Deus auctor horum mirabilium, est causa totius fortitudinis meæ in naturalibus atque fortuitis, cujus auxilio contra Pharaonem prævalui. Ipse quoque est laus mea, id est objectum ac materia laudum mearum, quibus eum in se ipso et in suis operibus laudo, non me ipsum. Ex ejus quoque judiciis, signis, effectibusque præclaris materiam habeo copiosam laudis divinæ; imo et si aliquid laude dignum in me est, hujus causa est ipse. Unde circa hæc, Fortitudo mea et laus mea Dominus, ait Glossa, Quia per ipsum fortis sum et laudabilis. Itaque Moyses, quum tot et tanta per eum Dominus perpetrasset, et vir eximius esset coram omni frequentia populi, noluit tamen in se ipso laudari, nec voluit commendare se ipsum, sed Dominum, cui adscribendum noverat esse omne bonum. Sic et sacratissima virgo Maria, quum Mater esset Altissimi facta, non se ipsam, sed Dominum glorificavit, dicendo: Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Et Psalmista: In Domino, inquit, laudabitur anima mea. Et factus est mihi in salutem, hoc est, potenter et gratiose salvavit me de manu Pharaonis, aliisque periculis. Moysi autem tanquam duci populi, instabat speciale periculum ex Pharaonis tyrannide, nisi Deus eum eripuisset: idcirco hæc singulariter loquitur et decantat, quum tamen fuerint communia beneficia Dei, sibi ac Hebræis collata. Nam et hoc ad servum Deo specialiter gratum, devotum, fidelemque pertinet, ut de generalibus beneficiis Creatoris, speciales laudes et grates referat Domino, quasi sint sibi soli condonata ab illo. Itaque Deus in se ipso invariabilis, æternus et non factus dicitur nobis fieri in salutem, seu refugium ac salvator, absque suæ deitatis mutatione: quando per gratiarum suarum charismata et effectus, subsidium et salutem nobis impendit.
paras.en: [[15:2|The Lord is my strength and my praise|Fortitudo mea et laus mea Dominus]]: that is, God Himself, the author of these wonders, is the cause of all my strength, in natural things and in what befalls by chance, by whose help I have prevailed against Pharao. He is also my praise, that is, the object and matter of my praises, with which I praise Him, in Himself and in His works, and not myself. From His judgments, too, His signs and His glorious effects, I have abundant matter for the praise of God; indeed, if there is anything praiseworthy in me, He is the cause of it. Hence on these words, [[15:2|The Lord is my strength and my praise|Fortitudo mea et laus mea Dominus]], the Gloss says: Because through Him I am strong and praiseworthy. So Moses, though the Lord had wrought so many and such great things through him, and he was a man eminent before the whole throng of the people, yet would not be praised in himself, nor commend himself, but the Lord, to whom he knew all good must be ascribed. So too the most holy Virgin Mary, when she had been made Mother of the Most High, glorified not herself but the Lord, saying: [[Luke 1:46|My soul doth magnify the Lord|Magnificat anima mea Dominum]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 33:3|In the Lord|In Domino]], he says, [[Ps 33:3|shall my soul be praised|laudabitur anima mea]]. [[15:2|and he is become salvation to me|Et factus est mihi in salutem]], that is, He has saved me mightily and graciously from the hand of Pharao and from other dangers. For a particular danger threatened Moses, as leader of the people, from the tyranny of Pharao, had God not delivered him: therefore he says and sings these things in the singular, though they were benefits of God common to all, bestowed on himself and on the Hebrews. For this too belongs to a servant especially pleasing to God, devout and faithful: that for the general benefits of the Creator he should render particular praises and thanks to the Lord, as though they had been granted to him alone. And so God, who in Himself is unchangeable, eternal and not made, is said to become salvation to us, or our refuge and saviour, without any change in His Godhead, when through the gifts and effects of His graces He bestows help and salvation on us.

paras.t: Iste, qui ita pugnavit pro filiis Israel, est Deus meus: qui quum sit universorum Deus jure creationis, gubernationis, et conservationis, specialiter tamen est Deus eorum, a quibus præcipue colitur, et ardenter amatur, et quibus ipse præcipua gratiæ dona largitur. Sicque fuit devotissimi ac sanctissimi Moysis Deus. Hunc et Elias orando locutus est: Deus meus, revertatur, obsecro, anima pueri hujus in viscera ejus. Et Paulus: Deus meus impleat omne desiderium meum in vobis. Et glorificabo eum, id est, gloriosum ac famosum, et omni gloria et honore dignum esse eum fatebor, describam, et opere demonstrabo, ei cum omni reverentia obsequendo. Deus patris mei: quasi Moyses dicat, Non solum ego per dona gratiæ fidelis sum, sed etiam natione, quoniam Deus verus, qui est Deus meus, fuit et est Deus patris mei. Quod tam de immediato Moysis patre, quam de quolibet sanctorum Patriarcharum, ex quibus duxit originem, accipi potest. Et exaltabo eum, id est, corde, ore, et opere per scripta testabor eum solum esse adorandum, et omnibus incomparabiliter digniorem ac altiorem. Qui solus in se ipso perfectionaliter infinitus, incircumscriptibilisque consistit, et universa infinite in omni perfectione ac claritate excedit, et omnis creati intellectus capacitatem interminabiliter superat. Itaque pronomen hoc, Iste, notat hic demonstrationem ad intellectum. Recitat tamen Lyra, quod secundum Hebræos, facit demonstrationem ad sensum. Nam dicunt, quod filii Israel transeundo per fundum maris, sensibiliter Deum videbant, atque cum digito demonstrabant: in quadam tamen similitudine sensibili assumpta, seu repræsentante, quia Deitas sensibiliter nequit videri. Dicunt quoque, quod populus ille tunc clarius vidit Deum, quam postea sancti Prophetæ. Sed istud nec probationem, nec apparentiam habet, præsertim quum populus ille fuit tam duræ cervicis.
paras.en: [[15:2|he|Iste]], who fought thus for the children of Israel, is [[15:2|my God|Deus meus]]: who, though He is the God of all things by right of creation, government and preservation, is yet in a special way the God of those by whom He is chiefly worshipped and ardently loved, and on whom He bestows the chief gifts of grace. And so He was the God of Moses, most devout and most holy. Elias too spoke to Him so in prayer: [[3 Kings 17:21|my God, let the soul of this child, I beseech thee, return into his body|Deus meus, revertatur, obsecro, anima pueri hujus in viscera ejus]] [the margin's reference is incomplete in the transcription (III. Reg. …); the words are 3 Kings 17:21]. And Paul: [[Phil 4:19|may my God supply all|Deus meus impleat omne]] my desire in you [so Denis, *desiderium meum in vobis*; the Vulgate has *desiderium vestrum*, "your want"]. [[15:2|and I will glorify him|Et glorificabo eum]], that is, I will confess, write and show by deed that He is glorious and renowned and worthy of all glory and honour, serving Him with all reverence. [[15:2|the God of my father|Deus patris mei]]: as if Moses were saying, I am of the faithful not only by the gifts of grace but also by birth, since the true God, who is my God, was and is the God of my father. This may be taken both of Moses' immediate father and of any of the holy Patriarchs from whom he took his origin. [[15:2|and I will exalt him|Et exaltabo eum]], that is, with heart, mouth and deed, and in writing, I will bear witness that He alone is to be adored, and is incomparably worthier and higher than all things: who alone in Himself is infinite in perfection and uncircumscribable, and infinitely surpasses all things in every perfection and splendour, and without limit exceeds the capacity of every created intellect. And so the pronoun *he* [Latin *iste*, "this one", a word that points] here points to Him for the understanding. Lyra, however, relates that according to the Hebrews it points to Him for the senses. For they say that the children of Israel, passing over the bottom of the sea, saw God with their senses and pointed to Him with the finger, though in a certain sensible likeness assumed for the purpose, or representing Him, since the Godhead cannot be seen by the senses. They say also that that people then saw God more clearly than the holy Prophets did afterwards. But this has neither proof nor likelihood, especially since that people was so stiff-necked.

paras.t: Dominus quasi vir pugnator, id est similis viro pugnatori, non nisi justa ac fortia prælia exercenti. Alibi autem dicit Lyra, quod in Hebræo non habetur, Quasi: sed translator hoc addidit, ad insinuandum quod Deus dicitur vir pugnator, non quod in eo sit sexus, aut corporeum aliquid secundum deitatis naturam. Unde sic dicitur vir pugnator, quomodo ait Salvator: Ego sum vitis vera, et Pater meus agricola est. Quod secundum Augustinum intelligendum est per similitudinem, non per proprietatem. Omnipotens nomen ejus. Hoc intelligi potest tam de nomine nominante, quam de nomine nominato.
