[[15:15|trembling seized on the stout men of Moab|Robustos Moab obtinuit tremor]]. By the stout men of Moab are understood the proud, who in a special way are called, and are, children of the devil. For Moab is interpreted 'from the father'. And to such the Saviour says: [[John 8:44|You are of your father the devil|Vos ex patre diabolo estis]] [the margin's reference here is partly unreadable: Joann. …]. [[15:15|all the inhabitants of Chanaan became stiff|Obriguerunt omnes habitatores Chanaan]]. Chanaan is interpreted 'commotion'. By the inhabitants of Chanaan, therefore, are rightly understood the lustful, who in a special way are unstable of heart, vain and foolish, tossed by various passions, never sincerely raised up to God. All these, hearing the law of the Gospel preached, in which the aforesaid vices are condemned and the opposite virtues, namely sobriety, liberality, poverty, humility and chastity, are taught, commended and commanded, were angered and troubled. And when they had seen this law prevail, and the Roman empire made subject to it, they were terrified and trembled. Countless of them, too, were converted, fearing to their salvation.

paras.t: Irruat super eos formido et pavor, in magnitudine brachii tui. Hoc accipi potest in bono, ut scilicet ex consideratione excellentiæ Christi, fiant veraciter timorati. Quod si converti noluerint, desuper terreantur, ita ut electos et Christifideles a spirituali profectu ac salutis internæ itinere nequeant impedire. Idcirco subjungitur: Fiant immobiles quasi lapis, quantum ad id quod prætactum est, et ne commune impediant bonum, donec pertranseat populus tuus, Domine, videlicet populus christianus, a via atque exsilio pertingendo ad patriam supercœlestem.
paras.en: [[15:16|Let fear and dread fall upon them, in the greatness of thy arm|Irruat super eos formido et pavor, in magnitudine brachii tui]]. This can be taken in a good sense, namely that from considering the excellence of Christ they may become truly God-fearing. But if they will not be converted, let them be terrified from above, so that they cannot hinder the elect and the faithful of Christ from spiritual progress and from the journey of inward salvation. Therefore it is added: [[15:16|let them become immoveable as a stone|Fiant immobiles quasi lapis]], as regards what has just been touched on, and so that they may not hinder the common good, [[15:16|until thy people, O Lord, pass by|donec pertranseat populus tuus, Domine]], that is, the Christian people, reaching from the way and from exile to the fatherland above the heavens.

paras.t: Introduces eos, et plantabis in monte hereditatis tuæ. Hic mons est Ecclesia militans, de quo loquitur Isaias: Erit in novissimis diebus præparatus mons domus Domini in vertice montium. Et Psalmista: Mons Dei, mons pinguis, mons coagulatus, mons pinguis. Abundant enim in monte hoc opulentissima et sacratissima virtutum charismata, supernaturalia dona, in quibus radicantur electi. Firmissimo habitaculo tuo, quod operatus es, Domine. Hic etenim mons, est solidissimum habitaculum a Christo constructum, qui dixit: Super hanc petram, videlicet super me ipsum, ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, et portæ inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam. Est quoque hic mons, sanctuarium tuum, Domine, quod firmaverunt manus tuæ, quum sit spirituale templum, de quo a Zacharia prædictum est: Ipse ædificabit templum Domino.
paras.en: [[15:17|Thou shalt bring them in, and plant them in the mountain of thy inheritance|Introduces eos, et plantabis in monte hereditatis tuæ]]. This mountain is the Church militant, of which Isaias speaks: [[Is 2:2|in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of mountains|Erit in novissimis diebus præparatus mons domus Domini in vertice montium]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 67:16|The mountain of God is a fat mountain. A curdled mountain, a fat mountain|Mons Dei, mons pinguis, mons coagulatus, mons pinguis]]. For on this mountain abound the richest and most sacred gifts of the virtues [Latin charismata, gifts of grace], supernatural gifts, in which the elect are rooted. [[15:17|in thy most firm habitation, which thou hast made, O Lord|Firmissimo habitaculo tuo, quod operatus es, Domine]]. For this mountain is the most solid habitation built by Christ, who said: [[Matt 16:18|upon this rock|Super hanc petram]], that is, upon Myself, [[Matt 16:18|I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it|ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, et portæ inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam]]. This mountain is also [[15:17|thy sanctuary, O Lord, which thy hands have established|sanctuarium tuum, Domine, quod firmaverunt manus tuæ]], since it is the spiritual temple of which it was foretold by Zacharias: He [[Zach 6:12|shall build a temple to the Lord|ædificabit templum Domino]].

paras.t: Dominus Jesus Christus regnabit in æternum et ultra, sicut Gabriel archangelus Virgini præelectæ ait: Regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum, et regni ejus non erit finis. Et Isaias: Multiplicabitur ejus imperium, et pacis non erit finis.
paras.en: [[15:18|The Lord|Dominus]] Jesus Christ [[15:18|shall reign for ever and ever|regnabit in æternum et ultra]], as the archangel Gabriel said to the chosen Virgin: [[Luke 1:32|he shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever|Regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum]], [[Luke 1:33|And of his kingdom there shall be no end|et regni ejus non erit finis]]. And Isaias: [[Is 9:7|His empire shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace|Multiplicabitur ejus imperium, et pacis non erit finis]].

paras.t: Ingressus est enim eques Pharao cum curribus, etc. Istius versiculi sensus patet ex præinductis. Filii autem Israel ambulaverunt per siccum in medio ejus. Filii Israel sunt, veri Christifideles, divina atque cœlestia contemplantes. Isti in medio sæculi hujus, quod est mare turbulentum ac periculosum, de quo loquitur Isaias, Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest: in medio, inquam, hujus maris gradiuntur per siccum, dum sæculi vitiis non fœdantur, neque in aquis concupiscentiæ volutantur; sed in medio nationis pravæ et perversæ irreprehensibiliter conversantur, lucentes inter illos tanquam luminaria gratiæ, verbum vitæ in se stabiliter continentes, ac Christi vestigia imitantes, atque dicentes cum Sponsa in Canticis: Lavi pedes meos, quomodo inquinabo illos? Qui autem Ægyptius est, id est carnalis et mente mundanus, et sequitur Pharaonem, consentiendo tentamentis diaboli, fluctibus mergitur vitiorum.
paras.en: [[15:19|For Pharao went in on horseback with his chariots|Ingressus est enim eques Pharao cum curribus]], etc. The sense of this verse is clear from what has been said before. [[15:19|but the children of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst thereof|Filii autem Israel ambulaverunt per siccum in medio ejus]]. The children of Israel are the true faithful of Christ, who contemplate divine and heavenly things. These, in the midst of this world, which is a turbulent and perilous sea, of which Isaias says, [[Is 57:20|the wicked are like the raging sea, which cannot rest|Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]]: in the midst, I say, of this sea they walk on dry ground, while they are not defiled by the vices of the world nor wallow in the waters of concupiscence; but [[Phil 2:15|in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation|in medio nationis pravæ et perversæ]] they live blamelessly, shining among them as lights of grace, holding [[Phil 2:16|the word of life|verbum vitæ]] steadfastly within themselves, and following the footsteps of Christ, and saying with the Bride in the Canticle: [[Cant 5:3|I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them|Lavi pedes meos, quomodo inquinabo illos?]]? [the margin gives Cant. v, 2]. But he who is an Egyptian, that is, carnal and worldly of mind, and follows Pharao by consenting to the temptations of the devil, is drowned in the waves of vices.

15.title: Elucidatio tropologica ejusdem cantici: Cantemus Domino
15.title_en: Tropological explanation of the same canticle: Let us sing to the Lord

paras.t: Tropologicus hujus cantici intellectus, ex præhabitis faciliter elici potest: ideo non nisi breviter tangam illum.
paras.en: The tropological [that is, moral] sense of this canticle can easily be drawn from what has been said before; therefore I shall touch on it only briefly.

paras.t: Itaque per Moysen, qui per aquam mortem evasit tam in sua infantia, quam in senio suo, intelligi potest quilibet Christifidelis, qui videns se per fontem Baptismi in Christo renatum, et tam illo sacramento quam in Pœnitentia seu confessione sacramentali, de spirituali Ægypto et fluctibus sæculi hujus, de potestate diaboli, de jugo et servitute peccati, de ignorantiarum et errorum caligine erutum, cum gratiarum actione Domino psallat, aliosque ad regratiandum secum et pro se invitet, dicendo: Cantemus Domino, gloriose enim magnificatus est, animam meam taliter eruendo, ac donis gratiæ decorando, ita ut grata et humili mente dicere queam: Protexisti me, Domine, a conventu malignantium, a multitudine operantium iniquitatem. Et item: Quoniam eripuisti animam meam de morte, et pedes meos de lapsu, ut placeam coram Deo in lumine viventium. Equum et ascensorem dejecit in mare: id est, visibilem ac invisibilem meæ salutis hostem prostravit, dando mihi virtutem resistendi ac prævalendi tentationibus eorumdem.
paras.en: So by Moses, who escaped death through water both in his infancy and in his old age, may be understood any one of Christ's faithful who, seeing himself reborn in Christ through the font of Baptism, and rescued, both by that sacrament and in Penance or sacramental confession, from the spiritual Egypt and the waves of this world, from the power of the devil, from the yoke and bondage of sin, from the darkness of ignorance and errors, sings to the Lord with thanksgiving, and invites others to give thanks with him and for him, saying: [[15:1|Let us sing to the Lord: for he is gloriously magnified|Cantemus Domino, gloriose enim magnificatus est]], by rescuing my soul in this way and adorning it with the gifts of grace, so that I can say with a grateful and humble mind: [[Ps 63:3|Thou hast protected me|Protexisti me]], O Lord, [[Ps 63:3|from the assembly of the malignant; from the multitude of the workers of iniquity|a conventu malignantium, a multitudine operantium iniquitatem]]. And again: [[Ps 55:13|Because thou hast delivered my soul from death, my feet from falling: that I may please in the sight of God, in the light of the living|Quoniam eripuisti animam meam de morte, et pedes meos de lapsu, ut placeam coram Deo in lumine viventium]]. [[15:1|the horse and the rider he hath thrown into the sea|Equum et ascensorem dejecit in mare]]: that is, he has laid low the visible and the invisible enemy of my salvation, by giving me the strength to resist and to overcome their temptations.

paras.t: Fortitudo mea et laus mea Dominus, cui dicere habeo: Quoniam in te eripiar a tentatione, et in Deo meo transgrediar murum. Et denuo: Laudabo Dominum in vita mea, psallam Deo meo quamdiu fuero. Et iterum: Laudabit usque ad mortem anima mea Dominum. Absit ergo, ut propriam quæram laudem, gloriamque humanam. Et factus est mihi in salutem: quia quum toties recidivaverim, tamque enormiter ipsum offenderim, non tamen juste damnavit me, sed pro malis retribuit bona; et jam per contritionem salvavit me a morte peccati, et a via meritoque gehennæ, quum tamen multos in æternum damnaverit, qui minus peccaverunt quam ego, ita ut illud sancti regis Ezechiæ dicere valeam: Tu autem eruisti animam meam ut non periret, projecisti post tergum tuum omnia peccata mea. Iste Deus meus: qui quum sit omnium Deus, tamen tanto specialius est Deus meus, quanto gratiosius egit mecum, ita ut dicere mihi incumbat: Adjutor meus, tibi psallam, quia Deus susceptor meus es, Deus meus, misericordia mea. Et glorificabo eum: quia quo plus peccavi in eum, et quo majorem mihi misericordiam gratiamque exhibuit, eo plus teneor ei esse subjectus et gratus. Deus patris mei: Christianus sum enim, filius hominis christiani. Et exaltabo eum, ipsum præ omnibus incomparabiliter diligendo, timendo, colendo, quærendo, omnique creaturæ ipsum totis præferendo præcordiis.
paras.en: [[15:2|The Lord is my strength and my praise|Fortitudo mea et laus mea Dominus]], to whom I can say: [[Ps 17:30|For by thee I shall be delivered from temptation; and through my God I shall go over a wall|Quoniam in te eripiar a tentatione, et in Deo meo transgrediar murum]]. And once more: [[Ps 145:2|in my life I will praise the Lord: I will sing to my God as long as I shall be|Laudabo Dominum in vita mea, psallam Deo meo quamdiu fuero]]. And again: [[Ecclus 51:8|My soul shall praise the Lord even to death|Laudabit usque ad mortem anima mea Dominum]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xiv, 8; the words are Ecclus 51:8]. Far be it from me, then, to seek my own praise and the glory of men. [[15:2|and he is become salvation to me|Et factus est mihi in salutem]]: for though I have fallen back so many times, and offended him so grievously, he did not justly condemn me, but rendered good for evil; and now through contrition he has saved me from the death of sin, and from the way to hell and the desert of it, although he has condemned for ever many who sinned less than I, so that I can say that saying of the holy king Ezechias: [[Is 38:17|but thou hast delivered my soul that it should not perish, thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back|Tu autem eruisti animam meam ut non periret, projecisti post tergum tuum omnia peccata mea]]. [[15:2|he is my God|Iste Deus meus]]: for though he is the God of all, he is all the more specially my God, the more graciously he has dealt with me, so that it is fitting for me to say: [[Ps 58:18|Unto thee, O my helper, will I sing, for thou art God my defence: my God my mercy|Adjutor meus, tibi psallam, quia Deus susceptor meus es, Deus meus, misericordia mea]] [the margin gives Ps. lxviii, 18; the words are Ps 58:18]. [[15:2|and I will glorify him|Et glorificabo eum]]: for the more I have sinned against him, and the greater the mercy and grace he has shown me, the more I am bound to be subject and grateful to him. [[15:2|the God of my father|Deus patris mei]]: for I am a Christian, the son of a Christian man. [[15:2|and I will exalt him|Et exaltabo eum]], by loving, fearing, worshipping and seeking him incomparably above all things, and preferring him with my whole heart to every creature.

paras.t: Dominus quasi vir pugnator, Omnipotens nomen ejus, qui hostes animæ meæ ac vitia expugnat in me. Ex me namque perditio mea, in ipso dumtaxat auxilium meum. Nec enim sufficiens sum aliquid cogitare ex me, quasi ex me. Ab ipso plane est omnis tentationum victoria.
paras.en: [[15:3|The Lord is as a man of war, Almighty is his name|Dominus quasi vir pugnator, Omnipotens nomen ejus]], who overcomes in me the enemies of my soul and my vices. For my destruction is from myself, my help is in him alone[[Osee 13:9||]]. For I am not [[2 Cor 3:5|sufficient to think any thing|sufficiens sum aliquid cogitare]] of myself, as of myself. Clearly every victory over temptations is from him.

paras.t: Currus Pharaonis et exercitum ejus projecit in mare, id est omnes adversarios meæ salutis, ut tactum est.
paras.en: [[15:4|Pharao's chariots and his army he hath cast into the sea|Currus Pharaonis et exercitum ejus projecit in mare]], that is, all the adversaries of my salvation, as was touched on above.

paras.t: In his ergo Dextera tua, Domine, magnificata est in fortitudine. Misisti iram tuam quæ devoravit eos sicut stipulam: quia per sanctum angelum tuum, zelo justitiæ tuæ accensum, atque in manu sua gladium flammeum tenentem, repulisti frequenter invisibiles hostes meos a me.
paras.en: In these things, then, [[15:6|Thy right hand, O Lord, is magnified in strength|Dextera tua, Domine, magnificata est in fortitudine]]. [[15:7|thou hast sent thy wrath, which hath devoured them like stubble|Misisti iram tuam quæ devoravit eos sicut stipulam]]: for through thy holy angel, kindled with the zeal of thy justice and holding a flaming sword in his hand, thou hast often driven my invisible enemies away from me.

paras.t: Et in spiritu furoris tui congregatæ sunt aquæ: id est, fluctus tentationum et tribulationum, quibus me sæpius repleverunt, in ipsos redacti sunt, quia ex ipsis non profecerunt finaliter in me, sed sibimet calamitatem tristiamque auxerunt. Stetit unda fluens: id est, gratia Dei exuberans quievit in corde devoto, imo et influxum suum ab indevoto retraxit. Congregatæ sunt abyssi in medio mari. Abyssi istæ, sunt exundationes atque profluvia inanium cogitationum et affectionum carnalium, quæ in medio mari, id est corde sæculari et amaro ac turbulento, coacervantur, quousque radio illuminationis supernæ et rore gratiæ dispergantur ac refrenentur.
paras.en: [[15:8|And with the blast of thy anger the waters were gathered together|Et in spiritu furoris tui congregatæ sunt aquæ]]: that is, the waves of temptations and tribulations with which they have often filled me were turned back upon themselves, for by them they gained nothing in me in the end, but only increased their own misery and sorrow. [[15:8|the flowing water stood|Stetit unda fluens]]: that is, the overflowing grace of God has rested in the devout heart, and indeed has withdrawn its inflowing from the undevout. [[15:8|the depths were gathered together in the midst of the sea|Congregatæ sunt abyssi in medio mari]]. These depths are the overflowings and floods of empty thoughts and carnal affections, which are heaped up in the midst of the sea, that is, in a worldly, bitter and troubled heart, until they are scattered and held in check by the ray of heavenly enlightenment and the dew of grace.

paras.t: Dixit inimicus: Persequar et comprehendam. Iste est spiritus malus unicuique ad exercitium datus, qui jugiter intra se cogitat persequi ac vincere animam ejus, cui ad exercitium ac probam est deputatus, ejusque spiritualia bona auferre molitur, et bona ejus proposita, salubres conceptiones, amorosos affectus interficere et auferre conatur; sed flante Spiritu Dei, succumbit.
paras.en: [[15:9|The enemy said: I will pursue and overtake|Dixit inimicus: Persequar et comprehendam]]. This is the evil spirit given to each man for his exercise [that is, to try and train him in the struggle], who continually plans within himself to pursue and overcome the soul of the man to whose exercise and proving he has been assigned; he strives to take away his spiritual goods, and endeavours to slay and take away his good resolutions, his wholesome thoughts, his loving affections; but when the Spirit of God blows [an allusion to v. 10, Thy wind (spiritus) blew], he goes under.

paras.t: Ascenderunt populi, et irati sunt. Injusti etenim justos persequi non desistunt; et multis non sufficit damnatio propria, imo et alios damnationi secum involvere enituntur.
paras.en: [[15:14|Nations rose up, and were angry|Ascenderunt populi, et irati sunt]]. For the unjust do not cease to persecute the just; and for many their own damnation is not enough, but they strive to entangle others with themselves in damnation.

paras.t: Dolores obtinuerunt habitatores Philistiim. Tunc conturbati sunt principes Edom, robustos Moab obtinuit tremor, obriguerunt habitatores Chanaan. Homines quippe vitiosi, gulosi, avari, superbi, libidinosi, per gentes præfatas signati, ut patuit articulo præcedenti, omni interna tranquillitate privantur, et variis passionibus agitantur: nunc inordinate et stolide metuentes, nunc inaniter præsumentes, nunc illicite gloriantes, nunc culpabiliter contristati, nunc inique concupiscentes, nunc concupiscentiarum suarum incommoda intra se sentientes: qui sunt tanquam pulvis ante faciem venti, et in circuitu ambulant, quos Deus ponit ut rotam, quoniam undique evagantur, nec in Deo eorum corda figuntur. Cetera patent, nec tropologiam exigunt specialem.
paras.en: [[15:14|sorrows took hold on the inhabitants of Philisthiim|Dolores obtinuerunt habitatores Philistiim]]. [[15:15|Then were the princes of Edom troubled, trembling seized on the stout men of Moab|Tunc conturbati sunt principes Edom, robustos Moab obtinuit tremor]], [[15:15|the inhabitants of Chanaan became stiff|obriguerunt habitatores Chanaan]]. For vicious men, gluttonous, avaricious, proud and lustful, signified by the nations named, as was shown in the preceding article, are deprived of all inward peace and tossed about by various passions: now fearing inordinately and foolishly, now presuming vainly, now glorying unlawfully, now sorrowing culpably, now lusting wickedly, now feeling within themselves the troubles their lusts bring: they are [[Ps 34:5|as dust before the wind|tanquam pulvis ante faciem venti]][[Ps 1:4||]], and they [[Ps 11:9|walk round about|in circuitu ambulant]], and God makes them [[Ps 82:14|like a wheel|ut rotam]], for they wander off on every side, and their hearts are not fixed on God. The rest is plain and calls for no special tropological reading.

15.title: Prosecutio expositionis hujus capituli a loco: Sumpsit ergo Maria
15.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this chapter from the place: So Mary took

paras.t: Quoniam non solum viri, sed feminæ quoque per maris divisi fundum profectæ sunt, congruum fuit ut ipsæ gratias agerent Deo. Sumpsit ergo Maria prophetissa soror Aaron: habuit enim gratiam prophetiæ, sicut et fratres ejus. Tamen gratia illa fuit major in Moyse: et forsan etiam fuit major in Aaron, quam in Maria sorore Aaron. Quare potius hic vocatur soror Aaron, quam Moysis? Dici potest, quod gratia brevitatis solus Aaron exprimitur: vel quia senior Moyse fuit. Recitat tamen Lyra, quod Judæi reddunt super hoc aliam causam, dicentes, quod Moyse nondum nato, quando non habuit fratrem nisi Aaron, hæc Maria prophetavit suæ matri, quod paritura esset filium, qui populum Israel liberaret. Sed incertum videtur, quod in ætate illa tam puellari habuisset gratiam prophetiæ. Et si ita fuit, tamen hoc parum facit ad istud, cujus nunc causa inquiritur. Tympanum in manu sua. Tympanum enim est musicum instrumentum factum de corio extento, siccato atque firmato, quod sonum emittit percussione pellis ita extentæ. Egressæque sunt omnes mulieres post eam: nam sicut Moyses fuit eminentior inter viros, sic soror sua ob suam sanctitatem et sapientiam inter feminas; cum tympanis et choris: non quod unaquæque illarum habuerit tympanum aut chorum, sed aliquæ inter eas. Per mulieres vero etiam puellæ et virgines intelliguntur. Porro chorus nunc sumitur pro musico instrumento, quod fit ex simplici pelle duas cutes habente, per quarum unam inflatur, per aliam reddit sonum. Potest tamen chorus nunc sumi pro concordi et pacata seu recte disposita societate, quoniam feminæ taliter se habendo sequebantur Mariam.
paras.en: Since not only the men but the women also had gone forth over the bed of the divided sea, it was fitting that they too should give thanks to God. [[15:20|So Mary the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took|Sumpsit ergo Maria prophetissa soror Aaron]]: for she had the grace of prophecy, as her brothers also had. Yet that grace was greater in Moses, and perhaps it was greater in Aaron too than in Mary, the sister of Aaron. Why is she called here the sister of Aaron rather than of Moses? It can be said that Aaron alone is named for brevity's sake, or because he was older than Moses. Lyra, however, relates that the Jews give another reason for this, saying that before Moses was born, when she had no brother but Aaron, this Mary prophesied to her mother that she would bear a son who would set the people of Israel free. But it seems uncertain that at so girlish an age she would have had the grace of prophecy; and even if it was so, this does little for the point whose reason is now being sought. [[15:20|a timbrel in her hand|Tympanum in manu sua]]. For a timbrel is a musical instrument made of hide stretched, dried and made firm, which gives out a sound when the skin so stretched is struck. [[15:20|and all the women went forth after her|Egressæque sunt omnes mulieres post eam]]: for as Moses was the more eminent among the men, so was his sister among the women, for her holiness and wisdom; [[15:20|with timbrels and with dances|cum tympanis et choris]] [*choris*, from *chorus*, which Denis goes on to take first for an instrument, then for a company]: not that each one of them had a timbrel or a *chorus*, but some among them. By the women, girls and maidens are also understood. Now *chorus* is taken here for a musical instrument made of a single hide having two *cutes* [literally "skins"; apparently the two openings of the bag], through one of which it is blown, while through the other it gives out the sound. Yet *chorus* can also be taken here for a harmonious and peaceful, or rightly ordered, company, since the women, behaving in such a way, followed Mary.

paras.t: Quibus præcinebat, dicens: Cantemus Domino hymnum victoriæ, gloriose enim honorificatus est: quia per opera præinducta ostendit præclare se super omnia honorabilem esse; equum et ascensorem dejecit in mare: sicut expositum est. An autem hunc versum dumtaxat præcinebat, an et sequentes omnes, aut quosdam, præcise quis novit? Forsitan præcinebat et alios versus, sed feminæ repetebant primum versum, vel etiam alios singulatim. Itaque simul ore cantabant, et manu in musicis instrumentis ludebant, quemadmodum David consuevit cum sono citharæ vel cum psalte, canere psalmos. Sic igitur illa præcinebat, et aliæ repetebant, sicut in choreis fieri solet. Nam et Durandus in Summa sua dicit eas choros duxisse, et addit quod illa fuit bona chorea. Aliqui quoque dicunt, quod eodem modo præcinebat Moyses viris; non tamen habetur ex textu, quod cum præfatis musicis instrumentis ipse et ceteri viri cecinerunt. Consueverunt autem feminæ Hebræorum scire hujusmodi musicos ludos. Unde et primo Regum habetur, quod mulieres egressæ sunt in occursum Saul regis et David cum tympanis, etc. Quidam præterea dicunt, quod Maria hæc per spiritum prophetiæ cognovit, Deum esse taliter collaudandum in via pro beneficiis post egressum ab Ægypto præstandis: ideo tulit tympanum secum, alias quoque feminas induxit ad asportandum secum præfata musica instrumenta. Sed sive per revelationem hoc præcognovit, sive non, dici potest quod portaverunt secum hujusmodi instrumenta, sicut et alia vasa ac utensilia sua, quasi in Ægyptum non redituræ.
paras.en: [[15:21|And she began the song to them, saying: Let us sing to the Lord|Quibus præcinebat, dicens: Cantemus Domino]] a hymn of victory, [[15:21|for he is gloriously magnified|gloriose enim honorificatus est]] [Denis's text reads *honorificatus*, "honoured"; the margin gives the reading *magnificatus*, "magnified", as in the Vulgate]: because by the works related above he has shown most clearly that he is to be honoured above all things; [[15:21|the horse and his rider he hath thrown into the sea|equum et ascensorem dejecit in mare]]: as has been explained. But whether she led off only this verse, or all the following ones as well, or some of them, who knows for certain? Perhaps she led off the other verses too, while the women repeated the first verse, or the others one by one as well. And so with their mouths they sang, and at the same time with their hands they played on the musical instruments, as David was wont to sing psalms to the sound of the harp or with the psaltery[[2 Kings 6:5||]] [the margin gives II Reg. vi, without a verse; 6:5 is where David plays on harps]. So then she led off and the others repeated, as is usually done in dances. For Durandus too says in his Summa that they led dances, and adds that it was a good dance. Some also say that Moses led off for the men in the same way; yet it is not had from the text that he and the rest of the men sang with the aforesaid musical instruments. Now the women of the Hebrews were accustomed to know musical pastimes of this kind. Hence in the first book of Kings too it is recorded that [[1 Kings 18:6|the women came out|mulieres egressæ sunt]] [[1 Kings 18:6|to meet king Saul|in occursum Saul regis]] and David [[1 Kings 18:6|with timbrels|cum tympanis]], etc. Some say besides that this Mary knew by the spirit of prophecy that God was to be praised in this way on the journey for the benefits that were to be bestowed after the going out from Egypt, and so she took a timbrel with her, and induced the other women too to carry the aforesaid musical instruments with them. But whether she foreknew this by revelation or not, it can be said that they carried instruments of this kind with them, as they did their other vessels and utensils, as women who would not return into Egypt.

paras.t: Tulit autem Moyses Israel de mari Rubro, id est, filios Israel fecit inde recedere per desertum versus terram promissam. Et ait quidam, quod ideo dicitur, Tulit, quia cum quadam violentia et importunitate fecit eos inde abire, quoniam ex avaritia erant nimis intenti ad Ægyptiorum spolia detrahenda et colligenda. Sed quum filii Israel fuerint plus quam duplo plures, quam submersi Ægyptii, ut patet in expositione præcedentis capituli, potuerunt infra modicum tempus illorum colligere spolia. Imo dictum est, quod septem diebus morati sunt juxta littus maris, venientes quotidie cum tympanis et musicis instrumentis ad littus, cecineruntque Domino canticum Moysis. Ideo propter spolia detrahenda non fecerunt nimiam moram ibidem, nec in eo quod dicitur, Tulit, aliqua violentia aut importunitas denotatur. Nam et capitulo duodecimo dictum est: Tulit populus farinam conspersam. Capitulo quoque tertiodecimo: Tulit Moyses ossa Joseph. In quibus orationibus in verbo hoc, Tulit, nulla violentia aut importunitas importatur. Et ingressi sunt in desertum Sur. Quod qualiter sit intelligendum, diffuse expressum est in præcedentis elucidatione capituli.
paras.en: [[15:22|And Moses brought Israel from the Red Sea|Tulit autem Moyses Israel de mari Rubro]], that is, he made the children of Israel withdraw from there through the desert toward the promised land. And a certain writer says that "brought" [*tulit*, literally "took" or "carried off"] is said because he made them go away from there with a certain force and insistence, since out of avarice they were too intent on stripping and gathering the spoils of the Egyptians. But since the children of Israel were more than twice as many as the drowned Egyptians, as is clear in the exposition of the preceding chapter, they could gather their spoils within a short time. Indeed it has been said that they stayed seven days by the shore of the sea, coming every day to the shore with timbrels and musical instruments, and sang to the Lord the canticle of Moses. Therefore they did not make too long a stay there for stripping the spoils, nor is any force or insistence denoted by the word *tulit*. For in the twelfth chapter too it was said: [[Ex 12:34|The people therefore took dough|Tulit populus farinam conspersam]]; and in the thirteenth chapter: [[Ex 13:19|And Moses took Joseph's bones|Tulit Moyses ossa Joseph]]. In these sentences the word *tulit* implies no force or insistence. [[15:22|and they went forth into the wilderness of Sur|Et ingressi sunt in desertum Sur]]. How this is to be understood was set out at length in the explanation of the preceding chapter.

paras.t: Ambulaveruntque tribus diebus per solitudinem, sequentes nubis ducatum; et non inveniebant aquam. Nam et raro pluit ibidem. Et si fuerit ibi aqua, ex solis ardore solet siccari. Et venerunt in Marath, id est locum quem paulo post sic vocaverunt, sicut patebit: nec potuerunt bibere aquas de Marath, id est, quæ erant in loco illo, eo quod essent amaræ. Unde et congruum loco nomen imposuit, vel Moyses, vel populus, vocans illud Marath, id est amaritudinem. Sicque a qualitate imposuit nomen substantiæ. Et quod ait, Vocans illud, sic potest exponi: vocando exprimens nomen loci illius. Porro Mara et Marath, idem est nomen. Mara autem indifferenter significat amaritudinem vel amarum. Siquidem scriptum est, Ne vocetis me Noemi, id est pulchram, sed vocate me Mara, id est amaram. Magister autem in historiis dicit: Vocaverunt locum illum Marath, ab amaritudine aquæ, vel potius pro amaritudine animi sui. […] namque est sitiens, quando non invenit potum, quam dum inventum gustare non valet. Josephus vero velle videtur, quod aquæ amaritudinem contraxerunt, quia non movebantur ab aliquo, sed stabant semper immotæ. Unde et dictum: Et vitium capiunt, ni moveantur, aquæ. Dicit equidem ibi fuisse puteum parvum, in quo fuit hæc aqua, et nomine putei intelligit forsitan lacum.
paras.en: [[15:22|and they marched three days through the wilderness|Ambulaveruntque tribus diebus per solitudinem]], following the guidance of the cloud; [[15:22|and found no water|et non inveniebant aquam]]. For it seldom rains there; and if there is water there, it is usually dried up by the heat of the sun. [[15:23|And they came into Mara|Et venerunt in Marath]], that is, to the place which they so named a little later, as will appear: [[15:23|and they could not drink the waters of Mara|nec potuerunt bibere aquas de Marath]], that is, those that were in that place, [[15:23|because they were bitter|eo quod essent amaræ]]: [[15:23|whereupon he gave a name also agreeable to the place|Unde et congruum loco nomen imposuit]], either Moses or the people, [[15:23|calling it Mara, that is, bitterness|vocans illud Marath, id est amaritudinem]]. And so he gave the thing its name from its quality. And the words "calling it" can be explained thus: by calling, expressing the name of that place. Now Mara and Marath are the same name, and Mara means "bitterness" or "bitter" without distinction. For it is written: [[Ruth 1:20|Call me not Noemi (that is, beautiful,) but call me Mara (that is, bitter)|Ne vocetis me Noemi, id est pulchram, sed vocate me Mara, id est amaram]]. But the Master says in the Histories: They called that place Marath from the bitterness of the water, or rather for the bitterness of their soul. For […] thirsting when he finds no drink than when, having found it, he cannot taste it [a word or more is lost in the print here; the sense seems to be that one who thirsts suffers less when he finds no drink than when he finds it and cannot taste it]. Josephus, however, seems to hold that the waters had become bitter because they were not stirred by anything but always stood still. Hence too the saying: And waters take on a fault unless they are stirred [a line of Ovid, Letters from Pontus I, 5, 6]. He says indeed that there was a small well there in which this water was, and by "well" he perhaps understands a pool.

paras.t: Et murmuravit populus contra Moysen, dicens: Quid bibemus? In quo patet eorum perversitas, impatientia, ingratitudo, inconsideratio. Debuerunt etenim tantum prælatum, patrem, ac ducem, quem viderunt Deo tam familiarem et carum, cum omni reverentia humiliter interrogare ac alloqui, et sperare in Domino, quem viderunt tanta fecisse pro eis. Murmuraverunt itaque propter potus, non propter cibi, defectum, quia adhuc reficiebant se parce cum cibo ex Ægypto allato. Jumenta quoque eorum aquæ poculo indigebant.
paras.en: [[15:24|And the people murmured against Moses, saying: What shall we drink?|Et murmuravit populus contra Moysen, dicens: Quid bibemus?]] In this their perversity, impatience, ingratitude and thoughtlessness are plain. For they ought to have questioned and addressed so great a prelate, father and leader, whom they had seen to be so familiar with God and so dear to him, humbly and with all reverence, and to have hoped in the Lord, whom they had seen do such great things for them. So they murmured for want of drink, not of food, because they were still feeding themselves sparingly on the food brought from Egypt. Their beasts too needed water to drink.

paras.t: At ille clamavit ad Dominum, ferventer orando. Nec impatienter respondit murmuratoribus illis, sed pro malis bona retribuit: quoniam tanta debet esse prælati perfectio, ut sua bonitate et probitate, subditorum malitiam improbitatemque vincat. Verumtamen non omnes filii Israel murmuraverunt, sed vulgares et imperfectiores. Qui ostendit ei lignum. Dicunt quidam, quod in eremo illa non erat lignum crescens, sed Deus miraculose illud adduxit. Quod et Augustinus sentire videtur, ut patet in Glossa. In Scholastica quoque historia fertur: Forte miraculose factum est, ut in solitudine, in qua non erat lignum, id est arbor crescens, inveniretur lignum. Quod lignum quum Moyses misisset in aquas, in dulcedinem versæ sunt, id est, dulces atque potabiles factæ sunt. Putant aliqui, quod lignum illud fuit naturaliter dulcorativum aquarum. Ad quod illud Ecclesiastici posset allegari: Nonne a ligno indulcata est aqua amara? Et loquitur ibi illa scriptura de naturalibus et medicinalibus terræ nascentium proprietatibus. Nempe verbis illis immediate præmittitur: Altissimus de terra creavit medicinam, et vir prudens non abhorrebit illam. Tamen (ut in Scholastica recitatur historia) Hebræus dicit lignum illud amarissimum extitisse, et ideo Deum jussisse, ut illud projiceret in aquam amaram, quatenus dum ex additione amari ad amarum, fieret dulce quod fuit amarum, clariusque ostenderetur divina potentia, quia majus erat miraculum. Sed quidquid horum dicatur, constat quod Deus solo imperio poterat aquam illam dulcificare. Ideo propter aliquid mysticum designandum, Origenes et alii putant Deum illud de ligno jussisse. Circa hæc Josephus scribit: Sumens Moyses virgam quam in præsenti habebat, scidit eam in longitudinem ejus per medium, et jecit in puteum, præcepitque fortibus viris ut aquam haurirent, et plurimam haustam prius effunderent, ut ultima remanens diu concussa, potabilis fieret. Verumtamen dictum hoc Josephi non est intelligendum de Moysis virga, per quam fecerat signa, sed de ligno sibi ostenso, in quo fecit incisionem per longitudinem ejus.
paras.en: [[15:25|But he cried to the Lord|At ille clamavit ad Dominum]], praying fervently. Nor did he answer those murmurers impatiently, but returned good for evil: for so great ought the perfection of a prelate to be that by his goodness and uprightness he overcomes the malice and wickedness of his subjects. Yet not all the children of Israel murmured, but the common sort and the less perfect. [[15:25|and he shewed him a tree|Qui ostendit ei lignum]] [*lignum*, "wood" or "tree"; Denis goes on to speak of it as a piece of wood]. Some say that in that wilderness there was no growing tree, but that God brought the wood there by a miracle. Augustine too seems to think so, as is clear from the Gloss. And in the Scholastic History it is said: Perhaps it was done by a miracle that in a wilderness in which there was no tree, that is, no growing tree, wood was found. [[15:25|which when he had cast into the waters, they were turned into sweetness|Quod lignum quum Moyses misisset in aquas, in dulcedinem versæ sunt]], that is, they were made sweet and drinkable. Some think that that wood had by nature the power of sweetening waters. In support of this, that saying of Ecclesiasticus could be alleged: [[Ecclus 38:5|Was not bitter water made sweet with wood?|Nonne a ligno indulcata est aqua amara?]] And that scripture speaks there of the natural and medicinal properties of the things that grow from the earth; for immediately before those words is set: [[Ecclus 38:4|The most High hath created medicines out of the earth, and a wise man will not abhor them|Altissimus de terra creavit medicinam, et vir prudens non abhorrebit illam]]. Yet (as is related in the Scholastic History) the Hebrew says that that wood was extremely bitter, and that God therefore bade him throw it into the bitter water, so that, when by adding bitter to bitter what had been bitter became sweet, the divine power might be shown more clearly, because the miracle was greater. But whichever of these be said, it is certain that God could have sweetened that water by his command alone. Therefore Origen and others think that God gave that command about the wood in order to signify something mystical. On these things Josephus writes: Moses, taking the rod which he had with him at the time, split it lengthwise down the middle and threw it into the well, and commanded strong men to draw the water and first to pour out the greater part of what they drew, so that what remained last, after being long stirred, might become drinkable. However, this saying of Josephus is not to be understood of Moses' rod, by which he had worked the signs, but of the wood shown to him, in which he made a cut along its length.

paras.t: Ibi constituit ei præcepta atque judicia: id est, in loco præfato post exhibitionem hujus beneficii atque miraculi, Deus per Moysen dedit ac posuit populo Israel quædam præcepta et judicia, id est judicialia instrumenta seu jussa, per quæ regerentur ad convivendum pacifice ac juste ad invicem. Sicque per præcepta, intelliguntur mandata ad Dei cultum directe spectantia. Et ibi tentavit eum: id est, Deus ibidem dedit ista præcepta populo, ut per observantiam aut transgressionem eorum Deus tentaret hunc populum, an vere obediens esset sibi, an non. Tentavit, inquam, non ut ipse cognosceret illud, sed ut innotesceret aliis, ad instructionem vel cautelam eorum, quemadmodum tentavit Abraham, Job, atque Tobiam. Deus autem neminem tentat tentatione ad fallendum tendente, aut ad vitium inclinante.
paras.en: [[15:25|There he appointed him ordinances, and judgments|Ibi constituit ei præcepta atque judicia]]: that is, in the aforesaid place, after the showing of this benefit and miracle, God through Moses gave and laid down for the people of Israel certain precepts and judgments, the judgments being judicial instructions or commands [the *judicialia*, the laws that governed dealings between man and man] by which they were to be ruled, so as to live together peaceably and justly with one another; and so by the precepts [*præcepta*, the Douay-Rheims' "ordinances"] are understood the commandments that bear directly on the worship of God. [[15:25|and there he proved him|Et ibi tentavit eum]]: that is, God gave these precepts to the people there so that by their keeping or breaking of them he might prove [*tentaret*, "try" or "tempt"] this people, whether it was truly obedient to him or not. He proved it, I say, not that he himself might know it, but that it might be made known to others, for their instruction or warning, as he tempted Abraham[[Gen 22:1||]], Job[[Job 1:12||]], and Tobias[[Tob 2:12||]][[Tob 12:13||]] [the margin gives Tob. ii, 12 and xii, 12; the trial of Tobias is spoken of at 12:13]. But God tempts no one with a temptation that tends to deceive or inclines to vice.

paras.t: Sic ergo tentavit populum illum, dicens per Moysen: Si audieris vocem Domini Dei tui, id est verba divina, auribus cordis et corporis; et quod rectum est coram eo feceris, et obedieris mandatis ejus, custodierisque omnia præcepta illius: qui enim transgreditur unum, fit omnium reus, quia mortaliter peccat: cunctum languorem quem posui in Ægypto, non inducam super te, id est, nullam infirmitatem et plagarum quas inflixi Ægyptiis, tibi infligam. Quod intelligendum est pro tempore quo fuerunt in deserto, et quantum ad justos et obedientes, sicut ex verbis immediate præhabitis eluxescit: de illis enim nunc loquitur. Unde et fertur in Psalmo: Non erat in tribubus eorum infirmus. Rebelles vero frequenter ac dire leguntur in deserto percussi: de quibus et constat, quod in solitudine obierunt, non utique absque præviis infirmitatibus. Verumtamen Augustinus super illud, Non erat in tribubus eorum infirmus, glossando addit, Sed corpore, non animo. Per quod insinuare et sentire videtur, verbum illud, etiam de iniquis esse intelligendum. Ad quod dici potest, quod etiam justi, qui inter illos fuerunt, natura fragiles erant, et aliquando peccaverunt, imo et quidam eorum mortaliter, ut patet de Aaron in vituli conflatione et incredulitate ad aquas Contradictionis. Ego enim sum Dominus salvator tuus, non solum ex Ægyptia servitute, et Rubri maris devoratione ac gladio Pharaonis, sed item ex servitute diaboli, jugo peccati, damnatione inferni.
paras.en: So then he proved that people, [[15:26|Saying|dicens]] through Moses: [[15:26|If thou wilt hear the voice of the Lord thy God|Si audieris vocem Domini Dei tui]], that is, the divine words, with the ears of the heart and of the body; [[15:26|and do what is right before him|et quod rectum est coram eo feceris]], [[15:26|and obey his commandments, and keep all his precepts|et obedieris mandatis ejus, custodierisque omnia præcepta illius]]: for he who transgresses one [[Jas 2:10|is become guilty of all|fit omnium reus]] [the margin's chapter number cannot be read; the words are those of Jas 2:10], because he sins mortally: [[15:26|none of the evils that I laid upon Egypt, will I bring upon thee|cunctum languorem quem posui in Ægypto, non inducam super te]] [*languorem*, "sickness"], that is, I will inflict on thee none of the infirmities and plagues which I inflicted on the Egyptians. This is to be understood of the time when they were in the desert, and as regards the just and obedient, as appears from the words immediately before: for it is of them that he now speaks. Hence too it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 104:37|and there was not among their tribes one that was feeble|Non erat in tribubus eorum infirmus]]. But the rebellious are often read to have been struck in the desert, and grievously; and of them it is certain that they died in the wilderness, and surely not without infirmities beforehand. Yet Augustine, on the words [[Ps 104:37|there was not among their tribes one that was feeble|Non erat in tribubus eorum infirmus]], adds in his gloss: But in body, not in mind. By this he seems to suggest and to hold that the saying is to be understood of the wicked as well. To this it can be said that even the just who were among them were frail by nature and sometimes sinned, and some of them indeed mortally, as is clear of Aaron in the casting of the calf[[Ex 32:4||]] and in his unbelief at the waters of Contradiction[[Num 27:14||]] [the margin gives Num. xxvi, 14; the waters of contradiction are named at Num 27:14, and the unbelief is told at Num 20:12]. [[15:26|for I am the Lord thy healer|Ego enim sum Dominus salvator tuus]] [Denis reads *salvator*, "saviour", where the Vulgate has *sanator*, "healer"], not only from the Egyptian bondage, from being swallowed up by the Red Sea and from the sword of Pharao, but also from the bondage of the devil, the yoke of sin, and the damnation of hell.

paras.t: Venerunt autem in Elim. Hoc loco quidam capitulum sequens incipiunt, aliqui vero ibi, Profectique. Venerunt autem filii Israel in Elim, id est in locum solitudinis istius sic nominatum. Ubi erant duodecim fontes aquarum, et septuaginta palmæ, et castrametati sunt juxta aquas: id est, mansionem et tentoria seu turmas suas ibi fixerunt ad tempus, ob loci amœnitatem et commoditatem: quia et aquæ fluenta, et arborum fructus præbuerunt eis refectionem; fuitque eis solatium quod juxta numerum duodecim tribuum suarum, repererunt ibi duodecim fontes, sic quod quælibet tribus potuit specialem fontem habere. Attamen Josephus scribit, quod modica fuit aqua in fontibus illis, et quod manibus inde sumebatur, cœnosum erat, inutile et impurum. Idcirco et palmæ erant parvæ staturæ, eo quod non satis irrigabantur ex aquis, nec humor ille sufficiebat ad terram conglutinandam.
paras.en: [[15:27|And the children of Israel came into Elim|Venerunt autem in Elim]]. Here some begin the following chapter, and others at the words "And they set forward". [[15:27|And the children of Israel came into Elim|Venerunt autem filii Israel in Elim]], that is, into a place of that wilderness so named, [[15:27|where there were twelve fountains of water, and seventy palm trees|Ubi erant duodecim fontes aquarum, et septuaginta palmæ]]: [[15:27|and they encamped by the waters|et castrametati sunt juxta aquas]]: that is, they pitched their quarters and tents, or their companies, there for a time, because of the pleasantness and convenience of the place: for both the streams of water and the fruit of the trees gave them refreshment; and it was a comfort to them that, matching the number of their twelve tribes, they found twelve fountains there, so that each tribe could have its own fountain. Josephus, however, writes that there was little water in those fountains, and that what was taken from them with the hands was muddy, useless and impure. And so the palms too were of small stature, because they were not watered enough by the waters, nor was that moisture enough to bind the soil together.

paras.t: Circa præhabita quæritur, quæ fuerunt præcepta in Marath data, quia textus non exprimit ea. Ad hoc Lyra allegat et sequitur Rabbi Salomonem, dicentem: Dominus videns filios Israel in solitudine otiosos, ne per otium laberentur ad deteriora, contulit eis duo præcepta, ut studerent in eis ad intelligendum atque implendum: unum fuit de observantia sabbati, quod plures observationes includit; alterum fuit de oblatione vaccæ rufæ, ex cujus cineribus aquæ injectis ac mixtis, aqua lustrationis fiebat, per quam purgabantur immundi, ut in Numeris describitur. Subdidit etiam eis copiam de pertinentibus ad judicia inter eos agenda, quatenus inter se juste conversarentur. Sed contra hæc Rabbi Paulus affirmat: Antiqui Hebræi communiter tenent, quod præceptum de sabbato, et quædam judicialia, data sint in hoc loco, non autem de vacca rufa. Nam de sabbato dicitur sequenti capitulo ante legis donationem: Videte quia Dominus dedit vobis sabbatum. De judicialibus quoque satis necessarium fuit, quatenus per ea tantus populus regeretur usque legislationem. Sed inter illa præceptum de vacca rufa, fuisset superfluum pro tunc, quousque tabernaculum fieret, et alia sacra, ad quorum ingressum aut tactum requirebatur purgatio immundorum per aquam lustrationis, ut præallegato Numerorum habetur libro.
paras.en: On what has gone before it is asked what the precepts given at Marath were, since the text does not state them. To this Lyra cites and follows Rabbi Salomon, who says: The Lord, seeing the children of Israel idle in the wilderness, lest through idleness they should slip into worse things, gave them two precepts to study, so as to understand and fulfil them: one was on the keeping of the sabbath, which includes many observances; the other on the offering of the red cow, from whose ashes, cast into water and mixed with it, the water of purification was made, by which the unclean were cleansed, as is described in Numbers[[Num 19:9||]] [the margin gives Num. xix, 9 and following]. He also furnished them with a store of things pertaining to the judgments to be given among them, so that they might deal justly with one another. But against this Rabbi Paul [probably Paul of Burgos, a converted rabbi, author of the Additions to Lyra] affirms: The ancient Hebrews commonly hold that the precept of the sabbath and certain judicial precepts were given in this place, but not that of the red cow. For of the sabbath it is said in the following chapter, before the giving of the law: [[Ex 16:29|See that the Lord hath given you the sabbath|Videte quia Dominus dedit vobis sabbatum]]. Judicial precepts too were quite necessary, so that so great a people might be governed by them until the giving of the law. But among them the precept of the red cow would have been superfluous for the time being, until the tabernacle and the other sacred things were made, for entering or touching which the cleansing of the unclean by the water of purification was required, as is had in the book of Numbers cited above.

paras.t: Insuper, juxta mysticam interpretationem, per Mariam Moysis sororem prophetissam, optime designabatur Deifera atque sanctissima virgo Maria, quæ de liberatione generis humani per Filii sui passionem atque baptismum, jugiter ac devotissime cecinit Deo gratiarum præconia cum tympano, id est plenissima suæ mundissimæ carnis crucifixi mortificatione: quam omnes mulieres virginesque devotæ in lege evangelica sunt secutæ cum tympanis, id est corporum suorum refrenationibus, et choris, id est sanctis concordationibus. Imo et quælibet devota anima eam imitari sic debet. Denique, juxta Boetium in primo Musicæ suæ, Omnis musica instrumentalis, fit nervorum tensione, aut spiritus inflatione, aut percussione rei concavæ. Si nervorum tensione, vel redditur sonus a superiori, et sic est psalterium; vel ab inferiori, et ita est cithara. Si spiritus inflatione, aut humano, aut aliunde attracto seu collecto: si humano, vel continuo, et ita est tuba; aut interpolato, et sic est chorus, per quem designatur concordia vocis et cordis in societate pacata. Si aliunde collecto per folles, sic sunt organa. Si vero sonant percussione pellis extensæ, tympana appellantur. Quæ autem percussione æris cavati, dicuntur cymbala: quæ ad invicem percussa, sonum reddunt acutum. Itaque, quoniam tympanum fit extensione corii siccati, per ipsum mortificatio carnis signatur. Qui autem Deo vult placitas laudes offerre, necesse habet carnem suam cum vitiis et concupiscentiis crucifigere, et scandalizantia membra abscindere.
paras.en: Moreover, according to the mystical interpretation, Mary the prophetess, the sister of Moses, very well signified the most holy Virgin Mary, the Mother of God [*Deifera*, "God-bearing"], who for the deliverance of mankind through the passion and baptism of her Son unceasingly and most devoutly sang to God the praises of thanksgiving with the timbrel, that is, with the fullest mortification of her most pure flesh [the print has *crucifixi*, "of the Crucified"; perhaps for *crucifixæ*, "crucified"]: whom all devout women and virgins under the law of the Gospel have followed with timbrels, that is, with the restraint of their bodies, and with *chori*, that is, with holy harmonies. Indeed every devout soul ought to imitate her in this way. Lastly, according to Boethius in the first book of his Music, all instrumental music is made by the stretching of strings, or by the blowing of breath, or by the striking of something hollow. If by the stretching of strings, either the sound is given from above, and so it is the psaltery, or from below, and so it is the harp. If by the blowing of breath, the breath is either human or drawn or gathered from elsewhere: if human, either continuous, and so it is the trumpet, or intermittent, and so it is the *chorus*, by which is signified the harmony of voice and heart in a peaceful company. If gathered from elsewhere by bellows, such are organs. But if they sound by the striking of a stretched skin, they are called timbrels; and those that sound by the striking of hollowed bronze are called cymbals, which, struck against one another, give a shrill sound. And so, since the timbrel is made by stretching dried hide, the mortification of the flesh is signified by it. Now those who wish to offer God praises that please him must crucify [[Gal 5:24|their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences|carnem suam cum vitiis et concupiscentiis]], and cut off the members that scandalize.

paras.t: At vero per hoc quod filii Israel post liberationem suam a Pharaone, inciderunt periculum sitis et venerunt in Marath, figuratur, quod fideles post divinorum infusionem charismatum, et consolationem Spiritus Sancti, interdum ruunt in gravem tentationem et afflictionem; nec aquam Marath bibere valent, nisi dulcoretur per lignum, id est, rigorosam et strictam pœnitentiæ refectionem ac fletum nequeunt sustinere, nisi dominicæ passionis et crucis meditatione ungantur, vel contemplatione sapientiæ, quæ significatur per lignum. Tamen per lignum illud missum in aquam, secundum Augustinum, figuratur crucis mysterium: quia per Christi passionem, omnis adversitas facta est non solum tolerabilis, imo et dulcis Christi fidelibus.
paras.en: But by the children of Israel's falling into the danger of thirst after their deliverance from Pharao, and coming into Marath, it is figured that the faithful, after the infusion of divine gifts [*charismata*] and the consolation of the Holy Ghost, sometimes fall into grievous temptation and affliction; and they cannot drink the water of Marath unless it is sweetened by the wood: that is, they cannot bear the rigorous and strict fare and the weeping of penance unless they are anointed by meditation on the Lord's passion and cross, or by the contemplation of wisdom, which is signified by the wood. Yet according to Augustine the mystery of the cross is figured by that wood cast into the water: because through the passion of Christ every adversity has become for Christ's faithful not only bearable but even sweet.

paras.t: Amplius, per promissionem illam filiis Israel factam, quod nullus eorum infirmaretur, si Deo in omnibus obedirent, hoc designatur, quod si Christi præcepta integre observemus, ab omni animarum languore efficiemur immunes. Nec putandum, quod corporalis sanitas promissa sit filiis Israel, tanquam finale principaleque præmium pro divinorum observatione præceptorum: quoniam corporalia et terrena ac transitoria bona, non sunt finis spiritualium bonorum, puta virtutum, virtuosorumque actuum: ideo nec sunt principalis merces eorum, quum finis sit dignior mediis. Sed sub corporalibus illis bonis, dona spiritualia et præmia æterna ac superna intelliguntur. Hebræis autem imperfectis ac rudibus, et nondum in fide constabilitis, promittebantur corporalia et terrena, ut per ea ædificarentur in fide, et exspectare discerent invisibilia ac æterna.
paras.en: Further, by that promise made to the children of Israel that none of them would fall sick if they obeyed God in all things, this is signified: that if we keep the precepts of Christ wholly, we shall be made free from every sickness of souls. Nor is it to be thought that bodily health was promised to the children of Israel as the final and principal reward for keeping the divine precepts: for bodily, earthly and passing goods are not the end of spiritual goods, such as the virtues and virtuous acts; and so neither are they their principal reward, since the end is worthier than the means. But under those bodily goods, spiritual gifts and eternal and heavenly rewards are understood. To the Hebrews, however, who were imperfect and unlearned and not yet firmly established in the faith, bodily and earthly things were promised, so that by them they might be built up in faith and learn to look for things invisible and eternal.

paras.t: Venerunt autem in Elim. Per Elim, ubi erant duodecim fontes, septuagintaque palmæ, designatur Christi Ecclesia, in qua est duodenarius numerus Apostolorum, qui splendidissimi fontes sunt saluberrimorum documentorum, de quibus accipi potest illud Psalmi: In ecclesiis benedicite Deo Domino de fontibus Israel. Et illud in Isaia: Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris. Per septuaginta vero palmas, figurati sunt totidem Christi discipuli, qui in prædicatione evangelicæ legis non mediocriter cooperati sunt sanctis Apostolis.
paras.en: [[15:27|And the children of Israel came into Elim|Venerunt autem in Elim]]. By Elim, [[15:27|where there were twelve fountains|ubi erant duodecim fontes]] and [[15:27|seventy palm trees|septuagintaque palmæ]], is signified the Church of Christ, in which is the twelvefold number of the Apostles, who are most splendid fountains of most wholesome teachings; of whom that saying of the Psalm can be taken: [[Ps 67:27|In the churches bless ye God the Lord, from the fountains of Israel.|In ecclesiis benedicite Deo Domino de fontibus Israel]] And that in Isaias: [[Is 12:3|Thou shall draw waters with joy out of the saviour's fountains|Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris]]. And by the seventy palms are figured as many disciples of Christ[[Luke 10:1||]], who worked together with the holy Apostles in no small way in the preaching of the law of the Gospel [the margin gives Luc. x; Luke 10:1 has seventy-two, where many Latin manuscripts read seventy].

16.title: Explanatio capituli sextidecimi: Profectique sunt de Elim
16.title_en: Explanation of the sixteenth chapter: And they set forward from Elim

paras.t: Qualiter Deus gratiose et miraculose providit populo suo necessaria victui in deserto, recitatur in isto capitulo.
paras.en: This chapter relates how God, graciously and miraculously, provided His people in the desert with what they needed for food.

paras.t: Profectique sunt de Elim. Nam ut in præcedenti dicebatur articulo, quamvis ibi fuerunt duodecim fontes, tamen modica aqua, quæ et impura erat in eis, et fructus arborum ibi inventi, a tanta multitudine fuerunt cito comesti: ideo processerunt, attamen juxta motum columnæ nubis. Et venit omnis multitudo filiorum Israel in desertum Sin, quod est inter Elim et Sinai. Verum, ut dictum est, omnia ista specialia loca, seu partialia deserta diversimode nominata, in uno illo totali deserto, quod est inter Ægyptum et Chanaan, continebantur ut partes. Ibi ergo venerunt quintodecimo die mensis secundi, etc., secundum computationem Judæorum, qui a Martio seu Aprili incipiunt menses anni, juxta sensum præhabitum. Et juxta hoc, mensis iste secundus fuit Aprilis vel Maius. Quum ergo de Ægypto egressi sint quintodecimo die mensis primi, ut duodecimo capitulo patuit, constat quod tricesimo die ab exitu de Ægypto venerunt in desertum Sin.
paras.en: [[16:1|And they set forward from Elim|Profectique sunt de Elim]]. For, as was said in the preceding article, although there were twelve fountains there[[Ex 15:27||]], yet the little water in them, which was also impure, and the fruits of the trees found there, were soon consumed by so great a multitude: therefore they went on, though following the movement of the pillar of the cloud. [[16:1|and all the multitude of the children of Israel came into the desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai|Et venit omnis multitudo filiorum Israel in desertum Sin, quod est inter Elim et Sinai]]. But, as has been said, all these particular places, or partial deserts named in different ways, were contained as parts in that one whole desert which lies between Egypt and Chanaan. They came there, then, [[16:1|the fifteenth day of the second month|quintodecimo die mensis secundi]], etc., according to the reckoning of the Jews, who begin the months of the year from March or April, in the sense given before. And accordingly this second month was April or May. Since, then, they went out of Egypt on the fifteenth day of the first month, as was shown in the twelfth chapter[[Ex 12:18||]][[Ex 12:51||]], it is clear that they came into the desert of Sin on the thirtieth day after leaving Egypt.

paras.t: Et murmuravit omnis congregatio filiorum Israel contra Moysen et Aaron in solitudine. Non simpliciter omnis congregatio illa sic murmuravit, sed tam multi in ea, quod ceteri comparative pauci fuerunt. Idcirco in hac computatione pauci illi non reputantur, soletque toti adscribi, quod convenit parti ejus majori.
paras.en: [[16:2|And all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness.|Et murmuravit omnis congregatio filiorum Israel contra Moysen et Aaron in solitudine]] Not that that whole congregation, simply speaking, murmured so, but so many in it that the rest were few by comparison. Therefore those few are not counted in this reckoning; and what belongs to the greater part is commonly ascribed to the whole.

paras.t: Dixeruntque filii Israel ad eos. De mulieribus non fit sermo, quum tamen verisimile sit, quod cum viris vel parentibus suis murmuraverunt, præsertim quum feminæ satis cito impatientes aut pusillanimes fiant; sed opera principalioris sexus describuntur communius. Utinam mortui essemus per manum Domini in terra Ægypti, id est, utinam Deus in Ægypto nos occidisset brevi et celeri morte, sicut occidit primogenita Ægyptiorum! Quasi dicant: Tolerabilior fuisset mors illa, quam tribulatio ista, et mori ex fame, juxta illud in Threnis: Melius fuit occisis gladio, quam attenuatis fame. Sed ista fuerunt verba diffidentiæ et nimiæ pusillanimitatis, imo et cujusdam desperationis. Non enim attendebant divina promissa, nec in adversis ostenderunt fidem et spem suam in Domino. Quando sedebamus super, id est prope, ollas carnium, quæ præparabantur nobis ad ignem in ollis. Solet autem Super, pro Prope sumi. Unde communiter dicimus: Colonia sita est super Rhenum. Et comedebamus panem in saturitate. Cur induxistis nos in desertum istud, ut occideretis omnem multitudinem fame? In hoc dupliciter mentiebantur. Non enim Moyses et Aaron, sed Deus per eos, imo per columnam nubis, magis autem per angelum nubis illius motorem, duxit eos in eremum illam. Et quamvis Moyses et Aaron hoc aliquo modo fecerunt, non tamen ut eos occiderent fame, sed ob alias rationabiles causas, in expositione litterali tertiidecimi capituli introductas.
paras.en: [[16:3|And the children of Israel said to them|Dixeruntque filii Israel ad eos]]. Nothing is said of the women, though it is likely that they murmured along with their husbands or parents, especially since women quite soon become impatient or faint-hearted; but the deeds of the principal sex are more commonly described. [[16:3|Would to God we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt|Utinam mortui essemus per manum Domini in terra Ægypti]], that is, would that God had slain us in Egypt by a short and swift death, as He slew the firstborn of the Egyptians! As if they said: That death would have been more bearable than this tribulation, and than dying of hunger, according to that in Lamentations: [[Lam 4:9|It was better with them that were slain by the sword, than with them that died with hunger|Melius fuit occisis gladio, quam attenuatis fame]] [Denis reads *attenuatis*, “wasted away”, where the Vulgate has *interfectis*, “slain”]. But these were words of distrust and of excessive faint-heartedness, nay, even of a kind of despair. For they paid no heed to the divine promises, nor did they show their faith and hope in the Lord in adversity. [[16:3|when we sat over|Quando sedebamus super]], that is, near, [[16:3|the fleshpots|ollas carnium]], the meats that were prepared for us at the fire in pots. Now *super* [over, upon] is often taken for *prope* [near]; hence we commonly say: Cologne is situated *super Rhenum* [on the Rhine]. [[16:3|and ate bread to the full: Why have you brought us into this desert, that you might destroy all the multitude with famine?|Et comedebamus panem in saturitate. Cur induxistis nos in desertum istud, ut occideretis omnem multitudinem fame?]] In this they lied in two ways. For it was not Moses and Aaron, but God through them, nay, through the pillar of the cloud, or rather through the angel who moved that cloud, who led them into that wilderness. And although Moses and Aaron did this in some way, yet it was not in order to kill them with hunger, but for other reasonable causes, set out in the literal exposition of the thirteenth chapter.

paras.t: Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen, qui murmurantibus illis condoluit, et Dominum invocavit: Ecce ego pluam vobis panes de cœlo, id est, materiam ex qua panes conficietis, faciam ex cœlo aereo pro vestra sustentatione in terram descendere, utpote manna: quod tamen angelorum ministerio factum agnoscitur. Bonus et pius Deus murmuranti populo condescendit, quia et aliquam habuerunt murmurandi occasionem, quia jam fame erant confecti. Nam infra triginta dies in via exactos, consumpserunt quæ ex Ægypto victualia detulerunt, etiam valde parce eisdem utendo, erantque in vastissima et sterilissima eremo, solo visu horribili. Egrediatur populus, et colligat quæ sufficiunt per singulos dies, id est, quotidie colligat tantum, ut pro illo die sufficiat ei, seu cuique colligenti pro se et sua familia, excepto tamen sabbati die, in quo non licebat colligere. Voluit autem Dominus, ut sine mundana sollicitudine, et absque guloso cupidoque affectu colligerent, utpote tantum, quantum putabant sibi sufficere: nec pro sequenti die colligerent, nisi in sexta die: quia non licuit inde servari in crastinum, quatenus de Dei providentia essent securi. Ut tentem eum, id est, idcirco istud præcipio, quatenus ex sequela hujus præcepti experiar, vel potius alios agnoscere faciam, et per modum tentantis me habeam, utrum ambulet in lege mea, an non. Quando Dominus dixit hæc, nondum contulerat legem, quæ in monte Sinai data est. Quomodo ergo ait, Utrum ambulet in lege mea? Et respondendum, quod jam dederat quædam præcepta in Marath, et protinus daturus erat legem concernentem hunc panem seu manna, videlicet quando et qualiter esset colligendus et accipiendus: imo jam aliquid tetigit inde; et paulo post, durante usu mannæ, daturus fuit legem in Sinai. Legem quoque naturalem et circumcisionis præceptum, ac alia quædam mandata, jam ante tradiderat Patriarchis in lege naturæ.
paras.en: [[16:4|And the Lord said to Moses|Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen]], who grieved at their murmuring and called upon the Lord: [[16:4|Behold I will rain bread from heaven for you|Ecce ego pluam vobis panes de cœlo]], that is, I will make the matter from which you shall make bread, namely manna, come down from the heaven of the air to the earth for your sustenance: which, however, is acknowledged to have been done by the ministry of angels. The good and kind God condescended to the murmuring people, because they did have some occasion for murmuring, being already worn out with hunger. For within the thirty days spent on the way they had used up the provisions they brought out of Egypt, though they used them very sparingly; and they were in a most vast and barren wilderness, horrible to look at alone. [[16:4|let the people go forth, and gather what is sufficient for every day|Egrediatur populus, et colligat quæ sufficiunt per singulos dies]], that is, let each one gather every day so much as suffices him for that day, or as suffices each gatherer for himself and his household, except, however, the sabbath day, on which it was not lawful to gather. The Lord willed that they should gather without worldly anxiety, and without a greedy and covetous disposition, namely as much as they thought sufficient for themselves; and that they should not gather for the following day, except on the sixth day, because it was not lawful to keep any of it until the morrow: so that they might be secure in God's providence. [[16:4|that I may prove them|Ut tentem eum]], that is, I command this so that from the keeping of this precept I may find out, or rather may make others know, and may behave as one who tests, [[16:4|whether they will walk in my law, or not|utrum ambulet in lege mea, an non]]. When the Lord said this, He had not yet given the law which was given on Mount Sinai. How then does He say, [[16:4|whether they will walk in my law|Utrum ambulet in lege mea]]? The answer is that He had already given certain precepts at Marath, and was straightway to give a law about this bread, or manna, namely when and how it was to be gathered and taken: indeed He has already touched on something of it here; and shortly afterwards, while the manna was in use, He was to give the law on Sinai. The natural law, too, and the precept of circumcision, and certain other commandments, He had already given to the Patriarchs in the law of nature.

paras.t: Die autem sexto parent quod intulerint, id est, de materia hujus panis congregent, quod in tabernacula seu tentoria sua reponant; et sit duplum quam colligere solebant per singulos dies, videlicet quinque diebus præcedentibus, ut sufficiat pro sustentatione, tam in ipsa feria sexta, quam in septima seu sabbato, quando non licet colligere. Hoc autem quod ait, Et sit duplum quam colligere solebant per singulos dies, etc., dupliciter potest exponi: Primo, quod sexta feria colligebant duplo plus, quam aliquo die præcedente: et ita videtur intelligere Origenes. Unde et in Glossa ex ejus verbis habetur: In die sexta duplum colligatur in repositione, quantum sufficiat etiam sabbato. Huicque sensui consonat, quod infra in isto continetur capitulo: In die autem sexta collegerunt cibos duplices, id est duo gomor per singulos homines. Secundo, sic illud quod collegerunt sexta feria, miraculose multiplicabatur, ita quod etiam pro sabbati retentione sufficiebat. Sicque non plus colligerant substantialiter sexta feria quam aliis feriis, sed virtualiter, in quantum illud multiplicabatur in duplum. Quid vero huic expositioni videatur favere, infra capitulo hoc tangetur.
paras.en: [[16:5|But the sixth day let them provide for to bring in|Die autem sexto parent quod intulerint]], that is, let them gather of the matter of this bread what they are to lay up in their tabernacles or tents; [[16:5|and let it be double to that they were wont to gather every day|et sit duplum quam colligere solebant per singulos dies]], namely on the five preceding days, so that it may suffice for their sustenance both on the sixth day itself and on the seventh, or sabbath, when it is not lawful to gather. Now what He says, [[16:5|and let it be double to that they were wont to gather every day|et sit duplum quam colligere solebant per singulos dies]], etc., can be explained in two ways. First, that on the sixth day they gathered twice as much as on any day before; and so Origen seems to understand it. Hence the Gloss too has, from his words: On the sixth day let a double amount be gathered to be laid up, as much as will suffice for the sabbath also. And with this sense agrees what is contained below in this chapter: [[16:22|But on the sixth day they gathered twice as much, that is, two gomors every man|In die autem sexta collegerunt cibos duplices, id est duo gomor per singulos homines]]. Secondly, thus: what they gathered on the sixth day was miraculously multiplied, so that it sufficed also to be kept for the sabbath. And so on the sixth day they had not gathered more in substance than on the other days, but in effect, inasmuch as it was multiplied to double. What seems to favour this explanation will be touched on below in this chapter.

paras.t: Insuper ex his verbis elicit Origenes quod manna cœpit dari ac pluere die dominica, utpote prima die hebdomadæ, quam nos ob Christi in ea resurrectionem, appellamus dominicam et festivam. Sic enim ait: Sexta dies appellatur, quæ ante sabbatum ponitur. Sabbatum autem septima dies est. Quæro ergo, qua die cœperit manna cœlitus dari, et volo comparare dominicam nostram cum sabbato Judæorum. Ex divinis namque Scripturis apparet, quod in die dominica primo datum est manna in terris. Si enim (ut ait Scriptura) sex diebus continuis collectum est, septima vero die, videlicet sabbato, cessatum est, constat quod cœpit dari dominica die. Intelligant ergo Judæi, jam tunc prælatam esse dominicam nostram Judaico sabbato; tuncque fuisse figuratum, quod in eorum sabbato non descendat ad eos gratia Dei. Hæc Origenes.
paras.en: Further, Origen draws from these words that the manna began to be given and to rain on the Lord's day, that is, on the first day of the week, which, because of Christ's resurrection on it, we call the Lord's day and a feast. For he says: The sixth day is the name of the day placed before the sabbath; and the sabbath is the seventh day. I ask, then, on what day the manna began to be given from heaven, and I wish to compare our Lord's day with the sabbath of the Jews. For it appears from the divine Scriptures that the manna was first given on earth on the Lord's day. For if (as Scripture says) it was gathered on six days in a row, and on the seventh day, namely the sabbath, it ceased, it is clear that it began to be given on the Lord's day. Let the Jews understand, then, that even then our Lord's day was preferred to the Jewish sabbath; and that it was then foreshown that on their sabbath the grace of God does not come down to them. Thus far Origen.

paras.t: Dixeruntque Moyses et Aaron ad omnes filios Israel: Vespere scietis, quod Dominus eduxerit vos de terra Ægypti. Quasi dicat Moyses: Imponitis mihi, quod quasi proprio capite vos induxerim in hunc locum, sed in hora hujus diei vespertina per evidentiam facti, utpote per miraculosam avium adventationem, certius cognoscetis, quia non nisi ex Dei imperio vos hucusque deduxerim. Et mane videbitis gloriam ejus, Domini, hoc est, præclaram ejus potestatem conspicietis in miraculoso descensu mannæ, quod cras mane videbitis. Causa quippe in suo cognoscitur et videtur effectu. Audivi enim murmur vestrum contra Dominum: quia in Deum et in ejus injuriam redundat murmuratio vestra contra me et Aaron facta, quia ex Dei præcepto in hunc locum vos duximus. Difficultatem tamen quamdam inducit conjunctio illa causalis, Enim. Nam quomodo Moysen audisse murmurationem filiorum Israel contra Deum, est causa quod vespere scient Dominum eduxisse eos ex Ægypto, atque quod mane videbunt gloriam ejus? Itaque quod ait, Audivi enim, etc., inducitur non tanquam causa beneficiorum tantorum, sed ut causa quod Moyses ista locutus est eis. Aliqui autem textus habent, Audivit enim: sicque sensus est, quod Dominus audivit murmurationem illorum contra Dominum, id est contra se factam. Si autem legatur, Audivi, quæstio est, cur singulariter dicitur, Audivi, quum pluraliter sit præmissum, Dixerunt Moyses et Aaron. Ad quod dici potest, quod Moyses tanquam principalis, de se singulariter ait, Audivi: quia ad eum præcipue pertinebat corripere populum, tanquam ad eorum prælatum. Nos vero quid sumus, quia mussitastis contra nos? Quasi dicant: Quum non simus nisi ministri Dei, cui in vestra eductione et deductione in cunctis obtemperavimus, male agitis contra nos murmurando, et inter vos basse adversum nos colloquendo.
paras.en: [[16:6|And Moses and Aaron said to the children of Israel In the evening you shall know that the Lord hath brought you forth out of the land of Egypt|Dixeruntque Moyses et Aaron ad omnes filios Israel: Vespere scietis, quod Dominus eduxerit vos de terra Ægypti]]. As if Moses said: You charge me with having led you into this place as it were on my own authority; but this evening, by the evidence of the deed, namely by the miraculous arrival of the birds, you shall know more surely that it is only by God's command that I have led you thus far. [[16:7|And in the morning you shall see the glory|Et mane videbitis gloriam ejus]] of the Lord [Denis's text reads “his glory”, which he glosses “of the Lord”], that is, you shall behold His glorious power in the miraculous coming down of the manna, which you shall see tomorrow morning; for a cause is known and seen in its effect. [[16:7|for he hath heard your murmuring against the Lord|Audivi enim murmur vestrum contra Dominum]] [Denis's text reads *Audivi*, “I have heard”; the Douay-Rheims follows the reading *audivit*, “he hath heard”, which Denis mentions below]: for your murmuring against me and Aaron overflows upon God and to His injury, since it was by God's command that we led you into this place. Yet the causal conjunction *for* raises a certain difficulty. For how is Moses having heard the murmuring of the children of Israel against God the cause why they will know in the evening that the Lord brought them out of Egypt, and will see His glory in the morning? So the words *For I have heard*, etc., are brought in not as the cause of such great benefits, but as the cause why Moses said these things to them. Some texts, however, have *For he hath heard*; and then the sense is that the Lord heard their murmuring against the Lord, that is, made against Himself. But if one reads *I have heard*, the question is why *I have heard* is said in the singular, when the plural went before: *Moses and Aaron said*.
