To this it can be said that Moses, as the principal one, says *I have heard* of himself in the singular, because it belonged chiefly to him to rebuke the people, as their prelate. [[16:7|but as for us, what are we, that you mutter against us?|Nos vero quid sumus, quia mussitastis contra nos?]] As if they said: Since we are nothing but ministers of God, whom we have obeyed in all things in leading you out and leading you on, you do wrong in murmuring against us, and in muttering against us in low voices among yourselves.

paras.t: Et ait Moyses: Dabit vobis Dominus vespere carnes edere: hoc est, volatilia faciet ad manus vestras venire hora præfata, ut capiatis ac præparetis ea ad comedendum: et mane panes in saturitate: hoc est, diluculo diei sequentis invenietis materiam panum, videlicet manna, quousque ad sufficientiam reficiemini; eo quod audierit murmurationes vestras, quibus murmurati estis contra eum: hoc est, querimonias vestras super defectu alimentorum cognovit, idcirco in hoc condescendet misericorditer vobis dando quæ appetistis. Nos enim quid sumus? Nec contra nos est murmur vestrum, sed contra Dominum, id est, non solum nec principaliter est contra nos, sed contra eum, cujus vices gerimus circa vos, et ex cujus commissione peregimus ea, propter quæ contra nos murmuratis. Qui enim tali casu murmurat contra suum superiorem, magis murmurat contra Deum, quam contra proprium superiorem. Nam inhonoratio servi, redundat in Dominum. Propter quod vicarius sui ait Salvator: Qui vos spernit, me spernit. Paulus quoque: Qui hæc spernit, non hominem spernit, sed Deum.
paras.en: [[16:8|And Moses said: In the evening the Lord will give you flesh to eat|Et ait Moyses: Dabit vobis Dominus vespere carnes edere]]: that is, He will make fowl come to your hands at the hour named, so that you may catch them and prepare them for eating; [[16:8|and in the morning bread to the full|et mane panes in saturitate]]: that is, at dawn of the following day you shall find the matter of bread, namely the manna, until you are refreshed to the full; [[16:8|for he hath heard your murmurings, with which you have murmured against him|eo quod audierit murmurationes vestras, quibus murmurati estis contra eum]]: that is, He has taken notice of your complaints about the want of food, and therefore He will mercifully condescend to you in this, giving you what you desired. [[16:8|for what are we? your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord|Nos enim quid sumus? Nec contra nos est murmur vestrum, sed contra Dominum]], that is, it is not only, nor chiefly, against us, but against Him whose place we hold towards you, and by whose commission we have done the things for which you murmur against us. For whoever in such a case murmurs against his superior, murmurs against God rather than against his own superior; for dishonour done to a servant overflows upon the Lord. Therefore the Saviour says to His vicars: [[Luke 10:16|he that despiseth you despiseth me|Qui vos spernit, me spernit]]. And Paul: [[1 Thess 4:8|he that despiseth these things, despiseth not man, but God|Qui hæc spernit, non hominem spernit, sed Deum]].

paras.t: Dixit quoque Moyses ad Aaron: Dic universæ congregationi filiorum Israel: quæ congregatio magna exstitit et late diffusa, nec bene intelligere poterat simul, nisi vocem tubalem; ideo Moyses commisit ipsi Aaron proferre hæc verba: Accedite coram Domino, id est, divinæ majestatis ubique præsentis et omnia intuentis conspectui vos repræsentate, attendendo ejus incircumscriptam præsentiam, atque ad eam erigendo cor vestrum. Iste fuit modus loquendi in veteri Testamento. Sic namque ait et Samuel primo Regum: Accedite huc coram Domino. Et Psalmista: Accedite ad eum. Aliqui tamen sic exponunt: Coram Domino, id est coram parvo tabernaculo, in quo Dominus Moysi loquebatur, magno tabernaculo, de quo infra habetur, nondum facto. Hinc Magister in historiis scribit: Aiunt Hebræi eos primo habuisse parvum tabernaculum, in quo Dominum consulebant, de quo infra habetur: Tollens Moyses tabernaculum, tetendit illud extra castra. Vel sic: Coram Domino, id est coram columna nubis. Dominus namque in nube illa, et item in tabernaculo illo specialiter fuisse asseritur, in quantum ibi specialiter apparebat, operabatur, aut loquebatur. Ideo coram nube aut tabernaculo accedendo, coram Domino accessisse dicuntur. Audivit enim, id est cognovit, murmur vestrum, quoniam omnia, nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus: atque ut scriptum est, Auris zeli audit omnia.
paras.en: [[16:9|Moses also said to Aaron: Say to the whole congregation of the children of Israel|Dixit quoque Moyses ad Aaron: Dic universæ congregationi filiorum Israel]]: which congregation was great and widely spread out, and could not well hear all at once anything but the sound of a trumpet; therefore Moses charged Aaron himself to deliver these words: [[16:9|Come before the Lord|Accedite coram Domino]], that is, present yourselves before the sight of the divine majesty, which is present everywhere and beholds all things, attending to His uncircumscribed presence and lifting up your heart to it. This was a manner of speaking in the Old Testament. For so Samuel too says in the first book of Kings: Come hither before the Lord[[1 Kings 10:19||]] [the margin gives 1 Reg. xv, 30, which does not fit; these words are not found in 1 Kings: the nearest is Samuel's “stand before the Lord” at 1 Kings 10:19, cf. 12:7]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 33:6|Come ye to him|Accedite ad eum]] [the margin gives Ps. xxxviii, 6, read for xxxiii, 6]. Some, however, explain it thus: [[16:9|before the Lord|Coram Domino]], that is, before the little tabernacle in which the Lord spoke to Moses, the great tabernacle, of which we read below, not yet having been made. Hence the Master writes in the Histories: The Hebrews say that they first had a little tabernacle, in which they consulted the Lord, of which we read below: [[Ex 33:7|Moses also taking the tabernacle, pitched it without the camp|Tollens Moyses tabernaculum, tetendit illud extra castra]]. Or thus: [[16:9|before the Lord|Coram Domino]], that is, before the pillar of the cloud. For the Lord is said to have been in a special way in that cloud, and likewise in that tabernacle, inasmuch as He appeared, worked or spoke there in a special way. Therefore, by drawing near before the cloud or the tabernacle, they are said to have drawn near before the Lord. [[16:9|for he hath heard|Audivit enim]], that is, has taken notice of, [[16:9|your murmuring|murmur vestrum]], since [[Heb 4:13|all things are naked and open to his eyes|omnia, nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus]]; and, as it is written, [[Wis 1:10|the ear of jealousy heareth all things|Auris zeli audit omnia]].

paras.t: Cumque loqueretur Aaron ad omnem cœtum filiorum Israel, respexerunt ad solitudinem. Jam in solitudine erant, qualiter ergo respexerunt ad eam? nisi forte dicatur, quod scribuntur ad solitudinem respexisse, quia ad quamdam ejus partem, oculis eorum oppositam, in qua erat columna nubis, cum speciali diligentia conspexerunt, quia insolitum aliquid ibi apparuit. Unde subjungitur: Et ecce gloria Domini apparuit in nube, id est, Deus majestatem suam monstravit in columna nubis, per supernaturalem et inconsuetum quemdam splendorem sensibilem, divinæ præsentiæ repræsentativum.
paras.en: [[16:10|And when Aaron spoke to all the assembly of the children of Israel, they looked towards the wilderness|Cumque loqueretur Aaron ad omnem cœtum filiorum Israel, respexerunt ad solitudinem]]. They were already in the wilderness: how then did they look towards it? Unless perhaps it be said that they are written to have looked towards the wilderness because they gazed with special attention at a certain part of it facing their eyes, in which the pillar of the cloud was, since something unwonted appeared there. Hence it is added: [[16:10|and behold the glory of the Lord appeared in a cloud|Et ecce gloria Domini apparuit in nube]], that is, God showed His majesty in the pillar of the cloud, by a certain supernatural and unaccustomed visible splendour, representing the divine presence.

paras.t: Locutus est autem Dominus ad Moysen, dicens: Audivi murmurationes filiorum Israel. Loquere ad eos: Vespere comedetis carnes, et mane saturabimini panibus; scietisque quod ego sum Dominus Deus vester. Circa hoc loquitur Origenes: Velim scire qualiter Judæi ista dicta suscipiant. Quid enim consequentiæ videtur habere, ut aut vespere carnes sine panibus comedant, aut mane panes absque pulmenti adjectione manducent? Et videtur Origenes insinuare, quod ista non valeant ad litteram proprie stare. Nihilo minus dici potest, quod ideo Dominus dixit, Vespere comedetis carnes, quia in vespera diei illius collegerunt comestibiles aves in copia. Ideo quoque disseruit, Mane saturabimini panibus, quia diluculo mox sequente pluit eis manna sufficiens, ex quo panes formabant. Et forsitan in vespera illa quidam illorum præ aviditate gulosa coxerunt avium carnes, comederuntque eas. Nam et quidam eorum adhuc aliquid habuerunt de pane, ut probabile reputatur.
paras.en: [[16:11|And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:|Locutus est autem Dominus ad Moysen, dicens]] [[16:12|I have heard the murmuring of the children of Israel, say to them: In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall have your fill of bread; and you shall know that I am the Lord your God.|Audivi murmurationes filiorum Israel. Loquere ad eos: Vespere comedetis carnes, et mane saturabimini panibus; scietisque quod ego sum Dominus Deus vester]] On this Origen says: I should like to know how the Jews take these sayings. For what sense does it seem to make that they should either eat flesh in the evening without bread, or eat bread in the morning without anything added to it? And Origen seems to hint that these words cannot properly stand according to the letter. Nevertheless it can be said that the Lord said, [[16:12|In the evening you shall eat flesh|Vespere comedetis carnes]], because in the evening of that day they gathered birds good to eat in abundance; and that He said, [[16:12|in the morning you shall have your fill of bread|Mane saturabimini panibus]], because at the dawn that followed soon after it rained manna for them in plenty, from which they made bread. And perhaps on that evening some of them, out of greedy eagerness, cooked the flesh of the birds and ate it. For some of them still had some bread, as is thought likely.

paras.t: Factum est ergo vespere, et ascendens coturnix, cooperuit castra, id est, multitudo copiosissima coturnicum, quæ sunt comestibiles volucres, veniens et pervolans mare Rubrum, per latum resedit super domos Hebræorum, et quievit in terra juxta eosdem, ita quod juxta beneplacitum suum aves illas ceperunt. De hoc in Scholastica narratur historia: Ascendens coturnix de sinu Arabico, id est a regione seu loco quodam Arabiæ, ubi præcipue alitur, transcenso medio mari operuit castra. Estque coturnix avis regia, quam Josephus ortygiam vocat, Græci ὀρτυγομήτραν, nos vulgo curleium dicimus, a currendo, quia videlicet frequenter cursitant super terram. Hinc in Sapientiæ libro legitur: Viderunt novam creaturam avium, quum abducti concupiscentia, postulaverunt escas epulationis. In allocutione enim desiderii ascendit illis de mari ortygometra. Quocirca scribunt expositores: Ortygia est regio seu insula, in qua habitant et abundant coturnices, duobus super terram cubitis volitantes.
paras.en: [[16:13|So it came to pass in the evening, that quails coming up, covered the camp|Factum est ergo vespere, et ascendens coturnix, cooperuit castra]], that is, a most plentiful multitude of quails, which are birds good to eat, coming and flying over the Red Sea, settled far and wide upon the dwellings of the Hebrews and rested on the ground beside them, so that they caught those birds at their pleasure. Of this the Scholastic History relates: The quail, coming up from the Arabian gulf, that is, from a certain region or place of Arabia where it is chiefly bred, crossed the middle of the sea and covered the camp. And the quail is a royal bird, which Josephus calls *ortygia*, the Greeks ὀρτυγομήτραν, and we commonly call *curleium* [curlew; Denis derives it from *currere*, “to run”], from running, because they often run about on the ground. Hence we read in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 19:11|they saw a new generation of birds, when being led by their appetite, they asked for delicate meats|Viderunt novam creaturam avium, quum abducti concupiscentia, postulaverunt escas epulationis]]. [[Wis 19:12|For to satisfy their desire, the quail came up to them from the sea|In allocutione enim desiderii ascendit illis de mari ortygometra]] [the word rendered “quail” is *ortygometra*]. Accordingly the expositors write: Ortygia is a region or island in which quails live and abound, flying two cubits above the ground.

paras.t: Quæritur, cur Dominus prius dedit eis carnes ad manducandum, quam panes. Dici potest, quod adhuc modicum quid habebant de panibus pro vespera illa, nihil autem de carnibus affectatis. Vel, quia in sua querimonia primo nominabant carnes, postea panes, dicendo: Utinam mortui essemus in Ægypto, quando sedebamus super ollas carnium, et comedebamus panes in saturitate! Iterum quæri potest, cur de carnium defectu murmuraverunt, et earum esum sic affectabant, quum haberent secum tot comestibilia pecora. Ad hoc Augustinus respondet: Cur in eremo carnes desideraverunt, quum de Ægypto cum multis pecoribus exierint, magna quæstio est. Nisi forte dicatur, quod in eremo non fuerant pascua: ideo minor pecorum fecunditas fecit eis parci, ne omnibus eis deficientibus, etiam sacrificiis necessaria deessent; vel, si quid aliud dici potest, unde solvatur quæstio hæc. Congruentius tamen creditur, quod non desiderarunt eas carnes quæ de pecoribus possunt haberi, sed eas quæ derant. Rursus asserit Augustinus: Aves illas multi Latine coturnices vocant, quum sit aliud genus, coturnicibus non usquequaque dissimile.
paras.en: It is asked why the Lord gave them flesh to eat before bread. It can be said that they still had a little bread for that evening, but none of the flesh they longed for. Or, because in their complaint they named flesh first and bread afterwards, saying: [[16:3|Would to God we had died|Utinam mortui essemus]] [[16:3|in the land of Egypt, when we sat over the fleshpots, and ate bread to the full|in Ægypto, quando sedebamus super ollas carnium, et comedebamus panes in saturitate!]] Again it can be asked why they murmured at the want of flesh, and longed so to eat it, when they had so many cattle with them fit to eat. To this Augustine answers: Why they desired flesh in the desert, when they had come out of Egypt with many cattle, is a great question. Unless perhaps it be said that there was no pasture in the desert, so that the lesser increase of the cattle made them spare them, lest, if all of them failed, what was needed even for the sacrifices should be lacking; or whatever else can be said by which this question may be solved. It is more fittingly believed, however, that they did not desire the flesh that can be had from cattle, but that which they lacked. Again Augustine asserts: Many call those birds in Latin *coturnices* [quails], though they are another kind, not altogether unlike quails.

paras.t: Mane quoque ros jacuit per circuitum castrorum. Hoc Lyra exponens, ait : Ros, id est manna ad modum roris congelati. Unde infra dicitur, quod habuit similitudinem pruinæ, quæ est ros congelatus. Ista est expositio Catholicorum, secundum quam manna cadebat immediate super terram, sicque per rorem vel pruinam designatur hic manna. Deinde subjungit : Rabbi Salomon exponit hunc locum subtilius, dicens quod primo cadebat pruina super terram, et postea manna desuper, et postea ros aliquantulum congelatus desuper, ita quod manna jacuit inter duo illa tanquam munde servatum. Unde in Hebræo habetur : Mane quoque fuit operimentum roris in circuitu castrorum, et ascendit operimentum roris, et ecce in solitudine minutum discoopertum. Sed circa hoc dico, quod multi doctores catholici adstruunt manna fuisse distinctum a rore, et illud cum rore pariter descendisse, præsertim quum scriptum sit in Numerorum libro : Quumque descenderet nocte super castra ros, descendebat pariter et man. Ubi satis evidenter docetur, manna fuisse distinctum a rore. Non ergo oportuit in hac expositione perfidum illum catholicis doctoribus sic præferre.
paras.en: [[16:13|and in the morning a dew lay round about the camp|Mane quoque ros jacuit per circuitum castrorum]]. Expounding this, Lyra says: *Dew*, that is, manna, in the manner of frozen dew. Hence it is said below that it was [[16:14|like unto the hoar frost|similitudinem pruinæ]], which is frozen dew. This is the exposition of the Catholics, according to which the manna fell directly upon the ground; and so here the manna is signified by the dew or the hoar frost. Then he adds: Rabbi Salomon expounds this place more subtly, saying that first the hoar frost fell upon the ground, and then the manna upon it, and then upon that a dew somewhat frozen, so that the manna lay between those two as if kept clean. Hence in the Hebrew we have: In the morning also there was a covering of dew round about the camp, and the covering of dew went up, and behold, in the wilderness something small, uncovered. But on this I say that many Catholic doctors maintain that the manna was distinct from the dew and came down together with the dew, especially since it is written in the book of Numbers: [[Num 11:9|And when the dew fell in the night upon the camp, the manna also fell with it|Quumque descenderet nocte super castra ros, descendebat pariter et man]]. Here it is taught clearly enough that the manna was distinct from the dew. There was no need, then, in this exposition, so to prefer that faithless man [that is, Rabbi Salomon, an unbeliever] to the Catholic doctors.

paras.t: Doctores vero catholici, qui dicunt manna per rorem intelligi, dicunt hoc per similitudinem unius cum alio. Nam et in Scholastica historia dicitur ex Josepho : Mane quum orasset Moyses, ros descendens, illinitus est manibus ejus, quem primo suspicatus est esse imbrem ; sed quum gustasset, sensit mellis dulcedinem, et panem promissum intellexit datum. Et jacuit ros per circuitum castrorum, et erat granum minutum quasi semen coriandri, album in modum pruinæ, et quasi pilo tusum. Hoc est quod in textu subjungitur : Quumque operuisset ros superficiem terræ, apparuit in solitudine minutum. Non ait : Apparuit in solitudine minutus, videlicet ipse ros, sed tanquam de re alia loquens : Apparuit, inquit, in solitudine minutum, et quasi pilo tusum, etc., id est res quædam minuta, ante incognita, neque visa, et quasi pilo tusa, id est quasi tali instrumento percussa, quoniam erat mundum ac lucidum, quasi fuisset in mortariolo tusum, folliculisque exutum, quemadmodum et a grano frumenti cortex percussionibus amovetur.
paras.en: But the Catholic doctors who say that the manna is meant by the dew say this by the likeness of the one to the other. For in the *Scholastic History* too it is said, from Josephus: In the morning, when Moses had prayed, the dew coming down was smeared on his hands, and at first he supposed it to be rain; but when he had tasted it he perceived the sweetness of honey, and understood that the promised bread had been given. And the dew lay round about the camp, and there was a small grain like coriander seed, white in the manner of hoar frost, and as it were beaten with a pestle. This is what is added in the text: [[16:14|And when it had covered|Quumque operuisset]] (the dew) [[16:14|the face of the earth, it appeared in the wilderness small|superficiem terræ, apparuit in solitudine minutum]]. He does not say, It appeared in the wilderness small [*minutus*, masculine, agreeing with *ros*, "dew"], meaning the dew itself; but as though speaking of another thing he says: [[16:14|it appeared|Apparuit]], [[16:14|in the wilderness small|in solitudine minutum]] [*minutum*, neuter: "a small thing"], [[16:14|and as it were beaten with a pestle|et quasi pilo tusum]], etc.; that is, a certain small thing, unknown and unseen before, and as it were beaten with a pestle, that is, as if struck with such an instrument, since it was clean and bright, as if it had been pounded in a little mortar and stripped of its husks, just as the husk is taken off a grain of wheat by beating.

paras.t: Quod quum vidissent filii Israel, dixerunt ad invicem : Manhu? quod significat, Quid est hoc? Ignorabant enim quid esset. Ideo admirando ita locuti sunt. Neque enim simile quid visum antea fuit, ejusdem videlicet speciei. Si autem fuisset idem quod ros, non sic admirati fuissent. Quibus ait Moyses : Iste est panis, id est materia panis ex eo fiendi. Vel nomine panis intelligitur quodlibet alimentum. Manna autem per se fuit aliqualiter refectivum, Quem Dominus dedit vobis ad vescendum.
paras.en: [[16:15|And when the children of Israel saw it, they said one to another: Manhu! which signifieth: What is this!|Quod quum vidissent filii Israel, dixerunt ad invicem : Manhu? quod significat, Quid est hoc?]] [[16:15|for they knew not what it was|Ignorabant enim quid esset]]. Therefore they spoke thus in wonder; for nothing like it, that is, of the same kind, had been seen before. If it had been the same thing as dew, they would not have wondered so. [[16:15|And Moses said to them: This is the bread|Quibus ait Moyses : Iste est panis]], that is, the matter of the bread to be made from it. Or by the name of *bread* any food is meant; and the manna was in itself in some measure nourishing: [[16:15|which the Lord hath given you to eat|Quem Dominus dedit vobis ad vescendum]].

paras.t: Hic est sermo quem præcepit Dominus, id est ejus significationem jussit a vobis impleri. Unde sermo hic sumitur pro re significata per ipsum. Deinde præceptum subjungitur : Colligat unusquisque ex eo quantum sufficit ad vescendum, gomor per singula capita, id est, pro unoquoque supposito colligatur tantum, sicut continet mensura nomine gomor, quæ secundum Glossam est mensura quinque sextariorum, et ut in fine hujus capituli scribitur, est decima pars ephi, quam mensuram Josephus vocat assarium. Nomina autem et modi mensurarum, apud diversos diversificantur, sicut numismata : ideo latet nos quantitas determinata illius mensuræ, secundum nostrarum maneriem mensurarum. Recitat tamen Lyra, quod secundum Rabbi Salomonem, gomor tenet quantitatem quadraginta duorum ovorum. Alii ex dictis Isidori ac Papiæ nituntur probare, quod gomor continet quartam Parisiensem cum media. Juxta numerum animarum vestrarum quæ habitant in tabernaculo, sic tolletis : hoc est, unusquisque paterfamilias accipiet omni die tot gomor repleta ex manna, quot sunt in domo sua personæ quæ vescantur hoc pane.
paras.en: [[16:16|This is the word that the Lord hath commanded|Hic est sermo quem præcepit Dominus]], that is, he has ordered that what it signifies be fulfilled by you. Hence *word* is taken here for the thing signified by it. Then the command is added: [[16:16|Let every one gather of it as much as is enough to eat; a gomor for every man|Colligat unusquisque ex eo quantum sufficit ad vescendum, gomor per singula capita]], that is, let as much be gathered for each person as the measure called a gomor holds. According to the Gloss this is a measure of five sextarii, and, as is written at the end of this chapter, it is [[16:36|the tenth part of an ephi|decima pars ephi]]; Josephus calls this measure an *assarium*. But the names and sizes of measures differ among different peoples, as coins do; so the exact quantity of that measure, reckoned by our kind of measures, is hidden from us. Lyra reports, however, that according to Rabbi Salomon a gomor holds the quantity of forty-two eggs. Others try to prove from the words of Isidore and Papias that a gomor holds a Paris quart and a half. [[16:16|according to the number of your souls that dwell in a tent, so shall you take of it|Juxta numerum animarum vestrarum quæ habitant in tabernaculo, sic tolletis]]: that is, every father of a family shall take each day as many gomors filled with manna as there are persons in his house who eat of this bread.

paras.t: Quamvis autem unus naturaliter multo plus manducet quam alter, Deus tamen præfixit universis et singulis eamdem mensuram : quoniam teste Josepho, quemadmodum manna supernaturaliter donabatur, sic supernaturaliter Deus disposuit, ut et fortioribus sufficeret illa mensura, et a debilioribus posset sine excessu consumi, ne fortiores cupiditate gulaque ducti, tam multum et impetuose colligerent, quod debiliores fraudarentur, fieretque inter eos turbatio. Nec his contrariatur quod subditur : Feceruntque ita filii Israel, et collegerunt, alius plus, alius minus. Quidam enim habuerunt plures domesticos, alii pauciores : ideo unus potuit plus mannæ de terra colligere, alius minus. Sed in hoc servabatur æqualitas, quod pro unaquaque persona æque multum dabatur et reservabatur de manna. Propterea sequitur : Et mensi sunt ad mensuram gomor : quia pro unoquoque tantum accipiebatur. Nec qui plus de manna collegerat, habuit amplius ; nec qui minus paraverat, hoc est, sibi procuraverat, reperit minus ; sed singuli juxta id quod edere poterant, congregaverunt, hoc est, unusquisque sibi assumpsit præfatam mensuram. Verumtamen sicut Magister in historiis subtiliter tangit, istud dupliciter intelligi potest. Primo, sic quod collecta ex manna, reponebantur in grandes acervos, ex quibus unicuique unum gomor mensurabatur atque dabatur. Secundo, sic quod quantumcumque quis pro se collegerat, tamen veniens domum, non reperit nisi mensuram unius gomor. Et secundum Josephum, quod ultra hoc fuit collectum et reservatum, ad nihil utile fuit in crastino, quoniam vermes et amaritudo illud consumpserant. Porro littera primo intellectui magis consonare videtur. Nam dictum est, Mensi sunt ad mensuram gomor.
paras.en: Now although one man by nature eats much more than another, yet God fixed the same measure for all and each: for, as Josephus witnesses, just as the manna was given supernaturally, so God supernaturally arranged that this measure should be enough for the stronger and could be eaten up without excess by the weaker; lest the stronger, led by greed and gluttony, should gather so much and so headlong that the weaker were cheated, and there should be disorder among them. Nor is this contradicted by what is added: [[16:17|And the children of Israel did so: and they gathered, one more, another less|Feceruntque ita filii Israel, et collegerunt, alius plus, alius minus]]. For some had more members of their household, others fewer; so one could gather more manna from the ground, another less. But equality was kept in this, that for each person an equal amount of manna was given and kept. Therefore there follows: [[16:18|And they measured by the measure of a gomor|Et mensi sunt ad mensuram gomor]]: because so much was taken for each one. [[16:18|neither had he more that had gathered more|Nec qui plus de manna collegerat, habuit amplius]]; [[16:18|nor did he find less|reperit minus]] [[16:18|that had provided less|nec qui minus paraverat]], that is, had procured for himself; [[16:18|but every one had gathered, according to what they were able to eat|sed singuli juxta id quod edere poterant, congregaverunt]]: that is, each took for himself the measure spoken of. Yet, as the Master touches on subtly in the *Histories*, this can be understood in two ways. First, that the manna gathered was laid up in great heaps, from which one gomor was measured out and given to each. Second, that however much a man had gathered for himself, yet when he came home he found only the measure of one gomor; and, according to Josephus, whatever was gathered and kept beyond this was good for nothing the next day, because worms and bitterness had consumed it. But the letter seems to agree better with the first understanding; for it is said: [[16:18|They measured by the measure of a gomor|Mensi sunt ad mensuram gomor]].

paras.t: Dixitque Moyses ad eos : Nullus relinquat ex eo in mane, hoc est, nullus vestrum reservet de mensura mannæ unius diei aliquid in diem sequentem. Cujus præcepti causa superius tacta est, ne scilicet solliciti essent de crastino, nec ex tali sollicitudine unus alterum defraudaret in colligendo, sed filialem habendo confidentiam in providentia Dei, et exonerati a cura et requisitione pro sustentatione futura, Deo liberius deservirent. Verumtamen sexta die servabant manna pro die sequenti, ut infra exprimitur. Qui non audierunt eum, hoc est, præcepto Moysis jam præfato non obedierunt : sed dimiserunt quidam ex eis usque mane. Et dicunt Hebræi, quod isti erant Dathan et Abiron. Potius autem puto, quod multi fuerunt, quum infra tot centena millia, factum duorum virorum non tantum reputaretur. Et scatere cœpit vermibus, atque computruit manna sic reservatum die sequenti. Hoc tamen (ut creditur) non venit ex natura mannæ, imo hoc conservabile fuit ex sua natura ad tempus diutius, sed in detestationem inobedientiæ, gulositatis, ac immoderatæ sollicitudinis reservantium manna, jussit Deus illud ita corrumpi, et ne amplius sic servarent. Et iratus est contra eos Moyses ira per zelum, ex caritate, et affectu justitiæ. Nam ut apparet, mortaliter peccaverunt sic reservando contra præceptum. Moyses autem excessum illorum cognovit, vel ex revelatione divina, vel ex revelatione humana.
paras.en: [[16:19|And Moses said to them: Let no man leave thereof till the morning|Dixitque Moyses ad eos : Nullus relinquat ex eo in mane]], that is, let none of you keep anything of one day's measure of manna for the following day. The reason for this command was touched on above: that they should not be anxious about the morrow, nor through such anxiety one cheat another in gathering, but, having a son's confidence in the providence of God, and freed from care and from seeking their future sustenance, they should serve God more freely. On the sixth day, however, they kept manna for the following day, as is stated below. [[16:20|And they hearkened not to him|Qui non audierunt eum]], that is, they did not obey the command of Moses just given, [[16:20|but some of them left until the morning|sed dimiserunt quidam ex eis usque mane]]. The Hebrews say that these were Dathan and Abiron. But I think rather that there were many, since among so many hundreds of thousands the deed of two men would not have been counted so much. [[16:20|and it began to be full of worms, and it putrified|Et scatere cœpit vermibus, atque computruit]], that is, the manna kept thus, on the following day. This, however (as is believed), did not come from the nature of the manna; on the contrary, by its nature it would have kept for a longer time; but in detestation of the disobedience, gluttony and immoderate anxiety of those who kept the manna, God ordered it to be so corrupted, so that they would not keep it like this any more. [[16:20|and Moses was angry with them|Et iratus est contra eos Moyses]], with the anger of zeal, out of charity and love of justice. For, as it appears, they sinned mortally by keeping it so against the command. And Moses knew of their excess either by divine revelation or by human report.

paras.t: Colligebant autem mane singuli manna, quantum sufficere poterat ad vescendum : puta mensuram gomor. Quumque incaluisset sol, id est sole paululum ascendente, et terram calefaciente, manna liquefiebat, (quum juxta ignem induraretur, quod rori non convenit : idcirco non fuit ros) : ideo mane colligebatur, statim quum ros ei admixtus, resolutus et consumptus esset a solis calore. In die autem sexta collegerunt cibos duplices, id est duo gomor per singulos homines. Qualiter hoc possit dupliciter intelligi, paulo ante inductum est. Qui autem exponunt hoc sic, quod sexta die non collegerunt plus quam aliis feriis, probant hoc per textum sequentem : Venerunt autem omnes principes multitudinis, et narraverunt Moysi. Quod ita exponunt : Principes vulgi admirantes de hoc, quod mensura mannæ sexta die collectæ, fuit in se ipsa sic duplicata miraculose, quod tantum invenerunt in domo, ac si ipsa sexta die duplum collegissent, venerunt et recitaverunt Moysi tantum miraculum. Præterea, qui vellet aliam expositionem tenere, posset hanc litteram aliter explanare, dicendo quod venerunt, nuntiaveruntque Moysi, duplicem quantitatem mannæ se collegisse in sexta die, sicut eis præcepit, ut ab eo audirent, quando et qualiter facerent panes ex duplo illo, et an esset periculum de mannæ putrefactione. Imo, quod iste sit sensus clausulæ hujus, videtur ex verbis sequentibus.
paras.en: [[16:21|Now every one of them gathered in the morning|Colligebant autem mane singuli]] the manna, [[16:21|as much as might suffice to eat|quantum sufficere poterat ad vescendum]]: namely the measure of a gomor. [[16:21|and after the sun grew hot|Quumque incaluisset sol]], that is, as the sun rose a little and warmed the ground, the manna [[16:21|melted|liquefiebat]] (whereas by the fire it hardened, which does not befit dew: therefore it was not dew); so it was gathered in the morning, as soon as the dew mixed with it had been melted and consumed by the heat of the sun. [[16:22|But on the sixth day they gathered twice as much, that is, two gomors every man|In die autem sexta collegerunt cibos duplices, id est duo gomor per singulos homines]]. How this can be understood in two ways was set out a little before. Those who expound it as meaning that on the sixth day they gathered no more than on the other days prove it by the text that follows: [[16:22|and all the rulers of the multitude came, and told Moses|Venerunt autem omnes principes multitudinis, et narraverunt Moysi]]. This they expound thus: the princes of the people, wondering that the measure of manna gathered on the sixth day had of itself been so miraculously doubled that they found as much at home as if they had gathered double on that sixth day, came and told Moses of so great a miracle. But anyone who wished to hold the other exposition could explain this letter otherwise, saying that they came and told Moses that they had gathered a double quantity of manna on the sixth day, as he had commanded them, so as to hear from him when and how they should make bread from that double portion, and whether there was any danger of the manna putrefying. Indeed, that this is the sense of this clause appears from the words that follow.

paras.t: Quibus ait eis : Hoc est quod locutus est Dominus : Requies sabbati sanctificata est Domino, id est, quies, qua die septima cessandum est ab operibus atque laboribus, ordinatur ad hoc, ut tunc Deo vacetur ; ejusque cultui dedicatur requies illa, idcirco in ea nihil coquendum est. Unde subjungitur : cras quodcumque operandum est, facite ; et quæ coquenda sunt, coquite. Hoc est, ea quæ die crastina, scilicet sabbato, faceretis et coqueretis, nisi præceptum celebrandi sabbatum impediret, facite et coquite sexta die. Quidquid autem reliquum fuerit, id est, quod de manna non consumitis, qua die illud collegistis, reponite usque in mane, id est, reservate pro die sequenti seu sabbato. Feceruntque ita ut præceperat Moyses, et non computruit, neque vermis inventus est in eo, puta in manna sic reservato, seu in pane formato : quæ formatio seu decoctio fiebat in die sexto, secundum modum qui in Numeris est descriptus, et paulo post tangetur.
paras.en: [[16:23|And he said to them: This is what the Lord hath spoken|Quibus ait eis : Hoc est quod locutus est Dominus]]: [[16:23|the rest of the sabbath sanctified to the Lord|Requies sabbati sanctificata est Domino]]: that is, the rest by which work and labour are to cease on the seventh day is ordained to this, that men may then give themselves to God; and that rest is dedicated to his worship, so nothing is to be cooked on it. Hence it is added: [[16:23|To morrow|cras]] [Denis takes *cras*, "to-morrow", with the words that follow], [[16:23|Whatsoever work is to be done, do it; and the meats that are to be dressed, dress them|quodcumque operandum est, facite ; et quæ coquenda sunt, coquite]]. That is, what you would do and cook to-morrow, namely on the sabbath, if the command to keep the sabbath did not forbid it, do and cook on the sixth day. [[16:23|and whatsoever shall remain|Quidquid autem reliquum fuerit]], that is, whatever of the manna you do not eat on the day you gathered it, [[16:23|lay it up until the morning|reponite usque in mane]], that is, keep it for the following day, or the sabbath. [[16:24|And they did so as Moses had commanded, and it did not putrify, neither was there worm found in it|Feceruntque ita ut præceperat Moyses, et non computruit, neque vermis inventus est in eo]], namely in the manna kept thus, or in the bread made from it: this making or baking was done on the sixth day, in the way described in Numbers[[Num 11:8||]], which will be touched on a little later.

paras.t: Dixitque Moyses : Comedite illud hodie. Istud dixit Moyses in ipsa sabbati die, ut sit sensus : Illud quod reservastis de manna ac alio cibo, a die præcedente usque in hodiernum, manducate hoc septimo die ; quia sabbatum Domini est : propter quod reservastis illud in hunc diem, in quo non licet manna colligere, imo nec invenietur in eo. Ideo subditur : non invenietur hodie in agro, id est in terra hujus deserti, in qua quasi in agro aliquid crescit graminis seu herbarum. Sex diebus colligite, etc., sicut expositum est.
paras.en: [[16:25|And Moses said: Eat it to day|Dixitque Moyses : Comedite illud hodie]]. Moses said this on the sabbath day itself, so that the sense is: What you have kept of the manna and of other food from the day before until to-day, eat on this seventh day, [[16:25|because it is the sabbath of the Lord|quia sabbatum Domini est]]: for which reason you have kept it for this day, on which it is not lawful to gather manna; indeed, none will be found on it. Therefore it is added: [[16:25|to day it shall not be found in the field|non invenietur hodie in agro]], that is, in the land of this desert, in which, as in a field, some grass or herbs grow. [[16:26|Gather it six days|Sex diebus colligite]], etc., as has been expounded.

paras.t: Venitque septima dies, et egressi de populo, ut colligerent manna, quum tamen esuriem non haberent, nec indigerent colligere, sed superflua sollicitudo, gulositas, aut etiam curiositas incitavit eos ad illum egressum, quatenus experirentur an prolata a Moyse, essent vera, non invenerunt. Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen : Usquequo non vultis, id est, aliqui ex vobis non volunt, custodire mandata mea, quæ vobis præcepi de modo et tempore colligendi, edendique manna, et legem meam de sabbati celebritate servanda ? Videte quod Dominus dederit vobis sabbatum, id est, diem sabbati celebrari præcepit, et in eo vos quiescere jussit : et propter hoc die sexta tribuit vobis cibos duplices. Maneat unusquisque apud semetipsum, id est, de loco suo non recedat. Unde expositorie subditur : nullus egrediatur de loco suo die septimo, id est, ad operandum non exeat, nec usque ad fatigationem conficiat iter, nec sine rationabili causa suæ habitationis exeat septa. Et sabbatizavit, hoc est, ab exterioribus quievit operibus, populus die septimo : ad recordandum beneficia Dei, specialiter creationis beneficium, atque ad quiescendum in Deo per exercitia devotionis. Sic utique quidam in populo illo sabbatizaverunt, videlicet justi. Alii corporaliter, non spiritualiter, sabbatizabant, qui et per mentis distractionem, inordinatas affectiones, ac alias culpas, a se ipsis longe digrediebantur.
paras.en: [[16:27|And the seventh day came; and some of the people going forth to gather|Venitque septima dies, et egressi de populo, ut colligerent]] manna (though they were not hungry and had no need to gather, but needless anxiety, gluttony, or even curiosity moved them to go out, to find out whether what Moses had said was true), [[16:27|found none|non invenerunt]]. [[16:28|And the Lord said to Moses: How long will you refuse|Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen : Usquequo non vultis]], that is, some of you refuse, [[16:28|to keep my commandments|custodire mandata mea]], which I gave you about the manner and time of gathering and eating the manna, [[16:28|and my law|et legem meam]] about keeping the feast of the sabbath? [[16:29|See that the Lord hath given you the sabbath|Videte quod Dominus dederit vobis sabbatum]], that is, he has commanded the sabbath day to be kept and ordered you to rest on it; [[16:29|and for this reason on the sixth day he giveth you a double provision|et propter hoc die sexta tribuit vobis cibos duplices]]. [[16:29|let each man stay at home|Maneat unusquisque apud semetipsum]], that is, let him not go away from his place. Hence it is added by way of explanation: [[16:29|let none go forth out of his place the seventh day|nullus egrediatur de loco suo die septimo]], that is, let him not go out to work, nor make a journey to the point of weariness, nor leave the bounds of his dwelling without reasonable cause. [[16:30|And the people kept the sabbath|Et sabbatizavit]], that is, rested from outward works, [[16:30|on the seventh day|populus die septimo]]: to recall the benefits of God, especially the benefit of creation, and to rest in God by the exercises of devotion. So indeed some among that people kept the sabbath, namely the just. Others kept the sabbath bodily, not spiritually: by distraction of mind, disordered affections and other faults they wandered far from themselves.

paras.t: Præterea, sicut fatur Andreas expositor, De manna contulit Deus octo præcepta : Primum, ut unusquisque colligeret manna quantum putaret sibi sufficere, utpote gomor pro quolibet homine. Secundum, ut unusquisque quotidie comederet unum gomor de manna præcise. Tertium, ut mane colligerent. Quartum, ut non reservarent ex manna in crastinum pro aliquo sex dierum. Quintum, ut sexto die colligerent duplum. Sextum, ut sexto die reservarent unum gomor pro sabbato. Septimum, ut illud gomor in sabbato manducarent. Octavum, ut unum vas continens mensuram gomor reservaretur de manna in tabernaculo, ad perpetuam rei memoriam. Itaque, qui in aliquo horum excesserunt, videntur peccasse mortaliter.
paras.en: Moreover, as Andrew the expositor [that is, Andrew of Saint Victor] says, God gave eight commands about the manna. First, that each should gather as much manna as he thought would suffice him, namely a gomor for each person. Second, that each should eat exactly one gomor of manna every day. Third, that they should gather it in the morning. Fourth, that they should not keep any manna for the next day on any of the six days. Fifth, that on the sixth day they should gather double. Sixth, that on the sixth day they should keep one gomor for the sabbath. Seventh, that they should eat that gomor on the sabbath. Eighth, that one vessel holding the measure of a gomor of manna should be kept in the tabernacle, for a perpetual memorial of the thing. So those who went beyond any of these seem to have sinned mortally.

paras.t: Appellavitque domus Israel nomen ejus, Man, id est, Israeliticus populus panem illum cum rore delapsum vocavit Man ; quia dum primo viderunt eum, dixerunt : Manhu ? quod est quid complexum, id est duæ dictiones, et sonat, Quid est hoc ? ita quod MAN, significat, quid ; HU autem, hoc. Nam et Josephus sic exponit. Posteriores tamen Judæi dicunt, per Man, significari præparatum (seu rem præparatam) ad comestionem : sicque diceretur panis hic, man, id est res a Deo præparata ad esum. Nos autem vocamus eum manna, id est panem cælestem. Quod erat quasi semen coriandri, id est simile semini illi in figura et quantitate, quoniam parvum fuit atque rotundum ; sed in colore differebat a semine illo quod nigrum est. Manna vero exstitit album, sicut in textu subjungitur : album, gustusque ejus quasi simila cum melle, id est, dulcissimi fuit saporis ad instar panis confecti ex simila melle mixta. Simila quippe est delicatissima atque purissima tritici farina. De hoc pane et ejus sapore ac confectione, legitur in Numeris : Erat man quasi semen coriandri coloris bdellii. Circuibatque populus, et colligens illud, frangebat mola, sive terebat in mortario, coquens in olla, et faciens ex eo tortulas saporis quasi panis oleati. Dicitur autem panis oleatus, in cujus pistratione oleum admisceatur.
paras.en: [[16:31|And the house of Israel called the name thereof|Appellavitque domus Israel nomen ejus]] *Man* [the Douay-Rheims has "Manna"; the Latin text reads *Man*], that is, the people of Israel called that bread which fell with the dew *Man*; because when they first saw it they said: *Manhu?*, which is a compound, that is, two words, and means *What is this?*; so that *man* means "what", and *hu* "this". For Josephus too expounds it so. But later Jews say that *man* signifies "prepared" (or a thing prepared) for eating; and so this bread would be called *man*, that is, a thing prepared by God to be eaten. We, however, call it *manna*, that is, heavenly bread. [[16:31|and it was like coriander seed|Quod erat quasi semen coriandri]], that is, like that seed in shape and size, since it was small and round; but in colour it differed from that seed, which is black. The manna was white, as is added in the text: [[16:31|white, and the taste thereof like to flour with honey|album, gustusque ejus quasi simila cum melle]], that is, it had a very sweet taste, like bread made of fine flour mixed with honey; for *simila* is the most delicate and purest flour of wheat. Of this bread, its taste and its making, we read in Numbers: [[Num 11:7|the manna was like coriander seed, of the colour of bdellium|Erat man quasi semen coriandri coloris bdellii]]. [[Num 11:8|And the people went about, and gathering it, ground it in a mill, or beat it in a mortar, and boiled it in a pot, and made cakes thereof of the taste of bread tempered with oil|Circuibatque populus, et colligens illud, frangebat mola, sive terebat in mortario, coquens in olla, et faciens ex eo tortulas saporis quasi panis oleati]]. Bread *tempered with oil* is bread in the kneading of which oil is mixed.

paras.t: Sed quæri potest, si panis ille fuit tam dulcis, cur quidam dixerunt de eo, Anima nostra nauseat, et arida est, super cibo isto levissimo. Respondetur, quod naturalis sapor mannæ, fuit dulcis valde et unicus, utpote talis, ut dictum est. Alius fuit sapor ejus supernaturalis ac multiplex, quem habuit in virtuosis ac justis, quibus sapiebat ut voluerunt. Si enim appetebant refici aliquo genere carnium aut piscium, sapuit eis ut cibus ille optatus : quod fuit ex gratia Dei, meritisque vescentium. Tertius fuit sapor ejus accidentalis, quem habuit in injustis, quibus propter eorum perversitatem fuit insipidus. Verumtamen in Scholastica historia legitur : Quod autem dicitur, quia sapiebat in ore cujusque quod desiderabat, non est multum authenticum. Forsitan ideo dictum est, quoniam liber Sapientiæ, ex quo dictum illud accipitur, non est de numero Scripturæ canonicæ. Verumtamen istud jam satis authenticum est, et viri catholici tenent sic communiter. Unde et Sapiens idem ait : Angelorum esca nutrivisti populum tuum, et paratum panem de cælo præstitisti illis sine labore, omne delectamentum in se habentem, et omnis saporis suavitatem : substantiam enim tuam, et dulcedinem quam in filios habes, ostendebas : et deserviens uniuscujusque voluntati, ad quod quisque volebat, convertebatur. Dicit autem et Josephus quod locus ille quo manna primum descendit, hactenus rigatur siccis imbribus et hujusmodi rore.
paras.en: But it may be asked: if that bread was so sweet, why did some say of it, [[Num 21:5|our soul now loatheth|Anima nostra nauseat]], and is dry, [[Num 21:5|this very light food|super cibo isto levissimo]] [Denis adds "and is dry" from Num 11:6, "Our soul is dry"]? The answer is that the natural taste of the manna was very sweet and of one kind, namely such as has been said. Another taste of it was supernatural and manifold, which it had for the virtuous and just, to whom it tasted as they wished. For if they longed to be refreshed with some kind of meat or fish, it tasted to them like that food they desired: and this was from the grace of God and the merits of those who ate. A third taste of it was accidental, which it had for the unjust, to whom, because of their perversity, it was tasteless. Yet in the *Scholastic History* we read: But what is said, that it tasted in each one's mouth of what he desired, is not very authoritative. Perhaps this was said because the book of Wisdom, from which that saying is taken, is not of the number of the canonical Scriptures [that is, it was not then received by all as canonical]. But this is now authoritative enough, and Catholic men commonly hold it so. Hence the Wise Man himself says: [[Wis 16:20|thou didst feed thy people with the food of angels, and gavest them bread from heaven, prepared without labour; having in it all that is delicious, and the sweetness of every taste|Angelorum esca nutrivisti populum tuum, et paratum panem de cælo præstitisti illis sine labore, omne delectamentum in se habentem, et omnis saporis suavitatem]]: [[Wis 16:21|For thy sustenance shewed thy sweetness to thy children, and serving every man's will, it was turned to what every man liked|substantiam enim tuam, et dulcedinem quam in filios habes, ostendebas : et deserviens uniuscujusque voluntati, ad quod quisque volebat, convertebatur]] [Denis's text reads "thou didst shew thy substance, and the sweetness which thou hast toward thy children"]. Josephus also says that the place where the manna first came down is still watered with dry showers and with dew of this kind.

paras.t: Dixit autem Moyses : Iste est sermo quem præcepit Dominus : Imple gomor ex eo : hoc est, Dominus mihi jussit, ut faciam mensuram gomor impleri hoc manna : et custodiatur in futuras retro generationes, id est per tempora futura, durante statu et ritu Israeliticæ plebis, ut noverint panem quo alui vos in solitudine, quando ducti estis de terra Ægypti : hoc est, quatenus posteri vestri recolant et perpendant, quam gratiose et miraculose nutrivi patres eorum in eremo, ut et grati sint Deo, et roborentur in fide.
paras.en: [[16:32|And Moses said: This is the word which the Lord hath commanded: Fill a gomor of it|Dixit autem Moyses : Iste est sermo quem præcepit Dominus : Imple gomor ex eo]]: that is, the Lord has ordered me to have the measure of a gomor filled with this manna; [[16:32|and let it be kept unto generations to come hereafter|et custodiatur in futuras retro generationes]], that is, through the times to come, while the state and rite of the people of Israel last; [[16:32|that they may know the bread, wherewith I fed you in the wilderness when you were brought forth out of the land of Egypt|ut noverint panem quo alui vos in solitudine, quando ducti estis de terra Ægypti]]: that is, so that your descendants may recall and weigh how graciously and miraculously I fed their fathers in the desert, that they may both be grateful to God and be strengthened in faith.

paras.t: Dixitque Moyses ad Aaron : Sume vas unum, hoc est receptaculum aptum : est equidem proprietas Hebræi sermonis, ut quod contentivum est alicujus rei, vas appelletur ; et mitte ibi man, id est, manna pone in vase illo, quantum potest capere gomor, videlicet mensura sic nuncupata ; et repone coram Domino, hoc est in tabernaculo, in quo Dominus specialiter esse et habitare censetur, ad servandum in generationes vestras, sicut præcepit Dominus Moysi. Posuitque illud Aaron in tabernaculo reservandum. Primo enim posuit manna illud in urna, imo in aurea urna, ut in historiis ait Magister. Unde in epistola ad Hebræos habetur : Urna aurea habens manna.
paras.en: [[16:33|And Moses said to Aaron: Take a vessel|Dixitque Moyses ad Aaron : Sume vas unum]], that is, a fitting receptacle: for it is a property of the Hebrew tongue that whatever contains anything is called a vessel; [[16:33|and put manna into it|et mitte ibi man]], that is, put manna in that vessel, [[16:33|as much as a gomor can hold|quantum potest capere gomor]], namely the measure so called; [[16:33|and lay it up before the Lord|et repone coram Domino]], that is, in the tabernacle, in which the Lord is held to be and dwell in a special way, [[16:33|to keep unto your generations|ad servandum in generationes vestras]], [[16:34|As the Lord commanded Moses. And Aaron put it in the tabernacle to be kept|sicut præcepit Dominus Moysi. Posuitque illud Aaron in tabernaculo reservandum]]. For first he put that manna in a pot, indeed in a golden pot, as the Master says in the *Histories*. Hence we have in the Epistle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 9:4|a golden pot that had manna|Urna aurea habens manna]].

paras.t: Denique jam in isto articulo dictum est, quod quando Moyses jussit hæc, fuit ibi tabernaculum parvum ; et in illo, quidam Catholici et Hebræi affirmant, urnam illam cum manna fuisse locatam, quousque magnum tabernaculum fuit constructum. Alii dicunt, quod non fuit positum vas illud cum manna, nisi in tabernaculo magno. Unde quod hic dicitur, intelligunt dictum per prolepsim, id est anticipationem, qua aliquid recitatur quasi antea factum, quum tamen factum sit postea, sicque Augustinus exponit : imo (ut fertur) Hebræi nonnulli testantur, quod Deus non dedit istud præceptum ante magni tabernaculi constructionem in monte Sinai facti, ut infra describitur.
paras.en: Lastly, it has already been said in this article that when Moses ordered these things there was a small tabernacle there; and some Catholics and Hebrews affirm that the pot with the manna was placed in it until the great tabernacle was built. Others say that the vessel with the manna was placed only in the great tabernacle. So they understand what is said here as said by prolepsis, that is, anticipation, by which something is told as if done before, though it was in fact done afterwards; and so Augustine expounds it. Indeed (as is reported) some Hebrews testify that God did not give this command before the building of the great tabernacle, made at Mount Sinai, as is described below.

paras.t: Filii autem Israel comederunt man quadraginta annis, videlicet toto tempore quo fuerunt in deserto. Ideo subditur : donec venirent in terram habitabilem. Hoc cibo aliti sunt usquequo tangerent fines terræ Chanaan. Verumtamen sicut in Glossa ex Augustino asseritur, non est intelligendum quod filii Israel cessaverunt comedere manna, statim ut introierunt habitabiles terras. Transierunt enim per Idumæam ex latere, et per regna Sehon et Og usque Jordanem, in quibus terris usi sunt manna. Additque Augustinus, quod in terris illis potuerunt fortassis uti tam manna, quam alio pane. Transito autem Jordane, et facta circumcisione secunda in Galgalis, celebratoque Pascha, defecit manna die sequenti, quum comedissent de frugibus terræ Chanaan, ut habetur in libro Josue.
paras.en: [[16:35|And the children of Israel ate manna forty years|Filii autem Israel comederunt man quadraginta annis]], namely the whole time they were in the desert. Therefore it is added: [[16:35|till they came to a habitable land|donec venirent in terram habitabilem]]: [[16:35|with this meat were they fed, until they reached the borders of the land of Chanaan|Hoc cibo aliti sunt usquequo tangerent fines terræ Chanaan]]. Yet, as is stated in the Gloss from Augustine, it is not to be understood that the children of Israel stopped eating manna as soon as they entered habitable lands. For they passed by the side of Edom, and through the kingdoms of Sehon and Og as far as the Jordan, and in those lands they used manna. And Augustine adds that in those lands they could perhaps use both manna and other bread. But when the Jordan had been crossed, the second circumcision made at Galgala, and the Pasch celebrated, the manna ceased on the following day, after they had eaten of the corn of the land of Chanaan, as we have in the book of Josue[[Jos 5:12||]] [the margin's reference is partly unread (Josue v, 1…); the passage is Jos 5:10–12].

paras.t: Postremo, circa hæc recitat Rabbi Paulus, quod inter Hebræos antiquos multum authenticos, fuit disceptatio grandis de manna. Nam quidam eorum, videlicet Rabbi Aquila, dixit manna fuisse panem quo vescuntur et angeli : quod alius nomine Rabbi Ismael reprobavit, dicens angelos non vesci corporeo cibo. Moderni autem Hebræi, ut Rabbi Moyses Gerundensis, et alii, sequuntur primam opinionem, dicentes quod manna fuit lumen divinum incorporatum : sicque filii Israel reficiebantur eodem pane, quo angeli reficiuntur : ii quidem lumine divino non incorporato, Israelitæ autem lumine divino incorporato. Sed ista opinio stulta et rudis est. Si enim per lumen divinum intelligunt lumen increatum æternum, quod Deus est, constat illud non esse incorporatum. Si autem per lumen divinum intelligunt lumen creatum, videlicet lumen gloriæ, aut aliquid tale angelis sanctis infusum sive inhærens, certum est, quod illud non sit substantia, sed accidens quoddam, cui non competit incorporari, neque corporaliter alere et augere. Ideo Sancti dicunt, quod manna fuit quid corporale, ministerio angelorum formatum in aere. Unde et panis angelorum vocatur, non quod illo vescantur, sed quia ad ejus formationem ac administrationem seu descensum, obsequebantur.
paras.en: Lastly, on these matters Rabbi Paul [that is, Paul of Burgos] reports that among the ancient Hebrews of great authority there was a great dispute about the manna. For one of them, Rabbi Aquila, said that the manna was the bread on which the angels also feed; this another, named Rabbi Ismael, rejected, saying that angels do not feed on bodily food. But the later Hebrews, such as Rabbi Moses of Gerona [that is, Nachmanides] and others, follow the first opinion, saying that the manna was the divine light embodied; and so the children of Israel were fed with the same bread with which the angels are fed: the angels with the divine light not embodied, the Israelites with the divine light embodied. But this opinion is foolish and crude. For if by the divine light they mean the uncreated, eternal light, which is God, it is plain that it is not embodied. And if by the divine light they mean a created light, namely the light of glory, or some such thing poured into or inhering in the holy angels, it is certain that this is not a substance but an accident, to which it does not belong to be embodied, nor to nourish and increase bodily. Therefore the Saints say that the manna was something bodily, formed in the air by the ministry of the angels. Hence it is also called the bread of angels, not because they feed on it, but because they served in its forming, its dispensing, or its coming down.

16.title: Spiritualis ejusdem capituli sextidecimi elucidatio
16.title_en: Spiritual explanation of the same sixteenth chapter

paras.t: Quum venissent filii Israel in desertum Sin, murmuraverunt contra Moysen propter victualium carentiam, et loci asperitatem atque infecunditatem. Per solitudinem illam, arcta via salutis, conversatio pœnitentialis, claustralis quoque religio designatur. Itaque per carnalium Judæorum murmurationem, figurata est impatientia, indignatio, murmuratio Christianorum modicam fidem habentium, qui adhuc sensualitatem non evicerunt. Isti post arreptum iter salutis, post pœnitentiam inchoatam, aut post religionis ingressum, tentantur de facili, dum adversitates, irrisiones, persecutiones aut infirmitates eis contingunt, dum non reficiuntur ad libitum, dum fame, siti aut frigore affliguntur, in tantum ut interdum suis superioribus indignentur, aut obloquantur, vel quod pejus est, in faciem injurientur eisdem. Non enim attendunt providentiam Dei, omnia justissime pro suorum electorum salute moderantis ac disponentis. Idcirco in tentatione deficiunt, et propria impatientia superantur. Denique sicut et Origenes conscribit, quando de intemperie cœli, de infecunditate terræ et arborum, de imbrium raritate, de aliorum prosperitatibus causamur, murmur contra Deum attollimus. Et sicut in filios Israel murmurantes, tandem sunt missi igniti serpentes: ita qui in præmissis permanent vitiis, immundissimis traduntur spiritibus et venenatis dæmonibus, qui eos occultis perimunt morsibus. Væ eis qui post conversionem suam ad ollas carnium, id est ad pristinas voluptates et vanitates, de quibus semper lugendum est, rursus adspirant, qui sunt canes reversi ad vomitum.
paras.en: When the children of Israel had come [[16:1|into the desert of Sin|in desertum Sin]], they [[16:2|murmured against Moses|murmuraverunt contra Moysen]] because of the want of victuals and the roughness and barrenness of the place. By that wilderness is signified the strait way of salvation, the life of penance, and also the religious life of the cloister. And so by the murmuring of the carnal Jews is figured the impatience, indignation and murmuring of Christians of little faith, who have not yet overcome their sensuality. These, after setting out on the way of salvation, after beginning a life of penance, or after entering religion, are easily tempted when adversities, mockeries, persecutions or sicknesses befall them, when they are not refreshed as they would like, when they are afflicted with hunger, thirst or cold; so much so that at times they are indignant with their superiors, or speak against them, or, what is worse, insult them to their face. For they do not heed the providence of God, who most justly governs and disposes all things for the salvation of His elect. Therefore they fail in temptation and are overcome by their own impatience. Lastly, as Origen too writes, when we complain of the inclemency of the sky, of the barrenness of the earth and of the trees, of the scarcity of rain, of the prosperity of others, we raise a murmur against God. And as fiery serpents were at last sent among the children of Israel when they murmured[[Num 21:6||]], so those who persist in the vices just named are handed over to most unclean spirits and venomous demons, who kill them with hidden bites. Woe to those who after their conversion aspire again to the [[16:3|fleshpots|ollas carnium]], that is, to their former pleasures and vanities, which are always to be mourned; who are dogs returned to their vomit[[Prov 26:11||]] [the margin gives Prov. xxvi, 11; Denis's wording, "returned to the vomit", is closer to 2 Pet 2:22].

paras.t: Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen: Ecce ego pluam vobis panes de cœlo. Sic Deus ex sua pietate immensa interdum quasi compatitur ita murmurantibus et aversis, atque per consolationem spiritualem, per visitationem internam, recreat, retrahit, ac roborat eos. Virtuosis autem et in via salutis ac religionis proposito jugiter proficientibus, multo copiosius atque frequentius pluit et infundit hujusmodi manna. Qui dicere possunt: Benedictus Dominus qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra. Itemque: Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine. Itaque, per manna potest intelligi divinæ consolationis suavitas, spiritualis dulcedo, affluentia munerum divinorum, prædicatio quoque verbi cœlestis, et potissimum Eucharistiæ sacramentum: imo ipse Dominus Jesus Christus, qui ait Judæis: Non Moyses dedit vobis panem de cœlo, sed Pater meus dat vobis panem verum. Ego sum panis vitæ. Qui manducat hunc panem, vivet in æternum. In hoc pane verissime est omne delectamentum, et omnis saporis suavitas. Iste est panis angelorum, cujus deitate angeli sancti æternaliter et insatiabiliter reficiuntur. Iste panis est Lumen divinum, Verbum æternum, incorporatum et incarnatum, quo veri Israëlitæ aluntur.
paras.en: [[16:4|And the Lord said to Moses: Behold I will rain bread from heaven for you|Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen: Ecce ego pluam vobis panes de cœlo]]. So God, out of His immense goodness, at times as it were takes pity on those who murmur thus and have turned away, and by spiritual consolation, by an inward visitation, refreshes them, draws them back and strengthens them. But on the virtuous, and on those who go steadily forward in the way of salvation and in the purpose of religion, He rains and pours this kind of manna far more plentifully and more often. These can say: Blessed be the Lord[[2 Cor 1:3||]], [[2 Cor 1:4|Who comforteth us in all our tribulation|qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra]] [the margin gives 2 Cor. i, 3, 4; where Denis says "the Lord", St. Paul has "the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ"]. And again: [[Ps 30:20|O how great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord|Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine]]! And so by the manna may be understood the sweetness of divine consolation, spiritual sweetness, the abundance of divine gifts, also the preaching of the heavenly word, and above all the sacrament of the Eucharist; nay, the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, who says to the Jews: [[John 6:32|Moses gave you not bread from heaven, but my Father giveth you the true bread|Non Moyses dedit vobis panem de cœlo, sed Pater meus dat vobis panem verum]]. [[John 6:48|I am the bread of life|Ego sum panis vitæ]]. [[John 6:59|He that eateth this bread shall live for ever|Qui manducat hunc panem, vivet in æternum]]. In this bread most truly is [[Wis 16:20|all that is delicious, and the sweetness of every taste|omne delectamentum, et omnis saporis suavitas]] [Denis takes these words, without naming the book, from what Wis 16:20 says of the manna]. This is the bread of angels, by whose Godhead the holy angels are fed eternally and insatiably. This bread is the divine Light, the eternal Word, embodied and incarnate, by which the true Israelites are nourished.

paras.t: Præterea, salubris doctrina, sacra Scriptura, verbum salutis, recte vocatur manna dulcissimum: quo quid dulcius esse potest, quum scriptum sit, Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua? Hinc Jonathas et veri Hebræi primo Machabæorum libro fatentur: Nos nullo horum indigemus, solatio habentes sanctos libros qui in manibus nostris sunt. Toties itaque Deus pluit, quoties verba ipsius prædicantur hominibus. Dulcissima autem ipsius pluvia est unctio Spiritus Sancti, allocutio ejus interna, illuminatio supernaturalis, qua divina intelliguntur secreta. Unde ait Propheta: Pluviam voluntariam segregabis, Deus, hereditati tuæ.
paras.en: Moreover, wholesome doctrine, sacred Scripture, the word of salvation, is rightly called most sweet manna: and what can be sweeter than it, since it is written: [[Ps 118:103|How sweet are thy words to my palate!|Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua?]] Hence Jonathas and the true Hebrews confess in the first book of Machabees: [[1 Mach 12:9|We, though we needed none of these things having for our comfort the holy books that are in our hands|Nos nullo horum indigemus, solatio habentes sanctos libros qui in manibus nostris sunt]]. So God rains as often as His words are preached to men. But His sweetest rain is the anointing of the Holy Ghost, His speaking within, the supernatural enlightenment by which divine secrets are understood. Whence the Prophet says: [[Ps 67:10|Thou shalt set aside for thy inheritance a free rain, O God|Pluviam voluntariam segregabis, Deus, hereditati tuæ]].

paras.t: Insuper, quodlibet manna præfatum debemus quotidie quærere mane, juxta illud, Quærite primum regnum Dei: et tantum manducare, id est mente capere, quantum possumus, ut ad meliora et viciniora saluti indefesse tendamus. Sexta autem die duplum oportet colligere, quoniam in profestis diebus debemus nos specialiter præparare ad ea quæ sunt cultus divini, atque ad sacram communionem, expediendaque corporalia expedire, ut in sancta festivitate solis divinis ac interioribus simus intenti. Quemadmodum autem manna servatum in diem sequentem computruit, servatum vero in sabbatum, integrum mansit: ita si bona agamus amore retributionis terrenæ, aut intuitu laudis humanæ, pereunt et putrescunt: si autem propter requiem regni cœlestis, quæ per sabbatum designatur, optime conservantur.
paras.en: Furthermore, each of the mannas named above we ought to seek daily, in the morning, according to that saying: [[Matt 6:33|Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God|Quærite primum regnum Dei]]; and to eat as much of it, that is, to take in with the mind as much, as we can, so that we may tend unwearied towards better things and those nearer to salvation. And on the sixth day we must gather double, since on the days before feasts [profesti dies, the working days, here those that go before a feast] we ought especially to prepare ourselves for the things of divine worship and for holy communion, and to dispatch the bodily business that is to be dispatched, so that on the holy feast we may be intent on divine and inward things alone. And as the manna kept until the next day putrefied, but that kept for the sabbath remained whole, so if we do good works for love of an earthly reward or with an eye to human praise, they perish and rot; but if for the sake of the rest of the heavenly kingdom, which is signified by the sabbath, they are kept perfectly.

paras.t: Vespere scietis, quod Dominus eduxerit vos de terra Ægypti, et mane videbitis gloriam ejus. Per Vesperam designatur sexta et ultima mundi ætas, in qua Filius Dei venit in mundum per incarnationis mysterium, de qua ait sanctus Joannes apostolus, Novissima hora est: in qua per Apostolos toti prædicatum est orbi, qualiter Christus nos de hoc sæculo nequam salvavit. Mane autem videbimus gloriam ejus, quia in resurrectione futura, et in exordio, quo eum resuscitati in die æternitatis sumus visuri, videbimus eum clare et beatifice sicuti est. Potest quoque per Mane intelligi inchoatio illuminationis supernæ, seu exordium diei gratiæ ac virtutum: in quo Mane videbimus gloriam ejus, excellentiam suæ divinitatis per donum sapientiæ contemplando. Rursus, impletum est istud quasi ad litteram, dum Christo in cruce defuncto, post innumerabilia quæ tunc fiebant, eodem die ad vesperam multi confessi sunt, quia hic homo vere Filius Dei fuit. Quod licet a solo Centurione dictum legatur, Nicodemus tamen, Joseph ab Arimathea, et alii multi utriusque sexus ita senserunt, saltem implicite et æquivalenter, quamvis in fide nutaverunt. Nam et omnis turba eorum qui aderant, percutientes pectora sua revertebantur. Mane autem tertiæ diei, qua Christus resurrexit, majestatem ejus viderunt sanctæ mulieres, quæ ad sepulcrum venerunt, quæ et angelos conspexerunt.
paras.en: [[16:6|In the evening you shall know that the Lord hath brought you forth out of the land of Egypt|Vespere scietis, quod Dominus eduxerit vos de terra Ægypti]]: [[16:7|And in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord|et mane videbitis gloriam ejus]]. By the evening is signified the sixth and last age of the world, in which the Son of God came into the world through the mystery of the Incarnation; of which the holy apostle John says: [[1 John 2:18|it is the last hour|Novissima hora est]]; in which it was preached by the Apostles to the whole world how Christ saved us from this wicked world. But in the morning we shall see His glory, because in the resurrection to come, and in the dawn in which, raised again, we are to see Him in the day of eternity, we shall see Him clearly and blessedly as He is. By the morning may also be understood the beginning of the enlightenment from above, or the dawn of the day of grace and of the virtues: in which morning we shall see His glory, contemplating the excellence of His Godhead through the gift of wisdom. Again, this was fulfilled almost to the letter when, Christ having died on the cross, after the countless things that were then done, on the same day towards evening many confessed: [[Matt 27:54|Indeed this was the Son of God|hic homo vere Filius Dei fuit]] [the margin gives Matt. xxvii, 54; Denis's wording, "this man", is that of Mark 15:39]. And though we read that this was said by the centurion alone, yet Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea[[John 19:38||]], and many others of both sexes thought so, at least implicitly and in effect, although they wavered in faith. For [[Luke 23:48|all the multitude of them that were come together|omnis turba eorum qui aderant]] [[Luke 23:48|returned, striking their breasts|percutientes pectora sua revertebantur]]. And on the morning of the third day, on which Christ rose again, the holy women who came to the sepulchre saw His majesty; they also beheld angels[[Mark 16:1||]][[Matt 28:1||]] [the margin gives only the chapters, Mark xvi and Matt. xxviii].

paras.t: Locutus est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens: Audivi murmurationes filiorum Israel. Timeamus ergo et nos, ne Deus audiat murmurantes, et impleamus illud Apostoli: Neque murmuraveritis, sicut quidam illorum murmuraverunt. Unde et Sapiens præcipit: Custodite vos a murmuratione quæ nihil prodest, quoniam sermo obscurus non ibit in vacuum. Nempe ut asserit Augustinus: Nulla re tantum offendit populus Israel Deum, ut murmurando. Præcipue quoque vitemus, ne contra prælatos et spirituales patres nostros aliquando murmuremus, ne et ipsi juste ac veraciter dicant nobis: Non contra nos est murmur vestrum, sed contra Dominum, et ne Deus illorum injuriam reputet sibi factam, et horribiliter vindicet eam.
paras.en: [[16:11|And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying|Locutus est Dominus ad Moysen, dicens]]: [[16:12|I have heard the murmuring of the children of Israel|Audivi murmurationes filiorum Israel]]. Let us too, then, fear lest God hear us murmuring, and let us fulfil that saying of the Apostle: [[1 Cor 10:10|Neither do you murmur, as some of them murmured|Neque murmuraveritis, sicut quidam illorum murmuraverunt]]. Whence the Wise Man too commands: [[Wis 1:11|Keep yourselves, therefore, from murmuring, which profiteth nothing|Custodite vos a murmuratione quæ nihil prodest]], [[Wis 1:11|for an obscure speech shall not go for nought|quoniam sermo obscurus non ibit in vacuum]]. Indeed, as Augustine asserts: In nothing did the people of Israel so offend God as by murmuring. Let us above all take care never to murmur against our prelates and spiritual fathers, lest they too say to us, justly and truly: [[16:8|your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord|Non contra nos est murmur vestrum, sed contra Dominum]]; and lest God count the wrong done to them as done to Himself, and avenge it terribly.

paras.t: Vespere comedetis carnes, et mane saturabimini panibus: quia in ultima mundi ætate Christi corpore enutrimur, cujus gratia ac virtute generatur in nobis spirituale mane, quum ipse sit Sol intelligentiæ atque justitiæ, sua præsentia diem gratiæ in anima causans. Nam eo ita præsente, sincera et clara in mente sunt omnia, et tunc panibus saturamur, quoniam pane sacramentali, pane vitæ et intellectus, pane lacrimarum et compunctionis, imo et internæ jucunditatis, pane virtutum, virtuosorumque actuum copiose reficimur. Itaque huic Vespere statim conjungitur istud Mane. Verumtamen in mane diei æternitatis felicius saturabimur, quando replebitur et plene contentabitur in bonis desiderium nostrum.
paras.en: [[16:12|In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall have your fill of bread|Vespere comedetis carnes, et mane saturabimini panibus]]: because in the last age of the world we are nourished with the body of Christ, by whose grace and power a spiritual morning is begotten in us, since He is the Sun of understanding and of justice, by His presence causing the day of grace in the soul. For when He is thus present, all things in the mind are pure and clear, and then we have our fill of bread, since we are plentifully refreshed with sacramental bread, with [[Ecclus 15:3|bread of life and understanding|pane vitæ et intellectus]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the words are those of Ecclus 15:3], with the bread of tears and of compunction, nay, of inward gladness too, with the bread of the virtues and of virtuous acts. And so to this evening this morning is at once joined. Yet in the morning of the day of eternity we shall have our fill more happily, when our desire shall be filled and fully contented with good things[[Ps 102:5||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; Denis's words recall Ps 102:5].

paras.t: Ascendens coturnix, cooperuit castra. Per coturnicem, avem regiam, pinguem et comestibilem, prope terras volantem, intelligitur Christi regis nostri humanitas, omni divino charismate superplenissima, quæ universas replet ecclesias, et omnium reficit mentes.
paras.en: The [[16:13|quails coming up, covered the camp|Ascendens coturnix, cooperuit castra]]. By the quail, a royal bird, fat and good to eat, flying close to the ground, is understood the humanity of Christ our King, more than full of every divine gift of grace, which fills all the churches and refreshes the minds of all.

paras.t: At vero per hoc quod manna venit cum rore, eratque rotundum, minutum, subtile, album et purum, quid aliud figuratur, nisi quod verbum Dei, gratia, virtutes, et consolationes internæ, sunt spiritualia bona valde subtilia, munda, parva quantitate, imo magis non quanta, sed magna virtute? Sed et ipsa Christi humanitas et incarnationis mysterium, nonne omni subtilitate, puritate, candore, perpetuitate replentur? Ex quibus unus plus colligit, alter minus, quia unus plus alio proficit atque intelligit. Verumtamen omnes idem suscipiunt Sacramentum, atque eodem in patria perfruuntur objecto.
paras.en: But by this, that the manna came with the dew, and was round, small, fine, white and pure, what else is figured but that the word of God, grace, the virtues and inward consolations are spiritual goods exceedingly fine and clean, small in quantity, or rather of no quantity at all [that is, not bodily things having size], but great in power? And are not the humanity of Christ itself and the mystery of the Incarnation filled with all fineness, purity, whiteness and lastingness? Of these one gathers more, another less, because one makes more progress and understands more than another. Yet all receive the same Sacrament, and in the fatherland enjoy the same object.

paras.t: Quumque incaluisset sol, liquefiebat. Sic quando Sol sapientiæ, Dominus Deus noster, solus ex se et per se lucens, ac cuncta illuminans, mentes nostras igne sanctæ dilectionis ac devotionis fervore accendit, omnis recedit duritia cordis, habitusque virtutum fluunt in actum. Et Eucharistiæ sacramentum per suos effectus liquescit in nobis, omnia interiora animæ penetrans, irrigans, atque in compunctionis jucunditatisque fletum resolvens.
paras.en: And [[16:21|after the sun grew hot, it melted|Quumque incaluisset sol, liquefiebat]]. So when the Sun of wisdom, the Lord our God, who alone shines of Himself and through Himself and enlightens all things, kindles our minds with the fire of holy love and the fervour of devotion, all hardness of heart departs, and the habits of the virtues flow out into act. And the sacrament of the Eucharist melts within us through its effects, penetrating and watering all the inward parts of the soul, and dissolving it into tears of compunction and of gladness.

paras.t: Requies sabbati sanctificata est Domino. Maneat unusquisque apud semetipsum. Itaque festis diebus Deo in omni tranquillitate interna vacemus, maneatque unusquisque apud se ipsum, id est, in cordis sui recollectione in Deo, sic ligat dispositiones, cordis distractiones abjiciat; orando, meditando, psallendo, communicando, celebrando, contemplando sit stabilis ac sincerus. Spiritualiter equidem communicandum est omni Christiano quotidie.
paras.en: [[16:23|the rest of the sabbath sanctified to the Lord|Requies sabbati sanctificata est Domino]]. [[16:29|let each man stay at home|Maneat unusquisque apud semetipsum]] [apud semetipsum, literally "with himself", which Denis goes on to take of the soul].
