So on feast days let us be free for God in all inward tranquillity, and let each one stay with himself, that is, in the recollection of his heart in God; let him so bind fast his inclinations [the printed text, sic ligat dispositiones, seems faulty; the sense is that he keeps his inclinations in check] and cast away distractions of heart; in praying, meditating, singing psalms, communicating, celebrating [that is, saying Mass], contemplating, let him be steadfast and sincere. Spiritually, indeed, every Christian ought to communicate daily.

paras.t: Iste est sermo quem præcepit Dominus: Imple gomor ex eo, et custodiatur in futuras retro generationes. Per repositionem et conservationem mannæ in aurea urna in tabernaculo et in templo, quid figuratum videtur, nisi quod verum ac divinissimum Manna, Dominus Jesus unigenitus Patris, in Sacramento jugiter in Ecclesia conservatur in repositorio aureo ad perpetuam suæ passionis et dilectionis memoriam, atque ad nostram saluberrimam refectionem? Et ut sciamus, qualiter ipsemet Dominus et Salvator, patres nostros sanctos Apostolos in Cœna novissima refecit hoc pane: deinde quotidie primitivam Ecclesiam, ceterosque fideles usque in præsens.
paras.en: [[16:32|This is the word which the Lord hath commanded: Fill a gomor of it, and let it be kept unto generations to come hereafter|Iste est sermo quem præcepit Dominus: Imple gomor ex eo, et custodiatur in futuras retro generationes]]. By the laying up and keeping of the manna in a golden urn, in the tabernacle and in the temple, what seems to be figured but that the true and most divine Manna, the Lord Jesus, the only-begotten of the Father, is kept continually in the Sacrament in the Church, in a golden repository [the vessel in which the Blessed Sacrament is reserved], for a perpetual memorial of His passion and of His love, and for our most wholesome refreshment? And this so that we may know how the Lord and Saviour Himself fed our fathers, the holy Apostles, with this bread at the Last Supper; and after that, daily, the primitive Church, and the rest of the faithful down to the present.

paras.t: Filii autem Israel manducaverunt manna quadraginta annis, donec venirent in terram habitabilem. Sicque Christifideles per omne tempus vitæ præsentis quæ degunt in hac terra, in via reficiuntur dominicis Sacramentis, quousque finito peregrinationis hujus curriculo, terram ultimate promissam, paradisum cœlestem introeant. Nunc enim Christi corpore et sanguine sub velamento sensibilium formarum spiritualiter nutriuntur, et ejus deitatem contemplantur per fidem, ea quoque fruuntur vicibus interpolatis et imperfecte per caritatem nondum perfectam. Porro in patria illa cœlesti ejus humanitatem glorificatam clarissime cernent, cujus intuitu foris reficientur, imo et intus, quantum ad accidentale pertinet præmium. Deitate autem ipsius beatifice perfruentur clare per speciem, quemadmodum repromisit: Qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo: et ego diligam eum, et manifestabo ei me ipsum.
paras.en: [[16:35|And the children of Israel ate manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land|Filii autem Israel manducaverunt manna quadraginta annis, donec venirent in terram habitabilem]]. And so the faithful of Christ, through the whole time of this present life which they spend on this earth, are refreshed on the way with the Lord's Sacraments, until, the course of this pilgrimage finished, they enter the land promised at the last, the heavenly paradise. For now they are spiritually nourished with the body and blood of Christ under the veil of sensible forms [that is, the appearances of bread and wine], and they contemplate His Godhead by faith, and enjoy it too, at intervals and imperfectly, through a charity not yet perfect. But in that heavenly fatherland they will most clearly behold His glorified humanity, by the sight of which they will be refreshed outwardly, nay, inwardly too, as far as concerns the accidental reward [that is, the joy added to the essential reward of the blessed, which is the vision of God Himself]; while His Godhead they will enjoy blessedly, clearly, by sight, as He promised: [[John 14:21|he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him and will manifest myself to him|Qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo: et ego diligam eum, et manifestabo ei me ipsum]].

17.title: Declaratio litteralis capituli septimidecimi: Igitur profecta omnis multitudo filiorum Israel de deserto Sin
17.title_en: Literal explanation of the seventeenth chapter: Then all the multitude of the children of Israel setting forward from the desert of Sin

paras.t: Descripto ac recitato in præcedenti capitulo, qualiter Deus providit Hebræis de cibo: nunc recitatur, quam miraculose providit eis de potu. Igitur profecta omnis multitudo filiorum Israel de deserto Sin per mansiones suas, id est per loca quædam ordinate perambulata, in quibus mansiones fecerunt, quieverunt, seu castrametati sunt. Quæ mansiones in Numeris nominatim exprimuntur, ubi legitur: Castrametati sunt in deserto Sin, unde egressi venerunt in Daphea, profectique de Daphea, castrametati sunt in Alus, profectique de Alus, in Raphidim fixere tentoria. Itaque duæ mansiones istæ, quæ intermediæ fuerunt inter Sin et Raphidim, in isto non exprimuntur capitulo, quia in eis non contigit populo aliquid specialiter magnum. Sic ergo profecti juxta sermonem Domini. Per sermonem Domini, non intelligitur hic (secundum Josephum) alicujus vocis expressio, sed ducatus columnæ, secundum quod stimulus dicitur vox asino, et calcar equo. Sed quoniam Deus jam ante præceperat Moysi, ut tam ipse quam populus sequeretur ducatum columnæ, potest nunc per sermonem Domini jussio seu locutio illa intelligi. Castrametati sunt in Raphidim, ubi non erat aqua ad bibendum populo. In aliis autem locis seu mansionibus aliquid aquæ pro necessitate habuerant. Nam in Marath fuit eis aqua dulcorata, in Elim autem fuerunt duodecim fontes, sed in Raphidim passi sunt specialem potus defectum.
paras.en: The preceding chapter having described and related how God provided the Hebrews with food, it is now related how miraculously He provided them with drink. [[17:1|Then all the multitude of the children of Israel setting forward from the desert of Sin|Igitur profecta omnis multitudo filiorum Israel de deserto Sin]] [[17:1|by their mansions|per mansiones suas]], that is, through certain places passed through in order, in which they made their mansions [that is, halting-places; Latin *mansiones*], rested, or encamped. These mansions are named one by one in Numbers, where we read: [[Num 33:11|They camped in the desert of Sin|Castrametati sunt in deserto Sin]], [[Num 33:12|And they removed from thence, and came to Daphca|unde egressi venerunt in Daphea]], [[Num 33:13|And departing from Daphca, they camped in Alus|profectique de Daphea, castrametati sunt in Alus]], [[Num 33:14|And departing from Alus, they pitched their tents in Raphidim|profectique de Alus, in Raphidim fixere tentoria]]. So these two mansions, which lay between Sin and Raphidim, are not mentioned in this chapter, because nothing especially great befell the people in them. So then they set forward [[17:1|according to the word of the Lord|juxta sermonem Domini]]. By *the word of the Lord* is not understood here (according to Josephus) the utterance of any voice, but the leading of the pillar, in the sense in which the goad is called a voice to the ass, and the spur to the horse. But since God had already commanded Moses before that both he and the people should follow the leading of the pillar, that command or speech can now be understood by *the word of the Lord*. They [[17:1|encamped in Raphidim, where there was no water for the people to drink|Castrametati sunt in Raphidim, ubi non erat aqua ad bibendum populo]]. In the other places or mansions they had had some water for their need. For in Marath they had water made sweet, and in Elim there were twelve fountains; but in Raphidim they suffered a special want of drink.

paras.t: Qui populus jurgatus contra Moysen, ait, id est, cum lite seu jurgio locutus est Moysi: Da nobis aquam ut bibamus. Non dixerunt humiliter, Orationibus tuis impetra nobis potum, sed tanquam passionati ac duri, valdeque proni ad vitia, ubique ex facili occasione, ad verba impatientiæ, murmurationis ac jurgii proruperunt. Quibus respondit Moyses: Quid jurgamini contra me? Tenebatur enim ex officio eos corripere. Cur tentatis Dominum? quasi dicat: Non solum peccatis in me jurgando, sed item in Deum, ipsum tentando.
paras.en: [[17:2|And they chode with Moses, and said|Qui populus jurgatus contra Moysen, ait]], that is, the people spoke to Moses with strife or chiding: [[17:2|Give us water, that we may drink|Da nobis aquam ut bibamus]]. They did not say humbly, Obtain drink for us by thy prayers; but, being passionate and hard and very prone to vice, they broke out everywhere, on slight occasion, into words of impatience, murmuring and chiding. [[17:2|And Moses answered them: Why chide you with me?|Quibus respondit Moyses: Quid jurgamini contra me?]] For he was bound by his office to rebuke them. [[17:2|Wherefore do you tempt the Lord?|Cur tentatis Dominum?]] As if to say: You sin not only against me by chiding, but also against God by tempting Him.

paras.t: Non enim solum dixerunt verba præmissa, sed (ut infra habetur in isto capitulo) tentaverunt Deum, dicentes: Estne Dominus in nobis, an non? Quum enim debuissent ad divinum auxilium humiliter confugisse, non ita egerunt, sed per murmurationes ac jurgia contra Moysen, voluerunt quasi extorquere necessarium potum, et experiri an Deus provideret eis de potu, sicut jam Moyses eis promiserat quod Deus non desereret eos.
paras.en: For they did not only say the words above, but (as is had below in this chapter) [[17:7|they tempted the Lord, saying|tentaverunt Deum, dicentes]]: [[17:7|Is the Lord amongst us or not?|Estne Dominus in nobis, an non?]] For when they ought to have fled humbly to God's help, they did not do so, but by murmurings and chidings against Moses they wished, as it were, to wring from him the drink they needed, and to put it to the test whether God would provide them with drink, as Moses had already promised them that God would not forsake them.

paras.t: Sitivit ergo ibi populus præ aquæ penuria, id est propter defectum aquæ, et murmuravit contra Moysen, dicens: Cur nos exire fecisti de Ægypto, ut occideres nos et liberos nostros ac jumenta siti? Quare non expresserunt etiam uxores suas atque filias? Sed forsitan expresserunt eas, quamvis Scriptura propter brevitatem non exprimat; vel per liberos subintelliguntur, vel murmuratio ista facta est communiter a viris atque uxoribus. Verumtamen non est putandum, quod omnes viri ibi præsentes, tam perverse locuti sint, sed major pars populi, quæ passionibus suis subjacuit. Attamen quæri potest, cur Deus permisit eos ad tantas inopias devenire, quum essent de regno opulento egressi, et cur non providit eis de quotidiano saltem poculo aquæ, sicut providit eis de manna quotidie. Respondet Andreas. Quia populus fuit duræ cervicis, subtraxit eis Dominus aliquid necessarii potus, ut in timore manerent. Cibus quoque magis necessarius est quam potus.
paras.en: [[17:3|So the people were thirsty there for want of water|Sitivit ergo ibi populus præ aquæ penuria]], that is, because of the lack of water, [[17:3|and murmured against Moses, saying: Why didst thou make us go forth out of Egypt, to kill us and our children, and our beasts with thirst?|et murmuravit contra Moysen, dicens: Cur nos exire fecisti de Ægypto, ut occideres nos et liberos nostros ac jumenta siti?]] Why did they not mention their wives and daughters as well? But perhaps they did mention them, though Scripture for brevity does not say so; or they are understood under *children*; or this murmuring was made by the men and the wives together. Yet we are not to think that all the men present there spoke so perversely, but the greater part of the people, which was subject to its passions. Still it can be asked why God allowed them to come into such want, when they had come out of a wealthy kingdom, and why He did not provide them at least with a daily cup of water, as He provided them with manna daily. Andrew answers: Because the people was stiff-necked, the Lord withheld from them some of the drink they needed, so that they might remain in fear. Food, too, is more necessary than drink.

paras.t: Clamavit autem Moyses ad Dominum, dicens: Quid faciam populo huic? id est, qualiter me circa eum habebo? qualiter procurabo ei quo eget? quomodo eum contentabo? Adhuc paululum, et lapidabit me. Hoc Moyses dixit non asserendo, sed conjiciendo et periculum allegando, ut Dei subventionem celerius impetraret. Et forte ex naturali mortis formidine dixit hoc. Nam et vir perfectus et constans, potest mortem irreprehensibiliter formidare naturali timore: quam et Christus sic timuit, tamen sponte.
paras.en: [[17:4|And Moses cried to the Lord, saying: What shall I do to this people?|Clamavit autem Moyses ad Dominum, dicens: Quid faciam populo huic?]] that is, how shall I bear myself towards it? how shall I procure for it what it needs? how shall I content it? [[17:4|Yet a little more and they will stone me|Adhuc paululum, et lapidabit me]]. Moses said this not as asserting it, but as conjecturing and pleading the danger, so as to obtain God's help the more quickly. And perhaps he said it out of the natural dread of death. For even a perfect and steadfast man can, without blame, dread death with a natural fear: and Christ too feared it in this way, yet willingly.

paras.t: Et ait Dominus ad Moysen: Antecede populum. Quasi dicat: Tu times aut suspicaris quod te lapidibus obruent, sed non est periculum, quia et quum præcesseris eos, non tangent te violenter. Et sume tecum de senioribus Israel: quos ad testificandum de veritate miraculi jam fiendi, putas magis idoneos: et virgam qua percussisti fluvium, tolle in manu tua. Si per fluvium intelligatur Nilus, dicitur Moyses fluvium percussisse cum virga, in quantum Aaron fecit hoc ex suo mandato, ut patuit capitulo septimo. Porro si nomine fluvii intelligatur mare Rubrum, illum fluvium Moyses personaliter cum virga percussit, ut supra patuit. Et vade. En ego stabo ibi coram te, id est, me ibi esse præsentem ad succurrendum tibi per effectum monstrabo. Vel forsitan angelus in Dei persona stetit ibi ad auxiliandum paratus. Est equidem specialis chorus angelicorum spirituum, per quorum obsequia fieri solent miracula. Supra petram Horeb. Per Horeb Glossa intelligit montem Sinai, qui et mons Horeb vocatur. Sicque petra illa fuisset in pede montis Sinai, quod et Magister in historiis sentit, dicendo: Petra Horeb, pars est montis Sinai. Sed his obviare videtur, quod infra et clarius in Numeris leguntur filii Israel post egressionem a mansione Raphidim castra fixisse in Sinai. Ergo adhuc notabiliter distabant a monte illo. Hinc per petram Horeb, quidam intelligunt aliud locum ejusdem nominis cum loco pedimontis Sinai, qui et petra Horeb vocatus sit. Vel dici potest, quod pes montis Sinai remote extenditur, et quod petra ista, ob suam ad pedem illum vicinitatem, appelletur hoc nomine. Præterea est et alius locus, petra Oreb nominatus, eo quod Gedeon ibi occiderit principem Madian, nomine Oreb, ut in libro Judicum scribitur.
paras.en: [[17:5|And the Lord said to Moses: Go before the people|Et ait Dominus ad Moysen: Antecede populum]]. As if to say: Thou fearest or suspectest that they will overwhelm thee with stones; but there is no danger, for even when thou goest before them they will not lay violent hands on thee. [[17:5|and take with thee of the ancients of Israel|Et sume tecum de senioribus Israel]]: whom thou thinkest the fittest to bear witness to the truth of the miracle now to be done: [[17:5|and take in thy hand the rod wherewith thou didst strike the river|et virgam qua percussisti fluvium, tolle in manu tua]]. If by *the river* the Nile is understood, Moses is said to have struck the river with the rod inasmuch as Aaron did this at his command, as was seen in the seventh chapter. But if by the name of *river* the Red Sea is understood, Moses struck that river in person with the rod, as was seen above[[Ex 14:21||]]. [[17:5|and go|Et vade]]. [[17:6|Behold I will stand there before thee|En ego stabo ibi coram te]], that is, I will show by the effect that I am present there to help thee. Or perhaps an angel stood there in the person of God, ready to help. For there is a special choir of angelic spirits by whose service miracles are commonly done. [[17:6|upon the rock Horeb|Supra petram Horeb]]. By Horeb the Gloss understands Mount Sinai, which is also called Mount Horeb. So that rock would have been at the foot of Mount Sinai, which the Master in the Histories [that is, Peter Comestor, in the *Historia scholastica*] also holds, saying: The rock of Horeb is part of Mount Sinai. But against this seems to be what we read below, and more clearly in Numbers, that the children of Israel, after setting out from the mansion of Raphidim, pitched their camp in Sinai. Therefore they were still a good distance from that mountain. Hence some understand by *the rock Horeb* another place, of the same name as the place at the foot of Mount Sinai, which was also called the rock Horeb. Or it can be said that the foot of Mount Sinai stretches out a long way, and that this rock is called by this name because of its nearness to that foot. There is moreover yet another place named the rock of Oreb, because Gedeon slew there a prince of Madian named Oreb, as is written in the book of Judges[[Judg 7:25||]].

paras.t: Percutiesque petram cum virga. Refert Lyra, quod Rabbi Salomon asserit quosdam de populo Israel fuisse ita malignos, quod dixerunt per virgam Moysis non potuisse fieri signa, nisi in aliorum perniciem, ut fuerunt plagæ Ægypti: ideo Dominum præcepisse, ut in eductione aquæ uteretur hac virga. Sive autem hoc fuerit verum, sive non, constat quod jam ante Dominus demonstravit per virgam illam posse fieri signa in salutem et subventionem, quoniam Deo jubente Moyses percussit mare Rubrum cum virga ut divideretur, quatenus per fundum ejus transeuntes filii Israel, evaderent manus Ægyptiorum, quemadmodum capitulo quartodecimo continetur. Ideo ratio Rabbi Salomonis non censetur apte inducta. Et exibit ex ea aqua, ut bibat populus. Fecit Moyses ita coram senioribus Israel. Et hoc fuit grande et præclarum miraculum, quod ex re illa tam dura et sicca tantus manavit humor, quod tot millia hominum ac pecorum potabantur ex eo. Nec apparet, quod aliquid petræ resolvebatur in aquam illam, sed quod Creator omnipotens aquam egredientem per creationem produxit in petra quasi in fonte; et facta fuisse videtur ruptura grandis in petra, ex qua vomebatur hæc aqua. Quod et ipsum erat miraculum, scilicet quod ex percussione cum virga, scissa fuit hæc petra: fuitque aqua illa ad potandum dulcissima, ut Josephus narrat.
paras.en: [[17:6|and thou shalt strike the rock|Percutiesque petram]] with the rod. Lyra relates that Rabbi Salomon [that is, Rashi, Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac] asserts that some of the people of Israel were so malicious that they said no signs could be done by Moses's rod except to the ruin of others, as the plagues of Egypt had been; and that therefore the Lord commanded him to use this rod in bringing forth the water. But whether this be true or not, it is certain that the Lord had already shown before that signs could be done by that rod for salvation and help, since at God's command Moses struck the Red Sea with the rod so that it was divided, in order that the children of Israel, passing through its bed, might escape the hands of the Egyptians, as is contained in the fourteenth chapter. Therefore Rabbi Salomon's reason is not thought aptly brought in. [[17:6|and water shall come out of it that the people may drink|Et exibit ex ea aqua, ut bibat populus]]. [[17:6|Moses did so before the ancients of Israel|Fecit Moyses ita coram senioribus Israel]]. And this was a great and glorious miracle, that from a thing so hard and dry so much moisture flowed that so many thousands of men and cattle drank of it. Nor does it appear that any of the rock was dissolved into that water, but rather that the almighty Creator, by creation, brought forth the water issuing in the rock as in a spring; and it seems that a great cleft was made in the rock, out of which this water gushed. And this itself was a miracle, namely that this rock was split by being struck with the rod; and that water was very sweet to drink, as Josephus tells.

paras.t: Et vocavit Moyses nomen loci illius, Tentatio, propter jurgium filiorum Israel, et quia tentaverunt Dominum, dicentes: Estne Dominus in nobis, an non? Sicque locus ille sortitus est nomina duo quia jam ante vocatus est Raphidim, et nunc ex eventu vocatur Tentatio.
paras.en: [[17:7|And he called the name of that place Temptation, because of the chiding of the children of Israel, and for that they tempted the Lord, saying: Is the Lord amongst us or not?|Et vocavit Moyses nomen loci illius, Tentatio, propter jurgium filiorum Israel, et quia tentaverunt Dominum, dicentes: Estne Dominus in nobis, an non?]] And so that place received two names, since it had already been called Raphidim before, and now from the event it is called Temptation.

paras.t: Venit autem Amalec, id est populus Amalecitarum, et pugnabat contra Israel in Raphidim, id est in loco deserti illius non multum remoto a Raphidim. Et quod ait Pugnabat, per anticipationem est dictum: quia non pugnavit contra Hebræos manu ad manum, ante id quod in textu subjungitur. Dixitque Moyses ad Josue: Elige tibi viros, et egressus pugna contra Amalec cras. Unde elicitur quod Josue, electis viris bellicosis ac strenuis, processit obviam Amalecitis in pugnam die sequenti. Dicitque Lyra: Noluit Moyses quod exspectaretur exercitus Amalec, sed quod iretur obviam ei, ne mulieres ac pueri, et timidi qui manserant in castris, nimis terrerentur ac fugerent. Ex quo sequi videtur, quod Josue obviavit Amalecitis antequam accesserunt ad Israel. Cui contrariari videtur quod in Deuteronomio legitur, quemadmodum Amalec extremos agminis Israel, qui lassi residebant, percussit: propter quod Dominus jussit, ut filii Israel tempore opportuno delerent semen et nomen Amalec de sub cœlo.
paras.en: [[17:8|And Amalec came|Venit autem Amalec]], that is, the people of the Amalecites, [[17:8|and fought against Israel in Raphidim|et pugnabat contra Israel in Raphidim]], that is, in a place of that desert not far from Raphidim. And when it says *fought*, it is said by anticipation, since he did not fight hand to hand against the Hebrews before what is added next in the text. [[17:9|And Moses said to Josue: Choose out men|Dixitque Moyses ad Josue: Elige tibi viros]]; [[17:9|and go out and fight against Amalec|et egressus pugna contra Amalec]] [[17:9|tomorrow|cras]] [Denis joins *tomorrow* to the fighting, as his gloss shows; the Douay-Rheims joins it to Moses's standing on the hill]. From this it is gathered that Josue, having chosen warlike and vigorous men, went out to meet the Amalecites in battle on the following day. And Lyra says: Moses did not want the army of Amalec to be waited for, but to be met, lest the women and children, and the fearful who had stayed in the camp, should be too much terrified and flee. From this it seems to follow that Josue met the Amalecites before they came up to Israel. Against this seems to be what we read in Deuteronomy[[Deut 25:17||]], how Amalec smote [[Deut 25:18|the hindmost of the army|extremos agminis]] of Israel, [[Deut 25:18|who sat down, being weary|qui lassi residebant]]: for which the Lord commanded that the children of Israel, in due time, should blot out the seed and the name of Amalec from under heaven.

paras.t: Quæritur, cur Moyses præfecit ipsum Josue pugnaturis contra Amalec. Quidam respondent quod ideo, quia prævidit in spiritu quod Josue futurus esset dux populi. Cui dicto obviare apparet, quod in Numeris legitur Moyses mox moriturus orasse: Provideat Dominus hominem qui sit super multitudinem hanc. Et tunc Dominus revelavit ei de Josue, sicque videtur ante nescisse. Alii dicunt quod ideo, quia prophetico spiritu novit ipsum Josue esse, de quo Jacob in benedictione Ephraim dixerat, Inde egressus est pastor. Quod satis redit in idem cum prima responsione. Plane autem dici potest quod ideo, quoniam scivit Josue esse virum justum, fortem, constantem ac bellicosum: unde et merita ejus credidit cooperatura communi triumpho.
paras.en: It is asked why Moses set Josue over those who were to fight against Amalec. Some answer that it was because he foresaw in spirit that Josue was to be the leader of the people. Against this saying appears what we read in Numbers, that Moses, when about to die, prayed: [[Num 27:16|May the Lord|Provideat Dominus]] [[Num 27:16|provide a man, that may be over this multitude|hominem qui sit super multitudinem hanc]]. And then the Lord revealed Josue to him; and so it seems that he did not know before. Others say it was because he knew by the spirit of prophecy that Josue was the one of whom Jacob, in the blessing of Ephraim, had said: [[Gen 49:24|thence he came forth a pastor|Inde egressus est pastor]] [the margin gives Gen. xix, 24; the words are Gen 49:24, in the blessing of Joseph, the father of Ephraim]. This comes to much the same as the first answer. But it can plainly be said that it was because he knew Josue to be a just man, strong, steadfast and warlike; and so he believed that his merits too would work together for the common triumph.

paras.t: Præterea circa hæc asserit Strabus, et habetur in Glossa: Amalec fuit filius Ismael, a quo Amalecitæ, qui et Ismaelitæ, ipsi sunt Sarraceni. Cui assertioni multa objiciuntur. Primo, quoniam in Genesi et primo Paralipomenon legitur, quod Eliphaz primogenitus Esau genuit Amalec. Secundo, quod secundo Regum adolescens qui nuntiavit regi David mortem Saulis, dixit se esse Amalecitem, fuitque adolescens ille, secundum expositores concorditer, filius Doeg Idumæi, et ita natus fuit ex Esau, non ex Ismaele. Tertio, quoniam Josephus secundo libro Antiquitatum affirmat, quod ab Amalec filio Eliphaz, dicti sunt Amalecitæ. Hinc quidam dicit, de Glossa illa Strabi non multum esse curandum. Porro Magister in historiis magis reverenter respondet, quod forte fuerunt sic appellati, et quod ex eis descenderunt forsitan duo populi Amalecitæ vocati. Quæ responsio, quamvis modesta sit, tamen ex Scriptura non habet auctoritatem. Idcirco est tutius sequi responsionem dicentium, quod Amalec iste et populus natus ex eo, descenderunt ab Eliphaz, quia hoc consonantius est Scripturæ canonicæ.
paras.en: Further, concerning these things Strabus asserts, and it is in the Gloss: Amalec was the son of Ismael, from whom come the Amalecites, who are also the Ismaelites; they are the Saracens. Many objections are made to this assertion. First, because in Genesis[[Gen 36:12||]] and in the first book of Paralipomenon[[1 Par 1:36||]] we read that Eliphaz, the firstborn of Esau, begot Amalec. Second, because in the second book of Kings the young man who brought King David news of Saul's death said that he was an Amalecite[[2 Kings 1:8||]]; and that young man, by the agreement of the expositors, was the son of Doeg the Edomite, and so was descended from Esau, not from Ismael. Third, because Josephus, in the second book of the Antiquities, affirms that the Amalecites were named after Amalec the son of Eliphaz. Hence someone says that not much heed need be paid to that gloss of Strabus. But the Master in the Histories answers more reverently that perhaps both were so called [that is, that there may have been two men named Amalec], and that from them perhaps two peoples called Amalecites descended. This answer, modest though it is, has no authority from Scripture. It is therefore safer to follow the answer of those who say that this Amalec, and the people born of him, came down from Eliphaz, since this agrees better with canonical Scripture.

paras.t: Ne autem Josue formidaret, et præsentiam Moysis peteret, ait Moyses ei: En ego stabo in vertice collis: quod juxta prædicta non potest intelligi de monte Sinai, sed de monte minori, qui Raphidim fuit; habens virgam Dei in manu mea. Quasi dicat: Orationibus te juvabo, per quod plus valeo, quam corporalibus viribus. Sed cur addidit, Habens virgam Dei in manu mea, quasi virga illa potuerit ad triumphum conferre? Respondetur, quod Moyses voluit se Deo repræsentare, ut prælatum ac principem populi, ut magis exaudiretur pro grege sibi commisso. Ideo tenuit virgam tanquam signum principatus sui in manu, et quia per virgam prævaluit Pharaoni. Cur autem ascendit in verticem collis, nisi quia ex situ hujusmodi loci, magis elevaretur mens ejus ad Deum? Vel ut inde conspiceret, qualiter ipsi Josue ac populo suo in bello succederet, sicque oraret pro eis instantius, si indigerent.
paras.en: And lest Josue should be afraid and ask for Moses to be with him, Moses said to him: Behold, [[17:9|I will stand on the top of the hill|ego stabo in vertice collis]] [Denis reads *En* (Behold) here, where the Vulgate has *cras* (tomorrow), which he has joined to the fighting]: which, according to what was said above, cannot be understood of Mount Sinai, but of a smaller mountain which was at Raphidim; [[17:9|having the rod of God in my hand|habens virgam Dei in manu mea]]. As if to say: I will help thee by prayers, by which I can do more than by bodily strength. But why did he add, [[17:9|having the rod of God in my hand|Habens virgam Dei in manu mea]], as though that rod could contribute to the victory? It is answered that Moses wished to present himself before God as the prelate and prince of the people, so as to be heard the more for the flock committed to him. So he held the rod in his hand as the sign of his rule, and also because by the rod he had prevailed over Pharao. And why did he go up to the top of the hill, unless that by the position of such a place his mind might be lifted up more to God? Or so as to see from there how things went in the battle for Josue and his people, and so pray for them more earnestly if they had need.

paras.t: Fecit Josue ut locutus erat Moyses, et pugnavit contra Amalec. Moyses autem et Aaron et Hur ascenderunt super verticem collis. Assumpsit autem Moyses secum duos illos, tanquam præ ceteris principales, et sibi propinquos ac meliores. Nam Aaron fuit frater suus, Hur autem maritus Mariæ sororis suæ, ut probabilius creditur, et Josephus protestatur. Et item, ut secum orarent, et opem sibi impenderent si necesse esset.
paras.en: [[17:10|Josue did as Moses had spoken, and he fought against Amalec|Fecit Josue ut locutus erat Moyses, et pugnavit contra Amalec]]; [[17:10|but Moses, and Aaron, and Hur, went up upon the top of the hill|Moyses autem et Aaron et Hur ascenderunt super verticem collis]]. Moses took those two with him as chief above the rest, and as near to him and better. For Aaron was his brother, and Hur the husband of Mary his sister, as is more probably believed and as Josephus declares. And also so that they might pray with him, and give him help if need be.

paras.t: Quumque levaret Moyses manus, vincebat Israel, id est Josue cum populo suo. Si autem paululum remisisset, superabat Amalec. Non dicitur, quod paululum remisit manus, sed, Si paululum remisisset. Unde videtur, quod interdum præ lassitudine cœperit parumper remittere manus, et tunc filii Israel minus fortiter et Amalecitæ fortius pugnaverunt. Et hoc Deus sic ordinavit ad ostendendum, quod victoria illa dabatur miraculose et gratiose a Deo; et item, quod oratio Moysis magnæ fuit efficaciæ apud eum, siquidem manibus elevatis oravit ferventius. Sunt et aliæ mysticæ causæ infra tangendæ. Manus autem Moysis erant graves, id est fatigatione gravatæ. Sumentes igitur lapidem Aaron et Hur, posuerunt subter eum, in quo sedit, id est, lapidem posuerunt ei ad sedendum. Aaron autem et Hur sustentabant manus ejus ex utraque parte. Ita Aaron sustentavit unum Moysis brachium, quod faciendo, sustentavit et unam ipsius Moysis manum. Aliud brachium ejus vel manum, Hur sustentavit. Et sic factum est, ut manus ipsius non lassarentur usque ad solis occasum: in quo pugna fuit finita.
paras.en: [[17:11|And when Moses lifted up his hands, Israel overcame|Quumque levaret Moyses manus, vincebat Israel]], that is, Josue with his people; [[17:11|but if he let them down a little, Amalec overcame|Si autem paululum remisisset, superabat Amalec]]. It does not say that he let his hands down a little, but *if he had let them down a little* [Latin *si … remisisset*]. Hence it seems that at times, from weariness, he began to let his hands down a little, and then the children of Israel fought less strongly and the Amalecites more strongly. And God so ordered this to show that that victory was given miraculously and by grace from God; and also that the prayer of Moses was of great efficacy with Him, since he prayed more fervently with hands raised. There are also other, mystical, causes, to be touched on below. [[17:12|And Moses's hands were heavy|Manus autem Moysis erant graves]], that is, weighed down with fatigue. [[17:12|so they took a stone|Sumentes igitur lapidem]], Aaron and Hur, [[17:12|and put under him, and he sat on it|posuerunt subter eum, in quo sedit]], that is, they placed a stone for him to sit on. [[17:12|and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands on both sides|Aaron autem et Hur sustentabant manus ejus ex utraque parte]]. So Aaron held up one arm of Moses, and in doing so held up one hand of Moses too; the other arm or hand Hur held up. [[17:12|And it came to pass, that his hands were not weary until sunset|Et sic factum est, ut manus ipsius non lassarentur usque ad solis occasum]]: at which the battle was ended.

paras.t: Fugavitque Josue cum adjutoribus suis Amalec et populum ejus, id est principem belli cum exercitu ejus, in ore gladii. Non dubium quin multi de Amalec fuerunt occisi, quoniam Moyse sic elevatis manibus exorante, prævaluit Israel, atque in ipsa fuga fuerunt multi prostrati. De populo autem Josue non videtur aliquis occidisse, quamvis aliquando fuerat ei difficultas in prælio illo ob causam prætactam. Præterea Josephus scribit, Amalecitas illos fuisse bellicosos, et a circumstantibus conductos ad impugnandum Hebræos. Quod item fecerunt, ne forte Hebræi damnum aut læsionem eis inferrent. Imo secundum Josephum, Amalecitæ incitabant alios ad impugnandum filios Israel. Victisque Amalecitis, filii Israel multa spolia obtinuerunt, et aliis terribiles sunt effecti, et nomen eorum undique divulgabatur, atque ab occisis arma detraxerunt, et nullus Israelitarum corruit, sed innumerabiles de exercitu hostium.
paras.en: [[17:13|And Josue|Fugavitque Josue]], with his helpers, [[17:13|put Amalec and his people to flight|Amalec et populum ejus]], that is, the prince of the war with his army, [[17:13|by the edge of the sword|in ore gladii]]. There is no doubt that many of Amalec were slain, since, while Moses prayed thus with hands raised, Israel prevailed, and in the flight itself many were struck down. Of Josue's people, however, none seems to have fallen, although at times he had difficulty in that battle for the cause touched on above. Moreover Josephus writes that those Amalecites were warlike, and were brought in by the peoples round about to attack the Hebrews. And they did this lest the Hebrews should perhaps do them damage or harm. Indeed, according to Josephus, the Amalecites were stirring up others to attack the children of Israel. And when the Amalecites were conquered, the children of Israel took much spoil, and became terrible to others, and their name was spread abroad everywhere; and they stripped the arms from the slain; and none of the Israelites fell, but countless of the enemy's army.

paras.t: Insuper de præfato Hur aliqui dicunt, quod fuit filius Mariæ sororis Moysis ex Caleph, eo quod primo Paralipomenon libro dicatur: Mortua uxore, Caleph accepit uxorem Ephrata, quæ peperit ei Hur; et dicunt, quod Ephrata illa alio nomine dicebatur Maria. Sed istud satis reprobatur ab aliis, præsertim quoniam vir iste fuit senior quam Caleph. Fuit enim avus Beseleel, sicut infra in textu habetur. Beseleel autem fuit virilis ætatis in exitu de Ægypto. Nam fuit vir sapiens, et electus a Deo ad construendum tabernaculum. Caleph vero quadraginta fuit annorum quando missus fuit ad explorandum terram, quod fuit tabernaculo jam completo, et ita Hur fuit multum senior eo. Correcti quoque textus primo Paralipomenon non habent Caleph, sed Caleb: et si habent Caleph, videtur vitium esse scriptorum; vel alius Caleph erat. Josephus quoque tertio Antiquitatum libro testatur, quod iste Hur fuit maritus Mariæ.
paras.en: Moreover, of the aforesaid Hur some say that he was the son of Mary, the sister of Moses, by Caleph, because it is said in the first book of Paralipomenon: His wife being dead, Caleph [[1 Par 2:19|took to wife Ephrata: who bore him Hur|accepit uxorem Ephrata, quæ peperit ei Hur]]; and they say that this Ephrata was called by another name Mary. But this is well refuted by others, especially because this man was older than Caleph. For he was the grandfather of Beseleel, as is had below in the text[[Ex 31:2||]]. And Beseleel was of man's age at the going out of Egypt; for he was a wise man, and chosen by God to build the tabernacle. But Caleph was forty years old when he was sent to spy out the land, which was when the tabernacle was already finished; and so Hur was much older than he. Also the corrected texts of the first book of Paralipomenon do not have Caleph but Caleb[[1 Par 2:18||]]; and if they have Caleph, it seems to be a fault of the scribes; or it was another Caleph. Josephus too, in the third book of the Antiquities, testifies that this Hur was the husband of Mary.

paras.t: Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen: Scribe hoc ob monumentum in libro, id est, hanc impietatem Amalec ad perpetuam memoriam describe, quatenus suo tempore a filiis Israel plenius vindicetur; et trade in auribus Josue, id est, ei committit ut memor sit horum, ut et ipse idem præcipiat populo tempore opportuno. Delebo enim memoriam Amalec de sub cœlo, id est, populum illum tam viros quam mulieres ac pueros faciam trucidari. Quod primo Regum legitur Deum per Samuelem jussisse Sauli. Sed quomodo verum est istud, quum usque in præsens perseveret memoria Amalec, præsertim dum ista leguntur? Nec omnes Amalecitæ fuerunt deleti, quum et Aman superbissimus fuit de semine Agag regis Amalecitarum, ut in libro Esther habetur. Et tempore David fuerunt quamplures Amalecitæ, ut primo Regum ostenditur. Respondendum, quod juxta Scripturas memoria impiorum dicitur deleri a terra, non quod prorsus in hominibus non permaneat, imo nonnullos infames malitia fecit famosos; sed quia non manent, nec sunt memoriæ quæ cedant in bonum eorum, sed magis in detrimentum ac vituperationem. Propter quod Salomon ait: Memoria justi cum laudibus; nomen impiorum putrescet. Dicitur demum memoria Amalec auferri, non quod posteritas ejus prorsus perierit, sed ob multitudinem peremptorum, et quantum ad ipsos iniquos in sua iniquitate occisos.
paras.en: [[17:14|And the Lord said to Moses: Write this for a memorial in a book|Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen: Scribe hoc ob monumentum in libro]], that is, write down this impiety of Amalec for a perpetual memory, so that in its time it may be more fully avenged by the children of Israel; [[17:14|and deliver it to the ears of Josue|et trade in auribus Josue]], that is, he charges him to be mindful of these things, so that he too may give the same command to the people in due time. [[17:14|for I will destroy the memory of Amalec from under heaven|Delebo enim memoriam Amalec de sub cœlo]], that is, I will have that people slain, men as well as women and children. This, as we read in the first book of Kings, God commanded Saul through Samuel[[1 Kings 15:3||]]. But how is this true, since the memory of Amalec lasts until now, especially while these things are read? Nor were all the Amalecites destroyed, since the most proud Aman was of the seed of Agag, king of the Amalecites, as is had in the book of Esther[[Esth 3:1||]]. And in David's time there were a great many Amalecites, as is shown in the first book of Kings[[1 Kings 30:1||]] [the margin's reference here is unread; the Amalecites who burned Siceleg, 1 Kings 30:1, fit Denis's words]. The answer is that, according to the Scriptures, the memory of the wicked is said to be blotted out from the earth, not because it does not remain among men at all (indeed malice has made some infamous men famous), but because the memories of them that remain, if any, do not turn to their good, but rather to their loss and reproach. Wherefore Solomon says: [[Prov 10:7|The memory of the just is with praises: and the name of the wicked shall rot|Memoria justi cum laudibus; nomen impiorum putrescet]]. Lastly, the memory of Amalec is said to be taken away, not because his posterity perished altogether, but because of the multitude of those slain, and as regards the wicked themselves, slain in their iniquity.

paras.t: Ædificavitque Moyses altare Domino, id est ad Dei honorem, ut super illud hostias laudis et gratiarum actionis Deo offerret pro concessa victoria; et vocavit nomen ejus, Dominus exaltatio mea, id est, ab eventu imposuit nomen illi altari, quod nomen significat tantum, sicut istud complexum, Dominus exaltatio mea: ad insinuandum, quod illo in loco Dominus exaltavit tam Moysen, per ejus preces dando victoriam, quam filios Israel, quos fecit hostibus fortiores; dicens: Quia manus solii Domini, id est potestas throni Domini omnipotentis, seu virtus Dei sedentis in throno, et bellum Dei erit contra Amalec a generatione in generationem: hoc est, Deus sua virtute et per manum atque exercitum hominum pugnatorum, dejiciet Amalecitas frequenter ac diu, et hoc propter præfatam eorum crudelitatem in Israelem, vel potius, quoniam patrum suorum iniquitates secuti sunt.
paras.en: [[17:15|And Moses built an altar|Ædificavitque Moyses altare]] to the Lord, that is, to the honour of God, so as to offer on it to God sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving for the victory granted; [[17:15|and called the name thereof, The Lord, my exaltation|et vocavit nomen ejus, Dominus exaltatio mea]], that is, from the event he gave that altar a name which means as much as this phrase, *The Lord my exaltation*: to suggest that in that place the Lord exalted both Moses, by giving the victory through his prayers, and the children of Israel, whom He made stronger than their enemies; [[17:15|saying|dicens]]: [[17:16|Because the hand of the throne of the Lord|Quia manus solii Domini]], that is, the power of the throne of the Lord almighty, or the might of God seated on the throne, [[17:16|and the war of the Lord shall be against Amalec, from generation to generation|et bellum Dei erit contra Amalec a generatione in generationem]]: that is, God by His own might, and through the hand and army of fighting men, will cast down the Amalecites often and for long; and this because of their cruelty to Israel spoken of above, or rather because they followed the iniquities of their fathers.

17.title: De spirituali ejusdem capituli septimidecimi intelligentia
17.title_en: On the spiritual sense of the same seventeenth chapter

paras.t: Ex præsenti capitulo edocemur in primis juxta historiam, quod fideles in hac vita multipliciter tribulantur. Per repetitam vero Hebræorum murmurationem et jurgationem contra Moysen, imo et contra Deum, designatur improba nimis ingratorumque carnaliumque perversitas, qui etsi interdum experiantur sibi subsidium desuper esse impertitum in una tentatione, tribulatione, penuria, alia tamen eis adveniente, quasi præteritorum Dei beneficiorum obliti, mox indignantur et murmurant : nec discunt ad Deum humiliter cum fiducia filiali confugere, sed contra eum et ejus vicarium faciliter concitantur : quorum perversitas, insipientia, ingratitudo longe a nobis sit. At vero Sin interpretatur tentatio, Raphidim autem sanitas judicii. Quemadmodum ergo filii Israel ex deserto Sin ingressi sunt Raphidim, ita qui tentationem devincens, ex eadem bene egreditur, ad sanum pertingit mentis judicium, quia ratio ejus non obscuratur fumo peccati, vitiorum caligine, inquietatione tentationis. Consideremus præterea, quod populo Dei ex terra Ægypti deducto, toties defuit aqua, et quod sola aqua in solitudine sunt potati. Non ergo quæramus delicias, non superfluitatem aut voluptatem in cibis ac potibus. Quod si exiguum nobis pro esu et potu proponitur, æquanimiter toleremus, et dona Dei, licet videantur tenuia, gratanter sumamus, pensantes quod tot electi Israelitæ justi, potentes, locupletes et nobiles, dux, pontifexque eorum exiguo aquæ poculo contentabantur. Denique exemplo Moysis, prælati et principes patientiam discant, et quantumlibet improbi et ingrati fuerint eorum subditi, ipsi tamen non cessent pro illis clamare ad Dominum.
paras.en: From the present chapter we are taught, first of all according to the history, that the faithful are afflicted in many ways in this life. By the repeated murmuring and chiding of the Hebrews against Moses, and indeed against God, is signified the exceedingly wicked perversity of the ungrateful and carnal, who, although they sometimes find that help has been given them from above in one temptation, tribulation or want, yet when another comes upon them, as though forgetful of God's past benefits, are straightway indignant and murmur: nor do they learn to flee to God humbly, with filial confidence, but are easily stirred up against him and against his vicar. Far from us be their perversity, folly and ingratitude! Now Sin is interpreted “temptation”, and Raphidim “soundness of judgement”. As, then, the children of Israel went from the desert of Sin into Raphidim, so he who overcomes temptation and comes well out of it arrives at a sound judgement of mind, because his reason is not darkened by the smoke of sin, the fog of vices, the disquiet of temptation. Let us consider besides that the people of God, once led out of the land of Egypt, so often lacked water, and that in the wilderness they were given nothing but water to drink. Let us not, then, seek delicacies, nor superfluity or pleasure in food and drink. And if little is set before us to eat and drink, let us bear it with an even mind, and receive the gifts of God gratefully, though they seem slender, considering that so many chosen Israelites, just, powerful, wealthy and noble, and their leader and their high priest, were content with a little cup of water. Lastly, by the example of Moses let prelates and princes learn patience, and however wicked and ungrateful their subjects may be, let them yet not cease to cry to the Lord for them.

paras.t: Ait autem Dominus ad Moysen : Antecede populum, et sume tecum de senioribus Israel. Sic Deus præcipit unicuique præsidenti, ut sibi commissis ostendat viam salutis, ducatque eos ad petram qui Christus est, ut aquam bibant sapientiæ salutaris, verbo et opere. Ergo qui præest, antecedat creditum sibi gregem, sicut ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus : Esto exemplum fidelium in verbo, in conversatione, in caritate. Assumere etiam secum debet de senioribus Israel, quoniam eos qui ætate, gradu, scientia, vel auctoritate excellunt, specialiter debet hortari, ut studeant in omni virtute præcedere juniores ac simpliciores, et ut sibi in aliorum directione adsistant.
paras.en: [[17:5|And the Lord said to Moses: Go before the people, and take with thee of the ancients of Israel|Ait autem Dominus ad Moysen : Antecede populum, et sume tecum de senioribus Israel]]. Thus God commands everyone who presides to show those committed to him the way of salvation, and to lead them to the rock which is Christ, that they may drink the water of saving wisdom, by word and by deed. Let him, then, who is set over others go before the flock entrusted to him, as the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[1 Tim 4:12|be thou an example of the faithful, in word, in conversation, in charity|Esto exemplum fidelium in verbo, in conversatione, in caritate]]. He ought also to take with him of the ancients of Israel, since he ought especially to exhort those who excel in age, rank, learning or authority to strive to go before the younger and simpler in every virtue, and to assist him in the guiding of the others.

paras.t: Percutiesque petram, et exibit ex ea aqua, ut bibat populus. Per petram Christus significatur, dicente Apostolo : Petra erat Christus. Per hoc ergo quod Moyses hanc petram cum virga percussit, atque ex ea egressa est exuberantissima aqua, qua refecti sunt populus ac jumenta : præfigurabatur, quod Deus Pater Filium suum pro omnibus nobis dedit in mortem, sicut per Isaiam prædixit : Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum. Propter quod princeps Apostolorum dignissimus ait : Deus qui prænuntiavit per os omnium Prophetarum pati Christum suum, implevit sic. Christus quoque in Psalmo ad Patrem : Quem tu percussisti, persecuti sunt. Percussit autem eum cum virga, id est juxta legis et Prophetarum oracula. Potest item per virgam paterna auctoritas, sed et lancea militaris, qua perforatum est sacratissimum Christi latus, seu lignum crucis, signari. Etenim Pater æternus propria auctoritate dictavit per Christi passionem redimere genus humanum. Omnia namque operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ. Propter quod loquitur : An non licet mihi, quod volo, facere ? Itaque de Christo in cruce vulnerato, suæ caritatis, passionis et obedientiæ merito, toti Ecclesiæ fluxerunt copiosissimi rivuli gratiarum, fluenta sapientiæ, et virtutum charismata. Hinc in Joanne habetur : De plenitudine ejus omnes accepimus. Unde et ipse in Apocalypsi protestatur : Qui sitit, veniat, et accipiat aquam vitæ gratis. Biberunt autem ex fontibus Christi non solum homines, id est electi ex Synagoga unius Dei cultores, sed et jumenta, id est ex gentilitate conversi atque carnales ac prædestinati.
paras.en: [[17:6|thou shalt strike the rock, and water shall come out of it that the people may drink|Percutiesque petram, et exibit ex ea aqua, ut bibat populus]]. By the rock Christ is signified, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 10:4|the rock was Christ|Petra erat Christus]]. By this, then, that Moses struck this rock with the rod, and that most abundant water came out of it, with which the people and the beasts were refreshed, it was prefigured that God the Father gave his Son unto death for us all, as he foretold by Isaias: [[Is 53:8|for the wickedness of my people have I struck him|Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum]]. Wherefore the most worthy prince of the Apostles says: [[Acts 3:18|God before had shewed by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ should suffer, he hath so fulfilled|Deus qui prænuntiavit per os omnium Prophetarum pati Christum suum, implevit sic]]. Christ too says to the Father in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:27|they have persecuted him whom thou hast smitten|Quem tu percussisti, persecuti sunt]]. Now he struck him with the rod, that is, according to the oracles of the Law and the Prophets. By the rod, again, may be signified the Father's authority, but also the soldier's lance with which the most sacred side of Christ was pierced, or the wood of the cross. For the eternal Father by his own authority decreed that the human race should be redeemed through the passion of Christ. For he [[Eph 1:11|worketh all things according to the counsel of his will|Omnia namque operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ]] [Denis writes “according to the purpose of his will”, joining two phrases of the verse]. Wherefore he says: [[Matt 20:15|is it not lawful for me to do what I will?|An non licet mihi, quod volo, facere]] And so from Christ wounded on the cross, by the merit of his charity, passion and obedience, there flowed to the whole Church most copious streams of graces, floods of wisdom, and the gifts of the virtues. Hence we have in John: [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received|De plenitudine ejus omnes accepimus]]. Whence he himself also declares in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 22:17|he that thirsteth, let him come|Qui sitit, veniat]], and [[Apoc 22:17|let him take the water of life, freely|accipiat aquam vitæ gratis]]. And not only men drank from the fountains of Christ, that is, the elect of the Synagogue, worshippers of the one God, but also beasts, that is, those converted from the Gentiles, carnal men, yet predestined.

paras.t: Venit autem Amalec, et pugnavit contra Israel. Per Amalec designantur tam visibiles quam invisibiles hostes justorum, qui populum christianum impugnant. Per Moysen vero designantur superiores prælati, qui inferioribus præsidentibus per Josue figuratis injungunt, ut plebes sibi commissas edoceant, qualiter hostibus suæ salutis, præsertim dæmonibus, debeant repugnare. Per hoc quoque quod Moyses in vertice collis oravit, monstratur, quod prælati debeant in virtutum cacumine esse firmati, sicque cum omni instantia et fervore pro inferioribus deprecari, manibus simul cum corde et oculis in cœlum erectis, juxta illud in Threnis : Levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Deum in cœlos. Imo et unusquisque taliter debet intercedere pro se ipso, sicque orando tentationibus viriliter reluctari. Nempe per hoc quod Moyse manus levante Israel vicit, econtrario autem Amalec, si Moyses manus paululum remisisset : ostensum est, quod virtus tentatoris tanto plus debilitatur, quanto tentatus indesinentius ardentiusque precatur : quo autem tentatus rarius orat atque remissius, eo tentator plus invalescit. Per idem quoque Dominus declaravit, quam vehementissime subditis prosit oratio assidua simul et fervens ejus qui præest. Ideo bonus subditus studeat suo prælato placere in Domino, atque instanter, humiliter, ac ferventer roget prælatum, imo et alios justos, ut jugiter ac ferventer pro se orare dignentur.
paras.en: [[17:8|And Amalec came, and fought against Israel|Venit autem Amalec, et pugnavit contra Israel]]. By Amalec are signified the enemies of the just, visible as well as invisible, who assail the Christian people. By Moses are signified the higher prelates, who enjoin the lower superiors, figured by Josue, to teach the peoples committed to them how they ought to fight against the enemies of their salvation, the demons above all. By this too, that Moses prayed on the top of the hill, it is shown that prelates ought to be established on the summit of the virtues, and so to pray for those beneath them with all urgency and fervour, with hands, heart and eyes alike lifted up to heaven, according to that word in Lamentations: [[Lam 3:41|Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens|Levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Deum in cœlos]]. Indeed each one ought to intercede in this way for himself as well, and so by praying to struggle manfully against temptations. For by this, that [[17:11|when Moses lifted up his hands, Israel overcame|Moyse manus levante Israel vicit]], but on the contrary Amalec, [[17:11|if he let them down a little|si Moyses manus paululum remisisset]], it was shown that the tempter's power is weakened the more, the more unceasingly and ardently the one tempted prays; but the more rarely and slackly the one tempted prays, the more the tempter prevails. By the same thing the Lord also declared how very greatly the constant and fervent prayer of him who presides profits his subjects. Therefore let a good subject strive to please his prelate in the Lord, and urgently, humbly and fervently beg his prelate, and indeed other just men, to deign to pray for him constantly and fervently.

paras.t: Verumtamen per hoc quod Aaron et Hur manus Moysis sustentabant : datur intelligi, quod ipsi prælato communi fragilitate circumdato, adstare et cooperari debent viri ad hoc magis idonei, præsertim qui regunt ac præsunt sub eo. Amplius, per hoc quod manus Moysis graves erant, rigor legis suæ insinuatur : qui rigor in novo Testamento per virtutem et caritatem Christi alleviatur. Quæ virtus et caritas per Aaron, qui interpretatur mons fortitudinis, et per Hur qui interpretatur ignis, apte intelliguntur.
paras.en: Again, by this, that [[17:12|Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands|Aaron et Hur manus Moysis sustentabant]], we are given to understand that the prelate himself, being compassed with the common frailty, ought to have standing by him and working with him men more fit for this, especially those who rule and preside under him. Further, by this, that [[17:12|Moses's hands were heavy|manus Moysis graves erant]], the rigour of his law is intimated: which rigour is lightened in the New Testament by the power and charity of Christ. This power and charity are fitly understood by Aaron, who is interpreted “mountain of strength”, and by Hur, who is interpreted “fire”.

paras.t: Postremo, per hoc quod filiis Israel, transito mari Rubro, a Moyse dictum est, State et videte, Dominus pugnabit pro vobis, et vos tacebitis ; eisdem vero post degustationem manna et potus supernaturaliter dati, præceptum est contra Amalec ire ad prælium : designatur, quod Dominus incipientes, pusillos, et nondum in virtutibus exercitatos, a tentationibus magnis præservat, quas novit eos ferre non posse : eos vero qui gustaverunt quam dulcis sit Dominus, et pro consuetudine sensus habent exercitatos ad discretionem boni ac mali, acrius sunt tentari. Ideo in Ecclesiastico rite docetur : Fili, accedens ad servitutem Dei, sta in justitia, et præpara animam tuam ad tentationem. Itaque Christi miles ad spiritualem pugnam sit semper accinctus, paratus, idoneus, quoniam tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Dominus, et quasi holocausti hostiam accepit illos. Unde et Judith asserit : Omnes qui Deo placuerunt, per multas tribulationes transierunt fideles. Illi autem qui tentationes non susceperunt in timore Domini et in patientia sua, exterminati sunt. Hinc loquitur Augustinus : Persevera usque in finem, quia tentatio durat usque in finem. Et si quæras, in quem finem, respondetur, quousque finias viam. Origenes quoque : Quum cœperis, inquit, manducare manna, et sapientiæ aquam potare, atque ad interiora spiritualis doctrinæ accesseris, pugnam exspecta, et ad prælium te dispone ac præpara.
paras.en: Lastly, by this, that when the Red Sea had been crossed Moses said to the children of Israel, [[Ex 14:13|stand, and see|State et videte]], [[Ex 14:14|The Lord will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace|Dominus pugnabit pro vobis, et vos tacebitis]], whereas the same people, after they had tasted the manna and the drink given them above nature, were commanded to go to battle against Amalec, it is signified that the Lord preserves beginners, the little ones and those not yet exercised in the virtues, from great temptations, which he knows they cannot bear; but those who [[1 Pet 2:3|have tasted that the Lord is sweet|gustaverunt quam dulcis sit Dominus]], and [[Heb 5:14|by custom have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil|pro consuetudine sensus habent exercitatos ad discretionem boni ac mali]], are to be tempted more sharply. Therefore it is rightly taught in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 2:1|Son, when thou comest to the service of God, stand in justice|Fili, accedens ad servitutem Dei, sta in justitia]], [[Ecclus 2:1|and prepare thy soul for temptation|et præpara animam tuam ad tentationem]]. Let the soldier of Christ, then, be always girded, ready and fit for the spiritual combat, since [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace|tanquam aurum in fornace]] the Lord hath proved his elect, [[Wis 3:6|and as a victim of a holocaust, he hath received them|et quasi holocausti hostiam accepit illos]]. Whence Judith too declares: [[Jdt 8:23|all that have pleased God, passed through many tribulations, remaining faithful|Omnes qui Deo placuerunt, per multas tribulationes transierunt fideles]]. [[Jdt 8:24|But they that did not receive the trials with the fear of the Lord|Illi autem qui tentationes non susceperunt in timore Domini]] and in their patience, [[Jdt 8:25|were destroyed|exterminati sunt]] [the margin gives Judith xi, 23; the words are Judith 8:23–25]. Hence Augustine says: Persevere unto the end, because temptation lasts unto the end. And if you ask, unto what end, the answer is: until you finish the way. Origen too: When thou hast begun, he says, to eat the manna and to drink the water of wisdom, and hast come to the inner things of spiritual doctrine, expect a fight, and dispose and prepare thyself for battle.

18.title: Expositio litteralis capituli octavidecimi: Quumque audisset Jethro sacerdos Madian
18.title_en: Literal exposition of the eighteenth chapter: And when Jethro the priest of Madian had heard

paras.t: Qualiter sanctus Moyses informationem et institutionem accepit, non solum a Deo per angelos, sed item ab homine, naturali, humana, et acquisita prudentia prædito, recitatur in isto capitulo.
paras.en: How holy Moses received information and instruction not only from God through the angels, but also from a man endowed with natural, human and acquired prudence, is related in this chapter.

paras.t: Quumque audisset Jethro sacerdos Madian, cognatus Moysis, id est socer ejus et ei affinis, quoniam filia ejus fuit Moysis uxor. De quo Jethro et diversis ejus nominibus, et qualiter fuit sacerdos in provincia Madian, diffuse dictum est supra. Omnia quæ fecerat Dominus Moysi: utpote qualiter prætulit eum Israeliticæ plebi, et quomodo multa et magna mirabilia per eum fecisset, atque diversis beneficiis ornasset eumdem: et Israeli populo suo, etc. Quod ait, Suo, referri potest ad Dominum, et item ad Moysen. Nam populus ille fuit specialiter populus Dei, tanquam cultor unius veri Dei, et multis specialibus donis desuper decoratus. Fuit quoque populus Moysis, tanquam grex ejus gubernationi ac prælationi commissus. Verumtamen non verisimile, quod Jethro percepit in speciali universa et singula quæ Deus fecerat Moysi et Israeli, sed in generali multa audivit, et quædam in speciali, videlicet qualiter Deus propter eos plagavit et submersit Ægyptios. Unde et paulo post in isto capitulo recitatur, qualiter Jethro ex Moysis relatione inde multa cognovit.
paras.en: [[18:1|And when Jethro the priest of Madian, the kinsman of Moses|Quumque audisset Jethro sacerdos Madian, cognatus Moysis]], that is, his father-in-law and kin to him by marriage, since his daughter was the wife of Moses. Of this Jethro and his various names, and how he was priest in the province of Madian[[Ex 2:16||]], much has been said above. [[18:1|had heard all the things that God had done to Moses|Omnia quæ fecerat Dominus Moysi]]: namely how He set him over the people of Israel, and how He had worked many great wonders through him, and adorned him with various benefits; [[18:1|and to Israel his people|et Israeli populo suo]], etc. His saying *his* can be referred to the Lord, and also to Moses. For that people was in a special way the people of God, as the worshipper of the one true God and adorned from above with many special gifts. It was also the people of Moses, as a flock committed to his governance and prelacy. Yet it is not likely that Jethro learned in detail each and every thing that God had done for Moses and Israel; rather he heard many things in general and some in detail, namely how God struck and drowned the Egyptians for their sake. Hence a little later in this chapter it is related how Jethro learned many things about it from Moses' account.

paras.t: Tulit, hoc est secum sumpsit ac duxit, Sephoram uxorem Moysis quam remiserat. Qualiter Moyses eam remiserit, quum tamen ipsa videatur quasi ex indignatione recessisse a Moyse, require supra in expositione secundi capituli. Et duos filios ejus, quorum unus vocabatur Gersam, etc. Istud totum in secundo capitulo continetur, atque expositum est.
paras.en: [[18:2|He took|Tulit]], that is, took with him and brought, [[18:2|Sephora, the wife of Moses, whom he had sent back|Sephoram uxorem Moysis quam remiserat]]. How Moses sent her back, when she seems rather to have left Moses as if in indignation, look for above in the exposition of the second chapter. [[18:3|And her two sons, of whom one was called Gersam|Et duos filios ejus, quorum unus vocabatur Gersam]], etc. All this is contained in the second chapter, and has been explained there.

paras.t: Venit ergo Jethro cognatus Moysis, et filii ejus, et uxor ejus ad Moysen in desertum, ubi erat castrametatus, juxta montem Dei. Quomodo verum est istud, quum sequenti capitulo legantur Moyses et populus Israel exisse de Raphidim, et venisse usque ad Sinai montem? Ergo apparet, quod Jethro venit ad Moysen in Raphidim, non juxta montem Dei, id est non prope montem Sinai: qui vocatur mons Dei, quia elegerat Dominus montem et locum illum ad dandum legem in eo, et ad apparendum ibidem, atque ad faciendum ibi mirabilia multa et magna, ad conferendum quoque hominibus beneficia gratiosa et varia gratiarum charismata. Ad istud quidam etiam inter Hebræos dixerunt, quod istud recitatur hic per anticipationem, ita quod Jethro non venit ad Moysen, nisi postquam filii Israel venerunt in Sinai. Dicuntque aliqui, quod venit lege jam data ibidem. Et apparentiam habet, quod non venit, nisi postquam filii Israel cœperunt in monte Dei notabilem facere moram, non ante, quando erant in assidua loci mutatione. In exordio quoque sequentis capituli innotescit, quod filii Israel venerunt in Sinai in principio tertii mensis, a tempore egressionis ex Ægypto, et ante illud tempus non videtur Jethro venisse, quum esset vir tantæ sublimitatis et grandævæ ætatis. Qui autem vult ordinem sequi historiæ, poterit dicere, quod locus Raphidim non multum distabat a Sinai, ideo fertur venisse ad Moysen prope montem Dei. Quæ tamen solutio non videtur magni valoris, quum in textu aperte dicatur, quod Jethro venit ad Moysen in desertum ubi erat castrametatus juxta montem Dei. Ergo Moyses jam fixerat ibi mansionem.
paras.en: [[18:5|And Jethro, the kinsman of Moses, came with his sons, and his wife to Moses into the desert, where he was camped by the mountain of God|Venit ergo Jethro cognatus Moysis, et filii ejus, et uxor ejus ad Moysen in desertum, ubi erat castrametatus, juxta montem Dei]]. How is this true, when in the following chapter we read that Moses and the people of Israel went out from Raphidim and came as far as Mount Sinai? It appears, then, that Jethro came to Moses in Raphidim, not by the mountain of God, that is, not near Mount Sinai, which is called the mountain of God because the Lord had chosen that mountain and place to give the law on it, to appear there, to work many great wonders there, and to bestow on men gracious benefits and various charisms of graces. To this some among the Hebrews have said that this is related here by anticipation, so that Jethro did not come to Moses until after the children of Israel had come to Sinai. And some say that he came when the law had already been given there. And it seems likely that he did not come until after the children of Israel had begun to make a notable stay at the mountain of God[[Ex 19:2||]], not before, when they were continually changing place. At the beginning of the following chapter too it is made known that the children of Israel came to Sinai at the beginning of the third month from the time of their going out of Egypt[[Ex 19:1||]]; and Jethro does not seem to have come before that time, since he was a man of such high standing and of great age. But whoever wishes to follow the order of the story can say that the place Raphidim was not far from Sinai, and so he is said to have come to Moses near the mountain of God. Yet this solution does not seem of much worth, since the text says openly that Jethro came to Moses [[18:5|into the desert, where he was camped by the mountain of God|in desertum, ubi erat castrametatus, juxta montem Dei]]. So Moses had already fixed his dwelling there.

paras.t: Et mandavit Moysi, dicens: Ego cognatus tuus Jethro venio ad te, et uxor tua, et duo filii tui cum ea. Probabile est, quod Jethro habuit etiam in comitatu quosdam ministros. Significavit autem Moysi suum adventum, an forsitan complaceret Moysi reditus suæ uxoris, et ut Moyses decenter reciperet socerum suum, uxorem, ac sobolem. Qui egressus in occursum cognati sui. Non misit alios in illius occursum, sed personaliter obviam ivit ex caritate et humilitate, et quia cognovit quam venerabilis et prudens vir esset socer suus. Adoravit, et osculatus est eum. Moyses adorationem duliæ, quæ debetur sublimibus personis, socero suo exhibuit, venerando eumdem cum inclinatione aut prostratione. Et puto, quod prævenit eum honore. Non enim oblitus fuit beatissimus Moyses pristinæ humilitatis, ex tam admirabili sua sublimatione apud Deum et homines; sed quo major, eo humilior fuit. Et osculatus est eum, ex amicitia speciali, imo ex spirituali dilectione: de qua osculatione frequenter scribit Apostolus: Salutate invicem in osculo sancto. Salutaveruntque se mutuo verbis pacificis: ita quod Jethro non objecit Moysi, quod uxorem suam remiserat, et quod non rediit ad se, nec prædixerat ipsi Jethro quod tamdiu absens maneret.
paras.en: [[18:6|And he sent word to Moses, saying: I Jethro, thy kinsman, come to thee, and thy wife, and thy two sons with her|Et mandavit Moysi, dicens: Ego cognatus tuus Jethro venio ad te, et uxor tua, et duo filii tui cum ea]]. It is probable that Jethro also had some servants in his company. He made his coming known to Moses, to learn whether the return of his wife would perhaps please Moses, and so that Moses might fittingly receive his father-in-law, his wife and his offspring. [[18:7|And he went out to meet his kinsman|Qui egressus in occursum cognati sui]]. He did not send others to meet him, but went out in person to meet him, out of charity and humility, and because he knew how venerable and prudent a man his father-in-law was. [[18:7|and worshipped and kissed him|Adoravit, et osculatus est eum]]. Moses showed his father-in-law the adoration of dulia [that is, the honour due to persons of high dignity, as distinct from latria, the worship due to God alone], honouring him with a bow or a prostration. And I think that he was the first to show him honour. For most blessed Moses did not forget his former humility in his so wonderful exaltation before God and men; but the greater he was, the humbler he was. And he [[18:7|kissed him|osculatus est eum]] out of special friendship, or rather out of spiritual love: of which kiss the Apostle often writes: [[1 Cor 16:20|Salute one another with a holy kiss|Salutate invicem in osculo sancto]][[2 Cor 13:12||]]. [[18:7|and they saluted one another with words of peace|Salutaveruntque se mutuo verbis pacificis]]: so that Jethro did not reproach Moses for having sent his wife back, and for not having returned to him, nor told Jethro beforehand that he would stay away so long.

paras.t: Quumque intrasset tabernaculum Moysis, narravit Moyses cognato suo cuncta quæ fecerat Dominus Pharaoni et Ægyptiis propter Israel, hoc est propter liberationem Hebræorum ex Ægyptiaca servitute, et etiam propter peccata quæ commiserunt Ægyptii in Hebræos: universumque laborem qui accidisset eis in itinere, et quod liberaverat eos Dominus, hoc est angustias et timores, inopiam victualium, difficultatem et asperitatem viarum, ac fatigationes, quas sustinuerunt a die quo exierunt Ægyptum, usque dum venerunt ad montem Dei. Quamvis enim Jethro de his multa jam percepisset, quoniam undique erant vulgata, petiit tamen aut appetivit de singulis plenius informari. Moyses quoque ex devotionis fervore libenter retulit ei omnia ista. Quæ et aptius potuit ei narrare in tabernaculo, quam in via: quoniam Aaron, Hur, multique alii principales ex Israel venerunt cum Moyse ad recipiendum ipsum Jethro honeste. Hinc in tanto tumultu non fuit aptitudo omnia recitandi.
paras.en: [[18:7|And when he was come into the tent|Quumque intrasset tabernaculum]] of Moses, [[18:8|Moses told his kinsman all that the Lord had done to Pharao, and the Egyptians in favour of Israel|narravit Moyses cognato suo cuncta quæ fecerat Dominus Pharaoni et Ægyptiis propter Israel]], that is, for the deliverance of the Hebrews from the Egyptian bondage, and also on account of the sins which the Egyptians had committed against the Hebrews; [[18:8|and all the labour which had befallen them in the journey, and that the Lord had delivered them|universumque laborem qui accidisset eis in itinere, et quod liberaverat eos Dominus]]: that is, the straits and fears, the want of victuals, the difficulty and roughness of the ways, and the weariness which they endured from the day they went out of Egypt until they came to the mountain of God. For although Jethro had already learned much about these things, since they had been spread abroad on every side, he nevertheless asked, or desired, to be more fully informed of each. And Moses too, out of the fervour of his devotion, gladly told him all these things. He could also tell them to him more fittingly in the tent than on the way, since Aaron, Hur and many other leading men of Israel had come with Moses to receive Jethro with honour; so in so great a throng there was no fit occasion to relate everything.

paras.t: Lætatusque est Jethro super omnibus bonis quæ fecerat Dominus Israeli, hoc est filiis Israel: per filios Israel intelligendo et filias, seu totam Israeliticam plebem illam, quam Jethro dilexit propter Moysen, imo potius propter Deum, in quem jam cœpit fidem et devotionem concipere ex tot mirabilibus ejus, ex quibus perpendit idololatriæ vanitatem, et quod soli summo, unique Deo cultus latriæ deberetur.
paras.en: [[18:9|And Jethro rejoiced for all the good things that the Lord had done to Israel|Lætatusque est Jethro super omnibus bonis quæ fecerat Dominus Israeli]], that is, to the children of Israel: understanding by the sons of Israel the daughters also, or that whole people of Israel, which Jethro loved for Moses' sake, or rather for God's sake, in whom he had now begun to conceive faith and devotion from so many wonders of His, from which he weighed the vanity of idolatry, and that the worship of latria [that is, the worship due to God alone] was owed to the one supreme God alone.

paras.t: Hinc subditur: Et ait Jethro: Benedictus Dominus, qui liberavit vos de manu Ægyptiorum et de manu Pharaonis, etc. Nunc cognovi quia magnus Dominus super omnes deos: hoc est, per hos divinæ potestatis effectus, soli Omnipotenti possibiles, scio quod Dominus quem colunt Hebræi, sit incomparabiliter altior cunctis diis, non solum falsis diis et idolis idololatrarum, sed et cunctis intellectualibus substantiis bonis, quæ per excellentiam sibi desuper datas participative dii vocantur. Porro quod subditur, eo quod superbe egerint contra illos, refertur ad illud, Benedictus Dominus qui eruit populum suum de manu Ægypti. Nam ideo eruit Hebræos, quia Ægyptii superbe egerunt contra illos, despiciendo, illudendo, opprimendoque eos quasi bruta vilissima.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[18:10|And he said|Et ait]] Jethro: [[18:10|Blessed is the Lord|Benedictus Dominus]], who hath delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of Pharao [these words are not in the Douay-Rheims, which gives the verse in short], etc. [[18:11|Now I know, that the Lord is great above all gods|Nunc cognovi quia magnus Dominus super omnes deos]]: that is, by these effects of divine power, possible to the Almighty alone, I know that the Lord whom the Hebrews worship is incomparably higher than all gods: not only the false gods and idols of the idolaters, but also all the good intellectual substances which, by the excellence given them from above, are called gods by participation. Further, what is added, [[18:11|because they dealt proudly against them|eo quod superbe egerint contra illos]], refers to [[18:10|Blessed is the Lord|Benedictus Dominus]] [[18:10|who hath delivered his people out of the hand of Egypt|qui eruit populum suum de manu Ægypti]]. For He rescued the Hebrews because the Egyptians dealt proudly against them, despising, mocking and oppressing them like the vilest beasts.

paras.t: Obtulit ergo Jethro cognatus Moysis holocausta, id est sacrificia, quæ ad divinæ majestatis honorem totaliter incendebantur, ad insinuandum quod vellet de cetero se totum exhibere cultui Dei veri, et hostias Deo, id est alia quæcumque sacrificia pro suis peccatis, quæ in paganismo contra verum Deum commisit: sicque fidem suam ore et opere professus est.
paras.en: [[18:12|So Jethro, the kinsman of Moses, offered holocausts|Obtulit ergo Jethro cognatus Moysis holocausta]], that is, sacrifices which were wholly burnt to the honour of the divine majesty, to signify that he wished henceforth to give himself wholly to the worship of the true God; [[18:12|and sacrifices to God|et hostias Deo]], that is, any other sacrifices for his sins, which he had committed against the true God in paganism. And so he professed his faith by word and deed.

paras.t: Si autem quæratur, qualiter licuit viro gentili officium sacerdotale assumere, et Deo talia sacrificia immolare, ad hoc in Scholastica historia respondetur: Augustinus non vult gentilem immolasse Domino, sed Moysen, secundum aliam translationem, quæ habet, Sumpsit Jethro hostias, id est, de oblatis a Moyse; sumpsit ab eo, et comedit. Et forte Moyses sacrificavit tunc prope montem, sicut prædixerat Dominus. Dicit enim Josephus Jethro venisse circa montem, ubi in rubo multas viderat Moyses visiones. Hæc ibi. Sed hæc verba intricata videntur. Quocirca pensandum, quod Septuaginta sic transtulerunt: Obtulit ergo et sumpsit Jethro socer Moysis holocautomata et sacrificia Domino. Circa quod loquitur Augustinus: Sumpsit, pro Obtulit, posuit. An forte sensus est, ut Jethro ea sumpsisse intelligatur, quæ Moyses intelligitur obtulisse? Legimus autem ipsum Jethro sacerdotem fuisse Madian. Mirum est autem, si ad ejus adventum cœpit Moyses sacrificare, et non potius ipse Jethro, qui jam sacerdos erat, sacrificavit. Ecce in his verbis Augustinus non negat ipsum Jethro sacrificasse.
paras.en: But if it is asked how it was lawful for a gentile man to take up the priestly office and to sacrifice such things to God, the answer given in the *Scholastic History* is this: Augustine will not have it that the gentile sacrificed to the Lord, but Moses, according to another translation, which has: *Jethro took victims*, that is, of the things offered by Moses; he took them from him and ate. And perhaps Moses then sacrificed near the mountain, as the Lord had foretold. For Josephus says that Jethro came to the region of the mountain where Moses had seen many visions in the bush. Thus far that work. But these words seem tangled. We must therefore consider that the Septuagint translated thus: *So Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, offered and took holocausts and sacrifices to the Lord.* On which Augustine says: He put *took* for *offered*. Or perhaps the sense is that Jethro is to be understood to have taken what Moses is understood to have offered? Yet we read that this Jethro was priest of Madian[[Ex 2:16||]]. And it would be strange if at his coming Moses began to sacrifice, and not rather Jethro himself, who was already a priest, offered the sacrifice. See, in these words Augustine does not deny that Jethro himself sacrificed.

paras.t: Itaque advertendum, quod in lege naturæ primogeniti fideles, erant sacerdotes Dei. Quoniam ergo Jethro jam credidit, potuit Deo sacrificare, præsertim si primogenitus fuit.
