Denique qui ex idololatria inter gentiles convertebantur ad cultum veri Dei, post suam conversionem poterant Deo sacrificare, quemadmodum quarto Regum recitatur de Naaman Syro, qui locutus est Eliseo: Non faciet servus tuus ultra holocausta ac victimas diis alienis, nisi Domino. Similiter legitur in libro Jonæ de viris gentilibus, quod visis mirabilibus quæ fiebant in subitanea tempestatis marinæ generatione et cessatione, immolaverunt hostias Deo, et vota voverunt, hoc est, plura se immolaturos Domino promiserunt. De quibus viris scribit ibi Hieronymus, quod promiserunt se amplius non recessuros a Deo, in quem tunc credere inceperunt. Præterea dici posset, quod Jethro pro tanto dicatur obtulisse holocausta ac hostias Deo, quoniam ea ex quibus fiebant sacrificia illa, dedit Moysi ad offerendum, quemadmodum in Job scribitur Deus præcepisse tribus amicis beati Job, ut sumerent septem tauros, totidemque arietes, et irent ad Job, qui offerret pro eis. Sic et in fine secundi Regum habetur, quod David ædificavit altare Domino, obtulitque holocausta atque pacifica. Postremo, quamvis Jethro dicatur conversus ad cultum Dei, non tamen legitur factus neophytus, nec legitur circumcisus fuisse: idcirco non tenebatur ad Mosaicam legem, sed in lege naturæ potuit salvari cum cultu unius Dei, et fide Christi venturi, sicut tunc multi salvati sunt.
paras.en: It is to be noted, then, that under the law of nature the believing first-born were priests of God. Since, then, Jethro now believed, he could sacrifice to God, especially if he was a first-born. Moreover, those among the gentiles who were converted from idolatry to the worship of the true God could sacrifice to God after their conversion, as is related in the fourth book of Kings of Naaman the Syrian, who said to Eliseus: [[4 Kings 5:17|thy servant will not henceforth offer holocaust, or victim, to other gods, but to the Lord|Non faciet servus tuus ultra holocausta ac victimas diis alienis, nisi Domino]]. Likewise we read in the book of Jonas of the gentile men that, having seen the wonders which took place in the sudden rising and calming of the storm at sea, they [[Jon 1:16|sacrificed victims to the Lord, and made vows|immolaverunt hostias Deo, et vota voverunt]]: that is, they promised that they would sacrifice more to the Lord. Of these men Jerome writes there that they promised never again to depart from God, in whom they then began to believe. Besides, it could be said that Jethro is said to have offered holocausts and victims to God inasmuch as he gave Moses the things from which those sacrifices were made, for him to offer; just as it is written in Job that God commanded the three friends of blessed Job to take seven bulls and as many rams, and to go to Job, who would offer for them[[Job 42:8||]] [the margin gives Job xiii, 8; the passage is Job 42:8]. So too at the end of the second book of Kings we have that [[2 Kings 24:25|David built there an altar to the Lord, and offered holocausts and peace offerings|David ædificavit altare Domino, obtulitque holocausta atque pacifica]]. Lastly, although Jethro is said to have been converted to the worship of God, we do not read that he became a neophyte [that is, a proselyte received into the people of Israel], nor that he was circumcised: so he was not bound to the Mosaic law, but could be saved under the law of nature with the worship of the one God and faith in the Christ to come, as many were saved then.

paras.t: Veneruntque Aaron, et omnes seniores Israel, ut comederent panem cum eo, hoc est, ut honorarent ipsum Jethro, manducando cum ipso, et congratulando suæ conversioni ac devotioni, et quoniam erat Moysis socer, virque multum notabilis, præsertim quia et ipse Jethro venit ad Moysen, ad congratulandum suæ prosperitati et prælationi. Venerunt ergo ad manducandum cum Jethro panem: per quem in Scripturis quicumque cibus significatur. Coram Domino. Circa hoc quærit Augustinus, qualiter factum est hoc coram Domino, quum tunc nondum fuerit tabernaculum factum. Ad quod respondet: Id factum est coram Domino, quod factum est ad ejus honorem. Origenes quoque circa hoc loquitur: Non omnes qui manducant, coram Domino manducant: sed perfecti, qui, sive comedunt, sive bibunt, ad Dei gloriam faciunt. Alii sic exponunt: Coram Domino, hoc est in tabernaculo parvo, in quo Moyses tunc responsa accepit, ut in expositione sextidecimi capituli dictum est plenius. Vel, coram altari ubi Jethro sacrificavit.
paras.en: [[18:12|and Aaron and all the ancients of Israel came, to eat bread with him|Veneruntque Aaron, et omnes seniores Israel, ut comederent panem cum eo]]: that is, to honour Jethro by eating with him and rejoicing with him in his conversion and devotion, and because he was the father-in-law of Moses and a very notable man, especially since Jethro himself had come to Moses to rejoice with him in his prosperity and his rule. So they came to eat bread with Jethro: by which any food at all is signified in the Scriptures. [[18:12|before God|Coram Domino]]. On this Augustine asks how this was done before the Lord, since the tabernacle had not yet been made. To which he answers: That is done before the Lord which is done to His honour. Origen too says on this: Not all who eat, eat before the Lord, but the perfect, who, whether they eat or drink, do it for the glory of God. Others explain it thus: *Before the Lord*, that is, in the little tabernacle in which Moses then received answers, as was said more fully in the exposition of the sixteenth chapter. Or: before the altar where Jethro sacrificed.

paras.t: Altera autem die sedit Moyses ut judicaret populum, expediendo et discernendo litigantium causas. Porro magistrorum ac judicum est sedere, tanquam majorum. Et item ad innuendum, quod corde tranquillato, passionibusque sedatis, debeant docere ac sententiare, quod per corporalem sessionem significatur. Qui adstabat Moysi de mane usque ad vesperam. Nam uno expedito, alter accessit. Et forsitan quidam adstabant ad audiendum sententias, quamvis probabile sit, quod expediti et nil causam habentes, removebantur, ut aliis pateret accessus. Verumtamen non apparet, quod sine interpolatione adsistebant per totam diem: alioqui, quando comedissent? Sed tota die adstitisse dicantur, quoniam omni hora ad hoc vacante adstabant.
paras.en: [[18:13|And the next day Moses sat to judge the people|Altera autem die sedit Moyses ut judicaret populum]], settling and deciding the causes of those at law. Now it belongs to masters and judges to sit, as to those who are greater; and also to signify that they ought to teach and pass sentence with a calm heart and with their passions stilled, which is signified by sitting in the body. [[18:13|who stood by Moses from morning until night|Qui adstabat Moysi de mane usque ad vesperam]]. For when one was dealt with, another came forward. And perhaps some stood by to hear the sentences, although it is probable that those whose cases were settled, and those who had no case, were sent away, so that others might have access. Yet it does not appear that they stood there without a break all day: otherwise, when would they have eaten? But they are said to have stood there all day because they stood there at every hour free for it.

paras.t: Quod quum vidisset cognatus ejus, ait: Quid est hoc quod agis in plebe? quasi dicat, Non est satis laudabile. Cur solus sedes, et omnis populus præstolatur de mane usque ad vesperam ad judicandum, quum possis tibi substituere adjutores? Et secundum Josephum, Jethro dixit ista secrete ad Moysen. Moyses vero tanquam vere humilis, omnibus patefecit se ista audisse ac didicisse a Jethro. Cui respondit Moyses: Venit ad me populus quærens sententiam Dei, hoc est justum judicium. Quumque acciderit eis aliqua disceptatio, veniunt ad me, ut judicem inter eos, et ostendam præcepta Dei et leges ejus, hoc est, doceam eos regulas juris et mandata judicialia, juxta revelationem divinam.
paras.en: [[18:14|And when his kinsman had seen|Quod quum vidisset cognatus ejus]], [[18:14|he said|ait]]: [[18:14|What is it that thou dost among the people?|Quid est hoc quod agis in plebe?]]? As if to say: It is not very praiseworthy. [[18:14|Why sittest thou alone, and all the people wait from morning till night?|Cur solus sedes, et omnis populus præstolatur de mane usque ad vesperam]] to be judged, when thou couldst appoint helpers under thee? And according to Josephus, Jethro said these things to Moses privately; but Moses, as one truly humble, made it known to all that he had heard and learned them from Jethro. [[18:15|And Moses answered him: The people come to me to seek the judgment of God?|Cui respondit Moyses: Venit ad me populus quærens sententiam Dei]], that is, a just judgment. [[18:16|And when any controversy falleth out among them, they come to me to judge between them, and to shew the precepts of God, and his laws|Quumque acciderit eis aliqua disceptatio, veniunt ad me, ut judicem inter eos, et ostendam præcepta Dei et leges ejus]]: that is, that I may teach them the rules of right and the judicial commandments, according to divine revelation.

paras.t: At ille: Non bonam, inquit, rem facis, id est, opus hoc judiciale, quo omnibus satisfacere solus conaris, non est satis discrete assumptum a te atque exhibitum. Ideo subditur: Stulto labore consumeris et tu, et populus iste qui tecum est, hoc est, indiscreto labore fatigatis vos invicem: illi, tibi causas proponendo; et tu, omnes solus determinando. Ultra vires tuas est hoc negotium. Solus illud non poteris sustinere. Non quod Moyses non fuerit satis sapiens ad discernendum omnia quæ proponebantur, sed quoniam tempus non sufficiebat ei ad proferendum sententias.
paras.en: [[18:17|But he said|At ille]]: [[18:17|The thing thou dost is not good|Non bonam, inquit, rem facis]]: that is, this work of judging, in which thou triest by thyself to satisfy everyone, has not been taken up and carried out by thee with enough discretion. So it is added: [[18:18|Thou art spent with foolish labour, both thou, and this people that is with thee|Stulto labore consumeris et tu, et populus iste qui tecum est]]: that is, you weary one another with indiscreet labour, they by putting their causes before thee, and thou by deciding them all alone. [[18:18|the business is above thy strength|Ultra vires tuas est hoc negotium]]; [[18:18|thou alone canst not bear it|Solus illud non poteris sustinere]]. Not that Moses was not wise enough to decide all that was put before him, but because the time did not suffice for him to give his sentences.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, an Moyses fuit in isto vere reprehensibilis atque culpabilis: et videtur quod non, alioqui Dominus reprehendisset eum. Respondetur, quod aliquid bonum est, et tamen est omittendum, ut aliquid melius fiat. Itaque quod Moyses fecit ex caritate atque justitia, non sine gravi labore, non videtur fuisse simpliciter malum. Poterat tamen in hoc Moysis opere aliquis defectus venialis peccati esse admixtus, videlicet indiscretio seu inconsiderata quædam: quod tamen Dominus ei non revelavit, quatenus inde instrueretur a viro gentili. Quod Deus sic ordinavit, ad magnam informationem omnium nostrum, ut infra tangetur. Nam et Augustinus circa hæc ait: Cur Dominus famulum suum, cum quo, et per quem, tanta ac talia loquebatur, permisit ab alienigena informari et admoneri? In quo Scriptura nos admonet, consilium veritatis non esse spernendum, per quemcumque præstetur. Videndum quoque, ne forte Deus voluerit ibi Moysen ab alienigena admoneri, ubi ipse Moyses posset tentari superbia, quæ in judiciaria potestate solet misceri. Hæc Augustinus. Aliqui vero dicunt, quod factum hoc Moysis non fuit culpabile, sed poterat melius fieri. Id vero quod est minus bonum, comparatione boni melioris dicitur quodammodo malum, videlicet respective, non tamen in se. Quemadmodum etiam minus malum, respectu pejoris, dicitur eligibile aliqualiter, respectiveque bonum.
paras.en: On this it is asked whether Moses was truly blameworthy and at fault in this. And it seems not: otherwise the Lord would have reproved him. The answer is that something may be good and yet be left undone so that something better may be done. So what Moses did out of charity and justice, not without heavy labour, does not seem to have been simply evil. Yet in this work of Moses some defect of venial sin could have been mixed in, namely a want of discretion or a certain lack of consideration; which the Lord nevertheless did not reveal to him, so that he might be instructed in it by a gentile man. God so ordained this for the great instruction of us all, as will be touched on below. For Augustine too says on this: Why did the Lord allow His servant, with whom and through whom He spoke such great things and of such a kind, to be instructed and admonished by a foreigner? In this the Scripture admonishes us that the counsel of truth is not to be spurned, through whomever it is given. We must also consider whether perhaps God willed that Moses be admonished by a foreigner at the point where Moses himself could be tempted by pride, which is wont to mingle with the power of judging. Thus far Augustine. But some say that this deed of Moses was not blameworthy, but could have been done better. And what is less good is in a manner called evil by comparison with a better good, that is, relatively, though not in itself; just as a lesser evil, with respect to a worse one, is called in some way choiceworthy, and good relatively.

paras.t: Sed audi verba mea, id est, increpationem seu admonitionem hanc benevole suscipe, atque consilia de agendis in gubernatione populi hujus. Consilium autem proprie dicitur inquisitio de agendis. Unde secundum Damascenum, est ignorantis naturæ. Sed nunc sumitur consilium pro informatione seu dictamine dirigentis. Et erit Dominus tecum, id est per gratiam ampliorem, si humiliter acquieveris imperfectiori, in eo quod veraciter dicit. Esto tu populo in his quæ ad Deum pertinent, id est, inter Deum ac populum tibi commissum sis mediator: ut referas quæ dicuntur, ad eum, hoc est, verba Dei referas populo, vel causas, vota, orationes populi offeras Deo, ejus misericordiam implorando; ostendasque populo cærimonias, id est cærimonialia Dei præcepta, observanda in celebrationibus solennitatum et oblationibus sacrificiorum, et ritum colendi, hoc est formam et morem servandos in præceptis moralibus, viamque per quam ingredi debeant, id est iter salutis, et opus quod facere debeant, hoc est, quid quo tempore sit agendum, ut omnia fiant ordinate.
paras.en: [[18:19|But hear my words|Sed audi verba mea]], that is, receive this rebuke or admonition with good will, [[18:19|and counsels|atque consilia]] about what is to be done in governing this people. Now *counsel*, properly speaking, is an inquiry about what is to be done; hence, according to Damascene, it belongs to a nature that does not know [that is, it is a seeking proper to a mind that lacks knowledge, and so is not found in God]. But here *counsel* is taken for the instruction or direction of one who guides. [[18:19|and God shall be with thee|Et erit Dominus tecum]], that is, by more abundant grace, if thou humbly yield to one less perfect in what he truly says. [[18:19|Be thou to the people in those things that pertain to God|Esto tu populo in his quæ ad Deum pertinent]]: that is, be the mediator between God and the people committed to thee: [[18:19|to bring their words to him|ut referas quæ dicuntur, ad eum]]: that is, bring the words of God to the people, or offer to God the causes, vows and prayers of the people, imploring His mercy; [[18:20|And to shew the people the ceremonies|ostendasque populo cærimonias]], that is, God's ceremonial precepts, to be observed in the celebration of the solemn feasts and in the offering of sacrifices, [[18:20|and the manner of worshipping|et ritum colendi]], that is, the form and manner to be kept in the moral precepts, [[18:20|and the way wherein they ought to walk|viamque per quam ingredi debeant]], that is, the road of salvation, [[18:20|and the work that they ought to do|et opus quod facere debeant]], that is, what is to be done at what time, so that all things may be done in order.

paras.t: Provide autem de omni plebe viros potentes, id est, diligenter considera, et elige ex populo universo sine personarum acceptione, et non solum ex tuis cognatis, viros eminentes, potentes, videlicet nobiles et magnates, qui (cæteris paribus) ad regendum alios sunt aptiores, quatenus sua potestate queant rebelles compescere, magisque timeantur. Propter quod in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Noli quærere fieri judex, nisi valeas virtute irrumpere iniquitates. Et timentes Deum, filiali timore, aut saltem initiali, ne ex humano timore a via æquitatis recedant; in quibus sit veritas triplex, videlicet veritas vitæ, doctrinæ, justitiæ; et qui oderint avaritiam, ne per munera corrumpantur. De explanatione autem horum verborum infra diffusius conscribetur. Et constitue ex eis tribunos, id est millenarios, utpote principes, quorum quilibet præsit mille viris: unde alia translatio habet, Constitue ex eis super millenos; et centuriones, quorum quilibet præsit centum hominibus; et quinquagenarios, et decanos: ita ut quilibet quinquagenarius princeps præsit quinquaginta, et unusquisque decanus præsideat decem; qui judicent populum omni tempore: hoc est, quorum principum unusquisque judicet causas eorum qui sibi subjecti sunt, tempore opportuno.
paras.en: [[18:21|And provide out of all the people able men|Provide autem de omni plebe viros potentes]]: that is, consider carefully, and choose out of the whole people without respect of persons, and not only from thine own kin, men who are eminent and powerful, that is, nobles and great men, who (other things being equal) are more fit to rule others, so that by their power they may restrain the rebellious and be the more feared. For this reason it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:6|Seek not to be made a judge, unless thou have strength enough to extirpate iniquities|Noli quærere fieri judex, nisi valeas virtute irrumpere iniquitates]]. [[18:21|such as fear God|Et timentes Deum]], with filial fear, or at least initial fear [that is, the fear of a soul beginning to love God, between servile fear of punishment and the filial fear of offending Him], lest out of human fear they turn aside from the way of equity; [[18:21|in whom there is truth|in quibus sit veritas]], threefold truth, namely truth of life, of doctrine and of justice; [[18:21|and that hate avarice|et qui oderint avaritiam]], lest they be corrupted by gifts. Of the explanation of these words more will be written below at greater length. [[18:21|and appoint of them rulers of thousands|Et constitue ex eis tribunos]], that is, *millenarii*, namely chiefs each of whom is over a thousand men; hence another translation has: *Appoint of them over thousands*; [[18:21|and of hundreds|et centuriones]], each of whom is over a hundred men; [[18:21|and of fifties, and of tens|et quinquagenarios, et decanos]]: so that each captain of fifty is over fifty, and each captain of ten over ten; [[18:22|Who may judge the people at all times|qui judicent populum omni tempore]]: that is, each of these chiefs is to judge the causes of those who are under him, at the fitting time.

paras.t: Quidquid autem majus fuerit, referant ad te: videlicet difficiliores causas, quas discernere nequiverint, vel quæ directe concernebant intelligentiam legis, cujus interpretatio pertinebat ad summum; et ipsi minora tantummodo judicent: sic tamen, quod inter hos principes subordinatio fuit, sicut nunc est inter prælatos Ecclesiæ, ita quod si decanus nequivit determinare causam eorum qui erant sub eo, habebatur recursus ad quinquagenarium: quod si ille nequibat discernere, ascendebatur ad centurionem: deinde si opus fuit, ad tribunum; sicque tandem ad Moysen, quod tamen contigit raro: idcirco non gravabatur. Unde subjungitur: leviusque tibi sit, partito in alios onere, id est officio judicandi, quod habet onus annexum. Si hæc feceris, implebis imperium Dei: hoc est, populum istum convenientius gubernabis secundum injunctum tibi a Deo officium; et præcepta ejus poteris sustentare; et omnis hic populus revertetur ad loca sua cum pace pectoris, et cum mutua pace expeditis eorum causis, et disceptationibus jam sedatis. Delectat quoque populum, ut superior dignitatem suam communicet aliis per congruos gradus, ne videatur solus velle præesse, aut præsumere quod ipse valeat omnia expedire, sicque elationis, invidentiæ, et præsumptionis redarguatur.
paras.en: [[18:22|and when any great matter soever shall fall out, let them refer it to thee|Quidquid autem majus fuerit, referant ad te]]: namely the more difficult causes, which they could not decide, or those which directly concerned the understanding of the law, whose interpretation belonged to the highest; [[18:22|and let them judge the lesser matters only|et ipsi minora tantummodo judicent]]: yet in such a way that there was a subordination among these chiefs, as there now is among the prelates of the Church, so that if a captain of ten could not settle the cause of those under him, recourse was had to the captain of fifty; and if he could not decide it, it went up to the centurion; then, if need be, to the tribune; and so at last to Moses, which however happened rarely: so he was not overburdened. Hence it is added: [[18:22|that so it may be lighter for thee, the burden being shared out unto others|leviusque tibi sit, partito in alios onere]], that is, the office of judging, which has a burden joined to it. [[18:23|If thou dost this, thou shalt fulfil the commandment of God|Si hæc feceris, implebis imperium Dei]]: that is, thou wilt govern this people more fittingly according to the office enjoined on thee by God; [[18:23|and shalt be able to bear his precepts|et præcepta ejus poteris sustentare]]; [[18:23|and all this people shall return to their places with peace|et omnis hic populus revertetur ad loca sua cum pace]] of heart, and with mutual peace, their causes being settled and their disputes now calmed. It also pleases the people that a superior should share his dignity with others by fitting degrees, so that he may not seem to wish to rule alone, or to presume that he can settle everything himself, and so be charged with haughtiness, envy and presumption.

paras.t: Quibus auditis, Moyses fecit omnia quæ ille suggesserat. In quo patet profunda et mira humilitas Moysis. Et electis viris strenuis de cuncto Israel: non dicitur quod Moyses per se eos elegit, quia ut in Deuteronomio habetur, commisit populo istam electionem: constituit eos principes populi, videlicet tribunos, et centuriones, et quinquagenarios, et decanos, etc. Approbavit enim electionem populi, et qui potentiores, justiores ac sapientiores reputabantur, pluribus præficiebantur. Putandum est autem, quod Jethro dixit Moysi præinductam increpationem et consultationem seorsum, ex quadam familiaritate et amicitia speciali: unde et tam confidenter locutus est. Deinde Moyses dixit ad populum ea quæ in Deuteronomio habentur, videlicet: Non possum solus sustinere vestra negotia ac jurgia. Date ex vobis viros sapientes et gnaros, et ponam eos vobis principes, etc.
paras.en: [[18:24|And when Moses heard this, he did all things that he had suggested unto him|Quibus auditis, Moyses fecit omnia quæ ille suggesserat]]. In this the deep and wonderful humility of Moses is plain. [[18:25|And choosing able men out of all Israel|Et electis viris strenuis de cuncto Israel]]: it is not said that Moses chose them by himself, because, as we have in Deuteronomy, he committed this choice to the people[[Deut 1:13||]] [the margin gives Deut. i; the people's choosing is at Deut 1:13–15]: [[18:25|he appointed them rulers of the people|constituit eos principes populi]], namely [[18:25|rulers over thousands, and over hundreds, and over fifties, and over tens|tribunos, et centuriones, et quinquagenarios, et decanos]], etc. For he approved the people's choice, and those who were reputed more powerful, more just and wiser were set over more. And it is to be thought that Jethro spoke the rebuke and counsel given above to Moses apart, out of a certain special familiarity and friendship; hence he spoke so boldly. Then Moses said to the people what is found in Deuteronomy, namely: [[Deut 1:12|I alone am not able to bear your business, and the charge of you and your differences|Non possum solus sustinere vestra negotia ac jurgia]] [Denis's wording, *Non possum*, differs a little from the Vulgate's *Non valeo*]. [[Deut 1:13|Let me have from among you wise and understanding men|Date ex vobis viros sapientes et gnaros]], [[Deut 1:13|that I may appoint them your rulers|et ponam eos vobis principes]], etc.

paras.t: Dimisitque cognatum suum. Per quod insinuatur, quod Moyses ex magna dilectione tenuit secum, quamdiu congrue potuit, socerum suum: et tandem redire absolute volentem, dimisit eum caritate et pace, deducens eumdem reverenter per aliquod spatium. Qui reversus, hoc est redire incipiens, abiit a Moyse in terram suam, videlicet Madian, relictis apud Moysen conjuge ejus ac filiis.
paras.en: [[18:27|And he let his kinsman depart|Dimisitque cognatum suum]]. By this it is suggested that Moses, out of great love, kept his father-in-law with him as long as he fittingly could; and at last, when he wished outright to return, he let him go in charity and peace, escorting him respectfully for some distance. [[18:27|and he returned|Qui reversus]], that is, beginning to return, [[18:27|and went|abiit]] from Moses [[18:27|into his own country|in terram suam]], namely Madian, leaving with Moses his wife and sons.

18.title: De tropologiis ejusdem capituli octavidecimi
18.title_en: On the tropological senses of the same eighteenth chapter

paras.t: Quid per Sephoram Moysis conjugem, et quid per ejus remissionem significatur, præhabitum est. Præterea, virtutes sanctissimi Moysis nobis ex isto capitulo multipliciter commendantur. In primis fervor suæ devotionis, quia narravit socero suo universa mirabilia Dei in Ægypto, marique Rubro, atque in solitudine facta. Discamus ergo et nos tanti Sancti exemplo non inaniter commendare nos ipsos, non proprias jactare virtutes, nec in verbositatibus et vitiosis confabulationibus tempus expendere, sed mirabilia Dei, beneficia ejus et pietatem, gratiamque ipsius cum omni alacritate ac devotionis ardore intra nos meditari, aliis recitare, ac pro viribus collaudare. Nempe, ut Tobiæ Raphael angelus contestatur, Sacramentum regis abscondere, bonum est: opera autem Dei revelare ac confiteri, honorificum est. Ideo ait Psalmista: Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo: narrabo omnia mirabilia tua. Ecclesiasticus quoque asserit: Nonne Dominus fecit Sanctos enarrare omnia mirabilia sua, quæ confirmavit Dominus omnipotens, stabilis in gloria sua?
paras.en: What is signified by Sephora, the wife of Moses, and by her being sent back, has been said already. Besides this, the virtues of the most holy Moses are commended to us by this chapter in many ways. First, the fervour of his devotion, since he told his father-in-law all the wonders of God done in Egypt, at the Red Sea and in the wilderness. Let us therefore also learn, by the example of so great a Saint, not to commend ourselves to no purpose, not to boast of our own virtues, nor to spend our time in wordiness and in sinful idle talk, but to meditate within ourselves on the wonders of God, His benefits and loving-kindness and His grace, with all eagerness and ardour of devotion, to recount them to others, and to praise them with all our strength. For indeed, as the angel Raphael testifies to Tobias, [[Tob 12:7|it is good to hide the secret of a king: to reveal and confess the works of God|Sacramentum regis abscondere, bonum est: opera autem Dei revelare ac confiteri, honorificum est]] [the Latin ends: "is a thing to be honoured", words the Douay-Rheims leaves out]. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 9:2|I will give praise to thee, O Lord, with my whole heart: I will relate all thy wonders|Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo: narrabo omnia mirabilia tua]]. Ecclesiasticus also declares: [[Ecclus 42:17|Hath not the Lord made the saints to declare all his wonderful works, which the Lord Almighty hath firmly settled to be established for his glory?|Nonne Dominus fecit Sanctos enarrare omnia mirabilia sua, quæ confirmavit Dominus omnipotens, stabilis in gloria sua?]]

paras.t: Insuper, cum Jethro audiamus mirabilia Dei cum gaudio spirituali, congratulemurque eis quibus Deus misericordiam suam impendit, et super his offeramus Deo sacrificium laudis, hostiam regratiationis, atque in toto corde convertamur ad ipsum.
paras.en: Further, with Jethro let us hear the wonders of God with spiritual joy, and rejoice with those on whom God bestows His mercy, and for these things let us offer to God the sacrifice of praise, a victim of thanksgiving, and turn to Him with our whole heart.

paras.t: Cum Aaron quoque et senioribus Israel, discamus comedere et bibere coram Domino, id est virtuose et sobrie cum prævia cibi et potus benedictione et sequente gratiarum actione, vitantes immoderantiam et verborum excessum, atque ad Dei gloriam referentes ipsam refectionem: ut scilicet corpore moderanter refecto, apti simus ad Dei obsequium, et ad omne opus virtutum, in tantum, ut et exteriora ac mechanica opera, ad spiritualem finem ac Dei honorificentiam ordinemus. Circa hæc loquitur Origenes: Non omnes manducant panem in conspectu Dei, sed qui meritis sunt probati, et implent illud Apostoli: Sive manducatis, sive bibitis, sive aliud quid facitis, omnia ad gloriam Dei facite. Omne ergo quod faciunt sancti, in conspectu faciunt Dei. Peccator autem fugit a Dei conspectu, quemadmodum Adam post transgressionem abscondit se, et Cain, fratre suo occiso, egressus est a facie Domini. Ego autem amplius locum istum discutiens, video quia qui pleniorem Dei scientiam accipiunt, pleniusque divinis imbuti sunt disciplinis, isti etiam si malum faciunt, coram Deo hoc agunt, quemadmodum ille qui dixit: Tibi soli peccavi, et malum coram te feci. Quid ergo plus habet, qui coram Deo peccat, nisi quod continue pœnitet, et dicit, Peccavi, ignosce mihi? Qui autem discedit a conspectu Dei, nescit converti. Hæc Origenes.
paras.en: With Aaron also and the ancients of Israel let us learn [[18:12|to eat|comedere]] and drink [[18:12|before God|coram Domino]], that is, virtuously and soberly, with a blessing of the food and drink beforehand and a giving of thanks after, avoiding immoderation and excess of words, and referring the meal itself to the glory of God: so that, the body being moderately refreshed, we may be fit for the service of God and for every work of virtue; so much so that we direct even outward and manual works to a spiritual end and to the honour of God. On this Origen says: Not all [[18:12|eat bread with him before God|manducant panem in conspectu Dei]], but those who are proved by their merits and fulfil that saying of the Apostle: [[1 Cor 10:31|whether you eat or drink, or whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God|Sive manducatis, sive bibitis, sive aliud quid facitis, omnia ad gloriam Dei facite]]. Whatever the saints do, therefore, they do in the sight of God. But the sinner flees from the sight of God, as Adam after his transgression hid himself, and Cain, when he had slain his brother, [[Gen 4:16|went out from the face of the Lord|egressus est a facie Domini]][[Gen 4:14||]]. But as I examine this place further, I see that those who receive a fuller knowledge of God and are more fully steeped in divine teaching, even if they do evil, do it before God, like him who said: [[Ps 50:6|To thee only have I sinned, and have done evil before thee|Tibi soli peccavi, et malum coram te feci]]. What more, then, has he who sins before God, but that he repents continually and says: I have sinned, forgive me? But he who departs from the sight of God knows not how to turn back. Thus far Origen.

paras.t: Amplius, ex isto capitulo commendatur nobis laboriositas et patientia Moysis, quia a mane usque ad vesperam sedit, ad decidendum ac mitigandum causas ac jurgia populi. Graviter itaque peccant principes ac judices terræ, qui causas habentibus faciunt tædiosas et irrationabiles moras, ludis vanitatibusque intenti.
paras.en: Further, this chapter commends to us the laboriousness and patience of Moses, since he sat [[18:13|from morning until night|a mane usque ad vesperam]] to decide and calm the causes and quarrels of the people. Grievously, then, do the princes and judges of the earth sin who put those who have causes to wearisome and unreasonable delays, being intent on games and vanities.

paras.t: Instruuntur demum ex isto capitulo præsidentes, præsertim prælati ac præsules, ne circa exteriora et lites immoderanter se occupent; sed talia quantum fieri potest, inferioribus ad hoc aptis committant, ne a melioribus vicinioribusque saluti actibus impediantur, sed vacent divinis, et pro subditorum salute coram Deo negotientur, illisque monstrent verbis et exemplis viam salutis, præcepta Dei, mandata Ecclesiæ, modum spiritualis profectus.
paras.en: Lastly, those who preside are taught by this chapter, above all prelates and bishops, not to busy themselves immoderately with outward affairs and lawsuits, but to commit such things, as far as can be done, to inferiors fit for it, lest they be hindered from better actions and those nearer to salvation; but rather to give themselves to divine things, and to do business before God for the salvation of their subjects, and to show them by word and example the way of salvation, the precepts of God, the commandments of the Church and the manner of spiritual progress.

paras.t: Præterea hic docemur, quales sint ad prælationem ac judiciariam potestatem eligendi ac promovendi. De quibus in primis fertur in textu, quod debeant esse potentes, ut queant perversos ac rebelles terrere, refrenare, corrigere. Si autem habuerint potestatem sine sapientia atque justitia, datur eis tyrannizandi occasio, et additur oleum igni. Verumtamen ubi nostra translatio habet, Provide viros potentes; alia continet, Provide viros sapientes. Sapientia quippe summe est necessaria judicibus ac prælatis. Propter quod, Væ terræ cujus princeps puer est. Et Plato beatam dixit rempublicam, cujus rectores sapientiæ student. Et quinto de Civitate Dei asserit Augustinus: Illi qui vera pietate præditi bene vivunt, si habent scientiam regendi populos, nil est felicius rebus humanis, quam si (Deo miserante) habeant potestatem. Verum ut ait sanctus pater Bernardus, rara est hujusmodi avis in terra: ideo si occurrat, injiciendæ sunt manus, ut apprehendatur.
paras.en: Moreover, we are taught here what sort of men are to be chosen and raised to prelacy and to judicial power. Of these it is said in the text, first, that they ought to be [[18:21|able|potentes]] [that is, powerful; Latin *potentes*], so that they can strike fear into the wicked and rebellious, curb them and correct them. But if they have power without wisdom and justice, an occasion of tyranny is given them, and oil is added to the fire. Yet where our translation has [[18:21|provide out of all the people able men|Provide viros potentes]], another has: Provide wise men. For wisdom is supremely necessary to judges and prelates. Hence: [[Eccles 10:16|Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child|Væ terræ cujus princeps puer est]] [Denis reads *princeps*, "prince", where the Vulgate has *rex*, "king"]. And Plato called that commonwealth happy whose rulers study wisdom. And Augustine declares in the fifth book of the City of God: If those who live well, endowed with true piety, have the knowledge of ruling peoples, nothing is happier for human affairs than that they should have power, by the mercy of God. But, as the holy father Bernard says, a bird of this kind is rare on the earth: therefore, if one turns up, hands must be laid on it so that it is caught.

paras.t: Secundo, de eligendis et promovendis fertur in textu, quod sint Deum timentes: alioqui cito a veritate recederent æquitatis, et timore periculi vel offensæ humanæ, judicia proferrent injusta. Hinc libro secundo Paralipomenon fidelissimus rex Josaphat legitur dixisse suis judicibus: Videte quid faciatis. Non enim hominum exercetis judicium, sed Dei; et quodcumque judicaveritis, in vos redundabit. Sit timor Domini vobiscum, et cuncta cum diligentia facite.
paras.en: Secondly, it is said in the text of those to be chosen and raised up, that they be [[18:21|such as fear God|Deum timentes]]: otherwise they would quickly depart from the truth of equity, and, for fear of danger or of giving offence to men, would pronounce unjust judgments. Hence in the second book of Paralipomenon the most faithful king Josaphat is read to have said to his judges: [[2 Par 19:6|Take heed what you do: for you exercise not the judgment of man, but of the Lord: and whatsoever you judge, it shall redound to you|Videte quid faciatis. Non enim hominum exercetis judicium, sed Dei; et quodcumque judicaveritis, in vos redundabit]]. [[2 Par 19:7|Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and do all things with diligence|Sit timor Domini vobiscum, et cuncta cum diligentia facite]].

paras.t: Tertio dicitur de eisdem, quod in eis sit veritas: veritas, inquam, vitæ, ita ut virtuosi exsistant, ne sint indigni alios judicare. Siquidem indignus est reum dijudicare, qui in eisdem aut majoribus est peccatis, ut ait Ambrosius. Sit quoque in eis veritas doctrinæ, quatenus secundum regulas juris procedant, et rationabiliter instruant partem utramque. Sit item in eis veritas justitiæ, sicut sanctus Job dixit: Justitia indutus sum. Nam et Philosophus protestatur, quod judex debet esse quasi animata justitia, et lex viva, ut a vera æquitate nusquam discedat, quia ad ipsum confugiunt homines, quasi ad regulam æquitatis. Hinc in Deuteronomio Moyses loquitur: Date ex vobis viros gnaros et sapientes, quorum conversatio probata sit in tribubus vestris; et ponam eos vobis principes. Quibus etiam ibi legitur præcepisse: Quod justum est, judicate: sive civis sit ille, sive peregrinus, nulla erit distantia: ita parvum audietis, ut magnum; nec accipietis cujusquam personam, quia judicium Dei est.
paras.en: Thirdly it is said of them, [[18:21|in whom there is truth|in eis sit veritas]]: truth, I mean, of life, so that they be virtuous, lest they be unworthy to judge others. For he is unworthy to judge a guilty man who is himself in the same or greater sins, as Ambrose says. Let there be in them also truth of doctrine, so that they proceed according to the rules of law and instruct both parties reasonably. Let there likewise be in them truth of justice, as holy Job said: [[Job 29:14|I was clad with justice|Justitia indutus sum]]. For the Philosopher too declares that a judge ought to be as it were justice alive and a living law, so that he never departs from true equity, since men flee to him as to the rule of equity. Hence Moses says in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 1:13|Let me have from among you wise and understanding men, and such whose conversation is approved among your tribes, that I may appoint them your rulers|Date ex vobis viros gnaros et sapientes, quorum conversatio probata sit in tribubus vestris; et ponam eos vobis principes]]. And there he is also read to have commanded them: [[Deut 1:16|judge that which is just: whether he be one of your country, or a stranger|Quod justum est, judicate: sive civis sit ille, sive peregrinus]]: [[Deut 1:17|There shall be no difference of persons, you shall hear the little as well as the great: neither shall you respect any man's person, because it is the judgment of God|nulla erit distantia: ita parvum audietis, ut magnum; nec accipietis cujusquam personam, quia judicium Dei est]].

paras.t: Quarto dicitur de eisdem, quod odiant avaritiam, ut scilicet non solum non sint avari, sed tam in se, quam in aliis, totis præcordiis avaritiam detestentur. Unde infra scribitur: Non accipias munera, quæ excæcant etiam prudentes, et subvertunt verba justorum. Verumtamen alia translatio habet, Qui oderint superbiam. Superbia namque tanto plus est præsidentibus ac judicibus odienda, quanto eis major est occasio superbiendi: quia in sublimitate quadam se intuentur, eisque plurimi blandiuntur, et magna eis libertas est faciendi quod volunt. Verum, si pensent quod Sapiens habet, formidabunt et humiles erunt. Scriptum est enim ibidem: Data vobis est potestas ab Altissimo, qui interrogabit opera vestra, et cogitationes vestras scrutabitur. Cito et horrende apparebit vobis, quoniam judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet; et potentes, potenter tormenta patientur. Hinc Ecclesiasticus ait: Rectorem te posuerunt? noli extolli; esto in illis, quasi unus ex ipsis; curam illorum habe, et sic considera.
paras.en: Fourthly it is said of them, [[18:21|that hate avarice|odiant avaritiam]]: that is, that they not only be not avaricious, but detest avarice with all their heart, as much in themselves as in others. Hence it is written further on: [[Ex 23:8|Neither shalt thou take bribes, which even blind the wise, and pervert the words of the just|Non accipias munera, quæ excæcant etiam prudentes, et subvertunt verba justorum]]. Yet another translation has: Who hate pride. For pride is to be hated by those who preside and by judges all the more as they have greater occasion of pride: since they see themselves in a certain eminence, and very many flatter them, and they have great freedom to do what they will. But if they weigh what the Wise Man has, they will fear and be humble. For it is written there: [[Wis 6:4|power is given you by the Lord, and strength by the most High, who will examine your works: and search out your thoughts|Data vobis est potestas ab Altissimo, qui interrogabit opera vestra, et cogitationes vestras scrutabitur]]. [[Wis 6:6|Horribly and speedily will he appear to you: for a most severe judgment shall be for them that bear rule|Cito et horrende apparebit vobis, quoniam judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet]]; [[Wis 6:7|the mighty shall be mightily tormented|potentes, potenter tormenta patientur]] [the margin gives Wis. vi, 6, 7; the first sentence is v. 4]. Hence Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 32:1|Have they made thee ruler? be not lifted up: be among them as one of them|Rectorem te posuerunt? noli extolli; esto in illis, quasi unus ex ipsis]] [[Ecclus 32:2|Have care of them|curam illorum habe]], and so consider [Denis reads *considera*, "consider", where the Vulgate has *conside*, "sit down"].

paras.t: Tales itaque sunt eligendi et promovendi, imo secundum forum conscientiæ tenetur unusquisque eligere meliorem seu digniorem, quamvis secundum forum contentiosum sufficiat eligere bonum et dignum. Alioqui electio semper posset cassari.
paras.en: Such men, then, are to be chosen and raised up; indeed, in the court of conscience [that is, before God, in the judgment of one's own conscience] each is bound to choose the better or worthier man, although in the contentious court [that is, in the external court of law, where disputes are tried] it is enough to choose one who is good and worthy. Otherwise an election could always be quashed.

paras.t: Postremo, in hoc capitulo commendatur nobis gloriosa humilitas, optimaque docilitas divinissimi Moysis, qui dum ad libitum divinis frueretur alloquiis, angelicisque instrueretur dogmatibus, nihilo minus dignantissime sumpsit, promptissime quoque implevit viri gentilis instructionem. Nemo igitur cornua sibi assumat, nullus in suis oculis tam sapiens exstet, ut increpationes et informationes suscipere dedignetur; imo et ab inferiori dignanter accipiat et gratanter, quidquid vere et salubriter ab illo audierit. Hinc Origenes disseruit: Satiari non possumus intuendo quod scriptum est, quam vehementer nos instruat. Etenim quum prospicio, quod Moyses propheta Deo plenus, cui Deus facie ad faciem loquebatur, consilium accepit a Jethro Madian sacerdote, admiratione nimia stuporem mentis incurro. Scriptum est enim: Audivit Moyses vocem soceri sui. Et non dixit socero suo: Mihi loquitur Deus, et cœlesti sermone defertur ad me, quid agere debeam: et quomodo consilium ab homine suscipiam, et a viro gentili? Et non quis dicat, sed quid dicat, auscultat. Unde et nos si forte aliquando invenimus aliquid sapienter dictum a gentilibus, non illud spernamus. Quis autem eorum qui præsunt, non dico, si jam aliqua ei a Deo sunt revelata, sed si in legis scientia aliquid meriti habet, dignatur consilium inferioris saltem sacerdotis accipere, nedum dixerim laici, nedum gentilis? Sed Moyses qui erat præ cunctis hominibus mansuetus, consilium accepit inferioris, ut et formam daret humilitatis principibus populorum, et futuri sacramenti designaret imaginem. Hæc Origenes.
paras.en: Lastly, there is commended to us in this chapter the glorious humility and excellent docility of the most divine Moses, who, though he enjoyed divine converse at will and was instructed by angelic teachings, nonetheless most graciously received, and also most promptly carried out, the instruction of a Gentile man. Let no one, then, take horns to himself [that is, grow proud], let no one be so wise in his own eyes as to disdain to receive rebukes and instruction; rather let him graciously and gratefully accept, even from an inferior, whatever he hears from him that is true and wholesome. Hence Origen discoursed: We cannot have our fill of gazing at what is written, how mightily it instructs us. For when I see that Moses, a prophet full of God, to whom God spoke [[Ex 33:11|face to face|facie ad faciem]], took counsel from Jethro, the priest of Madian, I fall into amazement of mind from exceeding wonder. For it is written: [[18:24|Moses heard|Audivit Moyses]] the voice of his father-in-law [Origen follows another version here; the Vulgate has: *Quibus auditis*, "when Moses heard this"]. And he did not say to his father-in-law: God speaks to me, and what I ought to do is brought to me by a heavenly word; and how shall I take counsel from a man, and a Gentile? And he listens not to who is speaking, but to what he says. Hence we too, if ever we find something wisely said by the Gentiles, should not spurn it. But which of those who preside, I do not say if some things have already been revealed to him by God, but if he has some merit in the knowledge of the law, deigns to take the counsel of a lesser priest at least, not to say of a layman, still less of a Gentile? But Moses, who was meek above all men[[Num 12:3||]], took the counsel of an inferior, both to give the princes of the peoples a pattern of humility and to sketch the image of a mystery to come. Thus far Origen.

19.title: Declaratio litteralis capituli nonidecimi: Mense tertio egressionis filiorum Israel de terra Ægypti
19.title_en: Literal explanation of the nineteenth chapter: In the third month of the departure of the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt

paras.t: Adventus filiorum Israel in montem Sinai, et præparatio eorumdem ad suscipiendum ibi legem a Domino, describuntur in isto capitulo.
paras.en: The coming of the children of Israel to Mount Sinai, and their preparation to receive the law there from the Lord, are described in this chapter.

paras.t: Mense tertio egressionis filiorum Israel de terra Ægypti, in die hac, scilicet prima die mensis illius, venerunt in solitudinem Sinai. Quemadmodum dictum est, tota eremus illa, fuit una grandis solitudo, seu unum desertum, longe ac late extensum: sed in diversis partibus suis sortita est diversa vocabula. Circa hæc ait Glossa: Quadragesimo septimo die postquam egressi sunt de Ægypto, primo die mensis tertii, scilicet Junii, pervenerunt ad montem Sinai, ibique peractis duobus diebus, quibus sanctificati sunt, hoc est ad legem suscipiendam purgati ac præparati, die tertio, id est quinquagesimo die ab egressu, videlicet die Pentecostes, legem receperunt. Receperunt eam, inquam, verbo tenus, ut infra patebit. Postea vero receperunt eam in scriptis, puta in tabulis, quum Moyses fuisset cum Domino in vertice montis quadraginta diebus ac noctibus.
paras.en: [[19:1|In the third month of the departure of Israel out of the land of Egypt|Mense tertio egressionis filiorum Israel de terra Ægypti]], [[19:1|on this day|in die hac]], that is, on the first day of that month, [[19:1|they came into the wilderness of Sinai|venerunt in solitudinem Sinai]]. As has been said, that whole wilderness was one great solitude, or one desert, stretching far and wide; but in its different parts it received different names. On this the Gloss says: On the forty-seventh day after they went out of Egypt, on the first day of the third month, namely June, they came to Mount Sinai; and when two days had been spent there, in which they were sanctified, that is, cleansed and prepared to receive the law, on the third day, that is, the fiftieth day from the going out, namely the day of Pentecost, they received the law. They received it, I say, by word of mouth, as will appear below. Afterwards they received it in writing, that is, on the tables, when Moses had been with the Lord on the top of the mountain forty days and nights.

paras.t: Nam profecti de Raphidim, et pervenientes usque in desertum Sinai, castrametati sunt in eodem loco, ibique tentoria sua fixerunt, eo quod columna nubis quiesceret ibi, e regione, hoc est ex opposito, montis Sinai. Unaquæque autem tribus atque familia, accepit locum et spatium congruum ad ponendum in eo suum tentorium. Erantque, ut dicitur, aliqui deputati, qui facerent hujusmodi divisionem et assignationem locorum; atque ut Lyra, Rabbi Salomonem sequens, affirmat, fixerunt tentoria e regione montis ad plagam orientalem, quatenus adorarent Dominum super montem Sinai, vultibus versis ad occidentem, quoniam versus occidentem adorabant Judæi. Sed his contradicit Rabbi Paulus, dicens rationem illam esse invalidam: quia Judæi (ut ait) adorabant versus occidentem, quando erant in tabernaculo vel in templo, in quo arca testamenti et propitiatorium erant in parte occidentali; sed quando erant extra templum, in parte occidentali, respectu templi, adorabant ad orientem: alias orando vertissent terga ad templum, quod valde inconveniens reputant. Unde hodie Hebræi existentes in partibus Europæ, quæ est in parte occidentali respectu Jerusalem, non orant versus occidentem, sed orientem, juxta quod tertio Regum libro Salomon ait: Adorabunt te contra viam terræ, quam dedisti patribus eorum, et civitatis quam elegisti, et templi. Melius ergo cum aliis expositoribus dicitur, quod castrametati sunt e regione montis Sinai circumquaque. Hoc dictum Rabbi Pauli, quantum ad aliqua, verum est; sed non videtur in toto huic litteræ consonare. Quod enim per circuitum rei figitur, non proprie dicitur figi e regione ipsius, sed magis in gyro ejus.
paras.en: [[19:2|For departing out of Raphidim, and coming to the desert of Sinai, they camped in the same place|Nam profecti de Raphidim, et pervenientes usque in desertum Sinai, castrametati sunt in eodem loco]], [[19:2|and there|ibique]] they pitched their tents, because the pillar of the cloud rested there, [[19:2|over against|e regione]], that is, opposite, [[19:2|the mountain|montis]] of Sinai. Each tribe and family received a place and space fit for setting up its tent in it; and there were, it is said, some men appointed to make this division and assignment of places. And, as Lyra affirms, following Rabbi Solomon, they pitched their tents over against the mountain on the eastern side, so that they might adore the Lord upon Mount Sinai with their faces turned to the west, since the Jews adored towards the west. But Rabbi Paul contradicts this, saying that this reason does not hold: for the Jews (he says) adored towards the west when they were in the tabernacle or in the temple, in which the ark of the testament and the propitiatory were in the western part; but when they were outside the temple, to the west of the temple, they adored towards the east: otherwise in praying they would have turned their backs to the temple, which they think most unfitting. Hence today the Hebrews living in the parts of Europe, which lies to the west of Jerusalem, do not pray towards the west but towards the east, in keeping with what Solomon says in the third book of Kings: They shall [[3 Kings 8:48|pray to thee towards the way of their land, which thou gavest to their fathers, and of the city which thou hast chosen, and of the temple|Adorabunt te contra viam terræ, quam dedisti patribus eorum, et civitatis quam elegisti, et templi]] [Denis reads *Adorabunt te*, "they shall adore thee"]. It is better said, then, with the other expositors, that they camped over against Mount Sinai on every side. This saying of Rabbi Paul is true in some respects; but it does not seem to agree wholly with this text. For what is set up round about a thing is not properly said to be set up over against it, but rather around it.

paras.t: Moyses autem ascendit in montem ad Deum, id est, partem montis ascendit, in qua Deus fuit per speciales effectus. Vocavitque eum Dominus de monte, id est, Dominus in superioribus montis existens, vocavit Moysen, jubens ut magis ascenderet. Qui non præsumpsit altius scandere nisi jussus, quia jam ante audivit a Domino circa rubum, Ne appropies huc. Et Josepho teste, mons Sinai tam altus est, tam proceros scopulos habet, ut non solum inaccessibilis exstet hominibus, quantum ad altitudinem suam, sed et videri vix queat sine visus labore. Et quum sermo esset, Deum habitare in eo, terribilis et inadibilis omnibus fuit. Deinde omnia ista ministerio angelorum facta creduntur, ita quod angelus in Dei persona apparens, et vocem sensibilem formans, Moysen est affatus.
paras.en: [[19:3|And Moses went up to God|Moyses autem ascendit in montem ad Deum]] [Denis reads "went up into the mountain to God"], that is, he went up to the part of the mountain in which God was present by special effects. [[19:3|And the Lord called unto him from the mountain|Vocavitque eum Dominus de monte]], that is, the Lord, being in the upper parts of the mountain, called Moses, bidding him go up higher. He did not presume to climb higher unless bidden, because he had already heard from the Lord at the bush: [[Ex 3:5|Come not nigh hither|Ne appropies huc]]. And, as Josephus testifies, Mount Sinai is so high and has such lofty crags that not only is it inaccessible to men by reason of its height, but it can scarcely be looked at without straining the sight. And since it was said that God dwelt on it, it was terrible to all and none would approach it. Further, all these things are believed to have been done by the ministry of angels, so that an angel appearing in the person of God, and forming a voice that could be heard, spoke to Moses.

paras.t: Et ait: Hæc dices domui Jacob, hoc est posteritati ipsius Jacob, et, pro id est, annuntiabis filiis Israel. Vos ipsi vidistis quæ fecerim Ægyptiis, hoc est, qualiter eos plagavi propter vos: quomodo portaverim vos super alas aquilarum, id est, ex Ægypto vos transtuli, et ab Ægyptiorum impugnationibus vos defendi, sicut aquila portat suos pullos de loco ad locum, et portando eosdem tuetur ne lædantur. Dicitur enim quod portat eos supra proprium dorsum, sicque corpus suum exponit pro pullorum defensione: ita et angelus columnam nubis posuit inter Ægyptios et Hebræos, ne Ægyptii impugnarent Hebræos ante transitum maris Rubri, quemadmodum supra patuit. Et assumpserim mihi, hoc est, gratiose et pie applicuerim vos cultui meo, ut mihi adhæreatis ad gloriam nominis mei, atque ad vestram salutem.
paras.en: [[19:3|and said: Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob|Et ait: Hæc dices domui Jacob]], that is, to the posterity of Jacob himself, [[19:3|and|et]] (put for *that is*) [[19:3|tell the children of Israel|annuntiabis filiis Israel]]: [[19:4|You have seen what I have done to the Egyptians|Vos ipsi vidistis quæ fecerim Ægyptiis]], that is, how I struck them with plagues for your sake; [[19:4|how I have carried you upon the wings of eagles|quomodo portaverim vos super alas aquilarum]], that is, I carried you over out of Egypt, and defended you from the attacks of the Egyptians, as the eagle carries its young from place to place, and in carrying them guards them from harm. For it is said that it carries them upon its own back, and so exposes its own body for the defence of its young: so too the angel set the pillar of the cloud between the Egyptians and the Hebrews[[Ex 14:19||]][[Ex 14:20||]], so that the Egyptians should not attack the Hebrews before the crossing of the Red Sea, as appeared above. [[19:4|and have taken you to myself|Et assumpserim mihi]], that is, have graciously and lovingly bound you to my worship, that you may cleave to me, for the glory of my name and for your own salvation.

paras.t: Si ergo audieritis vocem meam, hoc est, verbis meis obtemperaveritis, et custodieritis pactum meum, id est, legem meam vobis nunc dandam, memoriter efficaciterque servaveritis; eritis mihi in peculium de cunctis populis: id est, præ ceteris gentibus universis, eritis populus mihi specialiter carus, familiaris, et hereditarius, durante cursu veteris Testamenti, ita quod pascam atque custodiam vos, sicut custodit et pascit pastor proprium gregem. Hinc per Isaiam loquitur Dominus: Hereditas mea Israel. Unde (ut dicitur) in Hebræo habetur, Eritis mihi amicabilitas, ita quod per illud abstractum insinuetur, quam specialissime essent Deo dilecti. Hinc in Deuteronomio legitur: Te elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram. Porro peculium appellatur bonum speciale alicui appropriatum. Et ita plebs illa fuit Deo specialiter applicata.
paras.en: [[19:5|If therefore you will hear my voice|Si ergo audieritis vocem meam]], that is, obey my words, [[19:5|and keep my covenant|et custodieritis pactum meum]], that is, keep in mind and carry out my law, now to be given you, [[19:5|you shall be my peculiar possession above all people|eritis mihi in peculium de cunctis populis]]: that is, above all the other nations you shall be a people especially dear to me, my own household and my inheritance, while the course of the Old Testament lasts; so that I will feed you and guard you as a shepherd guards and feeds his own flock[[Is 40:11||]]. Hence the Lord says through Isaias: [[Is 19:25|Israel is my inheritance|Hereditas mea Israel]]. Hence too (as is said) the Hebrew has, *You shall be to me friendliness*, so that by that abstract word it is suggested how very especially they were beloved of God. Hence we read in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 7:6|The Lord thy God hath chosen thee, to be his peculiar people of all peoples that are upon the earth|Te elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram]]. Now *peculium* [a "peculiar possession": property set apart as one's own] is the name for a special good appropriated to someone. And so that people was especially bound to God.

paras.t: Mea est enim omnis terra: hoc est, universi habitatores terræ simul cum terra, mei sunt jure creationis et universalis imperii. Ideo possum vos ita conjungere mihi per gratiam. Et vos eritis mihi in regnum sacerdotale: hoc est, regnabo in vobis, et reges vobis præficiam, atque in regno vestro erunt sacerdotes mihi devoti, et vos consecrati eritis: et gens sancta: quoniam corda vestra virtutibus erunt repleta, et vos meo cultui eritis dedicati.
paras.en: [[19:5|for all the earth is mine|Mea est enim omnis terra]]: that is, all the inhabitants of the earth, together with the earth, are mine by right of creation and of universal rule. Therefore I can so join you to myself by grace. [[19:6|And you shall be to me a priestly kingdom|Et vos eritis mihi in regnum sacerdotale]]: that is, I will reign in you, and will set kings over you, and in your kingdom there shall be priests devoted to me, and you shall be consecrated; [[19:6|and a holy nation|et gens sancta]], because your hearts shall be filled with virtues, and you shall be dedicated to my worship.

paras.t: Hæc jam prædicta, sunt verba quæ loqueris ad filios Israel. Itaque Deus antequam legem plebi proposuit, commemoravit ei actus suæ justitiæ circa Ægyptios, et actus suæ misericordiæ circa eos, quatenus Deum timerent ut justum et omnipotentem, eumque diligerent ut pium ac liberalem, atque ut sibi grati consisterent, ac per hoc majora suscipere mererentur. Insuper fecit eis dulcissimam, excellentissimamque promissionem, si de cetero obedirent, ut sic provocarentur ad meliora, et ipsum ardenter diligerent, a quo in dilectione sic erant præventi.
paras.en: [[19:6|These|Hæc]], the things now said, [[19:6|are the words thou shalt speak to the children of Israel|sunt verba quæ loqueris ad filios Israel]]. So before God set the law before the people, He reminded them of the works of His justice towards the Egyptians and the works of His mercy towards themselves, so that they might fear God as just and almighty, and love Him as kind and generous, and remain grateful to Him, and so deserve to receive greater things. Besides, He made them a most sweet and most excellent promise, if from then on they obeyed, so that they might thus be roused to better things and love ardently Him by whom they had been so forestalled in love.

paras.t: Venit Moyses, et convocatis majoribus natu populi, exposuit eis omnes sermones quos mandaverat Dominus, hoc est verba præfata, quæ Deus jussit eis insinuari. Responditque omnis populus simul: Cuncta quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus. Compuncti enim erant ex verbis piissimis jam prædictis. Itaque ut omnia fierent ordinate, Moyses primo verba Dei retulit superioribus Judæorum, et illi ulterius retulerunt inferioribus, ut sic inferiores assuescerent superiores suos reverenter audire. Quumque retulisset Moyses verba populi ad Dominum. Quod Moyses fecit, non ut Domino ignota denuntiaret, sed ut a Domino aliquid plus audiret, et item, ut suum impleret officium, quoniam mediator fuerat constitutus inter Deum et populum. Et rursus, quatenus bona populi verba coram Domino recitando, gratiam impetraret a Domino ipsi plebi. Juxta quem modum angelus dixit Cornelio centurioni: Oratio tua et eleemosynæ tuæ commemoratæ sunt in conspectu Dei, ut legitur in Actis. Tobiæ quoque Raphael angelus: Ego, inquit, obtuli orationem tuam Domino.
paras.en: [[19:7|Moses came; and calling together the elders of the people, he declared|Venit Moyses, et convocatis majoribus natu populi, exposuit]] to them [[19:7|all the words which the Lord had commanded|omnes sermones quos mandaverat Dominus]], that is, the words given above, which God bade be made known to them. [[19:8|And all the people answered together: All that the Lord hath spoken, we will do|Responditque omnis populus simul: Cuncta quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus]]. For they had been moved to compunction by the most loving words just spoken. So, that all things might be done in order, Moses first reported God's words to the chief men of the Jews, and they in turn reported them to those beneath them, so that those beneath might grow used to hearing their superiors with reverence. [[19:8|And when Moses had related the people's words to the Lord|Quumque retulisset Moyses verba populi ad Dominum]]. This Moses did, not to tell the Lord what He did not know, but to hear something more from the Lord; and also to fulfil his office, since he had been appointed mediator between God and the people; and again, that by reciting the people's good words before the Lord he might obtain grace from the Lord for the people. In the same way the angel said to Cornelius the centurion: [[Acts 10:4|Thy prayers and thy alms are ascended for a memorial in the sight of God|Oratio tua et eleemosynæ tuæ commemoratæ sunt in conspectu Dei]] [Denis reads "thy prayer and thy alms have been remembered in the sight of God"], as we read in the Acts. And Raphael the angel says to Tobias: [[Tob 12:12|I|Ego]], he says, [[Tob 12:12|offered thy prayer to the Lord|obtuli orationem tuam Domino]].

paras.t: Ait ei Dominus: Jam nunc, id est cito post hæc, utpote tertio die, sicut patebit, veniam ad te in caligine nubis, id est in nube caliginosa, ut audiat me populus loquentem ad te ex ipsa nube, et credat tibi in perpetuum: certi quod ex divina revelatione locutus sis eis. Et quod ait, Ut credat tibi, intelligendum est tam de his qui ibi tunc aderant, quam de posteris eorumdem. Et quamvis multi eorum postmodum ad incredulitatem dilapsi sint, Dominus tamen fecit quod in ipso erat, ut et increduli inexcusabiles inveniantur. Qualiter autem istud sit factum, sequenti recitatur capitulo.
paras.en: [[19:9|The Lord said to him: Lo, now|Ait ei Dominus: Jam nunc]], that is, soon after this, namely on the third day, as will appear, [[19:9|will I come to thee in the darkness of a cloud|veniam ad te in caligine nubis]], that is, in a dark cloud, [[19:9|that the people may hear me speaking to thee|ut audiat me populus loquentem ad te]] out of the cloud itself, [[19:9|and may believe thee for ever|et credat tibi in perpetuum]], being certain that thou hast spoken to them by divine revelation. And his words, [[19:9|may believe thee|Ut credat tibi]], are to be understood both of those who were then present and of their descendants. And though many of them afterwards fell away into unbelief, the Lord nonetheless did what was in Him, so that the unbelievers too should be found without excuse. How this was done is told in the following chapter.

paras.t: Cur autem Dominus apparuit Moysi in nube aut nubis caligine, et ex ea locutus est ei? Respondetur, quod ad innuendum quod ipse Dominus sit cœlestium princeps, cujus magnificentia nubes discurrunt, quæ in aereo cœlo generantur atque moventur ad Dei imperium. Et item ad insinuandum, quod Deum in hac vita in se ipso clare cernere non valemus, sed (juxta Apostolum) videmus per speculum in ænigmate. Tamen ut Rabbi Paulus hic asserit, quando Dominus venit ad Moysen ad loquendum et apparendum ei dumtaxat, dicitur venisse in nube, non in caligine nubis: sed quando venit ad loquendum Moysi ex nube coram populo, dicitur venisse in caligine nubis, quoniam Moyses habuit clariorem Dei cognitionem quam populus. Verumtamen an ista proprietas in hujuscemodi locutione semper servetur, infra patescet.
paras.en: But why did the Lord appear to Moses in a cloud, or in the darkness of a cloud, and speak to him out of it? The answer is: to signify that the Lord Himself is the prince of the heavens, [[Deut 33:26|By his magnificence the clouds run hither and thither|cujus magnificentia nubes discurrunt]], clouds that are formed in the heaven of the air and are moved at God's command. And also to suggest that in this life we cannot see God clearly in Himself, but (as the Apostle says) [[1 Cor 13:12|We see now through a glass in a dark manner|videmus per speculum in ænigmate]]. Yet, as Rabbi Paul asserts here, when the Lord came to Moses only to speak to him and appear to him, He is said to have come in a cloud, not in the darkness of a cloud; but when He came to speak to Moses out of the cloud before the people, He is said to have come in the darkness of a cloud, since Moses had a clearer knowledge of God than the people. Whether this usage is always kept in speaking of such things, however, will appear below.

paras.t: Nuntiavit ergo Moyses verba populi ad Dominum, sicut jam dictum est. Qui dixit ei: Vade ad populum, et sanctifica illos, id est, exhortare et præcipe eis, ut sanctificent se, implendo quæ eis præcipies, utpote a carnalibus abstinendo amplexibus, et spiritualibus actibus insistendo, hodie et cras; laventque vestimenta sua: non quod in vestibus sit macula culpæ, vel quod exteriorem candorem rerum inanimatarum Deus per se aut principaliter curet, sed ut per vestimentorum lotionem corpoream, intelligerent se intus debere spiritualiter lavare et expurgare per conversionem et contritionem mentis ad Deum. Rudi etenim populo dedit Deus præcepta, eis proportionata. Et sint parati in diem tertium: ita ut tunc inveniantur per prævia virtutum exercitia dispositi, purgati, devoti ad occurrendum Domino, et ad suscipiendum legem ipsius. In die enim tertia descendet Dominus coram omni plebe super montem Sinai: non quod Deus in sua natura mutaverit locum, sed per quosdam effectus mirabiles circa montem Sinai factos, monstravit se aliquid novum operari ibidem, per quod cognoscebatur ibi præsens adesse. Itaque descendet, id est, præsentiam suam in loco inferiori ipso cœlo, monstrabit per effectus magnificos.
paras.en: [[19:9|And Moses told the words of the people to the Lord|Nuntiavit ergo Moyses verba populi ad Dominum]], as has just been said. [[19:10|And he said to him: Go to the people, and sanctify them|Qui dixit ei: Vade ad populum, et sanctifica illos]], that is, exhort them and command them to sanctify themselves by fulfilling what thou shalt command them, namely by abstaining from carnal embraces and applying themselves to spiritual acts, [[19:10|to day, and to morrow, and let them wash their garments|hodie et cras; laventque vestimenta sua]]: not that there is any stain of guilt in garments, or that God cares, in itself or chiefly, for the outward whiteness of lifeless things, but so that by the bodily washing of their garments they might understand that they ought to wash and cleanse themselves inwardly and spiritually, by the turning and contrition of the mind towards God. For God gave an untaught people precepts suited to them. [[19:11|And let them be ready against the third day|Et sint parati in diem tertium]]: so that they may then be found, by the foregoing exercises of the virtues, disposed, cleansed and devout, to go to meet the Lord and to receive His law. [[19:11|for on the third day the Lord will come down in the sight of all the people, upon Mount Sinai|In die enim tertia descendet Dominus coram omni plebe super montem Sinai]]: not that God changed place in His nature, but by certain wonderful effects wrought about Mount Sinai He showed that He was working something new there, by which He was known to be present there. So *He will come down*, that is, He will show His presence in a place lower than heaven itself by magnificent effects.

paras.t: Constituesque terminos populo per circuitum montis, et dices: Cavete ne ascendatis in montem, nec tangatis fines, id est partes seu extremitates illius. Omnis qui tetigerit montem, morte morietur, id est, corporaliter occidetur, imo et spiritualiter interibit, peccando mortaliter per divini violationem præcepti. Istud tamen præceptum ex sua natura fuit præceptum juris positivi, sicut et illud, quod Deus dedit in paradiso primis parentibus de non gustando fructum arboris scientiæ boni et mali: quem fructum comedere, non fuit malum in se, sicut nec tangere montem. Positiva quippe præcepta dicuntur, quæ sunt de rebus ideo debitis aut illicitis, quia jussæ sunt aut prohibitæ fieri; non autem idcirco jussæ aut prohibitæ fieri, quia ex sua ratione sint moraliter bonæ aut malæ. Manus non tangent eum, id est, nullus vestrum manibus suis montem attinget rependo aut innitendo; sed lapidibus opprimetur, sive confodietur jaculis, quicumque montem tetigerit. Hoc autem Deus tam rigorose præcipit, ad innuendum cum quanta reverentia sit accedendum ad ipsum, et ne aliquis cum præsumptione aut curiositate ad divina se ingerat, quoniam scrutator majestatis opprimetur a gloria. Item ad designandum, quam vehementer deficiat imbecillitas mentis humanæ, ab excellentia et comprehensione majestatis divinæ. Sive jumentum fuerit, sive homo, non vivet, si tetigerit montem, quousque fuerit data tangendi licentia. Nam subditur:
paras.en: [[19:12|And thou shalt appoint certain limits to the people round about|Constituesque terminos populo per circuitum]] the mountain, [[19:12|and thou shalt say to them: Take heed ye go not up into the mount, and that ye touch not the borders|et dices: Cavete ne ascendatis in montem, nec tangatis fines]], that is, the parts or edges, [[19:12|thereof|illius]]. [[19:12|every one that toucheth the mount, dying he shall die|Omnis qui tetigerit montem, morte morietur]], that is, he shall be put to death in body, and indeed shall perish in spirit too, sinning mortally by breaking the divine precept. Yet this precept was by its nature a precept of positive law, like that which God gave our first parents in paradise, not to taste the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil[[Gen 2:17||]] [the margin's verse number is lost: Gen. ii, 1…]: to eat that fruit was not evil in itself, any more than to touch the mountain. For those precepts are called positive which concern things that are due or unlawful because they have been commanded or forbidden, and not things commanded or forbidden because they are morally good or evil by their own nature. [[19:13|No hands shall touch him|Manus non tangent eum]], that is, none of you shall reach the mountain with his hands, by creeping up or leaning on it; [[19:13|but he shall be stoned to death, or he shall be shot through with arrows|sed lapidibus opprimetur, sive confodietur jaculis]], whoever touches the mountain. God commands this so strictly to show with what reverence we must approach Him, and that no one should thrust himself into divine things with presumption or curiosity, since [[Prov 25:27|he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory|scrutator majestatis opprimetur a gloria]]. Also, to show how far the weakness of the human mind falls short of the excellence and the comprehension of the divine majesty. [[19:13|whether it be beast, or man, he shall not live|Sive jumentum fuerit, sive homo, non vivet]], if he touch the mountain, until leave to touch it has been given. For it follows:

paras.t: Quum cœperit clangere buccina, tunc ascendant in montem. Circa hoc Rabanus scribit: Prius prohibet populum in montem ascendere, nunc jubet ut clangente buccina, ascendant in montem, per hoc humanam compescens audaciam, atque ad obediendum invitans, ad designandum, quod ad prædicationis vocem debemus nos ad superna erigere, nec sacramentorum investigationem ex nobis ipsis præsumere, sed Dei vocationem sequi. Alii sic exponunt: Quum cœperit clangere buccina in cacumine montis ab angelo, tunc ascendant in montem, id est ad terminos sibi præfixos accedant, per quod monti appropinquabunt, non tamen transeant ultra terminos ipsos. Sicque per hæc verba non dabatur eis licentia transgrediendi terminos illos, sed insinuatur quod ante clangorem buccinæ stent aliqualiter remote a terminis illis, et in ipso clangore eosdem accedant: quod nunc vocatur, In montem ascendere, quoniam termini illi erant in pede montis in aliquanto ascensu. Porro, ut Lyra refert, in Hebræo habetur: In protractu buccinæ ascendant. Quod quidam Hebræi exponunt, dicentes fuisse quemdam modum clangendi protensum, qui fuit signum recessus Dei a monte, tuncque licuit populo terminos præstitutos transcendere, atque in montem ascendere.
paras.en: [[19:13|When the trumpet shall begin to sound, then let them go up into the mount|Quum cœperit clangere buccina, tunc ascendant in montem]]. On this Rabanus writes: First He forbids the people to go up into the mountain; now He bids them go up into the mountain when the trumpet sounds: by this checking human boldness and inviting to obedience, to signify that at the voice of preaching we ought to raise ourselves to the things above, and not presume to search into the sacraments [that is, the sacred mysteries] of ourselves, but follow God's call. Others explain it thus: When the trumpet shall begin to be sounded by the angel on the top of the mountain, then let them go up into the mount, that is, let them come to the limits set for them, by which they will draw near to the mountain, yet not pass beyond those limits. And so by these words they were not given leave to pass over those limits; rather it is suggested that before the sounding of the trumpet they should stand some way off from those limits, and at the sounding itself come up to them: which is here called going up into the mountain, since those limits were at the foot of the mountain, a little way up its slope. Further, as Lyra reports, the Hebrew has: *At the drawing out of the trumpet let them go up*. Some Hebrews explain this by saying that there was a certain drawn-out way of sounding which was the sign of God's departure from the mountain, and that then the people were allowed to cross the appointed limits and go up into the mountain.

paras.t: Quæri potest, cur bestia montem tangens, fuerat occidenda, quum non peccasset in hoc. Respondetur, quod dominus bestiæ in re sua puniebatur, quam a montis contactu non custodivit. Et etiam jussum est hoc, ad incutiendum majorem timorem ac reverentiam divini præcepti: itemque ob misticam significationem, ad præfigurandum videlicet, quod homo carnalis indignus est ad divinorum communionem, et ad contemplandum superna.
paras.en: It may be asked why a beast touching the mountain was to be killed, since it had not sinned in this. The answer is that the owner of the beast was punished in his property, which he had not kept from touching the mountain. And this was also commanded to strike greater fear of the divine precept and greater reverence for it; and also for a mystical meaning, namely to foreshadow that the carnal man is unworthy of communion in divine things and of contemplating the things above.

paras.t: Descenditque Moyses de monte ad populum, et sanctificavit eum dispositive, sicut expositum est. Quumque lavissent vestimenta sua: ob causas inductas. Non autem jussi sunt nova induere vestimenta, sed per lotionem innovata seu candidata, quia per interiorem lotionem non mutatur anima quantum ad suam substantiam, sed in accidentalibus, et spiritualiter innovatur ac resplendescit. Voluit quoque Dominus in vestibus Hebræorum ostendere speciale miraculum, quia per tantum tempus ac spatium, quo in toto illo deserto fuerunt, non sunt attritæ. Ait ad eos: Estote parati in diem tertium, juxta sensum præhabitum, et ne appropinquetis uxoribus vestris, per carnalem copulam vel complexum, imo nec per inordinatam affectionem. Quamvis enim copula illa sine peccato fieri queat, tamen ob voluptatem adjunctam, deprimit mentem, et ad devotionem reddit ineptam, vel minus idoneam, etiam ad tempus actu cessante. Decuit quoque eos a carnalibus delectationibus abstinere ad aliquantum tempus, qui ad tantam divinorum speculationem et participationem fuerant admittendi. Certum est etiam, quod populus ille pro maxima sui parte fuit ita carnalis et pronus ad vitia, quod vix cognovit uxores sine admixtione peccati. Est etiam mystica ratio hujus mandati, videlicet quod populus christianus non debet Sacramentum altaris suscipere absque prævia abstinentia a copula etiam conjugali: quanto magis illegitima.
paras.en: [[19:14|And Moses came down from the mount to the people, and sanctified them|Descenditque Moyses de monte ad populum, et sanctificavit eum]] by way of disposing them, as has been explained. [[19:14|And when they had washed their garments|Quumque lavissent vestimenta sua]], for the reasons given. They were not bidden to put on new garments, but garments renewed or whitened by washing; for by the inward washing the soul is not changed in its substance, but in its accidents [that is, in its qualities, not in what it is], and it is spiritually renewed and shines again. The Lord also willed to show a special miracle in the garments of the Hebrews, since through all the time and the long way they spent in that whole desert they did not wear out.
