[[19:15|He said to them: Be ready against the third day|Ait ad eos: Estote parati in diem tertium]], in the sense given before, [[19:15|and come not near your wives|et ne appropinquetis uxoribus vestris]], by carnal union or embrace, nor indeed by disordered affection. For though that union can take place without sin, yet because of the pleasure joined to it, it weighs down the mind and makes it unfit, or less fit, for devotion, even for a time after the act has ceased. It was fitting, too, that those who were to be admitted to so great a beholding of divine things and a share in them should abstain for some time from carnal delights. It is certain also that that people, for the greatest part, was so carnal and prone to vice that it scarcely knew its wives without some mixture of sin. There is also a mystical reason for this command, namely that the Christian people ought not to receive the Sacrament of the altar without first abstaining even from conjugal union: how much more from unlawful union.

paras.t: Jamque advenerat tertius dies, et mane inclaruerat. Circa hoc scribit Lyra: Hic est dies sextus tertii mensis. Quarto enim die ejusdem mensis, dixit eis Moyses verba prædicta, ut Rabbi Salomon dicit. Sicque sexto die hujus mensis fuit lex data. Sed his repugnare videtur, quod ait Glossa: Hic est tertius dies tertii mensis ab exitu Israel de Ægypto. A die ergo quo Pascha fecerunt, videlicet a quartodecimo die primi mensis usque ad diem istum quo data est lex, dies quinquaginta fuerunt: utpote decem et septem dies primi mensis, et dies triginta mensis secundi, qui simul sunt dies quadraginta septem, et tres dies tertii mensis, in cujus tertio die data est lex. Cui computationi magis concordat, quod Magister in historiis scribit: uno […] præinducta Glossæ verba consonant prorsus verbis Augustini, vel potius ex verbis ejus sunt sumpta; concordant et textui. Ideo ita tenendum censetur.
paras.en: [[19:16|And now the third day was come, and the morning appeared|Jamque advenerat tertius dies, et mane inclaruerat]]. On this Lyra writes: This is the sixth day of the third month. For on the fourth day of the same month Moses spoke the aforesaid words to them, as Rabbi Solomon says; and so the law was given on the sixth day of this month. But what the Gloss says seems to go against this: This is the third day of the third month from the going out of Israel from Egypt. So from the day on which they kept the Pasch, namely from the fourteenth day of the first month[[Ex 12:18||]], to this day on which the law was given, there were fifty days: namely seventeen days of the first month and thirty days of the second month, which together are forty-seven days, and three days of the third month, on whose third day the law was given. With this reckoning what the Master writes in the Histories agrees better: one […] the words of the Gloss given above agree entirely with the words of Augustine, or rather are taken from his words; they agree also with the text. Therefore it is judged that this is to be held.

paras.t: Itaque tertio die valde diluculo, ut in Scholastica historia dicitur, ante solis ortum, id est, antequam sol ipse apparuit per se ipsum, non tamen ante auroram, quia in textu asseritur, Jam mane inclaruerat: et ecce cœperunt audiri tonitrua, et micare fulgura, et nubes densissima operire montem: quæ omnia angelico ministerio formabantur. Quumque tonitruum sit exstinctio ignis in nube, seu sonus factus in ea, facile fuit angelo sancto in nube illa formare tonitrua, et inde emittere fulgura. Magnique venti et pluviæ erant ibidem, ut Josephus scribit. Clangorque buccinæ vehementius perstrepebat. Angelus quippe formavit sonum hujusmodi. An tamen per veram tubam, an alio modo sibi placenti, quis novit? Verumtamen Judæi, juxta suarum consuetudinem fabularum, dicunt sonum illum factum per cornu sumptum de ariete pro Isaac immolato. Et timuit populus qui erat in castris. In Scholastica historia ex Josepho fertur, quod prædictis terribilibus auditis, putabant et ipsum Moysen ira Dei perisse. Tandem vero Moyses lætus apparuit, et aer serenus cum eo inter ipsos reversus est. Qui dixit ad eos: Hodie non audietis me Moysen, sed illum qui pro vobis percussit Ægyptum, qui dedit viam per mare, panem de cœlo, aquam de petra. Fiant ergo verba Dei vobis amabiliora, quam proprii filii et uxores.
paras.en: So on the third day, very early, as the Scholastic History says, before sunrise, that is, before the sun itself appeared in its own body, yet not before the dawn, since the text says, [[19:16|and the morning appeared|Jam mane inclaruerat]]: [[19:16|and behold thunders began to be heard, and lightning to flash, and a very thick cloud to cover the mount|et ecce cœperunt audiri tonitrua, et micare fulgura, et nubes densissima operire montem]]: all of which were formed by the ministry of angels. And since thunder is the quenching of fire in a cloud, or a sound made in it, it was easy for the holy angel to form thunders in that cloud and to send lightnings out of it. And there were great winds and rains there, as Josephus writes. [[19:16|and the noise of the trumpet sounded exceeding loud|Clangorque buccinæ vehementius perstrepebat]]. For the angel formed this sound. But whether by a real trumpet, or in some other way that pleased him, who knows? The Jews, however, after the manner of their fables, say that that sound was made with a horn taken from the ram sacrificed instead of Isaac[[Gen 22:13||]]. [[19:16|and the people that was in the camp, feared|Et timuit populus qui erat in castris]]. The Scholastic History relates from Josephus that, having heard these terrible things, they thought that Moses himself had perished by the wrath of God. But at length Moses appeared joyful, and clear air came back with him among them. And he said to them: Today you shall not hear me, Moses, but Him who struck Egypt for you, who gave a way through the sea, bread from heaven, water from the rock. Let the words of God, then, be dearer to you than your own children and wives.

paras.t: Quumque eduxisset eos Moyses in occursum Dei, id est, ut se reverenter ac devote præsentarent Deo, super montem Sinai descendenti per modum expositum, steterunt ad radices montis, videlicet juxta terminos eis præfixos, non ultra, sed citra eos. Totus autem mons Sinai fumabat, præsertim in vertice ejus ubi fumus ascenderat, eo quod descendisset Dominus super eum in igne, qui fuit alius a columna ignis, iter monstrantis in noctibus, et ascenderet fumus ex eo quasi de fornace. Ex quo videtur, quod ignis ille fuit spissus et satis obscurus, non multum subtilis et clarus, quatenus majorem incuteret formidinem duris Hebræis. Eratque omnis mons terribilis nimis, propter ea quæ fiebant et apparuerunt in eo. Et sonitus buccinæ paulatim crescebat in majus, et prolixius tendebatur. Omnia ista fecit Dominus coram plebe antequam legem dedit, ad demonstrandum suæ omnipotentiam majestatis, ut timeretur: quia lex illa fuit lex timoris et severitatis justitiæ imperfectis collata, qui per timorem et rigorem justitiæ fuerant ad legis observantiam inducendi. Lex vero evangelica, est lex caritatis et pietatis: idcirco a Christo sedente in monte cum serenitate et quiete est data, quia ad eam servandam inducendi sunt homines amore summi boni ac zelo virtutum. De hac re, id est utriusque hujus legis distinctione, multa scribit Apostolus ad Hebræos: Non accessistis, inquiens, ad tractabilem et accessibilem ignem, et ad turbinem, et caliginem, et procellam, et tubæ sonitum. Ex quibus probatur, quod ibi exstitit etiam turbo, id est vehemens ventus: quod tamen hic non fertur in textu.
paras.en: [[19:17|And when Moses had brought them forth to meet God|Quumque eduxisset eos Moyses in occursum Dei]], that is, that they might present themselves with reverence and devotion to God coming down upon Mount Sinai in the way explained, [[19:17|they stood at the bottom of the mount|steterunt ad radices montis]], namely by the limits set for them, not beyond them but on this side of them. [[19:18|And all Mount Sinai was on a smoke|Totus autem mons Sinai fumabat]], especially at its top, where the smoke had gone up, [[19:18|because the Lord was come down upon it in fire|eo quod descendisset Dominus super eum in igne]], a fire other than the pillar of fire which showed the way by night, [[19:18|and the smoke arose from it as out of a furnace|et ascenderet fumus ex eo quasi de fornace]]. From this it seems that that fire was thick and rather dark, not very fine and bright, so as to strike greater fear into the hard Hebrews. [[19:18|and all the mount was terrible|Eratque omnis mons terribilis]] exceedingly, because of what was done and appeared on it. [[19:19|And the sound of the trumpet grew by degrees louder and louder, and was drawn out to a greater length|Et sonitus buccinæ paulatim crescebat in majus, et prolixius tendebatur]]. All these things the Lord did before the people before He gave the law, to show the almightiness of His majesty, that He might be feared: for that law was a law of fear and of the severity of justice, given to the imperfect, who were to be brought to keep the law by fear and the rigour of justice. But the law of the Gospel is a law of charity and loving kindness: therefore it was given by Christ sitting on a mountain in serenity and quiet, because men are to be brought to keep it by love of the highest good and zeal for the virtues. Of this matter, that is, of the difference between these two laws, the Apostle writes much to the Hebrews, saying: [[Heb 12:18|you are not come|Non accessistis]], he says, [[Heb 12:18|to a mountain that might be touched and a burning fire and a whirlwind and darkness and storm|ad tractabilem et accessibilem ignem, et ad turbinem, et caliginem, et procellam]] [Denis's text has "to the fire that might be touched and approached", without *mountain*], [[Heb 12:19|And the sound of a trumpet|et tubæ sonitum]]. From which it is proved that there was also a whirlwind there, that is, a violent wind: which, however, is not told here in the text.

paras.t: Quæri potest, cur Dominus apparebat in igne, imo et in igne hujusmodi, atque in caligine et in nube. Respondetur, quod divina, per proprietates ignis specialiter designantur, in tantum quod et Deus ipse ignis consumens vocatur, ut alibi plenius dictum est. Cur autem in igne sic denso, et in caligine atque in nube, jam ante solutum est. Voluit namque Deus in veteri Testamento suæ justitiæ monstrare rigorem, et suæ incutere majestatis horrorem, quatenus et per hoc ostenderet se rerum humanarum esse provisorem ac judicem: quod a paucis tunc credebatur. Hinc tertio Regum Salomon ait: Dominus dixit ut habitaret in nebula. Pro quo, libro secundo Paralipomenon legitur: Dominus dixit ut habitaret in caligine. Unde et Nahum primo: Dominus, in tempestate et turbine viæ ejus. Porro Judæi dicunt Dominum apparuisse in igne et nube, quoniam ignis et nubes non habent fixam figuram. Idcirco in eis apparuit Dominus, id est per illa, ne Hebræi ad idololatriam proni, haberent occasionem formandi imagines Dei. Istud tamen non videtur magni valoris, quoniam ignis et nubes satis faciliter possunt formari ac pingi.
paras.en: It may be asked why the Lord appeared in fire, and indeed in fire of this kind, and in darkness and in a cloud. The answer is that divine things are signified especially by the properties of fire, so much so that God Himself is called [[Deut 4:24|a consuming fire|ignis consumens]], as has been said more fully elsewhere. Why He appeared in fire so thick, and in darkness and in a cloud, has been answered already. For in the Old Testament God willed to show the rigour of His justice and to strike men with dread of His majesty, so that by this too He might show that He is the provider and judge of human affairs: which few then believed. Hence Solomon says in the third book of Kings: [[3 Kings 8:12|The Lord said that he would dwell in a cloud|Dominus dixit ut habitaret in nebula]]. In place of which we read in the second book of Paralipomenon: [[2 Par 6:1|The Lord promised that he would dwell in a cloud|Dominus dixit ut habitaret in caligine]] [the margin gives II Paral. i; the verse is 2 Par 6:1, where Denis reads "said ... in darkness"]. And so Nahum too, in his first chapter: [[Nah 1:3|The Lord's ways are in a tempest, and a whirlwind|Dominus, in tempestate et turbine viæ ejus]]. The Jews, further, say that the Lord appeared in fire and cloud because fire and cloud have no fixed shape; and that the Lord appeared in them, that is, by means of them, so that the Hebrews, being prone to idolatry, should have no occasion to make images of God. This, however, does not seem of much weight, since fire and cloud can quite easily be shaped and painted.

paras.t: Moyses loquebatur ad Deum, et Dominus respondebat ei tanquam mediatori inter se et populum. Descenditque Dominus super montem Sinai in ipso montis vertice, et vocavit Moysen in cacumen ejus, scilicet montis, ad designandum quam familiaris et carus exsisteret Domino, et ut ejus verba attentius susciperentur a populo.
paras.en: [[19:19|Moses spoke|Moyses loquebatur]] to God, [[19:19|and God answered him|et Dominus respondebat ei]] as the mediator between Himself and the people. [[19:20|And the Lord came down upon Mount Sinai, in the very top of the mount, and he called Moses unto the top thereof|Descenditque Dominus super montem Sinai in ipso montis vertice, et vocavit Moysen in cacumen ejus]], that is, of the mountain, to show how intimate with the Lord and how dear to Him Moses was, and that his words might be received more attentively by the people.

paras.t: Quo quum ascendisset, dixit ad eum: Descende, et contestare populum, ne forte velint transcendere terminos sibi præfixos ad videndum Dominum, id est ad inspiciendum curiose aut præsumptuose, qualiter aut in qua forma ego Dominus tibi appareo: quod scire ad eos non pertinet, nec sunt digni: et pereat ex eis plurima multitudo, videlicet omnes qui fecerint hoc, aut consenserint ipsis, quia tales mox occiderentur, et propter suum excessum essent damnandi. Sacerdotes quoque qui accedunt ad Dominum, ingrediendo tabernaculum, templum, vel ad altare, offerendo ibidem, ubi Deus specialiter esse asseritur, sanctificentur, id est, se ipsos purificent modis prætactis, ne percutiam eos plaga mortis corporalis ac spiritualis. Si istud intelligatur de sacerdotibus Leviticæ stirpis atque Mosaicæ legis, per anticipationem est dictum, quoniam sacerdotes hujusmodi nondum fuerant instituti: ut sit sensus, quod sacerdotes tales post suam institutionem non præsumant ad Dominum nisi purificati accedere, nec sua officia indigne explere. Si autem intelligatur de sacerdotibus qui erant in lege naturæ, exponetur de primogenitis Israelitarum, qui officio sacerdotii fungebantur usque ad sacerdotii institutionem Levitici: nam usque ad id primogeniti fuerant sacerdotes. Jam quoque jusserat Dominus primogenitos Israel sibi sanctificari, ut capitulo tertiodecimo continetur.
paras.en: [[19:20|And when he was gone up thither|Quo quum ascendisset]], [[19:21|He said unto him: Go down, and charge the people; lest they should have a mind to pass the limits|dixit ad eum: Descende, et contestare populum, ne forte velint transcendere terminos]] set for them [[19:21|to see the Lord|ad videndum Dominum]], that is, to look curiously or presumptuously at how, or in what form, I the Lord appear to thee: which it is not theirs to know, nor are they worthy of it; [[19:21|and a very great multitude of them should perish|et pereat ex eis plurima multitudo]], namely all who do this or consent to those who do, since such men would at once be killed, and for their excess would be damned. [[19:22|The priests also that come to the Lord|Sacerdotes quoque qui accedunt ad Dominum]], by entering the tabernacle or the temple, or coming to the altar to offer there, where God is said to be in a special way, [[19:22|let them be sanctified|sanctificentur]], that is, let them purify themselves in the ways already touched on, [[19:22|lest he strike them|ne percutiam eos]] [Denis's text reads *percutiam*, "lest I strike"; the margin gives the reading *percutiat*, "lest he strike"] with the stroke of bodily and spiritual death. If this is understood of the priests of the stock of Levi and of the law of Moses, it is said by anticipation, since such priests had not yet been instituted: so that the sense is that such priests, after their institution, should not presume to approach the Lord unless purified, nor carry out their offices unworthily. But if it is understood of the priests who were under the law of nature, it will be explained of the firstborn of the Israelites, who performed the office of priesthood until the institution of the Levitical priesthood: for until then the firstborn were priests. And the Lord had already commanded that the firstborn of Israel be sanctified to Him, as is contained in the thirteenth chapter[[Ex 13:2||]].

paras.t: Dixitque Moyses ad Dominum: Non poterit vulgus ascendere in montem Sinai. Tu enim testificatus es et jussisti, dicens: Pone terminos circa montem, et sanctifica illum. Hoc ultimum verbum Moyses ante non scripsit; cetera clara sunt. Dominus enim jussit Moysi præfigere populo terminos, ultra quos non ascenderent montem. Sed quomodo intelligendum est quod dixit ad Moysen, Sanctifica illum, utpote montem? Et respondendum, quod sicut templum materiale dicitur sanctificari, dum divino cultui dedicatur, sic Moyses montem Sinai sanctificavit, denuntiando Judæis quod ille mons esset electus et deputatus a Deo ad peragendum in eo multa divina: quoniam ibi apparuit et locutus est Dominus, apparueruntque angeli, data est lex, et varia mysteria sunt expleta. Denique ex verbis jam habitis satis apparet, quod sanctus Moyses tam libenter fuit in vertice montis cum Deo, quod invite descendit. Ideo quasi excusando se de descensu, dicebat: Non poterit vulgus ascendere. Quasi dicat: Jam semel dixi hæc eis ex parte tui. Sed Dominus rursus jubet, Vade, descende, ut repetas populo quæ semel dixisti, quatenus diligentius ea observet.
paras.en: [[19:23|And Moses said to the Lord: The people cannot come up to Mount Sinai: for thou didst charge, and command, saying: Set limits about the mount, and sanctify it|Dixitque Moyses ad Dominum: Non poterit vulgus ascendere in montem Sinai. Tu enim testificatus es et jussisti, dicens: Pone terminos circa montem, et sanctifica illum]]. This last word Moses did not write before; the rest is clear. For the Lord bade Moses set limits for the people, beyond which they should not go up the mountain. But how is it to be understood that He said to Moses, [[19:23|sanctify it|Sanctifica illum]], that is, the mountain? The answer is that, as a material temple is said to be sanctified when it is dedicated to divine worship, so Moses sanctified Mount Sinai by declaring to the Jews that that mountain had been chosen and set apart by God for many divine things to be done on it: since there the Lord appeared and spoke, angels appeared, the law was given, and various mysteries were accomplished. Lastly, from the words just given it is clear enough that holy Moses was so glad to be on the top of the mountain with God that he came down unwillingly. So, as if excusing himself from going down, he said: [[19:23|The people cannot come up|Non poterit vulgus ascendere]]. As if to say: I have already told them this once on thy behalf. But the Lord bids him again, [[19:24|Go, get thee down|Vade, descende]], so that thou mayest repeat to the people what thou hast said once, that they may keep it more carefully.

paras.t: Cui ait Dominus: Vade, descende. Ascendesque tu, et Aaron tecum, ut sit socius tuus, audiendo ex me præcepta tibi nunc conferenda, quemadmodum hucusque fuit tibi associatus in faciendo prodigia, dirigendoque populum. Verumtamen cito descendit, nec fuit cum Moyse in vertice montis per quadraginta dies, de quibus infra dicetur. Sacerdotes autem et populus, non transeant terminos sibi præscriptos, nec ascendant ad Dominum in vertice montis, ne forte interficiat illos. Quod ait, Ne forte, non notat ambiguitatem, sed libertatem in Deo, qui omnia operatur non necessitate naturæ, sed secundum propositum suæ voluntatis atque liberrime. Descenditque Moyses ad populum, et omn[ia] narravit eis.
paras.en: [[19:24|And the Lord said to him: Go, get thee down; and thou shalt come up, thou and Aaron with thee|Cui ait Dominus: Vade, descende. Ascendesque tu, et Aaron tecum]], to be thy companion in hearing from me the precepts now to be given thee, as until now he has been thy companion in working wonders and in guiding the people. Yet he soon came down, and was not with Moses on the top of the mountain during the forty days of which we shall speak below. [[19:24|but let not the priests and the people pass the limits|Sacerdotes autem et populus, non transeant terminos]] prescribed for them, [[19:24|nor come up to the Lord|nec ascendant ad Dominum]] on the top of the mountain, [[19:24|lest he kill them|ne forte interficiat illos]]. His saying *lest perhaps* [Latin *ne forte*; the Douay-Rheims has simply "lest"] does not mark uncertainty, but freedom in God, who works all things not by necessity of nature but according to the purpose of His will, and most freely. [[19:25|And Moses went down to the people|Descenditque Moyses ad populum]], [[19:25|and told them all|narravit eis]].

19.title: De mystico hujus capituli nonidecimi intellectu
19.title_en: On the mystical sense of this nineteenth chapter

paras.t: Quadragesimo septimo die ab exitu de Ægypto, venerunt in Sinai. Certum est, per quadragenarium numerum tempus pœnitentiæ designari; per septenarium vero, septem dona Spiritus Sancti: per montem Sinai, altitudinem contemplandi. Qui ergo vult ad contemplationis apicem pervenire, primo in actibus pœnitentiæ se condigne exerceat, atque in donis Spiritus Sancti quotidie crescere enitatur, quatenus mente jam reformata, gloriam Domini speculetur facie revelata. Denique inter omnes Israelitarum mansiones, mansio in monte Sinai fuit præcipua: quoniam contemplationis quietem summe desiderant veri et spirituales Israelitæ, in quibus dolus non est, non hypocrisis, neque duplicitas, neque calliditas. Siquidem simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei.
paras.en: On the forty-seventh day after the going out of Egypt they came to Sinai. It is certain that the number forty signifies the time of penance; the number seven, the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost; Mount Sinai, the height of contemplation. Whoever, then, wishes to reach the summit of contemplation, let him first exercise himself worthily in the acts of penance, and strive to grow daily in the gifts of the Holy Ghost, so that, his mind now reformed, he may behold the glory of the Lord with open face. Moreover, among all the stations of the Israelites, the station at Mount Sinai was the chief: for the quiet of contemplation is what the true and spiritual Israelites most desire, [[John 1:47|in whom there is no guile|in quibus dolus non est]], no hypocrisy, no doubleness, no craftiness. For [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei]].

paras.t: Denique, sicut per Moysen Dominus dixit Judæis, Vos ipsi vidistis quæ fecerim Ægyptiis, quomodo portaverim vos super alas aquilarum: ita per chorum beatissimorum Apostolorum annuntiavit Christus universis hominibus, qualiter pro eorum salute impugnavit et vicit invisibiles hostes, imo et sæculi vanitates, hominesque perversos, persecutores justorum: de quibus dixit discipulis, In mundo pressuram habebitis, sed confidite, ego vici mundum; qualiter etiam sub alis misericordiæ suæ suscepit nos, ad fontem quoque Baptismi, et ad alia ecclesiastica sacramenta nos duxit, et nos ex gentilitate natos assumpsit sibi in populum, oleastrum inserens in bonam olivam, naturalibus ramis relictis. Idcirco si ei grati et obedientes fuerimus, erimus ei populus peculiaris præ cunctis hominibus, efficiemurque ei regnum sacerdotale et gens sancta. Multo enim carior est Christo Ecclesia, quam olim exstitit Synagoga. Numero quoque et merito et omni charismate Spiritus Sancti transcendit Ecclesia ineffabiliter Synagogam. Propter quod in Apocalypsi habetur: Christus dilexit nos, et lavit nos a peccatis nostris in sanguine suo. Princeps quoque Apostolorum: Vos, inquit, genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis, ut virtutes annuntietis ejus, qui de tenebris vos vocavit in admirabile lumen suum.
paras.en: Again, as the Lord said to the Jews through Moses, [[19:4|You have seen what I have done to the Egyptians, how I have carried you upon the wings of eagles|Vos ipsi vidistis quæ fecerim Ægyptiis, quomodo portaverim vos super alas aquilarum]], so through the choir of the most blessed Apostles Christ announced to all men how, for their salvation, he fought against and overcame the invisible enemies, and also the vanities of the world and perverse men, the persecutors of the just; of whom he said to the disciples: [[John 16:33|In the world you shall have distress. But have confidence. I have overcome the world|In mundo pressuram habebitis, sed confidite, ego vici mundum]]; how too he took us up under the wings of his mercy, led us to the font of Baptism and to the other sacraments of the Church, and took us, born of the gentiles, to himself for a people, grafting the wild olive into the good olive and leaving the natural branches[[Rom 11:24||]] [the margin's verse number is lost; the good olive is Rom 11:24, the grafting of the wild olive also Rom 11:17]. Therefore, if we are grateful and obedient to him, we shall be to him a peculiar people above all men, and shall be made to him [[19:6|a priestly kingdom, and a holy nation|regnum sacerdotale et gens sancta]]. For the Church is far dearer to Christ than the Synagogue once was. In number too, in merit, and in every charism of the Holy Ghost the Church surpasses the Synagogue beyond telling. Wherefore it is said in the Apocalypse: Christ [[Apoc 1:5|hath loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood|dilexit nos, et lavit nos a peccatis nostris in sanguine suo]]. And the Prince of the Apostles: You, he says, are [[1 Pet 2:9|a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people: that you may declare his virtues, who hath called you out of darkness into his marvelous light|genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis, ut virtutes annuntietis ejus, qui de tenebris vos vocavit in admirabile lumen suum]].

paras.t: Responditque omnis populus simul: Cuncta quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus. Ita et nos in Baptismo abrenuntiavimus omnibus pompis, operibusque diaboli, et universis Dei mandatis obtemperare condiximus: quod item post recidivum in sacramento Confessionis peregimus. Quid igitur nobis incumbit, nisi ut totis viribus ea, ad quæ nos toties obligavimus, impleamus, nec cessemus deflere, quod heu! tam enormiter ac frequenter ea transgressi sumus?
paras.en: [[19:8|And all the people answered together: All that the Lord hath spoken, we will do.|Responditque omnis populus simul: Cuncta quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus.]] So we too in Baptism renounced all the pomps and works of the devil, and promised to obey all the commandments of God; and this we did again, after relapsing, in the sacrament of Confession. What then is incumbent on us, but to fulfil with all our strength the things to which we have so often bound ourselves, and not cease to bewail that, alas, we have transgressed them so grievously and so often?

paras.t: Vade ad populum, et sanctifica illos hodie et cras; laventque vestimenta sua, et sint parati in diem tertium. Sic Dominus jubet prælatis et prædicatoribus in contemplationis exercitio constitutis, ut ab altitudine hujusmodi exercitationis paululum descendentes, ad creditum sibi dominicum gregem festinent, et cum hortando, instruendo, corripiendo, inflammando, sanctificent hodie et cras, hoc est statim sine periculosa dilatione, et non nimis cursorie, sed ad tempus sufficiens, quatenus in die tertio, utpote post veram confessionem et satisfactionem, sint parati Unigenitum Dei in Sacramento suscipere, atque in monte contemplationis Spiritum Sanctum salubriter intueri. Die enim tertia descendet Dominus coram omni plebe super montem Sinai: quia post dignam confessionem et satisfactionem idoneam, sanctificata jam mente, Spiritus Sanctus tam evidentia et præclara infundit charismata, ut dubitandum non sit, quin Dominus Deus in hujuscemodi mentem descenderit.
paras.en: [[19:10|Go to the people, and sanctify them to day, and to morrow, and let them wash their garments|Vade ad populum, et sanctifica illos hodie et cras; laventque vestimenta sua]], [[19:11|And let them be ready against the third day|et sint parati in diem tertium]]. Thus the Lord commands prelates and preachers who are set in the exercise of contemplation to come down a little from the height of that exercise and hasten to the Lord's flock entrusted to them, and by exhorting, instructing, correcting and inflaming them, to sanctify them today and tomorrow, that is, at once, without dangerous delay, and not too hurriedly but for a sufficient time; so that on the third day, namely after true confession and satisfaction, they may be ready to receive the Only-begotten of God in the Sacrament, and to behold the Holy Ghost with profit on the mount of contemplation. [[19:11|for on the third day the Lord will come down in the sight of all the people, upon Mount Sinai|Die enim tertia descendet Dominus coram omni plebe super montem Sinai]]: because after worthy confession and fitting satisfaction, the mind being now sanctified, the Holy Ghost pours in gifts so evident and so excellent that there can be no doubt that the Lord God has come down into such a mind.

paras.t: Constituesque terminos populo per circuitum, et dices: Cavete ne ascendatis in montem. Per hoc clarissime designatur, quod nulli licet transgredi mensuram et semitam sibi præfixas, nec incomprehensibilia fidei testimonia comprehendere velle, et suo ingenio ea metiri. Sed cum reverentia et modestia debemus ad contemplanda divina accedere, pensata propriæ capacitatis et defectuositatis materie, ut studeat unusquisque in primis ac maxime ea implere ac possidere, quæ Deus primo ac maxime requirit ab eo, sicque juxta sui status mensuram, et suæ vocationis exigentiam ac gratiam sibi concessam se occupet. Hinc quippe in Proverbiis jubetur: Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui. Et in Ecclesiastico: Altiora te ne quæsieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris; sed quæ præcepit tibi Deus, illa cogita semper. Hinc et Sapiens inducit: Sensum tuum, Domine, quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam, et miseris Spiritum Sanctum tuum de cœlis? Idcirco divinus et sacratissimus Dionysius contestatur in libro de Ecclesiastica hierarchia, quod nullus angelicorum spirituum audet quidpiam agere, nisi juxta legem ei desuper præstitutam.
paras.en: [[19:12|And thou shalt appoint certain limits to the people round about, and thou shalt say|Constituesque terminos populo per circuitum, et dices]]: [[19:12|Take heed ye go not up into the mount|Cavete ne ascendatis in montem]]. By this it is most clearly signified that no one may pass beyond the measure and the path set for him, nor wish to comprehend the incomprehensible testimonies of the faith and measure them by his own wit. Rather we ought to approach the contemplation of divine things with reverence and modesty, weighing the matter of our own capacity and deficiency, so that each one may study first and above all to fulfil and possess what God first and above all requires of him, and so busy himself according to the measure of his state, the demands of his calling and the grace granted him. Hence it is commanded in Proverbs: [[Prov 22:28|Pass not beyond the ancient bounds which thy fathers have set.|Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui]] And in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:22|Seek not the things that are too high for thee, and search not into things above thy ability: but the things that God hath commanded thee, think on them always|Altiora te ne quæsieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris; sed quæ præcepit tibi Deus, illa cogita semper]]. Hence too the Wise Man says: [[Wis 9:17|who shall know thy thought|Sensum tuum, Domine, quis sciet]] [Denis adds *Domine*, 'O Lord'], [[Wis 9:17|except thou give wisdom, and send thy holy Spirit from above|nisi tu dederis sapientiam, et miseris Spiritum Sanctum tuum de cœlis?]]? Therefore the divine and most holy Dionysius testifies in his book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* that none of the angelic spirits dares to do anything except according to the law laid down for it from above.

paras.t: Omnis qui tetigerit montem, morte morietur: id est, qui Deitatis altitudinem aut superglorlosissimæ Trinitatis mysterium irreverenter scrutari aut comprehendere velle præsumpserit, aut in Deum altissimum per hæresim, perfidiam, blasphemiamve peccaverit, disperibit. Lapidibus opprimetur, id est, efficacissimis argumentationibus atque acerrimis confutationibus convincetur; sive confodietur jaculis, id est, testimoniis Prophetarum et Apostolorum undique constringetur et dejicietur. Nempe ut Salomon ait, Verba sapientium sunt quasi stimuli, et quasi clavi in altum defixi. Manus non tangent eum: id est, qui adhuc solum activi sunt, nondum contemplationis secretum queunt attingere. Sive jumentum fuerit, sive homo, morietur. Per jumentum exprimitur animalis homo, qui non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei; per hominem vero potest intelligi, quicumque sola naturali et philosophica sapientia præditus, qui ad contemplanda christianæ fidei sublimia nequaquam idoneus invenitur, et propria præsumptione damnatur, si fidei alta scrutari, et judicare ac reprobare contendit. Unde et Apostolus: Videte, inquit, ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam secundum traditionem hominum. Quum cœperit clangere buccina, tunc ascendant in montem, id est, dum vox prædicationis cœlestis insonuerit, considerent divina quæ audiunt, secundum mensuram et intellectum Ecclesiæ.
paras.en: [[19:12|every one that toucheth the mount, dying he shall die|Omnis qui tetigerit montem, morte morietur]]: that is, whoever presumes irreverently to search into, or to wish to comprehend, the height of the Godhead or the mystery of the most supremely glorious Trinity, or sins against the most high God by heresy, faithlessness or blasphemy, shall perish. [[19:13|he shall be stoned to death|Lapidibus opprimetur]], that is, he shall be refuted by most effective arguments and most keen confutations; [[19:13|or he shall be shot through with arrows|sive confodietur jaculis]], that is, he shall be hemmed in on every side and cast down by the testimonies of the Prophets and Apostles. For, as Solomon says, [[Eccles 12:11|The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails deeply fastened in|Verba sapientium sunt quasi stimuli, et quasi clavi in altum defixi]] [the book in the margin is lost; the words are Eccles 12:11]. [[19:13|No hands shall touch him|Manus non tangent eum]]: that is, those who are as yet only active cannot yet reach the secret of contemplation. [[19:13|whether it be beast, or man|Sive jumentum fuerit, sive homo]], he shall die. By the beast is expressed [[1 Cor 2:14|the sensual man|animalis homo]] [Latin *animalis*, the 'animal' man, which answers to the beast], who [[1 Cor 2:14|perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God|non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei]]; by the man may be understood whoever, endowed only with natural and philosophical wisdom, is found in no way fit to contemplate the lofty things of the Christian faith, and is condemned by his own presumption if he strives to search into the deep things of faith, and to judge and reject them. Whence the Apostle too: [[Col 2:8|Beware|Videte]], he says, [[Col 2:8|lest any man cheat you by philosophy and vain deceit: according to the tradition of men|ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam secundum traditionem hominum]]. [[19:13|When the trumpet shall begin to sound, then let them go up into the mount|Quum cœperit clangere buccina, tunc ascendant in montem]], that is, when the voice of heavenly preaching has sounded, let them consider the divine things they hear according to the measure and understanding of the Church.

paras.t: Quumque lavissent vestimenta sua, ait: Ne appropinquetis uxoribus vestris. Sic et nos Deo volentes occurrere, et eum in thalamo cordis suscipere, debemus vestimenta nostra lavare, id est, per pœnitentiam et confessionem, emendationemque vitæ, omnem vitiorum impuritatem ab operibus nostris atque virtutibus removere, separantes pretiosum a vili, ut simus quasi os Dei, et impleamus quod Salomon ait: Omni tempore vestimenta tua sint candida. Unde et in Apocalypsi Dominus profitetur: Qui non inquinaverunt vestimenta sua, ambulabunt mecum in albis. Hinc et ei qui vestes suas ita non lavit, increpative dictum est: Amice, quomodo huc intrasti non habens vestem nuptialem? Denique tempore sacro, quo orationi et communioni est insistendum, pœnitentiæ quoque diebus ab amplexibus decet cessare, quum dicat Apostolus: Nolite invicem fraudare nisi ad tempus, ut vacetis orationi. Itemque: Tempus breve est: superest, ut qui habentes uxores, sint tanquam non habentes. Verumtamen salvo remedio his, qui pro infirmitate sua remedio indigent nuptiali.
paras.en: [[19:14|And when they had washed their garments|Quumque lavissent vestimenta sua]], he said: [[19:15|come not near your wives|Ne appropinquetis uxoribus vestris]]. So we too, wishing to go to meet God and to receive him in the bridal chamber of the heart, ought to wash our garments, that is, by penance and confession and amendment of life to remove all the impurity of vices from our works and virtues, separating [[Jer 15:19|the precious from the vile|pretiosum a vili]], that we may be as it were the mouth of God[[Jer 15:19||]], and fulfil what Solomon says: [[Eccles 9:8|At all times let thy garments be white|Omni tempore vestimenta tua sint candida]]. Whence in the Apocalypse too the Lord declares: [[Apoc 3:4|which have not defiled their garments: and they shall walk with me in white|Qui non inquinaverunt vestimenta sua, ambulabunt mecum in albis]]. Hence too it was said in rebuke to him who had not so washed his garments: [[Matt 22:12|Friend, how camest thou in hither not having on a wedding garment?|Amice, quomodo huc intrasti non habens vestem nuptialem?]] Lastly, in a holy season, when one must give oneself to prayer and communion, and in days of penance also, it is fitting to refrain from embraces, since the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 7:5|Defraud not one another|Nolite invicem fraudare]], [[1 Cor 7:5|for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer|nisi ad tempus, ut vacetis orationi]]. And again: [[1 Cor 7:29|The time is short. It remaineth, that they also who have wives be as if they had none|Tempus breve est: superest, ut qui habentes uxores, sint tanquam non habentes]]. Saving, however, the remedy for those who for their weakness need the remedy of marriage.

paras.t: Jam advenerat dies tertius, et mane inclaruerat; et ecce cœperunt audiri tonitrua et micare fulgura. Hæc dies tertia, est tempus evangelicæ legis. Nam prima dies, est tempus legis naturæ; secunda, tempus legis scriptæ. Mane tertiæ diei, est diluculum diei Pentecostes, quando factus est repente sonus vehemens, replens totam domum in qua primitiva sedit Ecclesia: qua Spiritu Sancto copiosissime adimpleta, cœperunt ab eadem emanare tonitrua evangelicæ prædicationis, et fulgura comminationum, ac præclara coruscare miracula. Tunc et nubes densissima operuit montem, id est copiosa multitudo millium Judæorum, qui tunc repente convertebantur, in quibus fuit mortalis infirmitas, et adhuc obscura cognitio, supervenit primitivæ Ecclesiæ, et baptizabatur ab ea. Clangorque buccinæ vehementius perstrepebat. Clangor ille fuit invictissima atque altisona prædicatio beatissimi Archiapostoli, confundentis et convincentis incredulos. Timuit populus qui erat in castris. Tunc enim omnes stupebant et mirabantur, dicentes: Quidnam vult hoc esse? Atque ut Lucas evangelista scribit, fiebat omni animæ timor. Eos vero qui credebant, eduxit chorus Apostolorum in occursum Dei, ita quod adventui et infusioni Spiritus Sancti se præparabant. Steterunt quoque conversi ad radices montis, hoc est in humilibus locis Ecclesiæ.
paras.en: [[19:16|now the third day was come, and the morning appeared: and behold thunders began to be heard, and lightning to flash|Jam advenerat dies tertius, et mane inclaruerat; et ecce cœperunt audiri tonitrua et micare fulgura]]. This third day is the time of the law of the Gospel. For the first day is the time of the law of nature; the second, the time of the written law. The morning of the third day is the dawn of the day of Pentecost, when suddenly there came a mighty sound, filling the whole house in which the primitive Church sat[[Acts 2:2||]]; and when she had been most abundantly filled with the Holy Ghost, there began to issue from her the thunders of the Gospel preaching and the lightnings of threatenings, and splendid miracles began to flash. Then too [[19:16|a very thick cloud|nubes densissima]] covered the mount, that is, a great multitude of thousands of Jews, who were then suddenly converted, in whom there was mortal weakness and as yet a dim knowledge, came to the primitive Church and were baptized by her. [[19:16|and the noise of the trumpet sounded exceeding loud|Clangorque buccinæ vehementius perstrepebat]]. That blast was the unconquerable and high-sounding preaching of the most blessed Chief Apostle, confounding and convicting the unbelievers. [[19:16|the people that was in the camp, feared|Timuit populus qui erat in castris]]. For then [[Acts 2:12|they were all astonished, and wondered|omnes stupebant et mirabantur]], saying: [[Acts 2:12|What meaneth this?|Quidnam vult hoc esse?]] And, as Luke the Evangelist writes, [[Acts 2:43|fear came upon every soul|fiebat omni animæ timor]]. And those who believed, the choir of the Apostles [[19:17|brought them forth|eduxit]] [[19:17|to meet God|in occursum Dei]], in that they prepared themselves for the coming and infusion of the Holy Ghost. The converts too [[19:17|stood|Steterunt]] [[19:17|at the bottom of the mount|ad radices montis]], that is, in the lowly places of the Church.

paras.t: Totus autem mons Sinai fumabat, eo quod descendisset Dominus super eum in igne. Tunc certe tota primitiva Ecclesia in monte Sion collecta, præ interiori cordis ardore, verba prædicationis ignita emittebat assidue, eo quod Spiritus Sanctus in igneis linguis descendisset in eam, qui præcordia ejus æstuantissime inflammavit. Moyses loquebatur, et Dominus respondebat ei. Sic et bonis ac sanctis prælatis Dominus pie respondet per occultum instinctum et sacras Scripturas, sanctosque angelos.
paras.en: [[19:18|And all Mount Sinai was on a smoke: because the Lord was come down upon it in fire|Totus autem mons Sinai fumabat, eo quod descendisset Dominus super eum in igne]]. Then indeed the whole primitive Church, gathered on Mount Sion, from the inner ardour of the heart sent forth without ceasing fiery words of preaching, because the Holy Ghost had come down upon her in tongues of fire, and set her inmost heart most fervently aflame. [[19:19|Moses spoke, and God answered him|Moyses loquebatur, et Dominus respondebat ei]]. So too the Lord answers good and holy prelates lovingly, by a hidden prompting, by the sacred Scriptures, and by the holy angels.

paras.t: Sacerdotes qui accedunt ad Dominum, sanctificentur, ne percutiat eos. Sacerdotes etenim evangelicæ legis tanto spiritualius et castius conversari oportet, quanto eorum sacerdotium divinius præstantiusque consistit, et quo dignior est Hostia quam consecrant, tractant, sumunt, et immolant Deo Patri. Quum igitur filii Israel etiam uxorati, jussi sunt abstinere a suis uxoribus usque in tertium diem, quando verba Dei fuerant audituri, suscepturique legem: qualis est sacerdotum evangelicæ legis impietas, qui incontinentiæ vitio subjacentes, Christum in Sacramento præsumunt tractare? O quanta est impudentia horum! et quam infinita damnatio, intolerabilisque punitio imminet eis!
paras.en: [[19:22|The priests also that come to the Lord, let them be sanctified, lest he strike them|Sacerdotes qui accedunt ad Dominum, sanctificentur, ne percutiat eos]]. For the priests of the law of the Gospel must live the more spiritually and chastely, the more divine and excellent their priesthood is, and the worthier the Victim whom they consecrate, handle, receive, and offer to God the Father. Since, then, the children of Israel, even the married, were ordered to abstain from their wives until the third day, when they were to hear the words of God and receive the law[[19:15||]], what is the impiety of priests of the law of the Gospel who, subject to the vice of incontinence, presume to handle Christ in the Sacrament? O how great is their shamelessness! and what endless damnation, what unbearable punishment hangs over them!

20.title: Expositio capituli vicesimi: Locutusque est Dominus cunctos sermones hos
20.title_en: Exposition of the twentieth chapter: “And the Lord spoke all these words”

paras.t: Jam datio legis describitur. Locutusque est Dominus cunctos sermones hos. In fine præcedentis capituli scriptum est, qualiter Moyses de celsitudine montis descendens, recitavit populo ea quæ ibi sunt scripta. Moyse itaque inferius exsistente cum populo, locutus est Dominus verba nunc exponenda, tam Moyse quam populo audiente, dicens : EEgo sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, de domo servitutis. Quemadmodum refert Lyra, Hebræi dicunt, quod istud sit unum et primum præceptum Decalogi, per quod affirmative præcipit Deus, ut ipse solus habeatur et colatur pro vero Deo, qui tam potenter et miraculose eduxit Israel de Ægypto. Quocirca Rabbi Paulus reprehendit Lyram, eo quod simpliciter narret prætactam Hebræorum opinionem, quasi probabiliter possit teneri, et non reprobet eam : quia si posset teneri, sequeretur secundum Rabbi Paulum, quod doctores catholici in enumeratione Decalogi deviassent a ratione. Verum hæc reprehensio est inepta, nec tenet consequentia illa : quia (ut infra patebit) etiam nostri doctores in modo numerandi, distinguendi, ac situandi decem præcepta, variis modis senserunt ; nec tamen hine sequitur, quod in hoc deviaverunt a ratione. Frequenter enim circa eamdem materiam diversæ opiniones possunt probabiliter teneri, absque errore et deviatione a ratione, quando non defenduntur cum incauta et temeraria assertione, ut patuit plenius in expositione exordii Geneseos, quod sancti doctores diversimode exposuerunt.
paras.en: Now the giving of the Law is described. [[20:1|And the Lord spoke all these words|Locutusque est Dominus cunctos sermones hos]]. At the end of the preceding chapter it is written how Moses, coming down from the height of the mountain, recited to the people what is written there. So, while Moses was below with the people, the Lord spoke the words now to be expounded, in the hearing of both Moses and the people, saying: [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, de domo servitutis.]] As Lyra reports, the Hebrews say that this is one commandment, the first of the Decalogue, by which God commands affirmatively that He alone be held and worshipped as the true God, He who so mightily and miraculously brought Israel out of Egypt. For this reason Rabbi Paul censures Lyra for simply relating this opinion of the Hebrews as though it could be held as probable, without rejecting it: for if it could be held, it would follow, according to Rabbi Paul, that the Catholic doctors had departed from reason in their numbering of the Decalogue. But this censure is beside the point, and the consequence does not hold: for (as will appear below) our own doctors too have held various views on the way of numbering, dividing and ordering the ten commandments, and yet it does not follow that they departed from reason in this. For often several opinions about the same matter can be held as probable, without error or departure from reason, so long as they are not defended with incautious and rash assertion, as was shown more fully in the exposition of the opening of Genesis, which the holy doctors have expounded in different ways.

paras.t: Deinde Rabbi Paulus reprobat præfatam Hebræorum opinionem, quia in verbis his, Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, non ponitur aliquod verbum imperativum aut præceptivum; sed est ibi solum denuntiatio quædam, qua Deus annuntiat populo quod ipse qui loquitur, sit Deus qui eos de Ægypto eduxit. Et in isto Rabbi Paulus catholice sentit, quia et Glossa ait: Non est istud mandatum, sed significatio cujus sit mandatum. Hoc idem asserit Augustinus et alii expositores communiter. Deinceps Rabbi Paulus tangit motiva Hebræorum, dicentium verba prehabita esse primum mandatum. Primum est, quia ad omnium divinorum observantiam præceptorum, necesse est præsupponere quod ille qui jussit ea, sit Deus qui Israel transtulit ex Ægypto : quoniam fides seu præsuppositio illa, est ratio obligandi ad servandum ipsius præcepta. Idcirco per verba hæc. EEgo sum Dominus Deus tuus, dicunt affirmative juberi, quod hoc firmiter credatur. Secundum eorum motivum est, quoniam antequam aliquis possit præcipere aliis, oportet ut recipiatur ab eis pro superiore. Ideo dicunt Deum primo jussisse per verba inducta, quod ipse haberetur ab Hebræis in Deum. Sed ista motiva quamvis aliquid contineant veritatis, non tamen concludunt propositumquia jam ante horum prolationem verborum filii Israel crediderunt, quod ille qui eos eduxit, esset verus Deus, et specialiter Deus eorum. Unde submersis Ægyptiis, cecinerunt : Cantemus Domino, gloriose enim magnificatus est. Quartodecimo quoque capitulo scriptum est, quod eis per maris fundum transductis, Ægyptiisque submersis, crediderunt Domino et Moysi servo ejus. Denique, præcedenti capitulo fassi sunt se velle esse subjectos imperio Dei, dicentes : Cuncta quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus. Itaque Deus tanquam præambulum quoddam pramittens, locutus est populo Israel : EEgo sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui licet sim universorum Dominus atque Deus per creationem et gubernationem, conservationem et judiciariam potestatem, tamen sum specialiter Dominus Deus tuus, quem elegi mihi in populum peculiarem, et cui nunc legem et præcepta hæc tribuo.
paras.en: Next, Rabbi Paul rejects this opinion of the Hebrews, because in the words [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus]] no verb of command or precept is used; there is only a kind of declaration, by which God announces to the people that He who speaks is the God who brought them out of Egypt. And in this Rabbi Paul thinks as a Catholic, for the Gloss too says: This is not a commandment, but a statement of whose commandment it is. Augustine and the other expositors commonly assert the same. Rabbi Paul then touches on the reasons of the Hebrews who say that these words are the first commandment. The first is that, for the keeping of all the divine precepts, it must be presupposed that He who commanded them is the God who brought Israel out of Egypt; for that belief, or presupposition, is the ground of the obligation to keep His precepts. Therefore, they say, by the words [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus]] it is affirmatively commanded that this be firmly believed. Their second reason is that before anyone can command others, he must be accepted by them as their superior; so they say that God first commanded, by these introductory words, that He be held by the Hebrews as God. But these reasons, though they contain some truth, do not prove the point, because even before these words were spoken the children of Israel believed that He who brought them out was the true God, and in a special way their God. Hence, when the Egyptians had been drowned, they sang: [[15:1|Let us sing to the Lord: for he is gloriously magnified|Cantemus Domino: gloriose enim magnificatus est]]. And in the fourteenth chapter it is written that, when they had been led across the bed of the sea and the Egyptians drowned, [[14:31|they believed the Lord, and Moses his servant|crediderunt Domino, et Moysi servo ejus]]. Finally, in the preceding chapter they professed that they were willing to be subject to God's rule, saying: [[19:8|All that the Lord hath spoken, we will do|Cuncta quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus]]. So God, setting this down first as a kind of preamble, spoke to the people of Israel: [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus]]; that is, though I am Lord and God of all things by creation and governance, by preservation and by power of judgment, yet I am in a special way the Lord thy God, thine whom I have chosen for myself as a peculiar people, and to whom I now give this law and these precepts.

paras.t: Consequenter exprimitur primum præceptum : Non habebis deos alienos coram me. Quasi dicat : Me solum pro vero Deo habebis, adorabis et coles ; omnes ceteros qui dii vocantur, refutabis adorare et colere per latriæ cultum, ita quod nec eos qui mendaciter dii vocantur, ut Jupiter, Mars, Saturnus, qui scelerati fuerunt, nec illos qui in Scripturis dii vocantur per participationem et gratiam, ut angeli et homines sancti, adorabis et coles latriæ cultu. Dæmones quoque a gentilibus dii mendaciter vocabantur. Corpora autem cælestia animata ponebant, sicque cælos, stellas, planetas, vocabant deos per quamdam participationem. De quibus in primo Timæi loquitur in persona Dei Plato philosophus : 0 dii deorum, quorum idem paer opifexque ego. Omnes hi possunt dii alieni vocari, in quantum per vitiosum cultum eorum homines alienantur, avertuntur et reprobantur a vero Deo: et item, quoniam Deus jussit, ut fideles sui ab illorum cultu se alienarent: rursumque, quia a vera deitate sunt alieni. Itaque ait : Non habebis deos alienos coram me, id est nullibi, quoniam ego ubique sum præsens, et cuncta intueor.
paras.en: Next the first commandment is stated: [[20:3|Thou shalt not have strange gods before me.|Non habebis deos alienos coram me.]] As if to say: Me alone shalt thou hold, adore and worship as the true God; all the others who are called gods thou shalt refuse to adore and worship with the worship of latria [the worship due to God alone]. So thou shalt adore and worship with latria neither those who are falsely called gods, such as Jupiter, Mars and Saturn, who were wicked men, nor those who in the Scriptures are called gods by participation and grace, such as the angels and holy men. The demons too were falsely called gods by the gentiles. And the gentiles held the heavenly bodies to be living things, and so called the heavens, the stars and the planets gods by a kind of participation; of these Plato the philosopher speaks in the person of God in the first book of the Timaeus: 'O gods of gods, whose father and maker I am.' All these can be called strange gods [dii alieni, literally 'alien gods'], inasmuch as by the sinful worship of them men are estranged, turned away and cast off from the true God; and again, because God commanded His faithful to estrange themselves from their worship; and again, because they are strangers to true divinity. Therefore He says: [[20:3|Thou shalt not have strange gods before me|Non habebis deos alienos coram me]], that is, nowhere, for I am present everywhere and behold all things.

paras.t: Non facies tibi sculptile, id est idolum aliquod ex quacumque materia, in qua sculpi potest. Et specialiter potest per idolum designari imago rei confictæ, quæ nullam exsistentiam habet, nec esse potest, quum dicat Apostolus : Idolum nihil est. Neque omnem similitudinem quæ est in cælo desuper, et quæ in terra deorsum, nec eorum quæ sunt in aquis sub terra : id est, nullam tibi formabis similitudinem per fusuram sive picturam cujuscumque rei creatæ, videlicet ad colendum aliquid tale, ita ut nec cælestium neque terrestrium neque aquaticorum imaginem tibi formes, aut fieri facias. Hinc subditur: Non adorabis ea neque coles, quia nec ipsam rem creatam, nec ejus imaginem. Aliqui namque putaverunt aliquid numinis esse in ipsis idolis, statuis seu imaginibus, ut Trismegistus, qui dixit : Statuas dico animatas sensu et spiritu plenas, imbecillitatem et sanitatem hominibus facientes. Aliqui vero hoc non credentes, coluerunt deos absque imagine eorumdem. Unde Varro, Valeriusque testantur, quod antiqui Romani deos diu absque imaginibus coluerunt.
paras.en: [[20:4|Thou shalt not make to thyself a graven thing|Non facies tibi sculptile]]: that is, any idol, of whatever material can be carved. And by 'idol' may especially be meant the image of a made-up thing, which has no existence and cannot exist, since the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 8:4|an idol is nothing|nihil est idolum]]. [[20:4|nor the likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or in the earth beneath, nor of those things that are in the waters under the earth|neque omnem similitudinem quæ est in cælo desuper, et quæ in terra deorsum, nec eorum quæ sunt in aquis sub terra]]: that is, thou shalt form for thyself no likeness of any created thing, by casting or by painting, for the purpose of worshipping any such thing; so that thou shalt neither form nor have made for thyself an image of things in the heavens, on the earth, or in the waters. Hence it is added: [[20:5|Thou shalt not adore them, nor serve them|Non adorabis ea, neque coles]]: neither the created thing itself nor its image. For some thought that there was something of divinity in the idols themselves, the statues or images; such was Trismegistus, who said: 'I speak of statues ensouled, full of sense and spirit, which bring sickness and health to men.' Others, not believing this, worshipped the gods without images of them; hence Varro and Valerius testify that the ancient Romans long worshipped their gods without images.

paras.t: Ego enim sum Dominus Deus tuus fortis, zelotes, id est, instar amatoris seu mariti aut sponsi zelotypi, volens solus amari et coli ut Deus et sponsus a fidelibus animabus : idcirco prohibeo eis fornicari cum diis alienis, quemadmodum sponsus non vult sponsam suam alteri commisceri. Qui autem accedit meretricem, non indignatur si et alter eam accedat, quia non habet ad illam amorem zelotypum qui socium et communicatorem excludit. Unde zelotes seu zelator nunc appellatur, qui sic vult solus amari, ita ut nihil secum ametur, in derogationem aut minorationem sui amoris. Sic igitur præcipit Deus se coli et honorari, ut ei dumtaxat tota mente adhæreamus, serviamus, atque vacemus, et non sit anima nostra dæmonum aut idolorum, alienorumve deorum adultera, sed Dei solummodo sponsa.
paras.en: [[20:5|I am the Lord thy God, mighty, jealous|ego sum Dominus Deus tuus fortis, zelotes]]: that is, like a jealous lover, husband or bridegroom, who wishes to be loved and cherished alone, as God and Bridegroom, by faithful souls. Therefore I forbid them to commit fornication with strange gods, just as a bridegroom will not have his bride joined to another. A man who goes in to a harlot is not indignant if another goes in to her too, because he has no jealous love for her, the kind that shuts out a companion and sharer. So He is here called jealous (zelotes, or zealous) who wishes to be loved alone in such a way that nothing be loved along with Him to the detriment or lessening of love for Him. Thus God commands that He be worshipped and honoured in such a way that we cleave to Him alone with our whole mind, serve Him and give ourselves to Him, and that our soul be no adulteress with demons, idols or strange gods, but the bride of God alone.

paras.t: Visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam et quartam generationem, eorum qui oderunt me. Non absolute ait, in tertiam et quartam generationem ; sed addit, Eorum qui oderunt me. Verumtamen additio ista, Eorum qui oderunt me, potest referri ad id quod dixit, Iniquitatem patrum, et etiam ad filios. Sed istud bonitati et æquitati Dei derogare videtur, ut iniquitatem parentum ulciscatur in sobolem, præsertim quum per Ezechielem locutus sit : Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris. Et per eumdem Prophetam ac Jeremiam : Omnis, inquit, qui comederit uvam acerbam, obstupescent dentes ejus. Nihilo minus idem Jeremias fatetur in Threnis : Patres nostri peccaverunt, et non sunt; et nos iniquitates eorum portavimus. Et in Josue leguntur filii Israel fugati, et quidam eorum occisi sunt propter peccatum Achan. Itaque circa materiam istam inveniuntur variæ auctoritates Scripturæ, quæ sibi invicem contrariari videntur. Nam et infra legitur, quod nunc in textu asseritur.
paras.en: [[20:5|visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me|visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam et quartam generationem eorum qui oderunt me]]. He does not say simply, 'unto the third and fourth generation,' but adds, 'of them that hate me.' Yet this addition, 'of them that hate me,' can be referred to what He said, 'the iniquity of the fathers,' and also to the children. But it seems to detract from God's goodness and fairness that He should avenge the iniquity of parents upon their offspring, especially since He has said through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:20|the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father|filius non portabit iniquitatem patris]]. And through the same Prophet, and through Jeremias: [[Jer 31:30|every man that shall eat the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge|omnis homo qui comederit uvam acerbam, obstupescent dentes ejus]]. Yet the same Jeremias confesses in the Lamentations: [[Lam 5:7|Our fathers have sinned, and are not: and we have borne their iniquities.|Patres nostri peccaverunt, et non sunt: et nos iniquitates eorum portavimus.]] And in Josue we read that the children of Israel were put to flight, and some of them slain, for the sin of Achan. So on this matter we find various authorities of Scripture which seem to contradict one another; and indeed what the text asserts here is read again below.

paras.t: Sed omnium horum solutio et concordantia ex dictis patet doctorum. Nempe, ut scribit S. Thomas in secunda secundæ, quod et ex dictis Alexandri de Hales habetur : Pœna potest considerari dupliciter : Primo, in quantum pœna, et prout per eam reparatur æqualitas justitiæ, dum peccator qui peceando nimis acquievit propriæ voluntati in derogationem justitiæ, aliquid patitur contra suam voluntatem, in ipsius justitiæ recompensam : sicque pœna pro proprio peccato infligitur. Secundo, consideratur pœna, ut medicina peccati, non solum curativa præteriti, sed etiam præservativa futuri, conservativaque boni : et sic aliqui puniuntur sine propria culpa, sed non sine causa. Per medicinam autem non est subtrahendum majus bonum, ut minus bonum obtineatur, sed econverso. Hinc aliqui absque propria culpa in temporalibus puniuntur per damna aut infirmitates, ut probentur, humilientur, aut alio modo gratiam sortiantur, sicque in spiritualibus bonis crescant, aut aliquo modo misericordiam consequantur. Nunquam tamen aliquis per spiritualium subtractionem bonorum punitur, nec in vita præsenti, neque futura, sine propria culpa. Sic ergo servi et filii in corporalibus aliquando puniuntur propter parentum aut dominorum suorum peccata, in quantum secundum corpus sunt aliquid seu res quædam illorum, ita quod parentes ac domini puniuntur in illis : unde in auctoritatibus dicitur, usque ad tertiam et quartam generationem, quia usque ad tot generationes vivere possunt parentes. Nec istud repugnat divine justitiæ, quoniam Deus hoc ipsum ordinat in ipsorum, sic patientium, bonum. Auctoritates autem contra hæc allegate, intelliguntur de pœnis spiritualibus et æternis.
paras.en: But the solution and harmonizing of all these is clear from what the doctors say. For, as St. Thomas writes in the Secunda Secundae [of the Summa], and as is also found in the words of Alexander of Hales, punishment can be considered in two ways. First, as punishment, inasmuch as by it the equality of justice is restored: the sinner who in sinning indulged his own will too far, to the detriment of justice, suffers something against his will in repayment to justice; and in this way punishment is inflicted for one's own sin. Secondly, punishment is considered as a medicine for sin, not only healing past sin but also guarding against future sin and preserving what is good; and in this way some are punished without fault of their own, though not without cause. But by medicine a greater good is not to be taken away to obtain a lesser, but the reverse. Hence some, without fault of their own, are punished in temporal things by losses or sicknesses, so that they may be tried, humbled or in some other way obtain grace, and so grow in spiritual goods, or in some way obtain mercy. Yet no one is ever punished by the withdrawal of spiritual goods, either in the present life or in the life to come, without fault of his own. So servants and children are sometimes punished in bodily things for the sins of their parents or masters, inasmuch as in the body they are something belonging to them, a kind of possession of theirs, so that the parents and masters are punished in them. Hence the authorities say 'unto the third and fourth generation,' because parents can live to see that many generations. Nor is this contrary to divine justice, since God ordains it for the good of those who suffer in this way. The authorities alleged against this are to be understood of spiritual and eternal punishments.

paras.t: Præterea Origenes solvit quæstionem hanc aliter, per patres peccantium, intelligens dæmones tentatores; per generationes, primam, secundam, tertiam et quartam, eos qui peccanti cooperantur, consentiunt, aut alio modo communicant.
paras.en: Origen, moreover, solves this question differently, understanding by the fathers of sinners the demons who tempt them, and by the first, second, third and fourth generations those who cooperate with the sinner, consent to him, or share in his sin in some other way.

paras.t: Et faciens misericordiam in millia his qui diligunt me, et custodiunt præcepta mea : id est, multo copiosius et protensius misereor posteris amantium me, et obedientium mihi, præsertim posteris prædestinatis. Nam ut ait Jacobus apostolus, Superexaltat misericordia judicium. Et Psalmista : Miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus. Verumtamen in hac re attendere possumus, quam mirabilia et incomprehensibilia sint judicia Dei, quia interdum immediati filii justissimorum patrum sunt pessimi, et econverso. Ecce quam sanctus vir fuit Josias, et tamen filii ejus pessimi erant. Sic et Ezechias rex sanctus, filius fuit vitiosissimi Achaz. Denique, infra discutietur de ordinatione, enumeratione et situatione Decalogi ; et utrum dicta hucusque, sint ad unum præceptum spectantia, an potius sint duo præcepta.
paras.en: [[20:6|And shewing mercy unto thousands to them that love me, and keep my commandments.|et faciens misericordiam in millia his qui diligunt me, et custodiunt præcepta mea.]] That is, I show mercy far more abundantly and far longer to the descendants of those who love me and obey me, especially to descendants who are predestined. For as the apostle James says: [[Jas 2:13|mercy exalteth itself above judgment|superexaltat autem misericordia judicium]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 144:9|his tender mercies are over all his works|miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus]]. Yet in this matter we may observe how wonderful and incomprehensible are the judgments of God: for sometimes the immediate sons of most just fathers are very wicked, and the reverse. See how holy a man Josias was, and yet his sons were very wicked; so too Ezechias, a holy king, was the son of the most vicious Achaz. Finally, below we shall discuss the order, numbering and arrangement of the Decalogue, and whether what has been said so far belongs to one commandment, or rather makes two.

paras.t: Sequitur aliud præceptum, et ut patebit, secundum in ordine. Non assumes nomen Dei tui in vanum : id est, nec falsum, nec sine rationabili causa jurabis per Deum. Nec enim insontem habebit Dominus eum, qui assumpserit nomen Domini Dei sui frustra : id est, talem tam inaniter jurantem, Deus non reputabit innoxium, sed transgressorem, damnationeque dignum ; imo decet ut nunquam sine reverentia et cordis attentione Deum nominemus, aut etiam nominari audiamus. Judæi vero affirmant hoc præcepto etiam prohiberi prolationem indebitam nominis Domini tetragrammaton, quod non licuit nominari nisi sacerdotibus, quando populum benedixerunt in templo.
paras.en: Another commandment follows, the second in order, as will appear. [[20:7|Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain|Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum]]: that is, thou shalt not swear by God either falsely or without reasonable cause. [[20:7|for the Lord will not hold him guiltless that shall take the name of the Lord his God in vain|nec enim habebit insontem Dominus eum qui assumpserit nomen Domini Dei sui frustra]]: that is, God will not count one who swears so idly as innocent, but as a transgressor and worthy of damnation. Indeed, it is fitting that we should never name God, or even hear Him named, without reverence and attention of heart. The Jews, moreover, affirm that this commandment also forbids the improper utterance of the Lord's four-lettered name [the Tetragrammaton], which none but the priests were permitted to pronounce, when they blessed the people in the temple.

paras.t: Sequitur præceptum tertium : Memento ut diem sabbati sanctifices : id est, in sanctis operibus diem illum expendas, et divino cultui applices illum. Per quod aliorum dierum solennium, et nunc dominicæ diei jubetur celebritas. Instituit autem Dominus sabbatum, id est diem septimum, celebrari, in signum quod ipse die septimo requievit a cunctis operibus suis, et in commemorationem beneficii creationis, imo et aliorum Dei beneficiorum, quorum jugiter memores debemus esse. Propter quod præcepto huic præmittitur, Memento : quod verbum etiam ideo præmittitur, quoniam cum summa diligentia cultui est insistendum divino. Vel, ut asserit Rabbi Paulus, ideo verbum istud præmittitur, quia jam ante in descensu manna datum fuit istud præceptum, ut supra patuit. Recitat quoque Rabbi Paulus : Hebræi credunt quod sanctificatio sabbati præcipua consistat in corporalibus delectationibus ; traduntque quod quilibet tenetur in illo die ter manducare, videlicet semel prandere, et bis cœnare, atque quod omnes hoc facientes, sint securi a judicio gehennæ, ut in libro eorum de sabbato, expresse habetur. Ecce quam ridiculosum et stultum est hoc.
paras.en: The third commandment follows: [[20:8|Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day.|Memento ut diem sabbati sanctifices.]] That is, spend that day in holy works and give it to divine worship. By this the keeping of the other feast days is commanded too, and now of the Lord's Day. The Lord instituted the sabbath, that is, the seventh day, to be kept as a sign that He Himself rested on the seventh day from all His works, and in remembrance of the benefit of creation, and indeed of God's other benefits, which we ought to remember continually. That is why the word 'Remember' is set before this commandment; it is set there also because divine worship must be attended to with the greatest diligence. Or, as Rabbi Paul asserts, this word is set before it because this commandment had already been given when the manna came down, as was seen above. Rabbi Paul also relates that the Hebrews believe the chief sanctification of the sabbath to consist in bodily pleasures, and teach that everyone is bound to eat three times on that day, namely to dine once and sup twice, and that all who do this are safe from the judgment of Gehenna, as is expressly stated in their book on the sabbath. See how ridiculous and foolish this is!

paras.t: Sex diebus operaberis, nisi in eorum aliquo aliqua solennitas occurrat, et facies omnia opera tua : unumquodque loco et tempore opportuno. Septimo autem die sabbatum Domini Dei tui est, id est, qui deputatus est cultui veri Dei. Non facies omne opus tu : id est, nullum servile aut mechanicum, præsertim nullum opus iniquum facies tu, id est facere tibi licet, et filius tuus et filia tua, servus tuus et ancilla tua, jumentum tuum, quia et pecora quæ laborant hominibus, voluit Deus tunc quiescere, convenienterque refici ; et advena qui est intra portas tuas, id est tibi cohabitat in villis, urbibus, aut domibus tuis. Et potest, per advenam intelligi quicumque ad Judaismum conversus. Deinde subjungitur ratio institutionis solennitatis sabbativæ : Sex enim diebus fecit Deus cælum et terram, mare et omnia quæ in eis sunt. Et requievit die septimo. Quod qualiter multipliciter possit intelligi, in expositione primi capituli Genesis diffuse expositum est. Idcirco benedixit Dominus diei sabbati, privilegiando eum præ ceteris diebus, et sanctificavit eum, id est divino eultui consecravit. Porro de expositione multiplici et plena intelligentia hujus præcepti et ceterorum præceptorum Decalogi, tot et tanta in aliis scripsi opusculis, imo et tanta inde habentur ubique, quod nequaquam stare intendo nunc in horum expositione hoc loco.
paras.en: [[20:9|Six days shalt thou labour|Sex diebus operaberis]], unless some feast falls on one of them, [[20:9|and shalt do all thy works|et facies omnia opera tua]], each in its proper place and time. [[20:10|But on the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God|Septimo autem die sabbatum Domini Dei tui est]], that is, the day set apart for the worship of the true God. [[20:10|thou shalt do no work on it, thou|non facies omne opus in eo, tu]]: that is, no servile or mechanical work, and above all no wicked work, shalt thou do; [[20:10|nor thy son, nor thy daughter, nor thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy beast|et filius tuus et filia tua, servus tuus et ancilla tua, jumentum tuum]], for God willed that even the beasts that labour for men should then rest and be suitably refreshed; [[20:10|nor the stranger that is within thy gates|et advena qui est intra portas tuas]], that is, who lives with thee in thy villages, cities or houses. By the stranger may also be understood anyone converted to Judaism. Then the reason for instituting the solemnity of the sabbath is added: [[20:11|For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them, and rested on the seventh day|Sex enim diebus fecit Dominus cælum et terram, et mare, et omnia quæ in eis sunt, et requievit in die septimo]]. The many ways in which this can be understood were set out at length in the exposition of the first chapter of Genesis. [[20:11|therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day|idcirco benedixit Dominus diei sabbati]], privileging it above the other days, [[20:11|and sanctified it|et sanctificavit eum]], that is, consecrated it to divine worship. As for the manifold exposition and full understanding of this commandment and of the other commandments of the Decalogue, I have written so much in other works, and so much on the subject is found everywhere, that I do not at all intend to dwell on their exposition in this place.

paras.t: Honora patrem tuum et matrem tuam, imo et ceteros progenitores, spiritualesque patres ac seniores, et benefactores ac magistros, cordiali affectu, decenti affatu, reali obtemperatione atque obsequio, et si opus fuerit, etiam sustentatione. De hac re infinita quodammodo dici possent. Subditur autem merces seu ratio hujus præcepti, ut sis longevus super terram, id est diu ac prospere vivas in terra. Non quod istud sit finale, principaleque premium observationis hujus præcepti, sed aliquantula retributio recte correspondens eidem : quoniam eum qui debite honorat principia suæ vitæ, puta parentes, decuit in ipsa sua vita prosperitatem et diuturnitatem sortiri, quemadmodum eum qui facit misericordiam, decet misericordiam consequi. Deus autem rudi populo veteris Testamenti temporalem promisit mercedem, ut vel sic ad obediendum alliceretur; tamen sub illa mercede subintellexit æternam ac spiritualem, quæ sola est premium condignum actuum virtuosorum, ex caritate Dei manantium, imo et ex actuali motione Spiritus Sancti. Unde quod ait, Ut sis longævus super terram quam Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi,rite exponitur de regione cælestis patrie. De qua fertur : Credo videre bona Domini in terra viventium. Itemque : Beati mites, quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram : in qua justi sunt longævi, quia in æternum vivent in ea. Et quamvis prædicta secundum communem legem ita se habeant, quandoque tamen contingit occulto Dei judicio, quod honoratores parentum brevis et ærumnosæ sint vite, inhonoratores vero eorum, longeva ac prosperæ. Quod Deus sic ordinat ad majorem obedientium felicitatem, atque ad graviorem inobedientium damnationem. Vel ex aliis abditis causis id accidit.
paras.en: [[20:12|Honour thy father and thy mother|Honora patrem tuum et matrem tuam]], and indeed thy other forebears, thy spiritual fathers and elders, thy benefactors and teachers: with heartfelt affection, with fitting speech, with real obedience and service, and, if need be, with support as well. Endless things, in a way, could be said on this. Then the reward, or reason, of this commandment is added: [[20:12|that thou mayst be longlived upon the land|ut sis longævus super terram]], that is, that thou mayst live long and prosperously in the land. Not that this is the final and principal reward for keeping this commandment, but a modest recompense rightly answering to it: for it was fitting that he who duly honours the sources of his life, namely his parents, should obtain prosperity and length in that very life, just as it is fitting that he who shows mercy should obtain mercy. God promised a temporal reward to the unschooled people of the Old Testament so that by this, at least, they might be drawn to obey; yet beneath that reward He meant the eternal and spiritual reward, which alone is the worthy reward of virtuous acts that flow from the love of God, and indeed from the actual movement of the Holy Ghost. Hence His words, [[20:12|that thou mayst be longlived upon the land which the Lord thy God will give thee|ut sis longævus super terram, quam Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi]], are rightly expounded of the region of the heavenly fatherland, of which it is said: [[Ps 26:13|I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.|Credo videre bona Domini in terra viventium.]] And again: [[Matt 5:4|Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the land|Beati mites: quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram]]; in which land the just are long-lived, for they shall live in it for ever. And though by the common law things go as described, it sometimes happens by the hidden judgment of God that those who honour their parents have a short and troubled life, while those who dishonour them have a long and prosperous one. God so ordains this for the greater happiness of the obedient and the heavier condemnation of the disobedient; or it happens for other hidden reasons.

paras.t: Præterea, post præcepta ad Dei cultum spectantia, recte ponitur immediate istud de honoratione parentum, quia post Deum sunt præcipue amandi ac honorandi. Et sicut a Deo suscipitur anima, ita a parentibus contrahitur caro ; et ipsi post Deum sunt causa præcipua sobolis suæ. Quemadmodum etiam Deus est causa omnium, sic ipsi propria prolis.
